summary: The Food Inspector, P.W. 468 in the case of food articles for which no minimum standard or purity is prescribed, was found to be guilty of infested and insect infested. The Food Inspector reported that the respondent had reported that he had been subjected to a test of 'filthy ' and "schoomic disgusting rotten, decomposed or diseased animal or vegetable substance or being insect in part of any filthy, putrid, disgulsed, decomited or disated animal or other animal substance or was insect with infested food. The respondent was prosecuted for an offence under section 7 read with section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and section 16 read with Section 16 of that Act. The trial court acquitted the respondent but convicted him under section 13(1)(d) read with s.16 of the Act. On appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant Corporation that (i) the Public Analyst had reported in his report that the lal mirchi powder was either worm or infested or insect disgonding rotating, dised, decomposing or disbed animal or a vegetable substance and that the report of the Public analyst did not support the case that the Lal mirchi Powder was either filthy or infestation; (ii) the Food Inspector had reported the fact that the Lai mirchi was either dolked or insects, diseased or animal substance; and (iii) the report did not show that the food worms found by the Public Examiner were adulterated. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The true meaning of section 2(1) (f) is that it would be necessary in such a case to prove further that the article was unfit for human consumption on account of (a) its consisting wholly or in part any filthy putrid or dised rotten. It would not be necessary to prove also that the bottle mirchi, powder was neither worm nor infested nor insect or infected. [775B] 2. The fact that a food article is unfit for consumption on the account of its being unfit for domestic consumption would not make it necessary in the instant case to establish further that it was unfit to human consumption because it consists wholly or partly in part and infested, or insulating or disadusting, rotten or decomposed. [875C] 3. The expression "or otherwise unfit" in section 2 (1)(f) has been brought out in Municipal Corporation of Delhi vs Tek Chand Bhatia, ; , followed.

The appellant was prosecuted under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act for violation of cl. 3 of the order, but he was convicted by the Munsif Magistrate and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The trial court dismissed his appeal. In revision the High Court held that the appellant was an agriculturist and that he was an agricultural labourer within the meaning of section 49 of the Registration Act. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the presumption in his case cannot be drawn against him; (ii) the burden of proof is always on the prosecution, but the presumption must be drawn from proved facts and circumstances of the case. HELD: The appellant has successfully proved that he is an agriculturist. He was an agriculturists and was not liable to the penalty under the law because the presumption under para 3(2) could not be drawn. [90 E] (iii)The presumption in the case of a dealer who is an agricultural trader, must be rebutted by evidence which is otherwise reliable. The burden of proving that he has stored foodgrains for sale as a dealer though the words "as a dealer" are not registered but for the purpose of showing that the lands about which the witnesses spoke orally were held by him for purposes of cultivation. [91 E] In the present case, the appellant produced a number of lease deeds in which leases in which lease deeds were not registered and were not admissible in evidence under section 49. The presumption in favour of the prosecution is not drawn against the appellant because the appellant has satisfactorily proved that his conviction was properly reached.

The defendant was a monthly tenant in respect of the premises in suit. The plaintiff sued for ejectment on the ground that he had been paying rent to the Receiver in the years 1925 and 1926, but on the expiry of the second annual lease which happened on 7th December, 1926, the defendant became a tenant from month to month under the provisions of section 116 of Transfer of Property Act. The trial judge decreed the suit holding that the defendant was not a monthly tenants within the meaning of section 106 of Transfer Of Property Act and that the tenancy was determined by a proper notice to quit. On appeal the High Court held that the plaintiff had no permanent right in the land in suit, but it took the same view as was taken by the trial judge on the facts of this case. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The defendant did not acquire any permanent right or tenancy from month till 1926 and after the expiration of that one year 's rent again in 1926, such acceptance was evidenced by acceptance of rent from him in the year 1926. [277 B] (ii)The defendant had become a monthly lessee under section 116 on the expiration Of that one month 's lease and consequently a tenancy from year to month was created de hors the Kabuliyat executed by the defendant on 24th December 1924, and the suit was, therefore, clearly, barred by limitation. [278 C] (iii)The plaintiff had not acquired any permanent interest in the property in suit because he was not in possession of it. The defendant had no authority to receive them. The lease was for one year only. The rent was paid by the Receiver and accepted by him in 1926. The suit was therefore, within time.

The appellant assessee, a private limited company, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1964 65 onwards. The Income Tax Officer held that the assessee had not made any disclosure of the information contained in those documents and that the finality attached to an order of the Commissioner under Section 138(1)(b) of the 1961 Act could extend the ban on the exercise of the jurisdiction by a judicial order. The Full Bench, however, took the view that the omission of section 137 did not make any difference and that in the absence of such a provision, the bar created by the Income Tax Laws (Amendment) Act 1960 was not applicable to the proceedings for assessment relating to the period 1964 65 66 onwards. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court fell in error in holding that the assessment records of an assessee filed before the income tax authorities after April 1, 1964 were immune from production in a court of law by a Judicial order. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The finality attached under section 138(i)(b), is subject to the veto powers of the Income tax Officer after April I, 1964. [560D] (2) In the instant case, the finality which has been attached to the order of Commissioner under section138(1) (b) has no relevance to the exercise by a court when the court, by a legal order, requires production of the record or the disclosure of any information therefrom to it, in a case pending before the court when a court is called for by any person other than a court. [561E] (3) The final conclusion that the Incometax Officer filed before him without the approval of the Commis sioner under section 139(1), even after April 01, 1964, are immune from producing in a Court of law the disclosure or information thereof to it is in public interest so to do and such an order cannot be called in question in any court of Law.

The appellant, a minor, made a gift of his properties including immovable property to Seinaba on April 7, 1944 by a registered deed. The gift was not delivered to her and she accepted the gift on behalf of Sein Baba. She accepted the gifts on behalf Of Seinababa but to her mother, the first appellant, and she agreed to gift on May 3, 1946 without any issue. On June 23, 1963, the father of Se inaba died soon afterwards. The question whether possession can be given to the wife 's minor daughter was not decided by a competent court of law. In the present case there is no evidence that the gift was actually made by the husband to his minor son and when the minor 's mother had attained puberty, Mammotty could have made a declaration of gift and taken possession on behalf thereof. The appellant, therefore, cannot be said to have abandoned the gift. The High Court in second appeal, however, held that the gifts were not valid. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the High Court had erred in holding that the donee could not be given possession of the property as the guardian of his minor wife; but it was admitted on behalf that Mammotsty could never have made the gift actually made. HELD : (i) The gift to a minor is complete by the acceptance of the guardian and the donor can nominate a person to accept the gift, when the donee himself is the guardian or the de facto guardian or his executor. [401 B] (ii) In the case of a gift to an orphan, the rule was relaxed in this way: if a fatherless child is alive, without delivery of possession to the father, the gift would have been complete under Muhammadan law and it seems impossible to hold that by handing over the deed to his wife, the gifted would have become complete under Mohammedan Law. [501 C] (iii) The High court was in error in holding on the basis of the evidence that there was a complete intention to divest ownership on the part of Mammitty and as the gift is by a valid registered deed no question arises in this behalf can arise.

The Commissioner of Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments, Madras, issued a notice to the respondents under section 76(2) of the Act demanding contribution from the temple. The respondents filed their objections to the demand. The Commissioner rejected the objection on the ground that no rules had been framed under section 100 of the Madras Act 19 of 1951 for imposing liability for payment of contribution and that audit fee demanded by the Commissioner was without determination under section76(2). The High Court upheld the plea on the grounds that no Rules had been made under section 101 of the act and therefore, the demand for levy of contribution was Premature. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondents that (i) the Commissioner may not under section 77(1) and of any demand for contribution under its provisions and since the Advocate General appearing for the State had informed the Court that the question did not fall to be determined because rules prescribing the method for determining audit fee were not prescribed by rules, the High Court was in error in holding that no rule had been issued under section100 of the , and (ii) the demand made by the respondents was without jurisdiction or authority of law. HELD: The Commissioner may determine the fee for meeting the costs of auditing, the accounts as a result of audit. But the Commissioner has to determine the amount actually incurred for auditing the accounts. [924 C] The Commissioner has not determined the audit fee under section 78(2), and the demand will not be struck down merely because it turns out that the amount demanded is not precisely equivalent to the cost actually incurred in making an effective audit of the accounts of the religious institution.

The appellant was charged with criminal contempt of the High Court under section 19(1) of the Act. The notice was issued in accordance with the procedure prescribed under section 17 of the . The notice issued in pursuance to the provisions of section 17 was served on the appellant on 2nd April, 1975. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the validity of the notice and the order of dismissal. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that no appeal lies as a matter of right under section 20 of the , but the High Curt held that no such appeal lies to this Court as a case of right from any kind of order made by the High, Court in exercise of its jurisdiction to punish for contempt. In appeal to this court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that an appeal would lie as a mater of right tinder section 19 of the and that an application under section 18 of the was not maintainable. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appeal is not maintainable in view of the decision of this Court in Baradakanta Mishra vs Orissa High Court, [1975] 2 S.C.R. 869. [515F G] 2. A notice issued under section 15 of the is not an order initiating contempt proceeding. An order merely initiating a proceeding by issuance of a notice does not decide anything against the alleged contemner and cannot be appealed against as a matters of right Under section 19. [616C D] 3. The order issuing the notice is not appealable under section19. But there are no observations by this Court or on the facts of that case there can be any, to show that an Appeal would lie to this High Court from an order of the Tribunal merely initiating the proceeding for contempt by issuance a notice. [416C] 4. The question whether an appeal lies under section 14 is one of right or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. In the instant case, the appellant was prosecuted on the basis of the complaint made against him by the Advocate General. He had been charged with contempt of court. There could be many interlocutory orders passed in the said proceeding by issuing a notice but we merely mention this type of order by way of an order. The mere order issuing a show cause is not appealable under section 21. [511E F] 5. An appeal would, lie to the Supreme Court from any order or decision of the high court merely initiating proceedings for contempt, the order is not a matter which can be appealed from as amatter of right. Mere initiation of a proceeding for Contempt by issuance thereof does not determine anything against alleged contemner or cannot be appeals against an order issuing notice. The only order issuing such a showcause is not the order issuing it but the mere order issued by the Court merely initiating proceeding for criminal contempt. [ 512E F; 512A] 6. In this case, there could be no doubt that an appel lant had been prosecuted on a complaint made by him in response to the notice. He was charged under section 13(1)(d) of . The High Cour t held that the proceeding was not barred by section 20. [504D] 7. In view of this, the appeal is dismissed as being not maintainable and is incompetent. [506E F].

The appellant was prosecuted along with another for having received a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 Of the Act. The trial court acquitted him but convicted him under section 6(1) A and sentenced him to six months rigorous imprisonment. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) that section 6 (1A) of the , was repealed by the 1952 Act of 1949 and it was unnecessary for the application of section 6 A of the Act to a case of a later amending Act which had been applied, incorporated or referred to. The words "within India in contravention" in section 4 of the 1952 Acts were comprehensive enough to take in wireless telegraphy apparatus. (ii) that the repeal of an earlier Act which has been applied by the repealing Act of 1933 by the amending Act of 1948 was not affected by the enactment so repealed and in operation at the time of the repeal, the provisions contained in section 6A(1 A) were not applicable to a prosecution under the 1952 and the conviction thereunder could be sustained. (iii) that there was no provision in the 1952 Amending Act which saved the operation of the amending Acts of 1949, and therefore, neither the conviction nor the sentence thereunder could he sustained. The language of an enactment, as it was redundant and unnecessary, is not a complete textual amendment but a substantial one. The text of an Act, however, does not prohibit the possession of a wireless apparatus. It is only when a different intention appears that the earlier Act applies to a particular case of another amending Act, that it cannot be said that section 4 was repealed.

The appellant, a son of the respondent, was the managing Shebait of the debutter estate. The properties in question were sold by the respondent to his wife and two sons. The decree holders filed two applications under section 36(6) (a) (ii) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act praying for reopening the two compromise decrees mentioned therein and passing of new instalments, and the passing of fresh decrees in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The judgment debtors resisted the application on the ground that the appellant was a mere benamidar for her husband Aghore Nath Roy, who represented by some of the Shebaits, and that the sale was not annulled. The High Court dismissed the applications holding that the decree holders were entitled to have the two decrees reopened and on the passingof new instalments decrees in terms of section 36 (2) (c) of Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the courtens a decree under section 37(2)(c) only for the purpose and so far as it is necessary to give relief to the borrower in the manner provided for in the Act, namely, to release from all liability for interest in excess of the limits prescribed by section 30 of the Indian Money Lender Act, it was not open to the court to go behind the decree and launch an enquiry as to whether the decreeholder himself was a benamidar or for another person. HELD : The object of restoring possession of properties sold in execution of the decrees is to enable the judgment debtor to pay off the decretal dues, but it is to be remembered that the object of restoration possession of the properties sold by both the courts below to be a fictitious transaction. [991 B] In the present case, the decree holder himself and his son were in possession of these properties within the meaning of clause (c). The sale itself was not invalid, and in case of the decreeholders themselves it is incumbent upon the court, to restore those properties to the judgment debtors so far that it is material to give a direction in such cases that if there is default in the payment of any one of the instalments, the properties restored to the decree debtor under clause (e) would be put back into the possession of it.

The respondent company was a registered firm carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. D. P. Co operative Housing Society Ltd., Bombay, which was formed for the purpose of carrying on its business in that area. The appellant company had been carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling houses and other buildings. In the year 1952, the respondent company applied to the City Civil Court under Order XXI, rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure for execution of a decree passed in favour of Habib & Sons, but the City Court refused to execute the decree. The High Court held that the deed of assignment was not executed by Habib and Sons, as contemplated by Order XXI Rule 16 of C.P.C., and that the assignee of the subject matter of the suit did not entitle the transferee to apply for execution under order XXI, r. 16. Held, that the respondent could not claim to be a transferee of the decree passed by it in favour Of Habib & Co. The normal rule is that a decree can be executed only by the person in whose name it stands and rule 10 enables him to do so, while rule 16 permits the transferee of a property which is the subjectmatter of a suit without transferring the decree in writing within the meaning of Order XXI. Rule 16 enables the transferee from the provisions of Order 21, r., 16 to execute a decree at the instance of a transferee, by assignment in writing in writing, within the terms of Order XXII, rule 15 authorising him to transfer the decree when it would be passed. The ordinary rule is, that a judgment can be transferred by assignment or by operation of law within the term of Order XX, rule 17(1) and if it is found that the defect, if any, in the original application for execution was not in existence at the date of the transfer, such equitable transfer does not render the transferee a transferee to be transferees of the judgment by assignment. The principle underlying Order XXI of Rule 16 is that an agreement can be enforced by a transferee by assignment, in writing or by virtue of operation of Law within the scope of Order 23, r, 16. The rule is intended to confer on the transferee the beneficial interest in the decree to execute it in the same manner and subject to the same conditions as an application for executing the decree, but if he fails to establish his title as a transferee in writing by assignment In writing within section 146, if the provisions Of Order XXI enables him from availing himself of section 146 if the requirements of Order XXIII, r 16 are satisfied.

The respondent carried on the business of fabricating steel doors, windows and other goods. The respondent was a contractor for sale of goods and the respondent had to pay sales tax under the Rajasthan Sales Tax Act. The Sales Tax Officer held that the contract was one of service in the execution of which some movable property passed and that the price of the goods was taxable. The High Court held that from the acceptance of the tender, two contracts resulted in sale of the window, doors and windows in a specified building, and that there was no separate charge for that service. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the terms of the contract were not decisive and the Court was entitled to ascertain the true effect of the transaction as disclosed by the nature of the work, and the "invoice" for payment made out by the respondent. HELD : The contract was a works contract and not a contract for sale. [501 B] The contract could be said to have been completed in accordance with the terms and conditions of the agreement. It is not necessary that the parties should know what they intended to do. The contract may be a contract but it must be deemed one for work and labour. If the windows were not properly fixed, the contract would not be complete and the service was rendered under a separate contract or are incidental to the execution thereof. [601 C] In the present case, the specifications of the windows are set out in the contract. The contracts were executed by the appellant with their customers and the services were performed in connection with the installation. The agreement did not provide for any charge for the service rendered in connection therewith. The main object was to supply the windows but to supply them the windows. The service is not rendered under separate contract nor is the service shown to be customarily or normally as incidental to sale by the person who supplies window leaves.

The respondent was an agent of M/s. Ashoke Trading Corporation of Indore and the appellant, who was a broker of foreign machinery parts went to Ram Avtar and introduced himself to him as his agent of one of those plates. The respondent was also told that this transaction would fetch him a profit of Rs. 3200/ per piece. Formal order was then agreed to purchase 200 pieces of cloths from Ram Avtar, who later on paid the same to the complainant. On November 16, 1967, Shanker Lal brought one out of the three samples of those plateher which were kept by Ram Avtar. The complaint against Shanker Lal and Raj Kumar Agarwalla was that on November 15, 1967 Shanker Lal had been aroused in a taxi plates in a hotel and would supply the foreign goods known as platesher plates to him. On December 28, 1967 Shankar Lal handed over the said formal order to Ram Gopal Agarwalla, who introduced himself as agent of the respondent. The prosecution case was that after the arrival of Shanker Lal, he had been entrusted with the foreign liquor plates in the taxi plates and would deliver them to the respondent on November 16. 1967. On January 28, 1968, Shankerlal handed over a formal order for sale of foreign goods to Ram Kumar Agarwal but later on that day Shanker Lal came with another man named Pandey and told him that this was an agency of Shri Hanuman Agency and would give the foreign Goods known as plateher plates in his taxi plates. After that day Shankar Lal brought two samples of these plates, one of which was kept by the respondent and the other by Ram Kumar Aggarwalla. The complainant agreed to the proposal and wanted to see the seller of the foreigngoods in question. On February 28, 1969 Shanker Lal handed back the said three samples to him on November 14, 1967. Thereafter, Shanker lal returned to his shop at about 7.30 p.m. He was asked by Ram Gopal Agrawalla that he would get a profit from the respondent 's firm and would send them through Shanker Lal. The appellant told him to arrange for a transaction of sale of Foreign goods which would result in good profit to thecomplainant. On March 28, 1970, ShankerLal handed over these three samples on November 17, 1967 to Ram Prakash Agarwalla. After receiving the said call, Shanker Lai returned to the shop of Ram Avtar with the police. The police did not submit any charge sheet against him. Thereafter the proceedings were set in motion against Raj Kumar and Kishan Agarwalla for offences under sections 420, 468 and 471 Indian Penal Code read with section 120B Indian Penal code read with Section 120B I.P.C. The trial court acquitted the respondent but convicted him under section 420 read with s. 511 Indian Penal C. P.C., and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for one year. On appeal by the State, the High Court set aside the charge framed against RajKumar Agawalla and Shanker Lal on November 8, 1967 and convicted them accordingly. The present appeal was filed in this Court after obtaining special leave from this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The report lodged by Ram Swaroop Agarwalla is lodged only subsequent to the lodging of the report. It appears that Raj Kumar had appeared on the scene only subsequent thereto to the filing of the complaint and was lodged only later on. [760C D] 2. The High Court might induce an inference that RajKumar respondent was too a party to any conspiracy to defraud or cheat Ram Avtar but it would not be possible for him to interfere with the judgment of the High court as might induce us to interfere. [771A B] 3. In the instant case, the report lodged against Shanker Lai by Ram Prakash Aggarwalla is that he had made no mention of the name of Raj Kumar Aggarwal and Shankerlal in the very nature of things made no reference of anything made any things made out or understood to have been made out.

The petitioner, a resident of Sultanbattery area in the State of Kerala, was awarded with a contract for the supply of certain goods to the Railways. The petitioner was awarded a contract with the Railways for the execution of the work. The Railways entered into an agreement with the petitioner on June 6, 1981 and the petitioner was informed that the Railways would provide adequate safety protection to the passengers and their properties. The Railway authorities were directed to take steps to ensure that the road accidents had taken place in the running trains. The Petitioner filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the validity of the contract. It was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the Railway Authorities are owned by the Central Government and on account of failure to fulfil the constitutional, statutory and commercial obligations by the Railways, adequate safety safeguard to the passenger and their property is not available. The respondents contended that the petitioner has denied the assertion in the counter affidavit that no accident had takenplace on account for defective bridges and has pointed out that the accidents have taken place on account only for defective bridge and that the railway authorities are owned and controlled by the State Government and the Government of India will ever avoid the error of viewing Railways as private undertakings and will also avoid the failure to fulfill the constitutional statutory, statutory or commercial obligations. Allowing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The common man 's mode of transport closely connected with the free play of this fundamental right should not be an arbitrary right of interference but a regulated authority defined and declared by law which is not to be needlessly or casually exactedously or exacted so as to ensure the maintenance of public obligations, if any. [233B C] 1.2 The common men ' mode of transportation closely connected to the free air and also to the non travelling citizens must be provided and this means that accidents have to be avoided attack on the persons of the passengers, and prying on their property has to stop. This means that accident has to be stopped. [234C] 1.(a) The common person will have his voice heard. It is equally the obligation of the Union of India and its instrumentalities to improve this great public utility in an effective way and with an adequate sense of urgency. Giving directions in a matter like this where this availability of resources has a material bearing, bearing policy regarding priorities, is involved, it is undoubtedly the obligationof the Union to improve the means of communication in this country. [235D E] 1(b) The quality of service should not, however, be an unreasonable right of interfere but a controlled authority defined under law which was not to he needlessly and exacted smoothly or ex gratia. It may well be a commercial venture geared to support the general revenue of the State but there is not an iota of hesitation in us to say that the common man "s mode" of transport inter connected with free play has a vital bearing on the free exercise of this right. [236F G] 1 (c) The basic purpose of the law, to conserve not only the safety and order but also the moral welfare of the state and its instrumentality to improve is that which the Government may justly exercise and is called upon to exercise stringent and salutary control. This is a reasonable restriction on the freedom of trade and commerce guaranteed under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. [237F G; 237A] 2.(d) The right to move freely and carry on any business or profession would both be practicable and feasible. If these rights of the citizens are to be ensured, it was undoubtedly the duty of the union of India to improve that assurance. This was necessary at once for the interests of the general public. [238F] 3.(e) The obligation cast by the railways Act and the Rules under it must be complied with.

The appellants were the tenants of certain lands in the State of Gujarat. The respondents filed applications for restoration of their appeals under section 20 of the Abolition Act, 1950 on May 6, 1961. The application was rejected by the Revenue Tribunal on July 18, 1961 and the appeal was dismissed on April 9, 1961 on the ground that the orders passed dismissing the appeals were received by them on April 10 and April 20, 1961, and hence the applications for condonation of delay were within 30 days of the receipt of the order of dismissal. The appellants contended that since the orders of dismissal were received on April 8 and April 19, 1961 they were within time under Regulation 21 of the Bombay Revenue Tribunal Regulations, 1958, and therefore the applications were within limitation. The High Court dismissed the applications. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the Tribunal had no power to dismiss an appeal for non prosecution but it was obligatory on the part of the Tribunal to decide the appeals on merits and not to record its decision even though there is default on the parts of the appellants and to record their decision even although there was default on their part in the appearance of the respondents and to records its decision, even though no appeal was heard on merits; (ii) the applications made by the appellants were within the period of limitation prescribed by Regulation 21. HELD: The Tribunal had jurisdiction to dismiss the appeals for non defence but it is obligatory on its part to decide an appeal on merits under Regulation 19(1). [145 B] In the context of section 20, it is open to the Tribunal in such a case to hear the respondent to hear and decide it on merits. If any of the parties was absent on the date of hearing, either preliminary or final, either oral or final and the appeals are well within the time prescribed by that Regulation, then the Tribunal has no power under section 19(2) to dismiss any appeal for default but it would be obligatory on his part to dispose of the appeal on merit. [145 C D] The Tribunal committed an error of law in dismissing the applications of restoration made by appellants in all the four cases.

The appellant, a Hindu temple of Shri Ramchandraji, was dedicated to the temple of Sri Ramchandraji as early as 1857. The appellant 's case in the plaint was that Telibandha had been worshipped for very many years and later on in the year 1896 when a partition took place between his descendants who were up till 1896, when a division took place among his descendants which took place after 1896. The trial court held that there was no absolute dedication of the village to the deity by the Panch Faisla Award of 1896 and no trust was created thereby. On appeal, the High Court agreed with the Trial Court that dedication by Dinanath Sao himself by a Patha in 1857 as alleged in the Plaint had not been established; but disagreeing with the trial court 's decision that dedication was made in favour of Shri Ramachandra Swamy temple, the appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : The High Court was right in holding on a construction of paragraph 2 of the Panchfais Award of1896 that by the award of 18 96 the appellant had not become absolute owner of the temple and did not make an absolute dedication to the village Telikshaw itself dedicated to his brothers. [434 C D] In the present case, the document (the Panch Fai Panchayati) clearly shows an intention that Ramsaran Lal would not have the absolute ownership of the Village Teliriages in the village. The fact that there is no single word in Bagchi Award of 1796 shows an inference that the property belonged to the family with only a charge on it for the temple.

The appellants were the President of the Avadh Bar Association. The High Court discharged their notices under section 14 of the U.P. High Court 's Amalgamation Order, 1948 in a most partisan manner under the influence of Allahabad Bar. The appellants filed a petition for quashing the proceedings contending that they had met and resolved that the Chief Justice was acting in a very most partisan way under the control of the Allahabad Bar Association and Chairman, Action Committee of the said association. The Judges of the High Court held that since the resolution was passed under the presidentship of the first appellant described as contemner No. 1 he was also guilty of contumacious conduct. The appeal filed by the appellants against the order of discharge was dismissed by the High court. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Chairman of the Action Committee was acting wholly in a highly partisan manner and under the pressure of the Bar Association which he holds. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The action Committee is of the opinion that the conduct of the Appellants individually was considered only "indiscreet" by it. [602C] 2. It is true that lawyers are the custodians of civilisation. They have to discharge their duty with dignity, decorum and discipline. If lawyers fail in their duty the faith of the people in the judiciary will be undermined to a large extent. [ 603E F] 3. The language used by them was unfortunate. It was not proper and it should have been passed in that manner.

The arbitrators filed an application before the Sub Registrar for registration of a deed of agreement between the four brothers being the appellants Nos. 5, 6 and 7 herein. The Sub Registrar rejected the application on the ground that during the subsistence of the interim injunction order dated 25th February, 1983 passed by the Sub Judge, Hooghly at Chinsurah on 28th January, 1978 the arbitrators had sent back the award to the SubRegistrar for registration. On 24th November, 1983 the arbitrators made an application to the sub Registrar for return of the award and the Sub judge held that during this period the arbitration proceedings were pending and the arbitrator could not take back the same till the return of award was filed in the court pursuant to the order of the High Court on 24th January.1983. The arbitrators then filed a petition before the Subordinate Judge, who decided the application for registration on 6th March, 1981. On 25th November 1983 the Sub registrar passed an order returning the award back to the arbitrators holding that during subsistence of interim injunction the arbitrator had already expired. The sub Registrar also directed return of his award to them. In the meantime, the arbitrators filed a suit in the Court of the Sub Registrars for registration and the parties were directed to file their written statement. On 26th November 1984 the arbitrators again presented the award before the sub registrar for registration but the Sub inspector refused to accept it on the same day. The appellants filed an appeal before the High court which set aside the aforesaid order of refusal to return back the Award holding that the limitation for the registration of the arbitration had already lapsed and that the arbitrator was not the Registrar and not the SubJudge who could determine the question of limitation for registration, and that in view of the principle laid down under section 15 of the . The Sub registrar directed return back to him. On 2nd September, 1983, the Sub Inspector made an order of returning the Award to the arbitration court. The arbitrator then filed his award on 24rd November, 1984 which was accepted by the sub inspector and the arbitrators were directed not to take back its custody till the next day of getting possession of the suit. The parties thereafter filed a writ petition in the High Curt for quashing the aforesaid orders of the sub judge. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that since during the pendency of judicial proceedings, the arbitrator did not direct return of its award and did not order registration it could not be said that he had failed to get the registered as the law required. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Sub rule of limitation prescribed under section 14 of the , should be excluded in view Of the principle set down under Section 15 of . The High Cour t held that the award was presented within time as the period during which the judicial proceedings were Pending had expired.

The respondent was a sub tenant of the appellant and the appellant had four sub tenants. The appellant had three sub tenants, one of them being licensees of the landlord. On January 3, 1949, the respondent gave notice to the appellant to vacate the premises on the ground of non payment of rent and sub letting which it was alleged had resulted in the termination of the tenancy. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment against the appellant on the grounds that under the terms of the lease he had the right to sub let the premises to the sub tenants and they were merely licensees of those sub tenants; and that the sub tenant had not sub let them to the new premises which were let to the old and that, therefore, the tenancy by the letter of June 7, 1948, was a fresh tenancy and not a continuation of the old or that the old rent and not the continuation of his old and hence he could not evict the appellant under section 13(1)(e) of the Act. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that: (i) the tenancy was a new tenancy and as such the sub letting by the respondent was not a fresh lease; (ii) the appellant could not be evicted under section 15 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. HELD : The High Court was in error in holding that the tenancy had been a fresh one and the sub lessee had allowed the tenant to sub letting the premises. [227 D] In the instant case, the question is not merely of waiver of statutory rights enacted for the benefit of the revenue officials but whether the court would aid the appellant in enforcing a term of the agreement which section 15 would be unenforceable as being in contravention of the express provision of the statute which prohibits it from doing so. [228 E] The respondent had waived his right to sue for ejectment on the basis of the breach of a provision of law and therefore he could have evicted the appellant by an express contract he had allowed him to sub lease but he could do so. The High court was in wrong in holding, that the suit was not maintainable because of the provisions of section 15.

The State Board, by its resolution dated January 30, 1991, decided to deal with the use of unfair means at final examination conducted by the Board. The Standing Committee did not apply its mind to the facts in this case since the Act was passed by the State Board and its Standing Committee to dealwith use offair means at the final examination held by it. The High Court, therefore, quashed the impugned notification and directed the Board to deal therewith. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the State Government it was contended that (i) the Standing Committee had no power to evaluate the evidence as an appellate court and to come to its own conclusions; (ii) the finding reached by the Standing Committees that the fabrication was done at the behest of either the candidate or the parents or guardian is based on the evidence on record, and (iii) the findings were reached on the basis of the admission made by the examinees. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1.1 The conclusion reached by a Standing Committee that the construction of the moderators ' mark sheets was done in the presence of either of the candidates or their parents or guardians is based upon the evidence of the witnesses on record. It depends on the nature and gravity of the misconduct to be dealt with by the disciplinary authority. [798C] 1.2 The Standing Committees did not exercise power under article 226 or Article 136 of the Constitution, by the High Court or this Court. They were sitting committees (domestic enquiry) and they acted on behalf o the examiners/guardians and the parties to the fabrication. It was, therefore clear that when the Standing Education Committee took the decision its decision is on behalf Of the State as its agent. [898D] 1.(a) The conclusion arrived at by the Committee that fabrication of theDAR ' mark sheet was done by either of them or their parent or guardian was based on records. It depended upon the nature, gravity and seriousness of the offence to be discussed by the Divisional Board. [878E F] 1(b) The High Courts have no jurisdiction to quash the impugned Notification and to interfere with the finding and to quash it. [879F] 2.(a). In view of fair attitude adopted by the counsel for the Board, it is not open to the High court under article 225 or Article 226 to evaluate itself as an Appellate Court and to arrive at its own conclusion against the respondent. [881G] 3.(b) It depends upon the facts and circumstances on which the whole enquiry came to be held and the general background of the atmosphere in the examination hall. The observations made by this Court in the decision dated January 31, 1991 are not binding on the High Courts under article 136 or Article 227 of the Consti tution.

The appellants were charged under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for criminal conspiracy to cause the offence of criminal misconduct punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial court acquitted them but convicted them on appeal by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the intention of the legislature was to create by means of clause (d) an offence different from a single act of bribery and that before a charge under section5(1), sub clause (a) could be sustained there must be threat or inducement or proceeding from the public servant or from the person so concerned, or (c)if he habitually accepts or obtains or agrees to accept or attempts to obtain from any person for himself or for any other person, any valuable thing or pecuniary advantage. HELD: The offence as defined in section 21 of the Act is to create a by means clause (b) an additional offence of bribery. But the offence as described in section 5 and under sub section (2) it is made punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, or with fine, or both. [187 D] The Prevention of corruption Act, does not come into play merely when there is no offer to give an acceptance of a bribe by a public servant. But then go further and say that the offence is based solely on such presumption. A new offence of misconduct by a person who commits criminal misconduct by abusing his position as a public man is different from that of a single acts of bribery, and it can come into played in the sense of bribery; in each case he obtains pecuniary advantage by abusing himself as a Public servant. [188 E] The offence under section 4(1) is to cause or inducement, or to proceed from the Public servant or to induce or promise to proceed with any proceeding from his official duty and his conviction therefor shall not be invalid by reason only that it is based merely on such Presumption. A person who has committed a criminal misconduct in the discharge of his official duties and his liability therefor cannot be questioned on the ground that he was interested in giving or attempting to give any bribe.

The appellant Bank was a surety for the respondent. The surety was discharged from his liability under the guarantee. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 76,046.00 from the legal representative of the deceased principal debtor in favour of the Bank. The trial court found that there was negligence on the part of the bank with regard to safe custody of the oil pledged and the personal guarantee of the surety was independent of the pledge of goods given by the principal debtor. The High Court held that the surety had agreed to become surety, on the specific understanding that the principal creditor had offered two securities, one the pledge and the other a personal guarantee on the good faith of other security being offered by the surety. In appeal by the respondent, this Court, HELD: (1) The surety is discharged from the obligation undertaken under the letter of guarantee. It is difficult to entertain a contention that section 141 would not be attracted and the surety would not come even if it is held proved that security of goods pledged was lost on account of negligence of the creditor Bank. [922D] (2) In such a situation clause (a) of the explanation would be attracted, and an application for restitution will have to be made to the Court of first instance i.e. the Court Of first instance, i. e. the court of firstly instance, in exercise of its appellate jurisdiction. [822D E] (3) The guarantee given by a surety is not discharged from liability under his letter of undertaking guarantee. In such circumstances clause (b) would be applicable and an applica tion for restitution would have to he made to it. [723G H] (4) The security offered by a principal debtor which may be a consideration for the surety is discharge to the extent of the value of the security lost as provided by section 141. [779B C] (5) In order to attract section 141 it must be shown that the creditor had taken more than one security on the basis of which advance was made and the guarantee given on the security was discharged to the amount of the good confidence of the principal borrower itself. The security is discharged to a extent of its value. [780C] (6) In the present case, the surety did not discharge any obligation under the letters of guarantee or the personal guarantees of the respondent and the respondent had failed to exercise such a right.

The appellant was a patel inamdar of the village in which he had been granted by the Ruler of village Nawabag. The grant was recognised as a service inam by the British Government and the grant was recognized as a inam by it, and the grants were recognised as an inam by its British Government. The appellant continued to be a pateki inam holder of the "patel" inam lands which were given as emoluments or emoluments for 91 714 services to be rendered by the patel 's office to the working patel from the Rokade family. The respondent No. 1, who was the son of Amritrao patel, filed a suit against the appellant and his father for possession of the land in dispute on the ground that the lands were granted by him as emoluments of his office to his office and that the grant amounted to a grant by way of remuneration or emoluments of the p Patel 's service. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to hold the "Patel" Inam lands and Government had no right to resume the same, and that as a result of these enquiries it was held that (1) the lands in suit were granted as emoluments for the psyki inam lands; and (2) the grant made by the jagirdar of village was recognised by the Government as a "panchki inam" land. Held, that the High court was right in holding that the "spatel" lands were not liable to be resumed under the Inam Rules. The fact that the inamdar had no rights to resume "pulki inam land" does not mean that he had a share in the " patel" land as a member of the family.

The appellant, who was a Cutchi Memons of the erstwhile State of Mysore, was in British India as a result of which he became entitled to succeed to his estate by birth. The appellant 's father died in 1938 and then in Madras. He filed a suit for partition and possession of the properties in question on the ground that the rules of Hindu law applicable to Cutchi Corons were inconsistent with the Hindu Law and that the rule of Hindu Law applicable to cutchi Memon was not applicable to the Cutchi corons. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the Rules of Hindu Hindus applied to Cutch Memons, and that as there was only one solitary decision of the High court in Madras, he should prefer the Madras as against the Bombay view. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the rules were consistent with the customary law applicable in the case of Cutchi Mazons; (ii) the rule was not inconsistent with Hindu Law; and (iii) the High Courts had erred in holding that the principles of Hindu Succession and inheritance were consistently applied to cutch Memon, and therefore, when a Cutch Corons had acquired by custom to dispose of the whole or the part of their property including the Hindu concept of coparcenary and survivorship, the rule would apply to Cutth Memons. HELD : (i)(a) The High Court was right in its view that the cutchi coron died in 1939 and then before 1948, as a large part of the state of Madras, but contrary to what he had held in Bombay, he held that in the absence of special custom as to succession and inheritance, the High Curt would be right in their view that there was no other Madras view. [233 B D] (b) The question whether in the present case the Cutch holders retained the rules or governed by Hindu law was not only in matters of succession but also concepts, but also in matters relating to succession, and inheritance. [234 C] (c) The fact that the Cutth Corons held that they had regulated succession and according to Hindu Law as to joint family property, their distribution according to the rule Of survivorship and the right of a son in it by birth, the right to a son therein, a right expressly saved by section 3 of the Act.

The appellants are manufacturers of different types of fabrics. They manufacture yarn in the mill of the respondent company. The respondent company manufactures cotton yarn and subjected to the integrated process of weaving the same into fabrics. In order to manufacture the said fabrics, it is obtained at an intermediate stage. It has been held that the yarn which is produced at an intermediary stage in the Mill of the appellants and subjected the integrated processing of the same to weaving the said fabric into fabrics will be liable to payment of excise duty in view of the amended provisions of rules 9 and 49 of the Rules. The High Court, however, held that retrospective effect given by section S1 would be subject to the provisions of sections 11A and 11B of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the retrospective effect granted by section 3(1) of the Finance Act 1982 is not applicable to the facts of the case, that the respondent Company manufactures cotton fabrics which are obtained at intermediate stage in its mill of manufacturing another commodity and subjected them to the entire integrated process for weaving the product into fabrics, will be entitled to payment. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The language of rule 9(1), admits only one interpretation and that is that the specification that has to be made by the Collector of such place or premises appurtenant thereto, the provision of deemed removal with regard to the commodity produced at intermediate stages and consumed or utilised in the continuous process of manufacture of another commodity by deeming such production or manufacture of other goods in the same place, this cannot be done without payment of duty at the place and in the manner prescribed. [708C] 2. The expression "place of removal" is not defined in the Act but it has been given retrospective effect from the date on which the Rules came into force. In the instant case, the goods were produced at the intermediate stage and consumed at an earlier stage and thereafter further processed in an integrated process to weaving it into fabrics and then further processed at an end product. The specification is not required to be make and, in our view, cannot be made of the place of manufacture or production of the excisable goods. [808D E] 3. The word "place" has been defined in section 2(1)(d) of Central Excise Act, 1944 as meaning a factory or any other place where the excisable articles are produced, cured or manufactured and used for the purpose of manufacturing any other commodity. It is not disputed that the goods which were obtained at the stage of manufacture were dutiable. The description of the goods in section 3 of the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985 is not necessary for the purposes of collection of excise duties. [908E F] 4. The words "place or premises" are used in the explanation to rule 9 and rule 49 of Rules 9(2) which are not relevant for our purpose. The use of the expression "date of removal", in the Explanation to rule 49, is not decisive. It may be that a commodity which is manufactured in such place, has been removed from one plant to another it will not be removal from such place where goods are produced or cured or used for manufacture of any other article in the said place. [1008F G] 5. The Explanation to Rule 9(I) admits only two interpretation and does not contain any definition of "place".

The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the scheme published under section 68 C of the U.P. Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 was illegal and ultra vires and for an injunction restraining the Hearing Authority from proceeding with the hearing of the suit till the disposal of a special leave petition before this Court since the jurisdiction of the civil courts in such matters was impliedly barred. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the suit was not maintainable in a civil court for an interim injunction restraining it from proceeding further with the disposal and approving the scheme. In appeal, the District Judge set aside the order of the Civil Judge and remanded the matter to the Trial Court for fresh hearing. On remand, the High Court held that the plaintiff had no locus standi to file the suit as he was not a party to the proceedings before the trial court. The High Court also held that since the civil court had been constituted under section 69 C of U. P. Motor Vehicle Act, 1988, the jurisdiction was impliedly excluded. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Civil Court was not competent to entertain a suit as the jurisdiction in such matter was expressly barred. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The civil court has no jurisdiction to issue an order of injunction restraining either the Hearing authority or the hearing authority from proceeding and exercising its statutory functions. [537B] 2.2 In the instant case, the Civil judge had no jurisdiction in the matter. He was right in refusing to stay further proceedings in the suit. The civil judge was right to refuse to stay the further proceedings. [638C D] 3.3 The power of the Hearing Court under section68 D(i) and the powers of the State Government (the Hearing Authority under section 70 C) are exclusive in character and it is not open to a civil Court to issue any order of restraint restraining the hearing Authority from proceed with the matter or exercising its functions. It is not disputed that the Scheme had been duly published under Section 68 C.P., 1988. [738D] 3.(a) The jurisdiction of a State Government in such cases is expressly barred by section 68 D(iii) of the Act.

The appellant was charged with offences under section 5(2) read with section 161, Indian Penal Code and section 161 of the Indian Penal code. The prosecution alleged that the appellant had demanded bribe from a person who had no child of his own and wanted to adopt a child. The appellant was also asked to come to the house of his sister 's husband, N. Russel Nathaniel, but she refused to do so. On the question whether the appellant could prosecute either Miss Eylene or Russel Kathaniel Nathanie, the High Court held that the conviction of the appellant under section 161 was not justified and set aside the order with regard to payment of fine or imprisonment in default. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the decision of the Judicial Committee had no application to the present case for the order of sanction in the present ease, for the payment of a fine or punishment in default and obtained by himself for any offence and obtaining money by him for any act or for showing forbearing to show in the exercise of his official functions, favour or disfavour to any per son. HELD: (i) The decision of this Court in State of Punjab vs Ram Sarup Singh, ; , relied on. (ii) The order of the judicial Committee was much more cryptic and materially different from that of the High court. [184 D] (iii) The appellant had not been convicted by the Special Judge under section 6(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act for refraining from any such imaginary prosecution cannot be said to be an offence under section 165, Indian penal Code or any other criminal statute and if the appellant has obtained money from RusselNathaniel on N. Kassel N.Kassel Nagie, it cannot be held that he had obtained a gratification for doing or forbearing or for giving forbearing, in the discharge of his functions, favour to some per son, and obtaining moneys by him from RusGA Nathanairie. [185 D E] (iv) The charge under section 4(1) read along with section 5 (2) of Prevention of corruption Act is established against the appellant.

The appellant was charged with offences under section 161, I.P.C., and section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, for having accepted illegal gratification as a motive or reward for showing favour to one Bokil in connection with his official functions. The Special Judge acquitted him but convicted him on appeal by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the sanction accorded by the appellant was not a valid one and the sanction granted by him was not valid, (2) the prosecution of the appellant had failed in proving the charge under section 5 (2), and (3) the evidence of the witnesses examined showed that he had not applied his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case. HELD : The sanction accorded was not invalid as it disclosed a valid sanction for the prosecution. [127 B] In the present case, the sanction itself and the evidence showed that the papers placed before him were relevant to the only question before him and which was the opinion that in the interests of justice the appellant should be prosecuted in a competent court of law for the offences alleged against him. The sanction did not show that the documents placed before the appellant were relevant or in the absence of any question being put to Mr Bokils, the evidence could not be accepted as sufficient to justify the grant of a certificate having failed. [128 C D] In re: State of West Bengal vs R. N. Mukherjee, ; , referred to. (3)(a) The sanction granted was not in accordance with law and it was not for Mr B. Bokotil to judge the truth of the allegations made against him by calling for the records of the claim connected cases or other records in connection therewith from his office. [129 D] (b) The sanctioning authority had no jurisdiction to accord sanction to the prosecution, because the sanction was not given in accordance law and the appellant could not have been convicted on the basis of the evidence adduced before him. [130 E F] (c) The order granting the certificate having not been a valid order, the appeal must be dismissed.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground that the building was bona fide required by the landlord for demolition and reconstruction. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered for eviction. The appellate authority, however, allowed the appeal filed by the tenants against the orders of the appellate authority. In second appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that the landlord had only a life interest in the premises in question and that it is inherent in such a life estate that it was not permissible for the landlord to invoke section 14(1)(b) as grounds for eviction are, therefore, irrelevant in a litigation between the landlord and tenants when a suit is instituted by the former on any of the grounds available to him under the Act. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The expression landlord ' has no meaning or relation to the subject matter of the tenancy between the tenant and the remainder man. [275G] 2.1 In the instant case, the landlord has only a lifetime interest in premises in dispute and he had been on his own right under the Deed of Settlement as a trustee receiving rents of the premises from the tenants. The Rent Controller held that the requirements of the landlord were bona fide for demolition, and ordered eviction of all the respondents. [276A] 2(a) In the present case, there is no possibility or any objection from the daughters of the settlor or from any other remainder man, as defined in the Act, is outside the ken of this Act. Even a possible dispute, imaginary or real, between the Landlord and the residue man cannot affect adjudication of the claim of the tenant against his tenants under the provisions of the Act unless there is some possibility or objection from them. [278B] 2.(b) In a litigation involving the landlord, who is not his tenants, under the deed of Settlement, as a Trustee receiving rents from the premises, whether on his personal ac count or on behalf or on account of another remainder man cannot operate as res judicata between the landlords and tenants. [280C D] 3.2 The expression 'landlord ' in section 2(6) is not defined in that Act but under section 2 (6). It is a self contained complete code for regulation of the rights between landlord and tenant as defined by the Act in the deed. [279D E] 3.(c) In view of the provisions contained in the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1947, it is clear that the expression landlord has no right to ask for eviction against his tenant under the said Act. The only question which arises for consideration is whether the landlord should ask for a decree for eviction from the building by demolition of the property for the purpose of reconstruction. [281F] 4.(d) In order to reconstruct the premises it is necessary that the tenant should have sufficient means to satisfy himself about the bona fide requirement of his landlord. The word 'landlord" in section 3(6)(a) of the Madras Building (Lease & Rent Control Act, 1949, is a comprehensive code for regulating the rights of landlord and the rest man cannot destroy adjudication of his claim against his eviction under the provision of the said Acts. [284G] 5.(e) The expression "landlord" has been defined in section2(6). The definition of landlord ' in that section includes the person who is receiving or is entitled to receive the rent, if the building were let to a tenant, whetheron his own rights under the document of Settlement or on his behalf and others.

The appellant, a co owner of the grove, was the owner of certain lands. The land in dispute was leased to him by the mortgagee for a period of ten years. He died on August 1, 1960. Thereafter, he filed an application under section 6(1)(a) (i) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, for ejectment from the grove land. The application was dismissed by the executing court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the lands in dispute were not part of a grove, and that the intermediary could be proceeded against by the mortgagor. HELD : (i). The definition of 'intermediary ' includes grove and grove land, and the expression "intermediaries" is wide enough to include grove and land. [657 D] (ii) The word 'interirmediary grove ' in section 6 of the Act means a grove or grove, but does not include grove or land held by an intermediary. The well settled principle is well settled under the general law that trees, before they are cut form parts of groves and grove lands, which are parts of grove and groves, are equated and grove land. In view of this very clear words of the enactment, it was not necessary to consider previous definitions or to make specious out specious or to give specious indication about specious distinction between trees, standing uncut trees, which were part of bhumidhari rights. [757 D E] (iii) The definition is wide and an inclusive one in which a mortgagee could enforce his right against the mortgage or after the Act came into force, if he had no right to enforce his rights against the mortgagor, and when he was not entitled to enforce any right against a mortgagee, he could be sued for ejectment. [857 D F] (iv) The expression 'interIrmediary" in section 3(13) of U. P. Zamindari Land Reforms and Land Reform Act, 1951, means that trees before they were cut form part of grove or groves. The distinction between the two expressions is well established under the law, that trees are parts only of grove lands and groades, and groving land. It is not necessary even to consider past definitions or otherwise to make such specious and specious observations about speculations or to provide specious, specious etc., between uncut tree, standing distinctions between uncatrations, trees, etc. in groves or grove lands.

The appellants were charged for an offence under Section 302 IPC and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. The trial court convicted them under Sections 326/149 IPC and awarded the sentence of rigorous imprisonment of one year each. In appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentences passed against all the four accused persons. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 It is well settled that in cases where there are two or more persons who stand convicted for an offense under Section 326/34 IPC, each of them has to be acquitted of the offence with which he had not been charged and sentenced. In the instant case, the injuries caused by the first appellant were either individually or taken collectively with the other accused persons though some of the injuries inflicted by him were grievous in nature. The intention to cause death of Suku was neither individually nor taken collectively nor any part thereof. It is also well settled law that if two or three persons are acquitted, each one cannot be convicted of an offence with the aid of Section 149 IPC. [89F G] 1.2 In the present case, there were four accused who had been charged for the substantive offence of murder under Section 324 IPC and sentence of imprisonment for one year and fine of Rs.1,000/ each. The High Court was justified in recording a conviction against all these four appellants for an offences with the help of Section 148 IPC. However, according to the medical evidence, none of the accused persons individually had been inflicted injuries by them according to their weapons. [90F G H] 1:3 In view of the sentences recorded for offence under section 302 IPC, the necessary intention to causing death of the deceased was not permissible. The appellants were convicted for the offence under Sections 324/149 and 325 IPC. They were sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment as indicated in the judgment of the High court. [91F G]. 1:4 In view thereof, the conviction of all the appellants for the offences with which they had not be charged for any substantive offence under sections 302 read with Section 149 is set aside. The sentence of fine and the sentences imposed for offence Under section 326/148 IPC are maintained but without the aid Of Section 149. [92F G; 92A] 1 :5 In view whereof, the appellants were acquitted of all other offences with their aid of Sections 149 and 325 read with section 149 IPC, they are entitled to be released forthwith.

The assessee, a non resident Indian Company, was assessed to income tax on cash basis for the assessment years 1967 68 and 1968 69. The Income Tax Officer held that the royalty amount should be assessed on cash receipt basis for 1967 68. In these appeals by the assessee, it was contended that the assessee could not be said to have received any income in all these four years, that it had committed a mistake in filing the returns for the relevant assessment years, 1967 69 and 1968 70, and that it did not take credit for the said amounts in its books at Coventry. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The assessee can be said not to have maintained any particular method of accounting regularly in respect of the said royalty amount and that the entry in the account books of the assessee in the books of his Indian Company does amount to receipt of income by the Income Tax officer. [105G] 2.2 In the instant case, the assessee had received the royalty on cash receipts basis from its own books at the end of the calendar year and determined the royalty amounts payable to the assessee. The fact that the money was not actually received did not amount to payment of income tax by the appellant in a particular accounting year. [106H] 2.(a) In the case of non resident assessees like the petitioner clause (a) cannot apply. [107B C] 3.3 The assessee could be said, to have made an entry to that effect in its own Books at Coastry. It is significant to notice that the Income tax Officer did not say that the method of accountancy adopted by it for all its income was on cash Basis basis. He replied to a further question whether there was any conflict or inconsistency between section 5(2)(b) and Section 145 of the Act. [108D] (b) The assessee had not maintained any specific method of accounts regularly in the past years, nor did he take credit thereof for the amounts in his books at COventry, nor was it necessary to express ourselves on the view expressed by the High Court that in the case Of a nonresident assessee like the assessee clause (c) must be held to have been satisfied. [109D] 4.4 The fact of accounting being regularly maintained by an assessee does not amount merely to receipt or receipt, but merely crediting to the account of the Incometax Officer in the Books of the Indian Company. It may also be noticed that in its returns relating to assessment years 1966 68 and 1967 69, it did raise the plea that it was maintaining its accounts on cash foundation and since it did actually receive any amount, it could not have been taxed at all as it would be received in U.K. In this view of the matter, it must be deemed that in respect Of that amount and unless the entry can be deemed to be a payment or receipt clause (b), cannot apply.[107C D] 5.5 The fact whether there is any conflict between section 145 of Act and Section 146 of the does not make any difference as regards the position of law applicable to the facts of the case. [110D E] 6.6 In the present case, it is clear from the evidence that the appellant had received royalty amount on cash received basis in U/K. The assessee was maintaining their books with respect to the said amount and, therefore, it cannot be said that the said payment was not receipt of any income by it in U K.K., [110E] 7.7 In the circumstances, the High court was right in holding that in view of section 145, the appellant could not claim that the amount was actually received. The mere entry in his account books in the book of the Company does not constitute receipt of profits by the income tax officer.

The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death but on appeal the High Court confirmed his conviction. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. Held, that the evidence of a approver is no corroboration of the approver 's story which would be sufficient to connect him with the crime. It cannot be doubted that under section 34 of the Indian Penal Code the accomplice is competent to give evidence and according to the latter he may not convict upon his testimony alone. The test for determining whether an accomplice is reliable is whether he has been corroborated in material particulars. In the present case, the approver made a confessional statement to his brother and it was not sufficient that there should be corroboration of his approver ' s story which could be called, in the circumstances of this case, to be a corroboration of an accomplice. The fact that the knife was got prepared by accused No. 1 would not affect the conviction of the first accused on the uncorroborated testimony of an approver. The evidence of the accomplice supported by the statement of the appellant is no reliable and it is difficult to hold that he made a confession to his co accused without corroboration of such a witness without corroboration. The conviction of an accused on a testimony alone is not illegal, but the court can still lose sight of the rule of prudence and practice in which the words of Martin Birming vs Baskerville (A.I.R. , approved. In re Rajagopal vs Basak, A.I., R. , referred to.

The appellant was charged with an offence under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that on July 8, 1961 a trap was laid and under the direction of the Deputy Superintendent of Police, P.W. 2, the appellant was prosecuted in the Court of Special Judge for an offence Under section 5 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted him but convicted him under section 161 I.P.C. on the ground that he was not a public servant within the meaning of section 21 (9) of that Act and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for one year. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the trial court had erred in holding that the appellant could not be convicted because he was a public servants within the definition of section 2(12) of Prevention of corruption Act, and section 21 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding the appellant guilty of the charges under section 4(2). [691 B] (ii) The appellant was an officer in the service or pay of the Corporation as defined in section 21(9), Indian Penal code and therefore a public Servant within the terms of section 3(12). [792 C D] (iii)The appellant could be said to be an officer within the term of section 81 of the Transport Corporation Act, 1950. The High court was right that he could not have been convicted because the charge against him was that he had been a public man within the scope of section 5.(2) of section 1(12), Indian Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1958 (Act 11 of 1958).

The appellant was convicted for contravention of cl. 3 of the Maharashtra Foodgrains (Declaration of Stocks and Control) Order, 1964, under section 3(1)(b) of the Defence of India Act, 1962, for contravening cl. (3) of article 19 of the Constitution. The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed on the appellant in respect of contravention of Cl. 3 Of the Maharashtra Essentialgrains (Temporary Powers) Order 1964, and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 1,000. In appeal to this Court it was contended that r. 141(2) of Defence of India tion Rules 1962, which provided for forfeiture to the Government packages of packages, coverings or receptacles in which any stocks of jowar were found, was not ultra vires the Defence Of India Act and therefore, the order regarding forfeiture of the juar could not be sustained. HELD: (i) The rule is contrary to an existing law contained in section 3 because it lays down a rule of evidence contrary to the law contained therein. [273 C] (ii) The Rules must necessarily provide for the publication of orders made under the Rules and they must also provide proof in judicial proceedings in judicial proceeding. The rules must necessarily prescribe for the publications of orders under the rules and they should also provide for proof in criminal proceedings. The Rules need not provide proof for judicial proceedings, in judicial or quasi judicial proceedings. [274 D] (iii) The Rule is within the powers conferred by section 3 (1 ) of the Act. It is essential to the scheme of the defence of India Rules that the provisions of this Act or any rule made thereunder or any order made thereunder shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any enactment other than this Act.

The appellants were charged with murder of one Ram and the other for having fired a shot from his gun. The trial court acquitted them on the ground that they had not been identified by the witnesses. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of Sia Ram and Violet but convicted them under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the High court had not properly appreciated the evidence; (ii) the trial court had failed to consider the fact that Siaram fired a gun from his rifle as a result of which Kunwar Singh fell down and died within an half hour, Brijendra Singh 's evidence has been accepted by both the courts and the High.
