Court was not impressed by the testimony of Om Prakash Dubey; (iii) the prosecution had failed in establishing the motive for murder of Kunwar Singh; (iv) the conviction of S as well as Violets were based on circumstantial evidence; and (v) the evidence of Om Parkash Dubey, who stated in his evidence that he knew Shri Ram and was therefore able to identify him. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The High Court ought not to have interfered with the order of acquittal passed by the trial Court. [87G] 2.1 In a case where the prosecution has failed to prove the motive or motive for the crime, it is not enough that an act on the part of the alleged abettor happens to facilitate the commission thereof, and thereby facilitates the commission of that act. The words attributed to Violetting do not, however, necessarily justify the inference that she was a party to the murderous design. [884C] 2(a) In order to hold that Shri Ram had played an important role in the murder of the deceased Kunwar Singh, it must be shown that he was aware of the nefarious design of S.ia Ram, and his associates. The fact that he had been told by some of the colleagues of the accused persons that they might accomplish their aim would not necessarily justify his inference that he is a party who had engaged him or who used to instruct him in the case or who use to instruct them in the cases. [894D E] 2.(b) The High court was not satisfied with the evidence on record and it was not possible for the Sessions Court to have gone into the question of motive or the motive of murder. [905E F] 3(c) In a criminal case, where the accused had been acquitted by the Trial Court, the presumption under section 114A of the Evidence Act would be that he did so by doing so by using his particular shout. The circumstances that S was aware that S had committed the murder were so flooded with that work that he could remember no details of an important murder trial. [914F] 4(d) In the instant case, the prosecution failed to establish the motive and the motive. The evidence of the eye witnesses is not sufficient to sustain the conviction. [925E] 5.2 The High Courts were not impressed with the testimony that S in order to holding that S did commit the murder, had played a important role. There was no evidence at all to show that S knew Shri R. Ram or his companions could have detected the presence of Kunwar singh. The mere fact that there was some other infirmity in the prosecution case would not justify the conclusion that he might be guilty of murder and convicted.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34, I.P.C., and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted him of the charge under section 307 read with Section 34, but convicted him under section 148, read with sections 149 and 147, and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for five years. In appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High Court was not justified in acquitting only one of the accused persons; (ii) the evidence was directed against the other named or unnamed persons, named or indicted, for committing the said offence and convicted under sections 302 read and section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. HELD : (i)(a) The High court was right in holding that the appellant was not guilty only one but he did not conjointly act with accused 2; (b) the conviction of the other persons was set aside by the High court on the ground that they did not have prior concert with each other or more persons named, named and unnamed, for commit the said crime. [682 B] (ii)(a). The appellant was acquitted under section 149, read along with section 149 because he had done the act pursuant to a pre arranged plan and therefore he could be convicted under Section 302 read, read alongwith section 34 because along with the other accused persons were acquitted either on the basis of constructive liability. [782 C] (b)(i) The appellant did not join the charge as required by section 149(1), nor was there any evidence in that regard. He had no prior concert or common intention with the others, named, or unnumbered, for commission of the said offences. [882 D E] (iii) The fact that two persons were convicted jointly with the accused did not necessarily displace the charge Under section 302, read together with section 109, and therefore they could be tried separately. [783 G H] (iv) The effect of acquittal of all the accused was that they do not conjointally act with each others named or unidentified persons, other than those acquitted, in the commission of that offence.

The petitioner, a manufacturer of electric cables, imported certain goods from the respondent State. The respondents were assessed to customs duty under section 14(1)(b) read with Section 16(2) of the Customs Act on the basis that the goods could not be released. The Customs authorities issued import licence No. 29598 for Rs.20,12,729 in favour of M/s Metalic metal Indus tries. The petitioner filed an application under Article 32 of the Constitution before the Customs Authorities claiming refund of the customs duty paid on the goods. The Assistant Collector of Customs and the Assistant Collector rejected the claim. The writ petition was filed by the petitioner against the order of the Income Tax authorities. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the customs authorities were right in taking the view that the rate applicable to the imported goods should be determined according to the law prevalent on the date they were actually removed from the warehouse after the amending Ordinance had come into force, and the customs officers and the Central Govern ment were right to take the view as well as the decision of this Court in Union of India vs M/S Metalic Metal Indus try. [1985] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 872 that relief under Article 226 was not available to enforcing a fundamental right which entitle a citizen to seek recourse to Article 32. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The relief under article 32 of t he Constitution is wholly inappropriate in the facts and circumstances of this case. [682D] 2.1 The petitioner has no fundamental fight to clear the goods on payment of duty when the goods are actually removed by the customs authority and the Customs authorities and the central Govern ment was right in accepting the view of the High Court that relief cannot be resorted to and this application does not lie under Article 14. [782E] 2(a) The petitioner 's grievance is that the Central Government had wrongly taken the view which it had taken on the ground that the rates applicable to imported goods were actually cleared from the warehouses after the amendment Ordinance had came into force. [882F G] (b) In a matter of this nature where liability of a citizen for payment of a particular duty depends on interpretation of law and determination or determination of questions of law as well, it cannot conceivably be contended that enforcing of those provisions of the Act would breach fundamental right to claim recourse to article 32. [820C] 2.(c) The relief sought under Article 33 is wholly misconceived in the circumstances and the writ peti tion is wholly unnecessary in the factual matrix and the provision of a specific statute for which elaborate procedure is pre scribed, it can conceivly be contended by the respondents that enforcing the provisions of those statutes would breach the fundamental right guaranteed to the petitioner. [825D] 3.(d) The claim under Article 16(1) is wholly untenable in the light of the prohibitory orders of the Central Govt. under section 102 of the . [825E F] 4.2 The relief claimed under Article 34 is wholly impermissible in the fact and circumstances. [826F G; 882A] 3. In a case of this kind where liability for payment is dependent on adjudication or determination or question of law or determination, it does not automatically involve breach of fundamental right for enforcement of which alone Article 32 would apply. [827B C] 4.(a) It is well settled that the remedy under article 226 is available only to enforcement of a fundamental rights and not to enforce a fundamental fight if the order challenged is a valid and legal order in spite of the allegation that it is a violation of law, it will not automatically be involved breach of the fundamental rights.

The appellant was the owner of a bungalow. The respondent 's father died in 1947 and his son was the sole surviving heir. He filed a suit for possession by partition against the respondent on the ground that the debt was not avyavaharika but it was due to the pious obligation under the Hindu law to discharge the debts of his father. The trial court decreed the plaintiff 's suit for partition by holding that the respondent had no interest in the bungalow and that the appellant was entitled to a decree for possession. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the debt which was avyaharika was not binding on the joint family as it was not an estate left by the sons; (2) that the debts were paid in discharge of their debts, and (3) that even if the debt had not been avyabalarika, the institution of the suit for division of the son 's power of disposition over the son was not dependent on what was the estate put up for sale. HELD: (i) The liability of a father to discharge his debts of the father which are not tainted with immorality or illegality is based on the pious duty of the sons who continue to exist in the lifetime and after the death of the mother, which does not come to an end as a result of partition of the joint Hindu family property. [419 C] (ii) The obligation of a son to discharge debts of a deceased father which were not tainted by immority or illegality was based on his pious obligation of the brothers which continues to exist and after his death the sons continue to remain in the possession of the estate. [420 D E] (iii)The liability of the respondent to discharge all the debts is that of the deceased father who has received a salary or remuneration from the family and therefore the right, title and interest of the defaulter i.e. of the brother alone could not include the share of the other members of the family.

The Delhi Administration was constituted under the Delhi Police Act, 1973. The Delhi Administration had to examine the conduct of various police officers and other persons and also the affidavits filed by them before it. The Committee submitted its report on December 29, 1988. The report stated that there were large number of persons who fall under section 8 B of the Act and have to be examined at the end of the inquiry. The committee submitted its Report on December 30, 1988 recommending suspension of the D.C.P. Kiran Bedi and Jinder Singh S.I., section I.P., Police Post, Tis Hazari. The petitioners in these cases were also given an opportunity of being heard before passing any order under section 9 B of Act. In their writ petitions filed by the Delhi Administration challenging the orders of the Committee, the High Court quashed the said orders of suspension and directed the Delhi Administrate to examine its witnesses first as provided by rule 5(5)(a) of the Rules referred to above. The respondents in these appeals contended that the Committee should have considered whether the petitioners were entitled to be treated as persons governed by section 8B of the Police Act. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Committee should consider whether the Petitioners were entitled for being treated as members governed by Section 8 B and 8 C of the Delhi police Act. [5G] 2.2 The Committee shall examine the entire conduct of all police officers, and other material before it and if at any stage of the proceedings the Committee has found that there are large number persons who were eye witnesses to the incidents and why could give evidence before the Committee in asking them to be cross examined, then they would not have been asked to get into the witness box for being cross examined till the endof the inquiry.[5G H] 2:1. The decision of the committee regarding filing of complaints by either of the petitioners is not contemplated under section8 B of Delhi Police act, 1973 and therefore cannot be sustained. [6H; 7A] 2(a) The Committee has clearly observed that it had to consider whether there were a large numberof persons who are eye witnesses and why can give evidence after the inquiry was held. It is obvious from the order of the Board that there was no justifiable reason to deny the same treatment to the petitioners. [7A B] 2.(b) The issue of such a notice is not envisaged under section S8 B and the criminal proceedings initiated against the petitioners before the Metropolitan Magistrate pursuant to the complaints filed on behalf of the Committees are to be considered at the beginning of the enquiry. [8C D] 3(a).

The first petitioner was a registered firm, petitioners Nos. 7 and 8 were registered dealers under the Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Act, 1959, for the purpose of carrying on business in motor cycles, rickshaw or a motor cab. The first petitioner, who was a dealer, challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that it was ultra vires the provisions of section 3 of the Rajasthan Goods and Taxation Act as unconstitutional and ultra vires certain provisions of the said Act, as unconstitutional. Held, that the proviso to sub section (3) of section 8A is not ultra vires any provision of the statute and the notification still retains the permissive character of the section, but only lays down what the amount of fare and freight charged it does not cease to be a tax on passengers and goods, though the measure of the tax is furnished by the amount or of fares and freight charges. The tax, however, remains on passengers, and goods which are transported by road or inland waterways. The words "in respect of all passengers carried and goods" in section 3(1) mean "the charge of the taxes on passengers carried or goods". The word "charge" is not defined in the Act but it has been used in the sense of a tax. The expression "charge of the Taxes" in the context of the proviso means "the amount of the lump sum paid by the owner of a motor cycle, rickshaw, or a Motor cab". The words 'charge of taxes" in that clause are not defined and they are capable of being understood as meaning "charge", but it is only so defined. The word 'charge ' has been defined in section 2(g) of the Indian Railways Act, 1890, to mean "a charge on goods carried or brought by road". The expression 'charge" in this clause means "any sum charged by a person for any purpose connected with the carriage of goods and includes any sum charged as a lump sum. The proviso to that sub section is not intended to cover cases where the owner has not plied his vehicle for a continuous period of not less than three months and produces a certificate from the authority competent under the Act, no amount by way of tax under the said act shall be payable for such period.

The appellant workmen were sought to be retrenched from 1st August, 1974 and the Labour Court directed their reinstatement effective from that date. The Labour Court also awarded full back wages to the workmen on its finding that the retrenchment was not bona fide and that the non availability of raw material or recurrent power shedding was a mere pretence or a ruse to torment the workmen by depriving them of their livehood, the real reason being the annoyance of the appellant consequent upon refusal of the workmen to be a party to a proposed settlement by which work load was sought to he raised. The appellant challenged the award in this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Labour court has rightly awarded full wages for full back salary. [567B] 2.2 The question whether the workmen concerned did not have any opportunity of explaining why their services should not be terminated and, therefore, reinstatement was held to be the appropriate relief. Once leave against relief of reinstatement is refused, the employer can not shirk his responsibility of paying the wages which the workman has been deprived of by the illegal or invalid action of the employer. [568C] 2.(a) The question is whether the Labour court in the facts and circumstances of this case was justified in awarding full back wage. It may well be that in appropriate cases the Court may, in the interest of industrial law requiring elucidation and final decision by this Court or discloses such other exceptional or special circumstances which merit consideration of this Court, or disclosessuch other exceptional and special circumstances as merit consideration whereof merit consideration thereof, or raises an important principle of industrial jurisprudence requiring elucidating and final decisions by this court or discloses some exceptional orspecial circumstances which merits consideration of the consideration of that Court or disclose such other special or special circumstance which merit Consideration of this court, or disclosed such other strong or special reasons which merit considered consideration of these courts or discloses any exceptional or exceptional special circumstances. [569E F] (b) The only question is what should be the guiding considerations for awarding full and back wages. It is no more open to debate that in the field of industrial adjudication a declaration can be given that the termination of service is bad and the relief of compensation for the loss is totally wiped out the Managing Director and the Directors shall not charge any fee for the services rendered as Director, no dividend shall be paid to equity shareholders, and the Managing Directors shall charge any fees for the service rendered as Directors, no bonus shall be payable to the workman. [570E F G] (c) The workmen concerned had failed to discharge their duties in accordance with the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. They were not entitled to the relief. [571F] (d) The Labour Courts have rightly awarded half back wages for the period when work was required to be done and the direction of reinstatement has become final.

The accused was charged with murder of his wife Churi. The prosecution case was that the deceased had come at the residence of the accused on the day of occurrence and that he was in a wet condition at the time when the accused left for Kotkhai, leaving his wife alone at the house of the deceased. The trial court acquitted the accused but convicted him under section 302 Indian Penal Code. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the State that the evidence of the prosecution witnesses was not sufficient to prove the guilt of the appellant beyond reasonable doubt and that the prosecution had failed to establish beyond any manner of doubt that the dead body of Churi deceased was recovered after the accused had visited the house. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The record of such a confession could not be put in evidence under sections 74 and 80 of the Indian Evidence Act. [734G] 2. The statement made by the accused before the police regarding the murder of Chururi deceased is admissible in evidence. It is in the evidence that only the accused in the case had visited his house on that evening and that there was nothing to show that the police was aware of the murder. There is no evidence to show as to whether the accused knew the murder or not. The version of the witness that he had gone to see film at Kotkha i, which had been arranged by the Publicity Department, according to Head Constable Bhag Singh PW 10, and Shri Mahajan (PW 15) on that day cannot be accepted because there is nothing to indicate that the Police was aware about the murder and believed that Joginder had been born to her as a result of her adulterous conduct. [834A B] 3. The evidence of PW 10 shows that he knew the deceased before the visit of the police. He did not deny that he would have insisted upon staying with him without the child. It was in the circumstances, that the accused could have had a natural affection for the child and it is difficult to believe that he should have insisted on staying with the child without the son of the father of the boy and the deceased abused him. [825E F] 4. The plea of the defence that he did not know the murder was not rightly rejected because there was no evidence that the appellant knew the death of Churauri. It could not therefore be accepted that there is no material to show how the accused came to the house on the date of occurrence. [934B C] 5. The High Court has rightly held that the record of the case and as it was not recorded in the manner prescribed by section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the same is inadmissible in evidence on behalf Of the respondent State.

The plaintiff, a co owner of certain properties, purchased certain properties from the defendants. The defendants claimed that they were liable to contribute in equal shares towards payment of the mortgage debt and the balance of Rs. 80,507 7 being the aggregate amount due and payable by the two defendants. They contended that the suit was not maintainable as the plaintiff had failed to prove that he was entitled to a mortgage decree up to a limit of Rs., 40,000 and also claimed interest on the said sum from the three mortgagors. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the plaintiff was entitled only to a sum of Rs, 2,500 and not the aggregate sum due and the defendants were liable for contribute in the balance amount of Rs 80,057 7 being their aggregate amount payable by them. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant (1) that the High court had no jurisdiction to entertain a suit under section 92 of the Transfer of Property Act read with section 82 of the Code; (2) that in the absence of an agreement to the contrary, the plaintiff 's remedy was only under section 91 of the Indian Contract Act and not under section 93 of the Specific Relief Act. HELD: (i) The High Court had no power to entertain the suit under sections 92 and 93 of Transfer of property Act read together with section 83 of the Evidence Act. [189 E] (ii) The declaration of charge by standing itself by standing themselves by itself is superfluous Order XXXIV though Order XXXIV, rule 2(1) does require that the decree in a mortgage suit shall be drawn up in the usual way affording either the right to redeem the whole of the balance or to any costs which may be necessitated by a further enquiry. The declaration as standing itself was by standing himself by itself and not expressly plead a case of subrogation in his plaint even in the alternative.

The appellants applied for the posts of Asstt. Engineers (Civil) and (Mech.) in all 9123 vacancies of Civil Engineers and 110 Mechanical Engineers in all 99.26 marks out of 150. The appellants applied before the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal for the post of Asstt., Engineer (Civil). The Tribunal dismissed their petitions holding that the percentage of marks for viva voce was excessive and in violation of the decisions of this Court, the appellants were not selected in merit as the last candidate selected for the above posts secured more than the appellants. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the marks awarded to the selected candidates for interview out of 100 marks out o f 150 were excessive and therefore the selections were made according to the Rules of 1973 and this practice is being consistently followed for the last 17 years and there is no allegation of any malafides in the matter of the impugned selections. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The selection was made as back as in 1987 and only the present appellants had approached the Tribunal for relief. [415C] 2.1 In view of the fact that appointments under the impugned Rules were made as early as in1987 and only this appellant had approached this Court for relief, the case of other candidates cannot be considered as they never approached for redress within reasonable time. The Rules are clearly in violationof the dictum laid down by this Court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., [1988] Sup. S.C.R., 657 and Mohinder Sain Garg vs State, of Punjab & Ors, J.T. 1987 (1) Sup.S.C., 657, followed. 2.2 The selection made according tain to the rules of 1973 was being consistently follow for the past 17 years. [515D] 3.3 The selections were not made according ly then both the appellants would have gone much lower in the merit list than the selected candidate. In view thereof, the selections made accordingto the Rules are also clearly in contravention of the dictum of this court in Ashok Yadav & Anr. vsState of Haryana and Ors., J.J.T., 1987 (2) Sup, S. C.R. 657 and Joginder Sain Garg v State of Punjab, [1988], Sup. SCR. 658, followed and applied.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 120 B I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction of the appellant but reduced his sentence to imprisonment for life. In appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the State that the prosecution had failed to prove the complicity of Sadanand in the murder of the Collector. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 It is not possible to accept a part of the confession as a complete one and on the basis of such incomplete evidence, the allegation of conspiracy cannot be accepted. [413D] 2.2 The High court has rightly held that the appellant was guilty of conspiracy to kill the Collector through Yadav. In these circumstances, it would indeed be hazardous to accept part of a link as a full and on its foundation the charge of conspiracy can be pressed into service only when the court is inclined to accept other evidence and feels the necessity of seeking assurance in support of its conclusion. [414B] 2:1 The High Courts have not been able to agree with the High Court that the evidence of Sadananda was satisfactory. It is a fact that a set of witnesses who according to the prosecution, were present when Yadav was taken into custody followed the incident, enforcement of rules became slack and there was regular flow of food from outside. This type of evidence cannot be accepta ble. [422C D] 2(i) The High Cou rt has rightly pointed out that the confession may be regarded as substantive evidence and can be admitted in evidence only when it has formed its opinion with regard to the quality and effect of the said evidence, then it is permissible to turn to the confession in order to receive assurance to the conclusion which the judicial mind is about to reach on the other evidence adduced by the prosecution. [411E F] 2.(ii) The confession may not be substantive evidence but if the prosecution relies upon circumstantial evidence, a clear link has to be established and the chain has to he completed, otherwise it would certainly be hazardous. [416F G] 3(iii) The fact remains that the jail records did not show that after the arrival of Sadanad at the jail, enforcement or rules becames slack. It was difficult to support the charge from direct evidence in every case but if there has been a regular flow and the link has been established and chain has also to be completed, it otherwise would indeed hazardous to accepted a part as a link. [420B] 4(iv) The mere fact that some of the witnesses were present at the time when Yadav had been taken into possession does not establish conspiracy. It may be hazardous in every respect to the charge but if it is difficult to accept any part of evidence, it can be concluded and the entire chain has lo be completed otherwise it will indeed be dangerous to accepta part of circumstantial evidence. [406C] 5(v) The prosecution has established by circumstantial evidence that the accused had an interview with his wife that day, the story of bribing the jail officials has been introduced. It would also be hazardous not to accept the criticism of counsel for the appellant that if the defence relies upon direct evidence, there is a clear nexus between the crime and the circumstances proved. [409E F; 409A] 6(vi) The conduct of Sadan in the instant case does not prove any conspiracy. The prosecution had further led evidence to show that the wife had an interviews with her husband and she was staying with him. It has also been admitted by the defence that the house was searched regularly at Sadanand. There is no direct evidence to establish conspiracy against Sadanand, therefore, the High court was right in holding that the charge against Sadananda is not proved. The conviction of Saddan is not sustainable.

The appellants, who were working as clerical and subordinate staff in the four companies with wages and dearness allowance prevalent in comparable concerns, filed references (IT) Nos. 123 and 132 of 1959 for fixation of their basic wage and dearness allowances. The Tribunal held that the total wage packet including basic wages and Dearness allowance was more than 15 months and that the Tribunal had gone wrong in applying the industry cum region formula which is the basis for fixing the same scales of dearness allowance and dearness Allowance together as it should have done, for the purpose of finding out whether the total pay packet in the appellants ' concerns could bear comparison with the total wages packet including dearness allowance. The High Court on reference held that there was no evidence to show that the average wage packet of the appellants concern was less than 15 days and that there were no comparable concerns in the same industry and that it had made the total price of comparable concerns as possible in different lines of business for the purposes of fixing the scales of wages and, dearness allowance together. The appellants contended (i) that the tribunal has gone wrong on the basis of the industrycum region formula and (ii) that there could be equal competition between the two groups and that in determining the total emoluments packet including the basic wage packet, the Tribunal should have taken into account the comparable concerns which it took into account. Held: (1) The Tribunal was right in applying a industry cum industry formula for fixing wages and the dearness allowance fixed by it as well as dearness allowance with respect to clerical staff and subordinate employees. (2) The tribunal has not considered what the total Wage packet of comparable concern would be on the ground that some exemplars were filed before it; but in doing so the Tribunal must have taken note of what was already prevalent in these concerns and also taking into account what was earlier prevalent in those concerns and then compare it with the Total wage packet. (3) The fact that there are different scales of pay and dearness, allowance fixed for clerical staff, and subordinate workmen, cannot be ignored by the Tribunal as well. (4) The fixation of basic wages, dearness allowances and other administrative expenses with respect thereto is not comparable to the total salary packet of industrial concerns. (5) The award of the tribunal was in accordance with the industry formula and it had applied the same scale of dearness Allowance for factory workmen as clerical staff. (6) The appellants were working under the control of the management of the two companies, one of which was the controlling company of the other three, and the other was the managing director of the company.

The appellants, who were the legal representatives of one Shiddappa, filed a suit against the respondents for redemption of certain mortgaged property and possession thereof free from encumbrances. The trial Court decreed their claim to an extent of half share in the suit land. On appeal by the mortgagees, the District Judge held that the Rajinama had not the effect of transferring the interest of Annappa to the mortgagees and hence he was entitled to redeem the mortgage on taking accounts. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Rajinamama was a complete relinquishment of his interest in the mortgaged property. The appellants could not claim redemption of the mortgage by adverse possession. [648 C] (ii) The High Court had refused to grant leave to appeal to the plaintiffs to make out such a new case. The finding that the appellants were bound to pay the amount also under the simple mortgage and that on taking account accounts, the mortgages had redeemed themselves was not correct. [749 D E] (iii) The appellants cannot claim redemption by adverse Possession. The High court rightly held that there was no evidence on record that Shiddppa intended to convey the title in the land to the mortgagors. [700 F G] (iv) The finding of the District judge that the plaintiffs were bound by the mortgage and did not extinguish the title of Ananappa to convey it in the property to the mortgagee, is not correct because the Rajiama was binding on his brother Annaappa.

The respondent, a dealer in carbon paper, was assessed to sales tax at the rate of 2 per cent. The Sales Tax Officer, Kanpur, did not accede to the conten tions of the respondent and holding that carbon paper could not be subjected to salestax at the rates specified in the Schedule to the Notification and (2) whether ribbon is an accessory or a part of the typewriter so as to attract tax at 5% prescribed inter alia for typewriters and parts thereof by Notification No. 2 of 1948, so as not liable to sales Tax at the point and at the same rate specified in that notification. The respondent filed writ petition before the High Court challenging the levy of tax on carbon paper at 6% and ribbon at 10%. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that Carbon paper does not lose its character as paper even after being subjected to chemical processes and that ribbon was a part thereof mechanically propelled by means of a typewriter. In appeal to this Court, it was contended for the respondent that carbon papers do not lose their character aspaper even after going through certain chemical processes, and that consequently ribbon cannot be subjected only to sales lax at the lower rate of 5 per cent prescribed for unclass fied goods and not at the higher rate of 6 paise per rupee. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The word 'paper ' has not been defined in the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1947 and that sale of stencil paper is not an essen tial part of a motor car in the same way, ribbon being used for printing or writing purposes. [838C] 2. The words 'popular sense ' in popular parlance, the word ' paper ' in the Notification No 8 of 1948 are not decisive of the question whether carbon paper is paper as envisaged by entry 2 of the aforesaid Notification. Just as aviation is not a part, aero plane or diesel is not part of that category compartment and a petrol is not necessarily a part. [938F] 3. The expression 'popsular sense" in popular literature means paper which is used for bearing writing, printing or purveying purposes. It does not mean paper made handless than otherpaper. Just because aviation has not even been defined either in the Act or Rules, and as such it has to be given the meaning which it has in ordinary parlance, meaning paper is used in the common parlance, but that it is to be construed according to the strict or technical meaning of the language contained in it. [977F G] 4. The High court was right in holding that a typewriter is not paper as contemplated by entry 3 of the Notification issued by the State Government under the first proviso to section 5(1) of the Act.

The appellant, a company, was carrying on the business of manufacturing sugar at Amroha. The respondents 1 to 4 were employed by the owners of the Sugar Mills at Amroha and were working as such in the Sugar Mill at Amroha for more than two years. On February 2, 1955, the General Manager made an order dismissing the respondents 1to 4 from service on the ground that they had disobeyed the order of transfer and thus they were properly dismissed by the management. The appellant contended before the Labour Appellate Tribunal that the management was within its rights and that as the respondents I to 4 had disobeying the order, they were rightly dismissed by it. Held, that in the circumstances of the case, the liability to be transferred must be deemed to be an implied condition of service within the meaning of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act. The essential distinction between that case and the present one is that every employer has the inherent right to transfer his employee to another place where the business was situated, unless there was an express condition to the contrary in the contract of employment. In such a case it was possible to imply the condition of right of the management to transfer the respondents to any of its concerns in any place and the records clearly indicated that transfer was one of the ordinary incidents of service in the Bank. The mere fact that there was no express agreement between the appellant and the respondents, did not prevent the employer from transferring the respondents ' employees to another. The question whether the appellant had the right to do so under the contract or under any statutory provisions, was a mixed question of law and fact. It was well within the powers of the Labour Tribunal to entertain the appeal.

The appellant company was incorporated in 1948 under the . The State Insurance Act, 1948, was enacted to provide for certain benefits to employees in the case of factories or establishments situated in areas in which the provisions of both Chapters IV and V were in force. Section 28 of the Act provided that the employer 's contribution payable under Chapter V A shall be in lieu of the employer "s contribution". The appellant company, a registered society, was incorporated under the , with effect from July l, 1973. The appellant Company made an application to the State Government for payment of special contribution under Chapter IV A of the . It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the contribution payable by it under Chapter VI A was not a fee and its levy was illegal as the Act did not contemplate rendering any service or the conferment of any benefit to the appellant company or its employees as quid pro quo for the payment. The High Court rejected this contention. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The contribution payable is a fee which is to be utilised for the benefits to be given to the employees under the Act. It is pursuant to the power entrusted in respect of entries 23 and 24 of List III, of their own force, of its own force. [1088B] 2.2 The scheme is confined to a few areas and though special contribution is levied from all employers wherever they are, in the cases of factories situated in any area in which there is no employer ' contribution under the provisions Of Chapter VA. It was not disputed that the contributions were directed to be made by the employer under Chapter VII A of that Act. The fact that the appellant Company had paid special contribution would not make it necessary for the Parliament to make certain transitory provisions, which it did by the introduction of Chapter V B of the , in order to attain legitimacy or not at all. Both Parliament and the Legislature of any State, subject to conditions with which we are not concerned, have power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List llI. It would be impossible for the legislature to decide in what areas and in respect thereof the employees ' State Insurance Corporation should be established. [ 1088C D] 2.(a) The scheme was confined to one few areas, though special contributions were levied from both employers wherever it be, in case of establishments situated within areas in whom the provisions are not applicable. It could not be said that the special contribution was, to be regarded as a tax or fee in order that it would have been impossible for Parliament to decide what in areas and on whom the Employees ' State insurance Corporation should have jurisdiction. [1188D] (b) The expression "tax" is used in Entry 23 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, which reads as under: "Taxes on the sale or purchase of goods". The word "taxes on sale or purchases" has been defined in Entry 24 of the Union List. It means taxes on the transfer or purchase by a person of goods for cash or deferred payment or other valuable consideration. [988G] (c) The words "tax on the purchase or purchase" are not defined in the Act but they have been used in different senses and their meaning is to include taxes on sales or purchases which are meant to be levied by the Parliament, by the Legislature. The word 'taxes ' has been used as a term of wide import and it has been so interpreted as to include tax on sale of goods. [889D] 3.(a)(i) The word `taxes" in Entry 25 of List I means taxes which are levied by Parliament, or the Legislature, or by both. It does not mean taxes on sale and purchase of any goods. The expression 'tax on purchase ' has not been defined under the Income Tax Act.

The petitioners are not regular employees, they do not have any specific job to do, work for a long time. The management has denied the petition ers ' claim and alleged that there is no vacancy in the establishment to absorb the petitioners and giving them the pay of regular workers. The High Court rejected the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 It is not the position that there are no vacancies or work available in the establishments for absorption of the petitioners. [654D] 2.2 In spite of our conclusion, keeping in view the offer made on behalf of respondent No. 2 in the counter affidavit together with Annexure R V thereto which was reiterated at the hearing before this Court and for some time they have been continued on rolls and paid in spite of there being no work available for them. The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment offered to the 63 daily rated workmen under this Scheme is purely on humanitarian grounds so far as there are not vacancies or works available in establishment for absorption. [554E] 2.(a) In view of the clear findings supported by the clear finding supported by evidence that there were no vacancies and work available, the petitioners cannot be regularised and their retention on the rolls is purelyon humanitarian grounds. [625B C] (b) The principle has been consistently followed in several decisions of this Court. [650E] 3.(a). In spite thereof, the principle of regularization of a Daily rated workman or payment offered by the employer to the temporary workmen does not arise. [600F G] 4.(b) It is well settled that regularisation of daily rated workers cannot be made on humanitarian ground so far it relates to the question of directing their absorption and regu larisation does not fall within the purview of Article 14 of the Constitution. [700G H] (c) The doctrine of regularisation has been repeatedly followed in many cases. In spite, this principle is not applicable to temporary employees. [760F G; 700A] 5.(d) The principles of regularisation are well settled and cannot be applied to temporary workers. [110E F] 6.(a)(i) The High Courts have rightly held that the petitioners being surplus to the requirement of the Project, they cannot be absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay for the period during which the same work is taken from them. [1160F] (ii) The petitioners are also running in heavy losses during the last three years and it is not possible to absorb them immediately as regular workmen.

The appellants, who were the co sharers of a tea estate, purchased certain lands in the suit for a consideration of Rs. 16,000/ . The plaintiffs claimed title to the property and the recovery of possession of the same from them. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court held that the sale was not the full owner of the entire interest effected by him under section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act and that in conse quence the sale passed the entire property and that the co heirs were estopped from questioning the validity of the mortgage. The appellants appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the transaction evidenced by exhibit 12(i) was not a full owner, but only the portion containing the description of the parties and the words of conveyance, with the words "in execution of the decree" in exhibit 12 (ii). [212 C D] (ii) The appellants had failed to raise any specific ground touching their right to this share. They did not raise any other ground touching the right to the share claimed by them. [212 E F] (iii) The appellant 's contention that when the sale in execution of a mortgage decree obtained by it and the sale under exhibit 12 was effected, the plaintiffs would be entitled to a decree for a declaration that the entire interests effected by them under exhibit 13(i), were not real, could not be accepted as frivolous. [213 D] The appellants ' contention that if the sale by the sale deed exhibit 12 is intended to pass title to Pir Baksh and in the event of the sale not being held to be real, it would stand on the same footing as the 8 pies share granted to them by the High court to a further transaction to which we must advert. [214 E F G] (iv) The first line of defence was that when a decree obtained against a co sharer in regard to which a decree was granted in favour of the plaintiffs by the trial Court, it was only the interest of a co heir which represented the interest in the property conveyed under exhibit12(i). [214 F G].

The appellant was charged with offences under sections 302 and 201 of the Indian Penal Code, for having committed an offence punishable under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and section 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The trial court acquitted him but convicted him on appeal by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the provisions of sections 173, 207A and 207A were not complied with because they had been prejudiced in showing that they had not been furnished with such documents or any of them, and (2) the trial was vitiated by the omission of non compliance with the provisions Of section 173(4). HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the provisions contained in sections 173 and 207 A(3), were mandatory but only directory. [293 B] In the present case, the appellant had been deprived of his defence and the trial had not proceeded on the basis that he had been adversely affected by the non compliance of the provisions. The High court was right to set aside the conviction and sentence passed against him. [294 C D] (3) The provisions of section 207 A were mandatory and the irregularity committed by the police officer in charge of the investigation did not vitiate the trial unless the accused had been furnished all the documents referred to in section 173, and that the irregularity was curable by reference to section 537 of the code. [295 E F] (4) The High Courts were right in taking a different view of the aforesaid provisions of the Cr. P.C. and that there was no scope for the argument that the failure of justice had caused substantial prejudice to the accused, in the interest of justice.

The respondent Municipality was constituted under the , for the purpose of carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling sugar. The appellant, who was a member of the Municipality, applied to the Special Officer for permission to discharge the effluent in accordance with the provisions of section 153A of the Act. The Special Officer rejected the application but refused to grant permission. On appeal by the respondent the Special officer held that the existence of a nuisance in the terms of sub section (1) of section153A was a matter for subjective satisfaction of the municipality and beyond the scope of his enquiry under section 153 A of the , he dismissed the petition. The respondent Municipality appealed to the High Court. Held, that the Special Officers had no jurisdiction to issue notice to the appellant as required by section 153B Of the Act and the order of the Special Judge refusing permission was not justified. The scheme of section 151A is to leave it to the subjective satisfaction or the owner of the factory within the fixed period or if a reply is received from the manager or the owners of the factories objecting or objecting subject to modification, the requisition specified in such notice. The order of refusal to go into the question whether a nuisance was one which ought to be set aside is one which is purely matter for the subjective opinion of the Municipal Authority and not the existence or absence of a public nuisance. The provisions of sections 153A and 153A are intended to protect the public health and fertility of the soil. The Act does not provide for any such restriction on the exercise of the fundamental right under article 19(1)(C) to prevent a nuisance which would affect the public Health and ferness of the land. The object of section 155A is that the Municipality should be given an opportunity to show cause against the existence, if it is satisfied that a nuisance exists in the manner specified by the notice. If the notice is objected to, the person on whom the notice has been issued does not deny the existence Of the nuisance in question and is prepared to comply with requisition in the form specified in the notice and not to showcause against the absence of any objection.

The appellant was charged with offences under section 3 of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955. The trial court acquitted him but convicted him under section 4 of the Act and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for one year. On appeal by special leave the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the prosecution had failed to prove that the articles were not railway stores within the meaning of section 2 of the . HELD: (i) The prosecution must first adduce evidence to show that there was reasonable suspicion of the stores being stolen or unlawfully obtained, and cannot satisfactorily account how they came by the same. [191 D] (ii) The evidence in this case did not establish that the goods were railway stores. There was no evidence before the courts to prove the fact that the contents of the report were correct. [192 E] (iii) The appellant failed to offer any satisfactory explanation of his possession of the goods. In most cases the burden of proof in respect thereof may be discharged by the prosecution. [193 A B] (iv) The defence is not called upon to prove a fact that there had been reasonable suspicion about the stores having been stolen or illegally obtained. It is only when the burden in respect of this is discharged by leading evidence about identifying the marks on the goods or some peculiarity of the same goods not to be found in cases of non railway goods that the onus shifts to the accused to account satisfactorily of his actual possession of those goods.

The appellants, who were the tenants of a shop in Jaipur, filed a suit for ejectment against the respondents on the ground that they had no right to continue in occupation of the demised premises as on the date of the suit as statutory tenants. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the tenancy was created by the respondent on the death of the tenant and the appellants were entitled to enjoy the protection under the Act. The High Court reversed the decrees of the courts below and decreeing the suit for eviction of the respondents. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 3(ii) of the Amendment Act introduced to Section 3 (ii) by which a contractual tenant on the termination of the tenancy is by virtue of succession under the provisions of the Rent Acts not liable to be evicted as a matter of course under the ordinary law of the land and he is entitled to remain in possession even after determination of his tenancy, as provided in section 13(1)(a) of that Act. [10D E] 1.2 The mere fact that in the Act no provision has been made with regard to the heirs of the tenants in respect of commercial tenancies on the demise of the landlord without any hiatus and restriction on the heritable interest in the tenanted premises governed by the Act subject to the rights and limitations prescribed under the Rent laws not liable for being evicted as such, does not bring about any change in the status and legal position of the statutory tenant on his death. [11E F] 1.(a) The mere existence of a contractual tenancy is not sufficient to bring about an change in status and ownership of the tenanted property governed by law subject to rights and restrictions prescribed under section 13 (1)(b). [10F G] 1(b) In the instant case, the appellants succeeded to the heritable right in the demised shop in question till the appellants are duly evicted in accordance with the provisions contained in the Rent Act as amended from time to time. The appellants succeeded in September 1966 to the estate of the respondent without any valid hiatu and restriction upon the heritable rights in the leased hold right held by the tenant. [12F G; 13A] 1:2 In the absence of any provision in the Transfer of Property Act, the tenancy rights are heritable and the heirs are entitled to enjoyed the protection of the Act as provided under the Transfer Acts. The respondents succeeded to their heritable interest on the demised property governed under the Rajasthan Premises (Control) Act, 1950. [13F G H] 1 :3 In the present case, there is no provision in any of the Transfer Of Property Act which provides that the heirs or successors of the appellants shall enjoy the right of a tenancy in respect thereof on the expiry of the contractual tenancy of the appellant. The succession having been opened to the appellants and succeeded in October 1966 to their original heritable interest, the respondents succeeded in December 1966 to be in possession of the premises in question. [14F G]. 1:4 In the facts of this case, it is not possible to hold that the appellants succeed to the leasehold right held on the basis of succession or tenancy rights in respect o commercial tenancies after the terminationof the tenancy of their tenancy.

The appellant Board was a public sector undertaking. The State Government had to provide for the development rebate scheme to all its employees except the Government servants who were on deputation and those to whom the Provident Fund Act applies. The appellant Board maintained a Contributory Provident Fund where the contribution is on the basis of basic wage, the Board and the balance sheet shows a very large amount in the shape of interest payable to the Government. The workmen claimed that all the employees of the Board should have the same and similar benefits and therefore there should be no distinction between the Board 's Provident Fund Scheme and the scheme under the Employees Provident Fund. The Industrial Tribunal held that the appellant Board had the financial capacity to implement the Provident fund scheme as demand ed by the Government of Bihar on 25th November, 1966. The Tribunal also found that the employees contributing more than what it was earlier and that therefore the Board would extend the benefits of the Contributory Provident Scheme to all the workmen of the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The employees of a public utility undertaking are entitled to the benefit of the Provident Funds Act. [47 G] (2) The contribution to the provident fund is an ordinary commercial concern to any credit amount to the depreciation reserve. It will also result in some reduction in profits and gratuity which will have to be paid and deduction of interest so paid will have been to be taken into account in calculating the profits. [48 C D] (3) The financial capacity of the employer to implement a Provident Fund scheme as demanded by the Board is not borne out by the provisions of the statute. It would, therefore, result in loss to the employer that burden must be borne by the employer like any other expense including wages and if the financial position shows that the burden of provident fund and gratuity does not result in losses to the employee like any others who are covered by the Act. The contribution is a statutory obligation and is a definite proportion whereas it is open to an ordinary industrial concern to some amount to be appropriated to a fund to be called the Development Fund to be utilised for (a) beneficial purposes, in the opinion of the board, to electrical development in the State; and (b) repayment of loans advanced to the Board under section 64, including arrears of such interest.

The respondent wife filed a petition for maintenance under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The Magistrate dismissed her application on the ground that she was impotent and was not just a cause for refusal of the wife to live with her husband and hence the wife was entitled to the grant of maintenance. On appeal by special leave, the High Court held that the husband having been found to be impotence which had been held by a number of authorities under the Civil law or other laws, it could not compel the wife not to live in her husband merely because she refused to live and hence she was entitled for maintenance if she refused. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has overlooked the legal effect of the second proviso to sub section (3) of section 125, which was also a proviso to the old section 488, clearly providing that it is incumbent on the Magistrate to consider the grounds of refusal and to make an order of maintenance if he was satisfied that there was just ground for refusing to live. [701C D] 2. The second proviso does not say that it would be a just ground. It only deals with maintenance only. If this could be a ground for divorce or for an action for restitution of conjugal rights, it can be said by any stretch of imagination that where a husband refuses to live without her husband, the wife is impotable and unable to discharge his marital obligations, this would not be a merely ground for refusal to live together with her. [801C] 3. The first proviso to section 125(3) makes it clear that it was incumbent on a Magistrate to decide whether or not he should live with the husband. If the second Proviso is not satisfied, the court may draw an inference of neglect or refusal to maintain the wife. But if this could not be said to be a reasonable ground for declining to live, the Court cannot compel the husband to live separately from his husband and the wife would be entitled to maintenance from her husband according to his means. [820E F] 4. The language of the proviso is clear and unambiguous that it does not mean that the court can compel the spouses to live independently without any ill will or coercion. It is a very different thing from holding that no evidence of cruelty can be admitted in a proceeding under the section. But, if this is so, it would not amount to both legal and mental cruelty which would undoubtedly be a proper ground for ordering maintenance. [825E F; 801A] 5. The words "in any way" are used in the proviso to Section 125(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code. It does not refer to any such situation as would justify the refusal of a wife to maintain her husband. The proviso is intended to protect the wife against cruelty which may be caused by her husband or taken a mistress before the amendment made in section 488. [823E F, 802A] 6. In the instant case, the ground of impotency which had not been held to be good law and are hereby overruled must be held to have been given by the courts below. The fact that the wife refused to stay with her would not justify the grant to live permanently with her wife.

The plaintiff, a Municipal Corporation, was granted permission to construct a compound wall on the land in question. The Municipality applied for permission under Section 80 of the Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925 to remove the structures and to take possession thereof. The Municipal Council, however, refused to grant permission. The plaintiff filed an appeal before the High Court which allowed the same holding that the vesting was not merely a right or an authorisa tion to sell the land but also a right of ownership over it. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the suit was barred by limitation and that the defendants had failed to prove their title. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in holding that there was no evidence to show that the Municipality was formally handed over the land to the State Government on 7th July, 1952 for use. [222B C] 2.1 The Municipal Corporation had not pleaded adverse possession of the suit building within 12 years prior to 3rd March, 1964 when the suit is filed. It was necessary for the Court to give a finding on title even if the defendants in possession had not alleged adverse possession. [223C D] 2(a) In the instant case, the plaintiff has not pleaded any adverse possession with the defendant but also there could not be any legal possession with him as the title to the suit property and the defendants have denied title of the land. The plaintiffs had not shown possession of these lands. Therefore, the suit for possession based on title to that property and they had denied title. [224D] 2.(b) In view of the fact that the plaintiff had not claimed adverse possession, the Municipal Council was entitled to give the same rent on 7.7.1952 for use in the ground and the land is vested and is in the possession of Government of India. [225G H; 227A] 3(a). The Municipal Board has not denied title to any property as it was not a vesting of the title itself in the Municipality. [227D] 4(b) The Municipal Committee had not denied the title of plaintiff even if they pleaded adverse posses sion to the land as claimed by them. In fact, the Resolution No. 37 dated 19th January, 1948 was only a right and an authori tion to selling the land was not vested in it. [228D] 5(c) The Municipality had not stated that the lands were vested in Bhavnagar Municipality. It is also not necessary for this Court to go into the question whether the vesting of title by Bhavnagar municipality was merely a legal possession and not a vested right. [226E F] 6(d) The High Courts have erred in holding, on facts, that the land vested in the Municipal Board under Resolution 37 dated 20th January 1948 was merely an interest or an owner to sell it. The resolution No.37 dated 19.1.1948 was only an interest and an owner of the property as stated in the plaint. [233F] 7(e) The plaintiff had also admitted that the structures in Rasala Lines were not shown to be that of the Municipality in the municipal records and even in the Plaint they did not claim any right or interest over it, nor there could be any dispute about the title. The defendants have claimed title of these structures as belonging to the Municipality and the plaintiff have denied their title of ownership of the lands as stated by them in the written statement.

The appellant was a lessee of a railway Carriage Workshop at Ajmer. He was charged with offences under section 5(1)(d) read with section 21(9) of the Indian Penal Code and was convicted by the Judicial Commissioner, State of Ajmer, under section 161 I.P.C., for having committed an offence punishable under section 165(2) (c) of Indian Penal code. The Judicial Commissioner granted a certificate to appeal to the High Court. The appellant contended that he did not fall within the terms of the last portion of clause (9) Of section 21 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and was therefore not an officer within the meaning of that term as used in section 21 (9). Held, that the words "officer in the service or pay of the Government" in section 2(d) of Act II of 1947, were wide enough to include all railway servants except for purposes of Chapter IX I, Indian Penal C. P.C. and therefore a public servant within the definition of a public Servant under section 21 Of the Indian penal Code could not be convicted of the offence under section5(1) (d) Of the Act II Of 1947. The words "any person employed to exercise, to some office for the performance of some pulice duty" in that clause were wide and wide enough respectively to cover all railway employees except those who were appointed to some offices for the discharge of certain pulice duties. The word "officer" in the section was wide enough and it could not mean any person employed by Government to exercise or perform any public duty entrusted to him by the Government. The expression "any officer" in this clause was wide and comprehensive enough to cover a railway servant within that term. The definition of "officer ' contained in section 3(1), Indian Penal, Code, which defines "public servant" as meaning an officer appointed to any office for performing duties immediately 'and includes a person employed in the discharge or pay to whom the Government is entrusted with the performance or pay. The phrase "any public duty" was wide so wide enough that it could be understood to include every act of duty performed by a public authority and not merely by an officer of the State Government.

The Respondent was granted a liquor vending licence for the year 1968 69 under the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887. The auction in respect of the said share of the Respondent was notified for June 14,1977. Just a day prior to the holding of the auction sale, the Respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge 1st Class, Patiala C, Patiala Division, in respect thereof. The Trial Court decreed the suit and held that the property attached and notified for sale was not exempt from attachment and sale under clause (ccc) of the proviso to sub section (l) of Section 60 set out the properties which were not liable to attachment and sell in revenue recovery proceedings adopted under the said Act. The Respondent filed an appeal before the District Judge, Patiala, who heard the said appeal, allowed the same holding that the portion of the building standing on the said plot of land was being used by him for his residence and he had no other residential house and, therefore, his said half share was exempt from attached under clauseccc of the Proviso to sub Section (l). The Respondent then filed a second appeal before a Division Bench. The Division Bench allowed the appeal holding that section 60 set forth the properties in which the liquor shop was situated. In the second appeal, the Division Bench held that section 61 sets out the property which are liable to attached and sold in execution of a decree of a civil court but were in pursuance of the order made by an officer authorized to adopt proceedings under the Act for recovery of revenue due to the State. The High Court allowed the second second appeal holding: (1) that section 59 set forth properties which are not liable or attachment and sales in revenue Recovery proceedings adopted thereunder; (2) that the said half portion of a building standing thereon was exempt therefrom from attachment, and (3) that in view of the provisions of section 60(l), the property should be attached and the sale notified in respect o f the said part of the house would only be such properties as are so exempted by the said law. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The opening words of sub section(1) of section 61 set out all the properties, which are exempt from the attachment and sold under any of her statute made expressly applicable thereto. [848F] 2. Section 60 sets out all properties which may not liable for attachment and Sale in revenue recover under the aforesaid Act. It is clear that section 58 sets out properties which have been exempted from attachment or sale in revenue proceedings under any such Act would be only such properties which arc so exempted. The provisions of sub sections (1), (c) and (ccd) of proviso to subsection (l), do not apply to an attachment and the property notified for auction sale in execution. [948G] 3. Section 61 sets forth all properties, whether movable or immovable, including buildings attached thereto. The said half is exempt from sale and the rest of the property is liable to be attached. [884C D] 4. The proviso to section 60 sets forth properties, if any, which may be exempted from sale or sale under any law made expressly apply to such attachment and selling in revenue recovered proceedings under that Act. [875D E] 5. Section 59 set out properties, where the property, if my, which is exempt therefrom, are exempt therefrom. The properties, when they are exempt, would only come within the purview of section 63(1). [886E F] 6. The expression "such attachment or sales" in the proviso refers to the attachment or sell mentioned in sub section 1 of Section 61 set forth all property which is liable for sale and in execution thereof would be merely such properties. [864D E; 848A] 7. The word "such attached" in sub clause (c), refers to a attachment and 'sale in revenue recoverable under the State Act.

The respondent, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1964 65 and 1965 66. The Income Tax Officer assessed the total income of the family at Rs.1,10,000/ per annum on the basis that the lands in question were undervalued. The respondent filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer but allowed the appeal holding that the enhanced compensation was not payable to the respondent. The High Court held that the enhancement of compensation by the Civil Court was illegal and invalid inasmuch as the respondent had issued it on the ground that such right to compensation had been undervalued on the earlier occasion and that having regard to the glaring enhanced compensation awarded by the civil court, the impugned notice issued under s.61 of the Act on the premise that such a right to receive compensation had not been properly valued as at the date of the death but was merely a mistake apparent from the record of the case and as such the enhanced amount was liable to be set aside. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) the High Court erred in holding that such valuation was really wrong in view of the enhanced market value on the date when the original assessment under s 73 A had been completed; (ii) the impugned notices were not valid because the respondent did not represent its correct market value which was clear from the records of the cases and as it was not a case of mistake apparent, the High court erred in relying upon the above decision. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The enhanced compensation by reference to the original award under s73 A is not a mistake of fact apparent from record of a case but a mistake discovered by reference. [331C] 2.1 In the instant case, the respondent was merely accepting the value of the acquired lands as determined by the Special Deputy Collector and the appellant had no objection to this course and, therefore, the enhanced land compensation was sought to be included in the principal value of estate by undertaking rectification proceedings. The impugned notice which was issued on a wrong assumption that the acquired land still formed part of the estate of the deceased properly under s,73A, which would otherwise be applicable to a notice under s61 with a view to get over the bar of limitation under s.,73A which would also be applicable in a notice Under s.59(a) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. [330E F] 2:1 The High court was right in holding on the facts and circumstances of the present case that the respondent himself did not estimate the market value of his own estimated value of lands on the previous occasion which was on the original valuation under s 76 A. [332F G] 3:2 The High ' Court erred by holding that in the instant cases, the re assessed compensation had actually been undervalued and as the same had escaped assessment, the same could not be regarded as proper evaluation of the right to the compensation as on the dates of death of the respondent, namely, the City Civil Court. [333G H] 3.3 The High Courts erred in taking into account the fact that the land was acquired by the Government and the lands were sold at a higher price than what was fixed by the Land Acquisition Officer. [431C D] 4:1 In view of this position, the State had no right to enhance the compensation on the land acquired by it. The State had not taken into account any other material which could be relied upon for enhancing the value. [328E F; 331A] 2(a). It is well settled that when a statute provides for enhanced compensation, the Court must resort to provisions of section 59 and proceed to make reassessment but such reassessment has to be done within the period of three years from the date on which it was made.

The appellant, a Cooperative Society, was elected as the Director of the Bank on 8.1.1987 and he was elected on 18.8.1986. The election of Directors to the District Central Cooperative Bank was challenged by the appellant in a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed the same holding that section 73FF(2) of the Maharashtra State Cooperative Societies Act, 1960, provided for setting aside an election as a Director and that as he had accepted that he paid the dues on 21.10.1986, on 18th August, 1986, he was disqualified to be elected or to continue as Director or Executive Committee Member of the Executive Committee of the Cooperative Society and that the appellant 's failure to pay the dues within 15 days as to why he should not be removed from the Board of Directors was without jurisdiction inasmuch as the Act prescribes a separate procedure for calling in question the appellant for election as the director of the bank. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the disqualification on account of his having repaid the entire loan before the impugned notice under section 78(1) of Maharashtra State Co operative Societies Act 1960, was without any jurisdiction inasmuch the Assistant Registrar could not have acted under section 73F(2), and that he had not been at all eligible to contest the election. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellant ' having repaid his entire loan on 21st October, 1986 and today on 19th August 1986, there was no room for holding that he was defaulter under section 74FF of the Act which did not envisage setting aside of an election. [680F] 2.1 Section 73FF of Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Rules, 1960 is not inconsistent with special provisions for setting up a separate machinery for calling the appellant to be Director or creasing to be director on account thereof. The special provision for settingaside an election must prevail over section 78 as there would be apparent conflict between the two maxim generalia specialibus non derogant non derogative general words do not derogate from special words in general terms. [ 680F] 1.2 Section 73F of Maharashtra Co operative Society Rules, 1961 is not repugnant to special provisions and the maxim generali specialibus Non derogant general words does not derogate therefrom general words. The Special provision for set aside an Election must prevailover section 78. [679G H] 2(a) In the instant case, there is no room of holding that appellant 'S having repaid this loan before it was issued would not be material for the purpose of taking action under section 76FF of Bombay Cooperative Societies act 1960. The Assistant Registrar did not issue notice to the appellant as a director or Executive committee member of the Managing Committee of a Cooperative society and that procedure had not followed the Assistant Registrars could not be followed. [681G H; 679A] 2.(b) In view of the matter the notice of the Deputy Registrar was in effect to say that the Appellant 's election has been set aside by the impugned order. The fact that he repaid the loan before issuing the impugned show cause notice would not, therefore, be material on the date of the notice and the provisions of section 78 (1) were not attracted. [685C D] 3(c) In a case where the term lending society is defined in Section 2(g) of Bombay Co operative societies Act, 1959, it has to be interpreted in the context of the provisions in the section. The word 'banking society ' has been defined in section 2(h) of that Act and the mere making of payment on 21 st October 1986 would not mean that the disqualifications on account whereof continued from 18th September 1986 to 21st November 1986 were subsisting, but it had been addressed to the Appellant as Director and his seat already fell vacant. [683D E] 4.(d) The appellant having repaid before the notice was issued did not contemplate setting aside the election as he was a defaulter under that section.

The respondent was in the service of the State Government. He retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation on September 1, 1977 and charges were served on him for the period he was in service of Maharashtra State. The State Government issued orders on December 4, 1982 reducing the pension payable to the respondent by 50 per cent. The respondent challenged the validity of the Government 's order dated December 4.1982 reducing the amount of pension payable by 50% by 50 percent. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the State 's orders reducing the respondent 's pension by 50%. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the State had no authority in law to take any disciplinary proceedings against the respondent as he had already retired from the service. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order reducing the pensionary benefits granted to a Government servant is expressly preserved by the aforesaid Rules. Rule 189 contemplates withholding or withdrawing of a pension or any part of it if the pensioner is found guilty of grave misconduct while he was not in service. [34D] 2.1 In the instant case, the State has power to reduce the pension granted to respondent but having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, it amounted to a serious default on his part as a Government Servant. The reduction of pension by 100 per cent would seriously affect his living. [35E F] 2(a) In the present case, there was no dispute that the respondent had already superannuated from service. He recommended that since the respondent has already retired, he should be reduced to the extent of Re. 1 per month. The Government had power to enhance the pension by taking proceedings against a Government employee even after his retirement is expressly retained by the said Rules. [36F G] 2.(b) In view of the fact and circumstances, the reduction of the pension was too harsh and disproportionate to the misconduct proved against the Respondent. [37G H] 3(c) The State has powers to reduce or withhold pension by an administrative order. The impugned order reducing pension by 25 per cent is too harsh. [38F G; 39A] 4.(d) In a case where the State government has power under Rule 189 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules, it is obligatory on the part of the competent authority to impose any punishment. The rule expressly confers power on the Government to withhold or withdraw any part thereof from the pension.
