[39C D] 5(e) The High Courts in exercise of its powers under Article 226 of the Constitution cannot interfere with the discretion exercised by the State. [40E F; 40A] 6.1 The State government should have taken into consideration the fact that the Respondent had already been retired from a service and the reduction in pension was not too harsh or disproportionate to his misconduct proved. [41F G H] 2 (a) The Government has power, to reduce, or withhold the pension, by taking proceeding against a public servant for misconduct which he may have committed while in service or after the completion of his service, provided that before any order reducing or withdrawing any part is made by the competent authorities the pensioner must be given opportunity of defence in accordance with the procedure specified in Note I to Rule 33 of Bombay Civil Service Rules. The provisions of Note 1 to Rule 3 of Bombay civil Services (Conduct, Discipline and Appeal) Rules are not applicable to the instant cases as in the present matter the State Govt.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the tenant on the ground that he was in arrears of rent and was not entitled to eject him. The trial court decreed the suit but the District Magistrate granted permission under section 3(3) of the U.P. (Temporary Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, to evict the tenant. On appeal by the landlord the High Court held that the permission granted by the Commissioner under section 7 F was invalid in law; and so he came to the conclusion that the appellant ' suit was incompetent. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the permission given by the commissioner under section 6(3)(a) of Act III of 1947, was invalid as it was not passed by a person who was not a District Magistrate; and (ii) the High court was in error in coming to the conclu sion that the order passed by the District magistrate without complying with the mandatory provision of the Act was invalid. HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the Commissioner could not deal with the question as to whether permission had been properly or validly granted or refused by the appropriate authorities exercising their powers under the relevant provisions of the , and in the face of such a statutory provision, if it is shown by a party impeaching the validity of the order in a civil court, then the plea that an order has been passed without notice to the tenant must be negatived. [501 B C] The High Courts were not justified in introducing a limitation pertaining to questions of jurisdiction in determining the scope of the revisionalvisional power conferred on the Commissioner by section 3 (3). That is why it must be held that a party can move the Commissioner only with regard to the legality, propriety or propriety of the orders passed by him completely invalid.

The appellant, a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission, was appointed as an Additional District Judge in the State Civil Service. He was promoted to the post of District Judge on May 1, 1983. On June 2, 1983 he was suspended by the Chief Justice of the High Court and was removed from his office by the order dated July 3, 1983 passed under Article 317(1) of the Constitution. The appellant challenged the said order in a writ petition before the High court which dismissed it. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the case of his client was not made out for obtaining a report from this Court on the question of misbehaviour; (ii) the Chairman or any other member, as the case may be ought to be removed from office only by the orders of the President on the ground of misbehaviour and ought to have obtained the opinion of a court on the questions of the alleged misbehaviour; and (iii) the order of removal could not be passed after the Supreme Court had reported on inquiry held in accordance with the procedure prescribed in that behalf under Article 145. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether the person concerned is guilty of misconduct and whether the misbehaviour is proved or not has to be decided by a court of first instance. [603G] 2. The power of the president to make a reference to this court under article 317(l) is not subject to the condition precedent that he must first have the facts examined by some other body or authority. That Article 317 (1) is neither subject to this condition precedent nor does it require him to cross examine witnesses on those aspects of the matter. [703G H] 3. The fact that the evidence has been examined and found upon by some body or authorities cannot conclude the issue as regards admissibility or relevance of that evidence. It will not be conducive to justice to decide the Reference on a consideration of affidavits only. [804B C] 4. The mere fact that evidence of any particular witness is recorded by the learned Judge will not conclude the issues as regards the admissibility or relevancy of that witness unless he is allowed to cross examination. [783C D] 5. The expression "in any other manner" in article 317 (l) means that the Chairman, or any member of a public service Commission can only be removed on such ground. If a full opportunity is given to the parties to prove and rebut the facts in issue as in a regular trial it is not over that by date, the charge of misbehaviour is made out and whether or the misbehaviour was of such a nature as to warrant the removal of the person from his appointment. [784E F] 6. The word "in" in Article 317 means "a situation where the Chairman is satisfied that there are circumstances which justify his removal". It is not necessary for him to show that he has been guilty of misbehaviour or incapacity, but it is sufficient if he is given an opportunity to cross-examine witnesses on such aspects of matter. The absence of any other procedure would not vitiate the order. [780E F;784A] 7. In the instant case, the High Courts have held that the appellant was guilty of the charge and had incurred the wrath of the Chief Minister of Punjab and the hostility of the Chairperson 's husband and that it would be impossible for him if he was allowed to examine witnesses at his own level.

The appellants plaintiffs instituted a suit under section 62(2) of the Orissa Religious Endowment Act, 1939 (Act No. VIII of 1939) for the recovery of certain sums from the respondents. The appellants contended that the endowment was a private endowment and not a public trust. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the dedication was a public nature and the temple was a purely charitable one and the intention of the founder was merely to dedicate the temple for the benefit of the members of the family or their descendants, and that extensive properties were dedicated for the purpose of the maintenance of the temple. The High Court dismissed the suit holding that the trust was not a private one and that the endowments were not public endowment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the approach made by the High court was wholly incorrect and it has misconstrued the evidence and documents produced in the case to show that the temple is a private or of a public character, and therefore, the mere factum of worship would not determine the nature of the endowment. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The question as to whether the dedication is of a private nature or of an a public body has to be decided with reference to the facts proved in each case and it is difficult to lay down any test or tests which may be in general application. [830E] 2.1 In a suit for declaration that the property was a personal endowment, the court must have regard to the nature and character of the trust and its recitals as also the recitals of the document. The mere fact that members of a Hindu public are allowed to worship at the shrine of the deity can only be the members or their representatives, and other factors that may be considered would be the nature or character of right. [ 830E F] 2(a) In a case where the origin of the endowments is not ascertained, the question whether the user of the public had a right to worship in the temple by itself will be a conclusive proof to show the nature, and the recitals as regards the private nature of endowment. [820B C] (b) The mere circumstance that members or the descendants of the community were allowed to perform all the work on the members and their descendants does not establish any such stipulation for taking offerings from the members. [821C D] 2.(c) In the instant case, the evidence shows that the founder of the Temple was merely managing a family deity in the village and there is nothing to show as to how the endowment came into existence. The fact that the trustees did not make any stipulation for offering offerings or contributions to be made by members of public to the temple belonging to the founder himself, this would be an important intrinsic circumstance to indicate the private character of a temple. [822E F G] 3.(d) In order to come within the purview of section 62 (2), it is necessary that there must be some evidence which may in some cases conclusively establish that the idol was of a purely religious nature. The burden of proving that the public or a stranger who had no right to perform the work of worship was on the person who was entitled to worship, and this onus was upon him to prove that the deity was not of a personal nature.

The appellant Bank was a contractor to finance contracts and the respondents were required funds for the execution of their contracts. The appellant Bank, however, did not pay the amount due under the bill. On December 12, 1952 the appellant received payment of all payments from the respondent Bank. The respondent Bank filed a suit in the court of the 1st Additional District Judge, Jabalpur against Malhotra and Takhatmal for recovery of the monies due to them under the bills. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the power of attorney dated July 13, 1946 coupled with endorsement on the bill dated July 19, 1948 amounted to an equitable assignment of the moneys due under a bill and amounted to a equitable assignment. HELD : (i) The power of Attorney dated July 18, 1948 was expressed to be irrevocable. It was not necessary for the appellant Bank to pay out of a specific fund in favour of the respondent. The agreement between the borrower and the lender was merely an equitable assignmen of the fund by way of security. [782 B] (ii) The principle to be deduced is that an agreement between a debtor and a creditor that the debt due shall be paid out of the specific fund of the borrower in the hands of the Government authorities. The power to attorney was expressed in the bill itself and the endorsement on it was a clear engagement by Malhotra to pay the appellant bank out of any specific fund. [777 D] (iii) The agreement did not create an equitable assigning of the debts or fund to which the order refers. It could only be implied from the terms of the contract. In construing the power conferred on attorney, it is necessary to bear in mind that the relationship of the two parties, Malhotra and lender was irrevocable.

The assessee was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gilland Arbuthnot & Co. Ltd., which had a Provident Fund Scheme for its employees. The Income tax Officer assessed this amount as the assessee 's income from other sources. He also assessed this sum as the income of his own contribution to the fund. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that the receipt in question was not a recognised one and therefore the same was exempt from payment of tax in view of section 17(3) (ii). On further appeal to the Tribunal, the High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee. In this appeal by certificate it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the receipts were income from all sources and that the same were not taxable as salary. HELD : The receipt of Rs. 27,948/ represents the interest on such contributions. [448 C] The receipt is undoubtedly an income. It follows that the payment of Rs., 27,947/ representing the interest thereon on such contribution. is undoubtedly a gain made by the investor and therefore it has to be considered as salary though it is undoubtedly that is an income from house proty. [441 D E] In defining the expression "Profits in lieu of salary" the legislature excluded from the scope of that expression any payments received by the assessee from a provident fund, his own contributions to the Fund or any interest on the securities. The receipt was therefore exempt from tax in respect of all receipts of profits in lieu Of salary.

The Bihar Act, 1950, was passed by the State Legislature of Uttar Pradesh in exercise of its powers conferred on it by article 246(1) of the Constitution. The provisions of the Act were amended by the Madhya Pradesh Act No. 1 of 1951 which came into force with effect from April 1, 1951. By section 3 of the amending Act, the State Government was empowered to make rules for regulating the slaughter of cows and calves of cows, male and female, and for that purpose it also made rules for the regulation of slaughter of bulls and bullocks in the interests of general public. The petitioners who were dealers in buffaloes, bulls and working bullocks (cattle and buffalo) who were carrying on their business as cattle and calvels of cows were granted a licence under section 3(1)(a) of that Act to sell them for consumption in the State of Uttar pradesh. The validity of the rules was challenged by the petitioners on the ground that they violated article 19 (1) (g) and (h) of article 19 of the constitution as it infringed their fundamental rights under articles 19 (2) (f), 19(1), 19 (6) and 31 of theConstitution. Held, that the impugned Acts were valid in so far as they prohibited the slaughter or calves for the period mentioned therein. The impugned Acts are not invalid on the grounds that they contravened article 19(2)(g). The petitioners were not entitled to any protection under article 19 because they had violated their fundamental right under articles 14 and 19 (5) of their Constitution. Held further, that in view of the provisions of section 3 (1)(b), the impugned Act was constitutionally valid in as far as it prohibits the slaughter for a period mentioned in it. The restrictions imposed by section 3 are not unreasonable or arbitrary. The State Legislature had no power to make any law imposing reasonable restrictions on the slaughter and caluse of cows. The Act is therefore invalid.

The respondent company, a public limited company, was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The Company had its registered office at Nagpur in Madhya Pradesh and its Manager was appointed as an employee of the Company. The company was to be governed by the provisions of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946. The respondent company was appointed on probation for a period of two years. On the expiry of the period of probation, the respondent company applied to the State Government under section 25 of the , for extension of the said period of one year. The State Government rejected the application and the appellant filed an appeal against that order before the High Court which was allowed by a Division Bench on September 26, 1956. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Standing Orders did not apply to the respondent and his services had been terminated in accordance with Standing Order No. (e) of Standing Order NO. (f) of standing order No. 42; (ii) the respondent was a 'employee ' within the meaning of section 2(1) of the local Act, and as the respondent did not fulfil the necessary condition of having his name and ticket number included in the departmental muster, he was not an employee within the definition of that expression in section 2 (1) Of the Local Act. HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the inclusion of the name and tickets in the Departmental muster was an essential characteristic of an 'employee as defined for the purpose of Standing Orders. [478 B] The essential content of the definition is employment in the office, Mains Department, Stores, Power House or Receiving Station of the company was not enough to make a person so employed an ' employee within that expression. The essential characteristics of an employee are employment in his office, mains Department and the mere fact of employment in that office, the subject or context of Standing orders, and the inclusion or exclusion of ticket numbers in the department must be considered as an essential element of an employment.

The appellant company was a private limited company. The workmen claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 for the year 1965 68 and claimed bonus on the basis of consolidated profits of all the units. The Tribunal held that alloy Steel Project was a separate establishment in respect of which separate balance sheets and profit and loss accounts were maintained, so that no bonus was payable until this Project itself earned profits, so far as separate balance sheet and profit loss account were maintained. On appeal by the workmen, the High Court held that the Tribunal went entirely wrong in holding that alloys Steel Project could not be treated as a separate Establishment for purposes of section 16 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that (i) the Tribunal had gone completely wrong in saying that all theseoy Steel Projects were a separate unit in respect whereof separate balance Sheet and profit & loss accounts are maintained; (ii) the proviso to sub section (2) of section 3 of the , did not apply in such a case. HELD: The Tribunal went wholly wrong in thinking that merely because Alloy Steel project was owned, controlled and managed by Hindustan Steel Ltd., it had to be treated separately as part of the same establishment for purposes Of computation bonus under the Act; (iii) the calculation of bonus on consolidated profits and loss statements is maintained; and (iv) the bonus paid on the foundation of consolidated accounts was Justified. [603 C D] The proviso to section 3 does not apply to separate units for which separate balances, separate profit and Loss statement are maintained.

The appellant, a sugar manufacturing company, was carrying on the business of manufacture of rayon grade pulp. The appellant, who is engaged in the manufacture of paper and paper industry, had been manufacturing rayor grade pinder for various purposes. The said product was subjected to levy of cess under the Punjab General Sales Tax Act, 1941. The cess was payable by every person carrying on any specified industry and every local authority and is calculated on the basis of water consumed by such person or local authority as the case may be for any of the purposes specified in column I of Schedule II to the Act, at such rate not exceeding the rates specified in the corresponding entries in column 1 thereof. The High Court held that the sugar manufacturing industries would come within Entry 15 of Schedule I to the Cess Act and the cess was leviable by every Person carrying on an industry. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the word 'vegetable ' in Entry 15 is used in opposition to the expression 'animal and 'analogous products ', and since the object of the cess Act and Cess Act were intended to control water pollution and since there was no industry within the meaning of Entry 15, the High Court had taken the view that the Sugar manufacturing industries will come within the Entry 15. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The word vegetable in Entry15 is used as a verb generally understood to mean that agriculture is an industry for certain purposes and vegetables are often indefinite and confusing, since it is based generally on how the plant or plant part is used rather than on what it is occurring and to the fitness of the thing to the matter to the statute. [501B C] 2. The term vegetable in entry 15 is not a word of art but every kind of plant life is to be given some wider meaning. It has a wide amplitude. It must be understood as referring to any and every kind or product which is covered by other entries could also be brought within Entry No. 15. [601D] 3. The expression vegetable in the context does not attract the botanic meaning. The words 'veliable product means of or made out of vegetable, but it has a wider amplitude. [525E F] 4. In order to bring an industry within any of these entries can also be taken within Entry 16. [401F G] 5. The object for which the Cess is imposed is to control the water pollution, and if the botsanic definition of vegetable products ' is used, it has to be understood in common parlance and it must be given its popular sense that sense which people conversant with the subject matter with which the statute is dealing would attribute to it. [504G] 6. The meaning of vegetables which are kept on the dining tables for dinner purposes, and it has wide amplitude, is not confined to vegetable products but includes fruit and vegetables. It is a well settled principle that in interpreting an entry, the court must look at the substance of the matter and not its object. [506B] 7. The question whether a particular industry falls within Entry15 or not is one of the main source of causing water pollu tion and since it has been used in connection with the production of alcohol from molasses could not be considered to be an industry under Entry 15 because the word vegetable is used for the purpose of consumption unless we say that it is an industrial product. [511E] 8.

The respondent landlord filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant on the ground that he required the premises for carrying on his profession as an Advocate. The Rent Controller rejected the application holding that the practice of the profession was not business within the meaning of Section 10(3) (a) (iii) and therefore, the respondent could not seek the eviction of him on the grounds that he needed the premises in question on the basis that he requires the premises. In revision, the High Court held that the use of the expression 'business ' in Section 10 (3)(a)(iii) was not a business within that meaning of section 10(1) (b) (ii). Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The word "business" is used in a wide sense so as to include the practice or profession of an Advocate or a Doctor. [14D] 2. Section 10 of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, does not bar the eviction by the landlord on the plea that he needs the premises bona fide for the purpose of carrying on a business. The expression ' Business ' in section 10 (1)(a) is used to include any profession. [15E] 3. Section 4 which provides for the determination of fair rent of a building on the application of the tenant or landlord, does indicate that it was for the purposes of carrying out a business and refers to the provisions of the Constitution or other statutes where the expression is used cannot be of any assistance in determining its meaning in section10(3)(b) of the Act. [16F] 4. The term 'business" has been defined in Section 2(a) of that Act, which includes a profession. It would also include the use by a person of any trade or business for which he is entitled whether under the Act or otherwise (a), for the time being, used for carrying out his profession. The words "business ' have not been defined either in the Act nor in the context of other statutes or in a manner alien to the context. [17F] 5. Section 3(1)(b)(iii), which bars the eviction from a non residential building where the landlord is not occupying a nonresidential building in a city or town concerned which is his own or to the possession of which he was entitled whether by the Act, or otherwise, (a ) for the use in that sense as a profession; and (b). for the non residential buildings owned by an Advocate but not Section 10. The legislature has used the expression business ' in a wider sense so that to include such profession. In the context, it would indeed be an "business". [17G H] 6. The High Court was right in holding that in the light of the provisions contained in the Andhra Buildings ( Lease, Rent & Eviction) Act 1960, the word 'business " has to be given a wide meaning so as not to include all profession.

The respondent was a debtor to the appellant. The respondent deposited a sum of Rs. 4,00,000 in its account with the appellant and the appellant was to place to credit the amount of Rs., 4,11,367.92 with interest and costs. The appellant filed the suit on 16 May, 1953 against the respondent for recovery of Rs 4,10,367 from India Supplies to the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed it on the ground that the appellant had not proved that the amount was deposited under an agreement and that it was a case where money was deposited in the name of India Supplies which was in the nature of deposit and therefore the suit was barred by time. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Courts were right in holding that there was no demand for a part of the amount in the year 1943 for a period of 1944. [575 B] (ii) The respondent had not established that the money was paid under an oral agreement and therefore it was improbable that the respondent would be entitled to withdraw the deposit on demand. [574 C D] (iii) The fact that the history of the transactions between the appellant, the respondent and Lakshmi Ratan Cotton Mills show that there were advances which were in the character of deposits and were not covered by the award did not make any difference because the history was not established. [576 E F] (iv) The statement of the respondent that he had to pay the dues of Lakshmi Ratan cotton Mills on the one hand and Lakshmi Rattan Cotton Mills on other, that moneys were lent and advanced by Lakshmi Ratan Spinning Mills to India Supplies would be relieved of the situation of repaying the money immediately. [577 C D].

The petitioner was detained by an order passed under sub section (1) of Section 3(1) on February 28, 1986. The grounds for detention were that the period of parole from May 15, 1986 to February 28 1987 could not be added to the maximum period of imprison ment of the detenu Shital Kumar for one year as specified in the impugned order of Detention. The petitioner 's husband was detained under sub s.(1) and since the detenu was already in custody at the time the order of detention came to be made, he was very keen to have the question of exclusion of the parole period decided by the Court. The petition was opposed on behalf of the respondents contending that the detaining authority had not applied his mind while passing the impugned detention order. It was contended that the petitioner 'followa tion was not justified in making an application under Article 32 of the Constitution and that the order was liable to be quashed. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The order of preventive detention could only be justified against a person in jail at the most one day. [845C] 2. In view of the positive case of the petitioner therein that there was suffi cient material to show that the detenu had been fully apprised of the fact that the peti tioner was already n custody, the order is liable to quashed. The fact that he was aware of the proceedings in the Court and did not dispute that the detention was imminent and the order being passed for preventive detention would not detract from the order having been passed for detention. [745C D] 3. In the facts of the present case there is sufficient material showing that the Detaining Authority was aware about the fact, that the Petitioner was already on bail and yet he was sub jectively satisfied that his detention was necessary. The question whether the order could be justified in a case of that type is to satisfy the court when detention is challenged on that ground that the authority was aware that the person was already In custody at that time. [820E F] 4. It is not possible to accept the contention that the mere fact that an accused in extradition is likely to get bail, an order of release under the National Security Act should not ordinarily be passed. If the apprehension of the detaining author it is true, court observed, the bail application had to be opposed and in case bail was granted, challenge against that order in the higher forum had to he been taken into custody. [822F G] 5. The detenu is al ready to have his detention in jail for one day as specified under the impugned Order of Detention and since he was already under custody at a time when the order came to he was made, yet he would not expect that he would be released forthwith. [825G H] 6. In fact, the detaining Authority was conscious of the facts that the detenue was already having been in custody when the detention order was passed and before the actual service of the order. The detaining authority was conscious that the fact whether the detenu is already in jail or not would not affect his subjective satisfaction that his release from detention was imperative. [823A B] 7. In a case where the detenu has to be detained for one month as specified by the impugnedorder of Detention, it is necessary that he should be released immediately on his executing a bond with two sureties. The first surety must be executed within three months from the date of detention and the second surety must execute a bond in the same form. [826B C] 8. In this case, there was no warrant for the detaining authorities to have passed an order under sub sec.(1), on February 27, 1986 without disclosing any reason as to why the detenu could not make an application for bail. The detention order is therefore bad and illegal. [827C D E] 9. The Court has clearly indicated that it was not a matter of jurisdition but had to been decided on its own facts.

The petitioners were working as casual labourers in the Telecom Department of the Union of India. They were engaged in digging, carrying and other similar types of work. The petitioners were employed on daily wages for a period of five years as casual labourer. Their services were terminated by an order dated 5th February 1986 issued by the Union Public Service Commission. The respondents filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the termination orders. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that since the petitioners belong to the category of casual labour and are not being regularly employed, they are not entitled to the same privileges which the regular employees are enjoying. In the appeals by special leave it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that since there is no scheme in existence for absorbing them as casual workers, the wages paid to them were very low and far less than the salary and allowances paid to the regular workmen of the Telecom department. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The employees of the Telecommunication Department are not eligible to the said privileges which they are enjoying in the Postal and Telegraphs Department at the rates equivalent to the minimum pay in the pay scales of semi skilled/skilled labour. [602C] 2. The benefit of increased rates of daily wages will not be admissible to the casual labourers who have been continuously working for more than six months. This would be without prejudice to absorption of casual labourers as and when they occur. [703E F] 3. The benefits of increased rate of daily wage are applicable to the semi skilled or unskilled workers in whose case the continuous spells of duty are intervene by a period not exceeding six months, where is any justification to keep them as Casual Labour in the Telegraphs department at the rate equivalent to minimum pay. [803E] 4. The Government agencies should not allow 610 workers to remain as casual labour for an unreasonably long period of time where is Any justification to keeping them as temporary or permanent employees for an unduly long period.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1950 52 and 1952 53. The Income tax Officer issued a notice under section 22(2) of the Act on January 5, 1950, calling upon him to make a " voluntary return" on the date he did, and to furnish a revised return on the basis of which he had made an assessment. The assessee filed a return showing the income below the taxable limit but it was not furnished within the time fixed by the notice. The High Court held that since the assessee had submitted a return under section 23(3) within the assessment year, and if no return was made within the period fixed by notice, the Department should have proceeded under section 24(1) or even section 24 (3). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that a " voluntarily return showing a non taxable income" could not be treated as a return of taxable income and that the Department ought to have issued a show cause notice under s.22(2), within the meaning of section 34(1)(a) of that Act, and that since no return had been made within time fixed, the department should have initiated proceedings either with a notice unders. 22(3). HELD: (i) The High court was right in holding on a construction thereof that a person who had no assessable income could not possibly be treated to be a "nil" of his income under the Act, because, as he had submitted the return under s 24(2)(a), if any return was filed within the prescribed time, the notice could have been issued. [854 C] (ii) The expression " voluntarily returning" in section 22 is not used in a sense to include a return which has been made before the assessment. It is only when the return is filed after a notice has been served that it can be treated that the assessee has made a voluntary return showing an assessable income. [954 D] (iii) The word " voluntarily" in s. 22 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, means "a return of income". It does not mean merely a return or a return but also a return for the purpose of assessment. If the return filed after notice has already been served, it can only be treated by the assessee as a true return and not a return. [1054 E] (iv) The words " voluntarily returned" in the section are wide enough to include an return which is made before assessment. In the present case, the general notice under S.22 of the Income tax (Central) Act was served on the assessee and it was filed after the expiry of the period prescribed by the notices.

The respondent State of Maharashtra issued a notification dated 23.8.1983 inviting applications for appointment to the post of Directors of the Reserve Bank of India, in the State of Bombay. The appellant was one of the candidates who had applied for the said post. The respondent State Government issued an advertisement on 7.9.1983 calling for applications from eligible candidates for appointment as Directors of a nationalised bank. The last date for receipt of applications was 3.10.1983. The appellants were informed that the respondent State had not received any applications and that the applications would be considered in accordance with the procedure laid down by the ReserveBank of India. The State Government, however, rejected the applications on the ground that the appellant had not submitted the applications within the time stipulated under the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the respondent. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the Act and the Scheme were ultra vires the Act as they were framed in exercise of the powers conferred upon them by Article 162 of the Constitution, and that they had no statutory force to make any scheme for the constitution of the Board of Directors. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The scheme was not violative of Articles 19(1)(c) and 43(A) of the Consti tution of India Act, 1950. [857F] 2.2 The scheme could not be said to be ultra vires Article 162 as it was not a matter for the Central Government to provide for election in the manner chosen by it so as to restrict the choice of appointment to certain categories of persons mentioned in the Act, and if the Central Govern ment had intended to make such an order, it would have been open to the Central Gov ernment to amend the Scheme suitably for that purpose. [957F G] 2.(a) The scheme is not a mere formality but a discretion which must be reasonably exercised so as t he true intent of the legislature as to the composition of the board of Directors is to enable it reasonably exercise its discretion in such a way as to give the maximum scope for the concerned employees to exer cise their choice in the selection of their representatives. [757F H] (b) The Central Government was to provide the best form of repre sentation to every category of persons specified in the Scheme, and it would be perfectly in order for the State Government to continue the practice followed by it prior to the circular in question or to hold election of its employees. [758A B] 2(a) In the instant case, the Central Govt. was to make a scheme for constitution of Board of directors so as not to restrict choice of appointments to the three persons specified on the panel furnished by the representative Association of workmen or Association of non workmen, as the case may be, would not be a perfect representation in keeping with the principle of election. [759C] (c) The Scheme was not intended to give an opportunity to the employees to make their representations before the Central Gover ment. It is open to them to do so and they cannot be allowed to take advantage of the same.

The respondent was imposed penalties in the sum of Rs. 1,000/ on an assessee during the pendency of an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and made an interim prayer for stay of collection of the penalty imposed by the departmental authorities on an 'assessee during the course of an assessment proceedings. The Appellate Tribunal allowed the application for stay and directed that the recovery proceedings should be stayed till the disposal of the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) Section 220(6) of the Income tax Act, 1961 empowers the Appellate Tribunal to regulate its own procedure but it does not confer any power on the Appellate Authority to stay the recovery of taxes or penalties payable by or imposed on the assessees as a matter of practice prevailing in the department. [69E F] (2) The Appellate Assistant Commis sioner is entitled to stay as incidental or ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction. He cannot, however, be put at par with a statutory power as is contained in section 220(7). [70F G] (3) Section 254 confers appellate jurisdiction on the Income Tax Officer who can give the necessary relief of staying recovery of tax or penalties due from an assessee. It does not empower the Appellate Tribu nal to entertain an appeal against the order of stay by treating the assessee as not being in default during the disposal or in a routine way as is embodied in section 254. [70G H] (4) The power of stay can be spelt out from that provision. The appellate Tribunal must be held to have the power to grant stay as ancillary or incidental to its Appellate jurisdiction. It may also be that when an appeal is pending before the Income Commis nioner, but the Act is silent in that behalf when an application is pending at the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner and not to the AppellateTribunal.

The respondent was charged under section 7 of the Police Act with remissness in the discharge of his duty and unfitness for the same. The trial was conducted by the Superintendent of Police, in accordance with the following rules: "Rule 489 A. (1) The Superintendent of police may be departmentally tried under section7 of the . . . , . . " . . ." The respondent submitted his explanation on September 12, 1953, and the Superintendent made an endorsement to the Superintendent that the respondent was receiving bribes in the performance of his duties and unf fitness for the said purpose. On November 17, 1952, the District Magistrate sent a endorsement to him stating that the Sub Divisional Magistrate had found substantial complaints against the integrity of the respondent, that he had also received such complaints and that his general reputation for integrity was not good but that his General reputation for thesame was not satisfactory. The Superintendent made a endorsement on the report and communicated the same to the respondent. On December 17, 1953 the District magistrate sent an endorsement on his report and communicate the same in his turn to the Inspector of Police. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad praying that the order of dismissal be quashed as it was not passed by a police officer junior in rank to a Superintendent, and for quashing the order dismissing him. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the departmental inquiry was only a further step in respect of the misconduct of the Respondent and that the District Magisterial inquiry was vitiated by a number of serious irregularities; and that as no case had been made out against the respondent in the police station, the Superintendent could not proceed with a departmental trial without complying with the provisions of subparagraph (1). Held, that the High court was right in holding that there was no magisterial inquiry in respect to the matter which was the subject matter of the departmental trial. The District Magis trate had no jurisdiction to proceed with the departmental enquiry and the departmental proceedings were not therefore illegal. The order of the Superintendent was invalid as it did not affect the validity of the order. The State of Uttar Pradesh vs Ram Chandra Srivastava, A.I.R. 1953 S.C. 1021, distinguished.

The appellant was appointed as a Specialists Grade II in the Central Government Health Service on February 8, 1971. He was promoted to supertime grade I on February 9, 1971 and thereafter he was confirmed in that post by an order dated March 31, 1972. The appellant challenged his promotion before the Central Administrative Tribunal which allowed him to continue in super time grade II on February 10, 1971 as Specialists ' Grade ' posts in supertime Grade II. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the promotion of the appellant and the order of his confirmation. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that since the appellant was fully qualified for promotion to super time scale I he should have been promoted from that date. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that (i) the promotion to Supertime Grade I on March 31 and July 30, 1972 was not a promotion but only a transfer from one post to another; (ii) the appellant had not put in 8 years ' service in the category of specialists grade ' posts which meant specified in the speciality in which he had sought promotion; and (iii) the post could only be filled in by promotion from amongst those belonging to Specialists grade, i.e., by transfer from unspecified Specialists, Grade ' officers ' grade and added to super Time grade II. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant was not qualified for being promoted to Super time scale II because he had not been put in a specified post in specialists ' grade or general duty officers ' grades. [53G H] 2.2 The appellant is fully qualified and, therefore, he must be considered eligible for promotion from the date on which he claims as being eligible for supertime scale I. [54A B] 2(a) The appellant had been fully qualified to be promoted to the super time Scale II because his refusal to accept promotion at Simla was never superseded by any one junior to him in his speciality. He must have been considered for the post which is deemed to have fallen vacant in September 1971 on the invalidation of promotion of Dr. Sen and was not unqualified for the posts to which each one of them was promoted. [55C D] 2.(b) The order of promotion could only mean that the person to be appointed to such a post would be one who is eligible to be selected in the respective speciality in Which the post was created, he could be said to have been superseded in violation of article 16. [56F G] 3(a)(i) The promotion to the Supertime grade II must be made by way of promotion from which promotion is offered by way Of promotion. It is implicit in this arrangement that the appellant should be considered for such post which was deemed to be a specifiedpost in super Time Grade II and added as a specified vacancy in superTime grade II.[56F] 4(b) In passing a contention that when a post from unsspecified Specialists' posts was converted into a specified Post it can only be filling in, it could only been filled in, by promotion, that would only be from amongst the originally created Specialists (Grade 's Grade ') officers ' Grade and added in super scale II.

The appellants were tenants of certain lands in the State of Punjab. The land inherited by them was not hit by section 10A and section 19B of the Act. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the soundness of the High Courts 's approach. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the surplus area which became surplus subsequent to April 15, 1953 was not affected by section 20A and Section 19B. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the land inherited in excess of the permissible limit was saved from utilisation by the State. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: The High Courts took the view that area which become surplus subsequent thereto was not covered by section 19 B. [603C] The thrust of section 19A is that even if the source of the excess area inheritance is dependent on the permissible limits, there was no frustration of the policy of the law. [704D] The saving clause is cumbersome but the sense and is the sense, and is, having regard to the conspectus, can only be that though in the hands of the propositus, it is surplus land, if among the heirs it is Surplus land, it was not, then their transfers will not be affected by the interdict of section 10 A. [613E F] The object of the saving clause was to give some time to the son or the husband or the latter had only lands within permissible limits. It was not possible to say that if after the commencement of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, any person acquires any land by inheritance or bequest by inheritance, then his transfers will be affected. [503B C] The language of section 20 B is plain and unambiguous. The saving clauses are cumbersable but the meaning of the savings clause is clear and unambiguous that the legislature intended to give certain time to a son or husband or other persons in possession of any land to whom he is an heir, to make a declaration of his lands within a prescribed time. [643B C].

The plaintiffs claimed the other estate of Amarshah in devisees under the will of Amarhah executed on December 3, 1950. They contended that the geneal table set up by the plaintiffs represented the true relationship between the descendants of Gangashah and that the suit was not barred by the decision of the Governor of Madhya Pradesh dated November 9, 1951, and that as the plaintiffs were entitled to receive compensation in respect thereof, they were not entitled to claim any compensation or payable in respect of the Malguzari lands which vested in consequence of the enactment of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals Alienated Lands) Act 1 of 1951. The trial court held that the plaintiffs had become entitled to the Zamindari on the death of Amrashah as an impartible estate and that they were entitled only to the estate devised in their favour by Amarsh. On appeal the High Court held that there was no evidence to show that the adoption of Am Rashah was genuine and the plaintiffs could not be reopened in a suit for setting aside that decision because no suit was filed within two months from the date of such order, and since no suit had been filed within one month from that date and if no suit is filed within three months from that day, the order became final and conclusive. Held: (i) The High Court was in error in not reducing the amount of mesne profits awarded to the plaintiffs because no appeal or revision lay against the decision. (ii) The order of the Compensation Officer did not oust the jurisdiction of the Civil Court to determine competing claims of persons claiming proprietary rights to the property vesting in the Government by operation of section 3 of the Act.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for recovery of possession of the premises on the ground that the respondent was not entitled to raise any dispute as to standard rent. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court held that the provisions contained in section 12(3)(a) were applicable to the suit, but that the suit was governed by the provisions embodied in section 13(3) (b) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that the dispute as regards standard rent is to be raised within one month from the service of notice under section 12 (2) (a) of and therefore, the suit is governed by sections 12(1)(b), 12(4) (c) and (d) of Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court was in error in holding that the question whether the dispute raised as to Standard rent was a dispute within the meaning of section 12 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, was not limited only to a dispute raised within two months from the date of service of the notice under Section 12(2) of. The latest point of time when according to Ambalal 's case (supra), the tenancy was excessive and standard rent should be fixed, the Court shall and in any other case if it appears to the Court that it is just and proper to make such an order directing the tenant to deposit in court forthwith such amount as the Court may specify. [603 H] In the instant case, the respondent landlord had made an application to the court under sub section (3) of section 11 and paid the amount of rent or permitted increases specified in the order made by the Court. The last point of Time when according by Ambalals 's Case (supra) the dispute in question was raised at any time prior to the expiry of one month, the operation of section 13 (3)(b) would be excluded. [703 H; 704 A] In view of the fact that the appellant landlord had filed a written statement in answer to the plaint and in such a case the provisions of section12(3), (a), 12 (3A) (d), 12, (4) and 12(5) (e) of Bombay Rents Hotel and lodging House Rates Act, 1948 would apply.

The respondent company was a director of the appellant company. The Aluminium Ltd. appointed three permanent directors on the board of directors of the respondent company at all ordinary or extraordinary general meetings of the shareholders of the company and on behalf of the Aluminium Ltd., appointed three directors on its board of Directors, who held majority of the shares in the respondent Company. In exercise of the power conferred by article 105 of the articles of association of the Company, the appellant was a Director of the Respondent company nominated by the Aluminium Limited as its Chairman. The question for decision was whether in the facts and circumstances of these cases, the Income tax Appellate Tribunal was right in holding that the directors of respondent company had a controlling interest in it as contemplated by section 2 (21) of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, read with section 66(1) of that Act. Held, that the managing director of a company may well be regarded as having "a controlling interest" in the company when such a person acquires, by purchase or otherwise, the majority of shares which under the articles Of association of tile company is concerned, and as such have "a Controlling interest" therein, the controlling interest remains vested in the Aluminium LTD. and is at no time vested in him, though as between them and their beneficiaries, he may hold the majority shares of theshares held by it in the Company when they hold and are entered in the share register as holders of the majority. The control interest remained vested in a company which was not revoked, as long as its authority is not revoked.

The respondent was appointed as an Assistant Director of the Electricity Board on 30th December, 1966. He was promoted to the post of Accounts Superintendent on 30.12.1966 and was confirmed in that post with effect from that date. On 1st October, 1957, some persons junior to him were promoted on their having passed Part I and II of the S.A.S. Examination. The respondent opted to the Service under the Board and ceased to be an employee of the Government with effectfrom that date and was denied promotion to the respondent as he had not passed the examination. On 30th November, 1966, some of the persons junior were promoted to that post. The resolution required the passing of the Departmental Exami nation and Kannada language test for the purpose of earning increments and for promotion. The Resolution provided that the posts of Accounts Superintendents were to be filled by promotion from the cadre of I Division Clerks on the basis of seniority cum merit cum seniority cum senioritycum merit cum meritcum meritcum seniority cum fitness. On 31st December, 1967 some persons senior to him had passed Part II and II examinations. The Board resolved to grant promotion to all those who were eligible for promotion as Accounts Superintendent. The appellant challenged the resolution by a writ petition before the High Court which allowed the writ petition holding that the respondent was not entitled to be promoted as an Superin tendent as on 30st December 1966, and that the Resolution did not apply in the present case as the Regulations framed under section 79(c) of the Act were not relaxed by amending the Regulations. The Division Bench dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant. In the appeal before this Court it was contended for the respondent that the High court was in error in construing the relevant provisions of the Regulations and holding that there was no ground for not accepting the view of the High Curt that the Board was in breach of the relevant regulations and the resolutions passed by the Board under section 80(c). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was in wrong in construing a relevant provisions in the Regulations as the resolution had modified a Regulation which was passed by it in exercise of the powers conferred by the statute. [510C D] 2.1 The Resolution does not have the effect of modifying a Regulation and the decision of the Board cannot have the effects of modifying the Regulation. It is not possible to infer from the Resolution there is nothing to indicate that the allottees were not required to pass the examination and Kannad language test. [610F G] 2(a) The resolution does not require the passing or passing of a Departmental Exam cation. The passing of an S.S., Examination was not insisted upon in all cases. [511E F] (b) The Resolution requires the passing o r examination and the Kannada Language test for promotion to cadre of Accounts Officers as before being insisted in future also, and if passing of such a Departmental Examination is insisted in all other cases. It cannot be said that the resolution does have the impact of modifying an Regulation which is passed by a Board under s 79(C). [511D] 2.(b) In any event the plea of the respondent will have to be rejected as it is incumbent on him to pass such examination and passing of S.L.S Examination was insisted in some cases. The decision of this Court in State of Mysore vs V. N.K.V.N. Murthy, [1963] Supp. 1 SCR 872, relied on. 2.(c) The High court had not applied its mind to the question whether the Regulations were mandatory or directory.

The petitioner 's son Suman Behera was taken from his home in police custody at about 8 a.m. on 1.12.1987 by respondent No.6, Sarat Chandra Barik, an Assistant Sub Inspector of Police attached to Jaraikela Police Station under Police Station Bisra, Distt. Bisra. The petitioner 'S son SumanBehera was arrested and sent to judicial custody in police remand at about 9 a. m. on the same day. On 1.1.1987, respondent No 6, Sarats Chandra Bariar, aged about 22 years, in police force, filed an application for compensation under Article 32 of the Constitution before the High Court. The petition was dismissed by the High court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The relief of monetary compensation as exemplary damages, in proceedings under Article 226 of the constitution is a remedy available in public law based on strict liability for contravention of fundamental rights to which the principle of sovereign immunity does not apply, even though it may be available as a defence in private law in an action based on tort. [610C D] 2. The right to compensation in proceedings relating to violation of fundamental right is claimed by resort to the remedy in public Law under the Constitution for establishing infringement of the indefeasible right guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution Act, based on the strict liability of the State for the breach of its public duty to protect the fundamental rights of the citizen. [710D E] 3. The compensation is in the nature of Adjudicatory damages awarded against the wrong doer for the violation of the fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution and is independent of the rights available to the aggrieved party to claim compensation under the private law. [811E F] 4. The payment of compensation in this proceeding is in public interest and is based on a strict liability towards breach of fundamental Rights to which it is guaranteed in the Constitution, notwithstanding the right of the citizens, notwithstanding, the right to remedy by way of a civil suit or criminal proceedings. Of course, relief in exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 14 or 226 would be granted only once it is established that there has been an infringement of fundamental freedoms and fundamental rights. [783F G] 5. The claim based on statutory provisions for compensation in respect of violation of human rights is a constitutional right guaranteed to the citizen under Article 19(1)(g) of the Indian Constitution, as also the right under Article 22 of the People 's Right to Property guaranteed by Part III of the Limitation Act, 1908. [784A B] 6. The Court is not helpless and the wide powers given to this Court by Article 32 or 226 are not fettered by any other form of appropriate redressal by the court in the facts and circumstances of the case. [773B C] 7. The High Courts being the protectors of the civil liberties of the petitioner, notwithstanding his right to claim damages under the public law for violation of their fundamental rights, it does so under the Public Law in an act based on private law, based upon strict liability, for contraventions of fundamental and indefeasible rights guaranteed by Article 21. [771C D E] 8.

The petitioner was convicted for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The sentence was confirmed by the President of India in revision. In a petition filed by him before the High Court, the petitioner contended that the two prisoners had been sentenced to imprisonment for life and that the petitions filed by them were premature. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The constitutional right to means of information through the medium of an interview of the two convicts who are sentenced to murder is not an absolute right nor does it confer any right on the Press unless in the first instance, the person sought to be interviewed and indeed, if it was thought necessary that such a search should be taken, a person who desires to interview a prisoner may have subject himself to the rules and regulations governing the interviews. [1187G H] 2. The petitioner has been asking permission for interview the prisoners as he is willing to be interviewing them. He does not want to know what he wants to do so. It does not imply or spell out any legal obligation on the citizens to supply information to the Press, and indeed it does confer any rights on the press to have an unrestricted access to meansof information. [1087A] 3. The right claimed by the petitioner is not the right to express any particular view or opinion but the right of an association or opinion and the right can be claimed by a member of the community, who desires that interview a person may have Subject himself to search in accordance with the rules governing the interview. [1105C D] 4. The freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution is not absolute or unqualified right nor indeed does it impose any right upon the Press to have such an unrestricted right. It only confers on the citizen right to mean of information Through the medium in accordancewith the rules regulating the interviews, and regulations contained in the Jail Manual. [111D E] 5. The expression "in the first place" is not a word of indefinite import but it does not confer any absolute right or authority. It merely means that they can always be permitted only subject to the Rules and Regulations contained in Jail Manual for the Superintendence and administration of Jails, which is applicable to Delhi. [112E F] 6. The Constitution has no application to the case of a prisoner who wants to interview the prisoner. The provisions of article 19 (1)(b) are not intended to confer any fundamental right on him but only have an express or implied authority to do what he does in his capacity as a member. [113G H; 113A] 7. The words "in accordance with" in article 19 are not meant to be used in the sense of expression and it is not necessary that they should be used to describe them as friends of the society. It is only when the person wants to interviewed a prisoner that he can have an opportunity to interview him. [114B C] 8. The presence of a free Press does not mean that they could always be allowed to interview those prisoners who are convicted of murder. The existence of a Free Press does no imply or spells out any right or opinion, but the rights of an Association or opinion are not expressly referred to in clause (4) but that does not means that it can always have an absolute or unrestricted access thereto. [115E F; 116A] 9. The protection of article 21 is not available to a prisoner unless he wants himself to interview his prisoners. It cannot be said that the prisoner has been asked to interview them. If such an application is made to the Superintendent of Jail, he will be free to consider the same on merits and in accordance the jail regulations contained therein. [117F G] 10. The petition filed before the President was rejected by the High court.

The appellant was the Receiver of a tea garden. The respondent instituted a suit against the Receiver for recovery of the amount due under the mortgage bond and the appellant filed an application for damages to the extent of Rs. 22, 1956. The Subordinate Judge decreed the suit on May 31, 1956 but he also allowed the respondent 's application for compensation in respect of the loss caused to the tea garden by fire. On appeal the Subordinate Judge held that the Receiver was not answerable for the loss occasioned to the Tea garden by the fire and dismissed the objections. In second appeal the High Court held that as the Receiver had no duty or obligation in relation to the plantation, the appellant was liable to make good the loss suffered by the Receiver 's negligence in the performance of his duties. The High Court also held that since the Receiver did not perform his duties, the suit was incompetent to enforce the bond and directed that the damages awarded to the respondent be recovered from the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Subordinate judge who tried the suit is incompetent to enforcing the surety bond executed by the appellant as he was neither the successor nor the successor in office nor the assign of the District Judge; and (ii) the Receiver owed no duty, obligation or obligation to pay the damages caused to tea garden due to the Receiver. HELD: The surety bond has undoubtedly, to be construed strictly but it is impossible to accept the contention that the receiver owed no obligation or duty in respect thereof. [360 E] In the present case, the surety Bond was executed six months after the tea Garden was damaged by fire and the Receiver gave effect to the loss on March 22, 1950 being the date when the Receiver took possession of the property. The surety Bond is both a part of the proceedings pending before the District judge and on the transfer of the suit and the entire proceedings including the bond stood validly transferred to the Court of the Subordinate Judges.

The appellant, a dealer in food grains supplied to the Regional Food Controller diverse quantities of wheat were sold to the State Government. The sales tax Officer levied tax under the U.P. Sales Tax Act on the aggregate of the price of wheat by the appellants. The Additional Judge (Revisions) Sales Tax held that the turnover resulting from supplies of wheat was not taxable since there was no "sale" within the meaning of section 2(h) of the U P. Sales tax Act and that no tax was exigible on such transactions. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The sales made to the Central Food Controller were liable to pay sales tax on the sales made by the appellant to the Controller or a person authorised by him in that behalf. [517 D] (2) The State Government had no volition in the matter. It was not open to the dealer to contend that there was any contract between the parties but subject to restrictions, the transaction could be regarded as a sale. [593 E] (3) The expression "sale of goods" in section 2 (h) means the money consideration for sale of goods, and where under a contract of sale property in the goods is transferred from the seller to the buyer, the contract is called an agreement to sell" occurring in section 3(1). [593 F] (4) The word "sale ' in section 4 means the price paid or agreed to be paid for the goods sold. The expression 'sale ' has not been defined in the UP. Act. The definition of the word 'sale' is wide enough to include a transfer of property in goods and it includes a transfer by way of sale, but where the transfer of the property in a goods is effected by a contract, the agreement is called a sale but where there is no such contract, then the transaction can be regarded to have been completed.

The petitioner was convicted by the trial court for offences under sections 302, 201 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code. He was sentenced to death on May 26, 1986. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that he had been in jail from November 12, 1985 onwards awaiting trial on a charge of murder. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that: (1) the Advisory Board and sec tion 11 of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985 which provides for detention of a person for a longer period than three months unless an Advisory Board consisting of persons who are or have been qualified to be appointed as Judges of a High Court has reported before the expiration of the said 206 period of 12 months; (2) the report of the Advisory board was more than three weeks after the date of detention, though it was within three months of the subsequent order of detention; and (3) the detaining authority had not applied its mind to which the Advisory Boards had to be obtained before the expiry of three months from the date on which the detention order was made. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The report of an Advisory board is not a sufficient answer to say that it is necessary to continue the detention of the person beyond the period of three month after the day on which its report or within three weeks was received before the hearing of the case. [10E] 2.2 The report must be obtained within three days from the time of the order of the detention and therefore, the detention cannot be sustained as constitutionally valid unless it is made within three years after the expiry thereof. [11F G] 3.1 In a habeas corpus proceeding, it is not sufficient answer tain that the procedural requirements of the Constitution and the statute have been complied with before the date when the order was revoked and a subsequent order is made. The report may be obtained in time but it cannot be said to be an affidavit or an affidavit. [12F] 3:2. In a Habeas Corpus proceeding, the Court is not confronted with the present situation at all. It is only when the Advisory Commis sioner has reported within the period specified therein that it was necessary to continued the detention. If the report is received before a hearing of case, it cannot he said to have been obtained within 3 months from its date of its receipt. [13F] 4:3. The question as to whether there was sufficient cause for the detention or not has to be answered in the light of the facts that the report was made within 3 weeks and if the report had been received before it was received, it would not answer to saying that the representation, though not made within six months, was disposed of before the hear ing of the matter.

The respondent was the father of the petitioner. He filed a suit for specific performance of an agreement dated 14th August, 1978 between the parties and the appellant. The respondent claimed that he had agreed to such entrustment and that he was entitled to receive the balance amount of Rs. 1,00,000/ from the appellant as per the award. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the revision application. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the notice was already given to the respondent and the petitioner had torn off the award and therefore, the respondent was compelled to rely upon a photo copy of the original award; (2) the arbitrator had not drawn up any factual dispute, reiterated the fact that the parties had agreed that both of them should abide by the award dated 20th January, 1977 in respect of which award there had been continued objections but now they have agreed to refer the disputes to arbitration. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The conduct of the parties that there was an arbitration agreement and by signing the award it could be said that the dispute had not amicably settled and no such agreement was made, is clear from the narration of facts that the respondent had agreed not to refer any disputes in writing to the arbitration of the named arbitrator. [527B C] 1.2 The conduct and the fact of the matter that there were an arbitration agreements between the appellant and the respondent clearly showed that both the parties should abide with the award on 20th August 1977, and that their interpretation should be left to the arbitrator himself. [628D E] 2.1 In the instant case, it is clear that the conduct of parties that the agreement had been duly signed by both the sides and that the entire responsibility of the arbitrator will lie on Shri Kantibhai Vaidya and legal philosophers weep. With respect, we cannot agree more in the facts and circumstances of this case. [728F G] 2(a) The conduct or the fact as to whether the parties agreed to reference to arbitration or not is a proper arbitration agreement in terms of section 2(b) of the Act. But in the instant context, it was clear that both sides had agreed on referring the disputes in written to the named Arbitrator and that they did decide it. [428F] 3(a). The conduct as well as the fact about which there is no factual dispute are reiterated by both parties. [541G H] 4(b). In the present case, the conduct and fact of parties clearly showed the existence of an arbitration clause in the agreement. It was clear from a reading of the award that it could not have been challenged in execution proceedings only on the ground that the Court which passed the decree was lacking in inherent jurisdiction in respect thereof. [543G H; 543A] 5(c) The High Court was right in dismissing the application in the manner it did.

The respondent instituted a suit against the appellants on January 2, 1941, for recovery of a loan advanced before or after the commencement of this Act. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the respondent was not an assignee within the meaning of section 2 (22) of the Act and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the petition (exhibit 2a) was not a proceeding in execution for any of the purposes mentioned in clauses (a) or (b) of section 28, sub section (1), as amended by the Calcutta High Court. HELD : The words "all the rights of the mortgagee" used by their Lordships in Promode Kumar Roy vs Nikhil Bhusan Mukhopadhya (I.L.R. , approved. In the present case, the respondent had not received the notice referred to in clause (a), and therefore, he was not entitled to exemption under proviso (ii) to sub section(1) of sec tion 36 of the Calcutta Act. [582 C D] The words 'all the right of the mortgagor" used in section 28(1)(b) are wide enough to include a mortgage debt. It is well settled that a "proceeding in execution" is an application for execution and not a suit for recovery. In this case, as the respondent did not receive the notice under clause (b), he was entitled to recover the debt from the original mortgagor. [682 C] The word 'all ' includes a proceeding for execution. It means a proceeding which affects any decree of a Court unless such decree is one which was passed in a suit to which this Act applies and which was not fully satisfied by January 1, 1939. In other words, the expression "all rights of an assignee" used therein must be construed as including a proceeding relating to execution. [782 D E] The respondent 's claim to exemption from the mortgage debt under proviso(ii) of sub section 2(22) was pending on January 30, 1937, and the petition of June 2, 1939, amounted to a proceeding within the definition in section 2.(22) as amended.

The appellant was the Karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his sons. The properties conveyed by the two deeds were executed without consideration or for the transfer of jewels. In 1947, after the execution of exhibit A 1 and exhibit A 2, the appellant transferred to the appellant certain properties belonging to the joint family. On the death of Venkatacharyulu, the respondents filed a suit against his widow and sons for recovery of possession of the properties conveyed in favour of the appellant. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal, the High Court held that the transfers were made by Venkatacwarulu in favour Of the appellant and that the subsequent severance of joint status between Venkatachariulu was valid. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The transfer under exhibit A1 and exhibit B 2 were not supported by any consideration by way of cash delivery or delivery of jewel properties. The past cohabitation was the consideration for the subsequent promise to transfer the properties to her. The previous cohabitation could not validate them. [45 D E] (ii) The transfers under exhibit 1 and A 2 were invalid. The original partitions in 1947 could not invalidate them. The transfers were without consideration and were by way a gift of his undivided interest in the coparcenary properties to his concubine. The subsequent severance was valid, but in holding that the gifts were not hit by section 6(h) of the , the High court rightly held that past cohabitations were invalid, because they were motivated by a desire to compensate the concubate for her past services. [46 E F] (iii) The properties gifted under exhibit B 1 and Exhibit A 2 are not hit on sec. 6(i) of Act. The transfer was without consideration. The family properties gifted thereunder were not validated by the disruption of joint family in 1947. The partitions were invalid and the subsequent partitions did not invalidate the gifts.

The respondent, a company incorporated in the United Kingdom, was carrying on business as a dealer in the manufacture of pharmaceutical products. The respondent, who was the managing agent of the appellant, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1961 62 under section 23(1)(vi) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The Income Tax Officer issued notice under section 226(3) of that Act on 5.12.75 and served a notice on the respondent under section 227(3). The respondent filed writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice on various grounds including the delay in payment of interest for the period after 5.11.75, which was beyond the time prescribed by section 226 (3) and also to make a statement on oath under clause (vi) thereof. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the delay was not attributable to the respondent and that the notice issued under section 22(3)(vi), of the Act was without jurisdiction. In appeal to this Court, it was contended for the appellant that the High court had no power to condone the inordinate delay in making the requisite statement under section 225(3), as the same was made after the expiry of the date of maturity of insur ance policy, and that there fore, the L.I.C. had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ application. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The delay in filing the requisite Statement under section226(3 ) of the income Tax Act is not governed by Section 244 of the Incometax Act, 1922. [114B] 2.1 In the present case, the inordinate delayed statement on the basis of the registered assignment was made by the L I.I C., in the present matter only after the L 1.I .C. did not belong to the assessee inasmuch as it was payable only to the assignee and not the defaulter. [117D] 2(a) The delay, if any, in making a statement under clause(vi) is not covered by Section 245 of the I.T.O. [118F] 3.2 In the instant case, there was no justification for the inordinate delays in making this statement on its behalf and on the contrary, the delay had been satisfactorily explained by the appellant. The explanation given by the respondent that such a statement was not made since it involved the likelihood of exposing the LI.I.,C. or any of its officers to personal liability has therefore, no merit. [119F] 4(b) In the absence of any material on record to justify the inordinate unexplained delay in raising the requisite statements under section 228(3 ), the High Courts were not justified in holding that such an explanation was not forthcoming since it did not relate to the likelihood or exposing the appellant to personal responsibility. [120D] 5.3 The delay is a matter of discretion and has to be exercised judicially, reasonably and in accordance with law. It is not possible for the Court to interfere with the discretion of the Court in exercise of its discretion under Article 226(1) of Constitution.
