[122F] 6.4 In the facts and circumstances of the case, it is obvious that the inordinate lapse in making an application under clause ((vi) was not due to any mala fides or deliberate inaction on the part of the respondent. The inordinate delay was a matter which had to be considered by the Court at the time of passing the requisite order. [123F] 5(a).

The respondent was a member of the Madhya Pradesh Legislative Assembly. He was elected as a member to the Lok Sabha. The appellant filed an election petition in the High Court challenging the election of the respondent on the ground that he had been disqualified under section 29(2) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 and that the first proviso to section 29 (1) of that Act applied only to cases where the First Schedule prescribed a period of limitation for such an appeal. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the second proviso to sub section (2) was applicable to the case where the first Schedule had not prescribed any period of time for determining any period for which a period was prescribed in the First schedule and that, therefore, the second limb of section 29 of the Act would apply even to cases when the First Scheduled prescribed a maximum period of three years. The respondent appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD: (i) The first proviso is not applicable to an appeal under the Representation Of the People act, 1951. It does not fall under article 156 of the First Schedules to the Limitation Act because it does not apply even though it is not of a type for which period a period is prescribed in that Schedule. [144 B] (ii) The second limb is concerned only with proceedings of this kind, that is, that the First and Second Schedule prescribe a period within which a limitation of three months would be provided in the first schedule. In order to deal with the second ground given by the respondent, it is necessary to reproduce the provisions of section29(2), sub section(2). The first limb of sub section 2 provides that where any special or local law prescribes for any suit, appeal or application by any special and local law for which time a period prescribed therefor by the first scheduled has not been prescribed therefor, then, the provisions contained in section 3 shall apply as if such period were prescribed therefor. [145 C D] (iii) The proviso to s.29(1) does not prescribe any period within the meaning of that sub section. It only provides for an appeal or revision by any general or local laws. Therefore, what has to be seen whether a suit, Appeal or application under a particular local law is of a kind different from one for which limitation is prescribed for such a suit.

The appellant, a private operator, was directed to stand for the purpose of allowing the passengers of Baldev to get into and to get down from the stage carriages in a writ petition, Civil Miscellaneous Writ Petition No. 501 of 1986. The District Magis trate passed an order fixing the places for the bus stand/halting place. The appellant challenged the said order before the High Court which was dismissed by the Single Judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the District Magistrate had no power to fix any area as a bus stand under section 76 of the Act and that the place where the appellant and other bus operators were asked to stop their buses at the bus stands fixed by the District Magistrate. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in upholding the impugned order passed by the Dist. Magistrate. [707C] 2. Section 76 of Act confers power on the State Government to make rules for the purposes of the said chapter. It only authorises the District Magistrates to exercise the powers under section 68(2)(r) of the . The High court was therefore, in error and upholding the order passed against the appellant. [ 707C D] 3. Section 78 of the is in Chapter IV of the , which is confined to the question of determination of parking places and halting places which are not the same as bus stand which can only be notified by the Regional Transport Authority. Such a power should be specifically given by the statute and that, therefore, rules could be framed by the State Transport Authority for determining any convenient place or places within the Town Area of Baldev (Mathura) as a Bus stand. [779E] 4. The Regional Transport Authorities having jurisdiction over the area and not in the District magistrate cannot be equated with the Regional Trans port Authority constituted under the Act. It merely authorises the district Magistrate to exercise powers under Section 76. [780F G] 5. The power conferred on the District Collector by section 68 (2)(t) of is confined only to the questions of determination or parking places which were not the similar bus stand and halting place which are neither the same nor the same. It could be exercised only by the regional Transport Authority constituted in accordance with the provisions relating to the said subject under section 70(2). [779G] 6. The State Government had power to issue a notification fixing a bus stands under section76 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 and that too was a sort of radiating centre of all the bus traffic in the town. It is open to the Regional transport Authority to take action immediately for determining or convenient places within its Town Area. [777A] 7. The order passed under section 78 of Motor Vehicles Rules, 1939 is not confined to a question of fixation of parking place and halting stations which are outside the Town area of Baldev. [771C D; 778D] 8. The provisions relating thereto have no application to a permanent bus stand as a vehicle stand. It cannot be said that in the instant case no order has been passed by any Regional Transport Officer, Mathura to determine the area in question as a motor vehicle stand and the power to prescribe a bus stood vested in the Regional Authority constituted Under the Act, therefore rules could have been framed by it regarding the said Subject under section 75 of the. The impugned order is therefore set aside.

The appellants were convicted under section 7 of the Punjab Paddy (Export Control) Order, 1959. The trial court convicted all the accused persons but on appeal the Additional Sessions Judge set aside the conviction and sentenced them to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and also to fine. On appeal by the State, the High Court set aside their conviction and sentence of Qimat Rai and of the two appellants. In appeal to this Court it was contended that there had been an attempt on the part of the appellants to commit the offence of export and that the prosecution had failed to prove that the appellants were guilty of an attempt to commit a crime, and that in any case, the conviction of Qinat Rai was bad as he was not present at the time when the offence was committed. HELD: (i) The sufficiency of the act reus of a criminal attempt is different from attempt to committing it. It is merely a preparation on the parts of the appellant 's luggage and coverings or receptacles in which they are actually preparatory to the commission of a crime. [682 B] (ii) There has been an effort on the portion of the accused appellants to committing the offence. The sufficiency is not a question of law which had led to difficulty because of the necessity of distinguishing between acts which are merely preparatory to commission of the crime, but that is only a preparation at the stage when the offences were actually committed. [782 C] (iii) There was an attempt at the part in committing the crime of export. The evidence showed that Qin at the relevant point of time, at about the 18th mile from Delhi, had no connection with the commission or preparation of the offence and as a matter of fact, Qimats Rai had no intention to commit it. [882 D] (iv) There is nothing in the Act which shows that the Act was intended to apply to the export of paddy within the meaning of Para 2(a). The sufficiency has not been shown by the prosecution to show that the appellant was a person who could be convicted of an offence under section7. [667 G H] (v) There had been no attempt on his part to commit any offence of attempt to export. It was merely a preparing on the whole or, as a mater of fact he must be shown first to have intended to commit that crime and secondly to have done an act which constitutes the act which constituted the act constituting the act. [666 A] (vi) The adequacy of the acts which constitute the act is a question which had leading to difficulty since the necessity for distinguishing between actions which are simply preparatory to carrying paddy, and those which are sufficiently proximate to it.

The appellant, a company, was incorporated in the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The appellant was carrying on business as Managing Agents of the Company and was managing agents of the said Company. In the accounting year of the company, the appellant had been paying commission to the transferees and were not liable to tax in respect of the same. The Income tax Officer held that the Sassoons had not earned any part of the Managing Agency commission which had accrued to them during the chargeable accounting period. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that as the Sas soons had no income, they would be their income and no part of such income could ever be said to have accrued to the Sas Soons during the relevant chargeable accounting periods. The Appellate Tribunal, however, held that in any event what was transferred by the Sasstsoons to the transferee was merely expectations of earning commission and not any part thereof. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Managing Agency had been referred back to the period in which it was earned and the portions of the remuneration or commission which were earned by the transferees were merely expectations and not some part of it. [345 D] (ii) The managing agency agreement shows that the assignor is to be responsible only to the assignee for the payment of the entire year 's remuneration, but by the very terms of the managing Agency Agreements it could be referred back either as part of a term between the transferor and the assignee, but on the fact that what was retained was an income bearing asset which carried with it a right to the whole income that fell due after the date of assignment. [346 E] (iii) The remuneration for the entire period of the agency which is the source of income must be regarded as one entity and on the facts of this case, it could reasonably be said that the remuneration for that part of its remuneration was not by itself enough to vest in the assignee a beneficial right to remuneration of the year. [347 G] (iv) The word "income" in section 10 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, is wide and comprehensive enough to include income from business. It is well settled that the term "income", in section 2(g) of the Act, includes income from any business carried on by a company which is a firm or a Company. [348 C] (v) The expression "income from business" in the definition of "business" in s.2(g), includes income derived from business carried out by a firm. It does not include income derived by a partner from business, but it is only income derived therefrom.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge, on a consideration of the entire evidence came to the conclusion that Sahoo killed Sunderpatti. The High Court confirmed both the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the soliloquy of the accused admitting his guilt was not an extra judicial confession as the Courts below held it to be. HELD: (1) It is implicit in the concept of "confession" that something which the prisoner had been over muttering to himself, or saying to his wife or to any other person in confidence, will be receivable in evidence only on proof. [975 B] (2) The extra judicial confessions are not a rule of law and they cannot be used as corroborative piece of evidence. They are often true. But the probative value of an admission or confession can be offered only by witnesses who heard the admission or confessional statement, as the case may be. If so in the case of a statement made by an accused admitting guilt is not admitted in evidence merely on proof, there cannot be any difference in principle in the cases of an oral statement. [977 E] (3) The probative value attached to it is always true. It may be used only as a corroborative piece or evidence. But so, at the trial the statements of the witnesses who hear the admission and confession can certainly be proved as a piece ofevidence.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk in the respondent 's General Insurance Co. Ltd., on May 1, 1976. He was later transferred to another office of the respondent on June 29, 1976 and was confirmed in that post on July 30, 1977. The respondent challenged the validity of the order of termination by tendering one month 's salary in lieu of notice and also a direction to pay all the allowances upto that date including the period of his suspension. The appellant contended before the High Court that the service of the appellant was terminated in terms of the existing rule 5 of the Rules, and that the Board of Directors had to take a decision whether the need to continue the employee 's service was terminated or the terms and conditions were duly altered by any other scheme framed under the Act. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the appellant having been appointed as an officer/employee of the Indian Insurance Co., in accordance with the provisions of the Act, the termination of his service was illegal and void offending Article 14 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "in the event of the Society not having any further need of any employee ' s service whether permanent or temporary, which shall be decided by the Board, the Principal Officer shall give 30 days ' notice in writing for termination of service or in lieu thereof. [225B] 2.1 The word "in" is susceptible of two interpretations. The words "in case of the society not having an any further requirement of any employees 's services whether permanent, temporary or temporary which shall he kept would be put to an end by giving one month notice or pay in lieu thereto. [226D] 2(a) The word 'in" in Rule 5 means a person who is employed for a fixed period and has been paid wages in lieu whereof the employer may terminate his service on the expiry of the period specified in that rule. If the provisions are construed in such a way as would make it consistent with the constitution and another interpretation would render the provision or the rule unconstitutional, the court would lean in favour of the former construction. [227E] 2.(b) The expression 'in the case of a society not possessing any further necessity of any employment 's work whether permanent and temporary which should be decided either by the Principal officer or by the employee is occupying no further need for the services of a particular employee, in consequence the service is abolished. [228F] 2 (c) The words 'in case the Society has not any further demand of any person 's employment whether permanent nor temporary, have an option to leave or discontinue by giving 30 days notice in advance of his intention to do so, would entail forfeiture of the pay of the month. If there is no need for such services of any individual employee, the post would be abolished. The word `in case ' does not mean that the employee has an option either to leave and discontinue by give one month's notice or salary in addition thereto.

The appellant, a manufacturer of country liquor, was granted licences for the sale of country spirit and for the use of country Liquor. The State Government issued a fresh order dated August 19, 1970 under section 22(1) of the Orissa Excise Act, 1915, directing that the licence be granted for an exclusive privilege to manufacture and sell liquor. The appellant challenged the said order by way of writ petitions before the High Court which were dismissed on April 16, 1971. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the State Government had no authority to issue a notice under section 23(1), as the power of the Board to disregard the decision in Ajodhya Prasad 's case had been delegated to the Board of Revenue; and (ii) the Collector had no power to issue such a notice. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that section 6(a) of Orissa Excise Rules, 1915 was ultra vires the powers of the Legislature. [723C] 2. Section 6(1)(b) of Act and Rule 103(1 of the Excise Rules were ultra vires. It is not necessary to deal separately with the judgment of the High court dated April 16. 1971 in Jaiswal 's Case (supra). The High Courts have held that as section 6 was not made retrospective, the effect of section 6 amounted to a direction by the Legislature to disregard its decision in Sajodhya Prasads case that the amount realised by auction was illegal and that section6 was ultravio sion. [779C D] 3. Section 5 of the Amending Act of 1970 was not enacted retrospectively. The power of State Government to disregard an order passed under section 6 is a legislative function and it has the exclusive right and privilege of manufacturing and selling liquor. It cannot be said that the State had the exclusive power or privilege of manufacture and sale of liquor. [780E] 4. Section 2 to 5 of Amending Act, 1970 was ultra virus the powers conferred on the Legislature by section 22 of the Act. The amendment of 1970 did not affect the effect or validity of section 3 of the amending Act of 1971. It was therefore ultra vires that power of Parliament.

The prosecution case was that the deceased was a good opportunity to commit theft of articles in the house of Dr. Nanavati and that he used to wash clothes of accused No. 3. The trial court acquitted all the three accused except accused Nos. 1 and 2. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that there was corroboration of the evidence of Dinkar and accused No., 2 and that the High Court had rightly come to the conclusion that there were corroboration in regard to accused No,. 3 and that even if there was some corroboration in material particulars, the prosecution could not be said to have proved that accused No .3 was guilty of the offence. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The evidence of the prosecution established that accused Nos 1 and 3 were guilty of murder. The discovery of articles by accused No 2 is not to be lost sight of. Accused No. 1 was found in the tailor 's shop of Takalkar. The fact that Dr. Narendra was seen alive in the company of accused NO. 3 is not a good evidence. [618 D] In view of the fact that there is sufficient corroboration of evidence of PW 2 and his wife, it cannot be said that accused no. 3 was guilty. [719 G H] The discovery by accused Nos 2 and 3 was as a result of a statement by accused NO .3 to the shop of P.W. 1. The evidence in regard thereto is not of importance in view of death of Narendra. Dr. Shahher was found as a witness and it was proved that he had seen alive the articles in his godown and gave the key of the godown to accused Nos .2 and 3. [819 G] In the absence of any corroboration, the evidence relating to the recovery of articles from the shop is not reliable. The High Court rightly came to the finding that there are corroboration in respect of accused Nos,. 1 and 4.

The appellant was the owner of a plot in question. The Town Planning Officer, Surat, made an estimate of the market value at its market value on the basis of the average value of the original plots. The town planning officer assessed the market price at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per sq. yard and determined the market rate at Rs. 2,000 for each plot. The appellant challenged the assessment by a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the decision of the Town Planning officer determining the amount of compensation in the appellant 's case was not appealable. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court was right in finding that the determination of the value of a part of the plot at the date of declaration of the final scheme was made. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The principle for determining the market values of the land at the time of declaration is whether an owner of land is given a reconstituted plot or not compensation. [874C] 2. The Act specifies a principle of compensation, it is observed in Shantilal 's Case at page 357 of the report that the value determined by the Town planning Officer under section 32 (1) (iii) has to find out the marketvalue of each of the plots included in the final Scheme and not the final plot. [884D] 3. The principles for determining compensation are: (i) that the land is likely to be affected by the making of a town planning scheme; (ii) that it is necessary to determine the amount payable to the owner for loss of land; and (iii ) that the market valuation of each plot at its date of the declaration is determined on the market Value of the entire plot. In determining the difference between the total values of original plots and the total value of each plots included, in the Final scheme, the Town Development Officer may determine the compensation to be paid to the owners for loss. [894E F] 4. The scheme determines the amount to be payable by the local authority in cash or in such other way as may be agreed upon by the parties. In fixing the amount on each plot included in a final scheme, it would be the value which is estimated to accrue in respect of each Plot included in an Final scheme and not that the final plots are the same. [904G H] 5. The fact that under the Act the market cost of the whole plot has to be determined on its market price is not a ground for determining any compensation payable by a local authority or partly from such person as the Town Plan Officer may in each case determine. [851A B] 6. The provisions of section 69 are not intended to be exhaustive and they do not require that the owner should have an opportunity of being heard before making a scheme. It is only when he makes a claim before the Town Planner that the amount has to he determined, that it may be necessary for him to make a scheme, or the date on which the declaration was made, [852C D] 7. The object of section 64 is to enable the owner to make an application for compensation in respect thereof from the local authorities or partly by persons benefited or partlyfrom the local area and partly from the public authority which is beneficial partly to the general public, which shall be included in costs of the scheme. [864D E] 8. The mere fact that section 64 has been enacted with a view to making a town Planning scheme in accordance with the provisions of the Act does not make any difference between an owner and a person benefited by the framing of a scheme under section 68. [952E F G] 9.

The appellant, a brother of the testator, was the third son of Seetharama Iyer. He had two daughters and one daughter. The widow died in 1934. The appellant filed an application for a certificate under section 66(1) Of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, which was granted by the High Court on the ground that the will was void for uncertainty. The High Court held that the English rule of benevolent construction that a legatee has a right to choose in such circumstances applied to India also and also held that on the construction of the will in this case the right of selection was in Seetharams or in the legatees, and not in Seethrama. Held, that the testator intended that each daughter should get the area of land devised to take them into account the good and bad quality of the land. The gift cannot be said to be void for uncertain within the meaning of section 89, for uncertainty within the definition of section 90, for it can be made certain. The will in such cases is a case where on the constructions of the Will it was held that there were no words in the will which would lead to the inference that the legatee intended that the daughters should get their lands after taking into account good and good quality of land. Held further, that even though the words are different in the case of daughters as compared to the words used in the testator 's case, the intention of the settlor was clearly to select the house himself to be given to each son and there could be no question of the legatee in making the selection. The word "he shall give" in the context of the mother would mean that the Will should have been made by the legatee and once the selection is made by him, the lands devised out of one or more of the three children will be in possession so long as the three sons were minor and shall deliver possession of the properties to the children. The words "he will deliver possession" in section 89 are wide enough to include a person who has no male issue but only a female issue. The expression "he should give" is not defined in the Act, because it is well settled that a testator must be given the right to select his house himself and he can make the selection by the Selection Committee appointed by him. The intention of testator was clearly that the sons would get their properties after taking in account the bad good and poor quality of lands.

The appellant, a co bhumidar of the plots in dispute, was allotted to one Smt. Bashir and Mohd. Bashri for the purpose of consolidation operations. The land in dispute was recorded as a co sharer with the respondents. The appellant 's name was also recorded as co sharers with the defendants. In the consolidation proceedings, separate plots were carved out and she was never informed about any proceedings by the defendants and was never intimated about any proceeding by the respondents nor was there any judicial proceedings under which the name of the plaintiff was suddenly deleted after 1359 Fasli. The District Judge found that on the admitted facts even after the abolition of zamindari, the position was that in 1357 Fasli the plaintiff 's names were clearly recorded as an co sharner with the defendant and continued to be so till 1359 Fasli as would appear from exhibit 2. The High Court also held that the name was actually deleted after 1356 Fasli and there was no order of any authority or court to show the circumstances under which, the plaintiff came to know that her share was being properly looked after by them and on this footing the District Judge dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in law in holding that the present suit was barred by section 49 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, because after the abolished zamindari, there were no judicial proceedings pending under which any name was suddenly omitted or there were any judicial proceeding under which such name was subsequently deleted. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High court erred in holding on facts that a clear fraud had been committed during the consolidation operations either by the defendant or somebody else as a result of which the rights of the parties were sought to be extinguished. [867F] 2.2 In the present case, it is manifest that the possession of the defendants as co tenants was never specifically recorded as joint sharers in the consolidation operation either by them or by someone else as such. The fact remains that the District judge has come to a clear conclusion that some sort of fraud must have been committed by the parties and on that footing the High court rightly reversed the decision of the District Court. [767F G] 2.(a) In view of the clear decision of this Court, the High Courts erred in not holding that there was any evidence on the record to prove that the plaintiff had practised a fraud on the consolidation authorities. The finding of the learned District Judge is not sustainable in law and the judgment of the High Curt cannot be allowed to stand. [783A B] (b) In the instant case, the possession was never expressly recorded as the co share with the respondent. There was no evidence on record that any fraud was committed during consolidation operations in the village by anybody else as the defendants were co shared with the plaintiff.

The petitioner in his writ petition challenged the appointment of Respondent No. 1 as Deputy Prime Minister of India, on the ground that he was still functioning as Chief Minister when the oath register was administered to him as Deputy Cabinet Minister. The respondent No. I filed a writ petition challenging the appointment and the practice which has been followed evince the Constitution came into force. The petitioner in person contended that the oath administered to Respondent No 1 was not the oath in accordance with the prescrip tion of the Constitution; and (ii) he was yet functioning as the Chief Minister of Haryana when the Oath Register was administered, while being sworn into office, he describes himself as Prime Minister and all other Ministers signa blely as Ministers. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The oath register is by the incumbent signed as Prime Ministers and all others signa nations are merely descriptive of the person and of his nomination as a candidate. [318C] 2. The requirement of Article 75(4) of the Consti tution is only for a Minister of the Union and there is no separate form even for the Prime Minister. It is only in respect of the Prime Ministers that the prescribed oath register has to be divided into two parts, one which contains the sub stantial part. [036E] 3. The expression "other Ministers" in the Third Schedule means the person taking the oath or making the affirmation and the other who also contains the Sub stanial part. It does not confer on him any powers of the Chief Prime Minis ters, along with his other submis sions, signaations as Prime Mini ter. [618F] 4. The word "other Minister" in Article 75 (4) is merely descriptive and the latter which contains sub st antial part is properly followed. It would vitiate the oath. [519G H] 5. The words "other than Ministers" are merely academic and not merely descriptive. The language of Article 77(4), read with Form VII A, in the third Schedule, is merely a descriptive and not the other which contains a sub stature. [720H; 721A B] 6. The use of the word "Other Minister" as used in Article 77 (4), in the fourth Schedule, indicates that the person takes the oath as Prime Secretary and allother Ministers sign aations as Ministers, though he has been described as Prime minister.

The appellant, a factory, was engaged in the manufacture of sugar. The respondent workmen were dismissed from service on the ground that they had failed to comply with the provisions of the Factories Act and the rules framed thereunder. The management put up a notice that the stoppage of work on 1st November, 1948 amounted to an illegal strike and a break in service within the meaning of the Act. The appellant contended that the closure of the factory was not a concerted action on the part of the workers who participated in such strike but had failed in doing so because the workers were not entitled to annual holidays with pay under section 49 B (1) of the , and that the management had decided that the workers whose services were terminated within the definition of the word "strike" as given in section 2(q) of Factories Act, 1948, would have completed a period of twelve months ' continuous service in the factory. Held, that the appellant was not entitled under the provisions Of the Factories Acts to deprive them of the holidays under the rules and that no substantial question of law arose for decision in respect of the construction of section 49 A (1). The workmen were entitled to the annual holidays at full rates as provided for in section 49B (1), but they would have got under the Rules. The workers who had participated in the strike could not be denied the benefit of holidays under section 48 B (2) because, by a notification of the Government of Madras dated 23rd August, 1946, the Buckingham an Carnatic Mills had been exempted from the provisionsof Chapter IV A of the and the provisions were therefore attracted to it. The workmen who had failed before the coming into force of the Factory Act could not claim any privilege under section 47 B (3) because they had no right to deprive their workers on 1th November, 1949, as a result of an illegal lock and did not cause any interruption in the work on that night.

The appellant was convicted under section 292 I.P.C. and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court dismissed the petition, holding that the film had been given 'A ' certificate by the Central Board of Film Censors acting within their jurisdiction under the Act, thereby sanctioning the public exhibition of the film, did not constitute an offence under section 293 I. P.C., and that no prosecution could be legally sustained in the circumstances of the case. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that once a certificate sanctioning public exhibition has been granted by the competent authority under the (for short, the Act), there is justification for its displaying the film even if it be obscene or not, and that any prosecution could legally sustain in the circumstance of the present case, the film having been duly certified for public exhibition, the sanctions and pursued in good faith, believes himself to be justified by law, i.e., by some other provision, then section 79 I.A.C.; and that the certificate holder is justified by Law, because if the act was done by one "wholly believed himself to he believed himself on sound faith in good belief it would be justified either by law or otherwise, that he entertained a mistake of fact and not by reason of a mistake which is an offence. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The prosecution is unsustainable because section 79 is reformative and does not require any further proof to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. [503B] 2.2 In the present matter, the prosecution is justified because section 80 I.C of the Act provides that no court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 3 or 4 unless the ground covered by the two laws are satisfied. The section does not contemplate any further evidence to prove the guilt beyond reasonable doubts. [403D] 2(a) In order to attract section 79, the accused must have been guilty of a criminal charge and he should be punished with imprisonment for life. [303E F] (b) Section 79 is a special provision which provides that where any offence alleged to have been committed by a person who is not duly qualified under the rules made thereunder, or by virtue of any rule made under this Act, is punishable with death, then, unless the court finds that such person has caused an injury which is likely to cause death, it shall presume that he had caused such injury.

The petitioner, a Government Pleader in the Patna District, was given short shrift by the High Court in a laconic order, but undaunted by this Court in utter nudity, his case was a claim of monopoly of all government cases in the Bihar District including lucrative land acquisition. The petitioner 's claim as the sole representative of Government Pleader was that the official income expected from this heavy harvest of cases was not a legal cover for seeking lucre but for vindicating the inviolability of the high public office of Government pleader by politicisation of government Pleaders by counsel for the petitioner. The High Court rejected the claim as being devoid of merit and dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that: (1) the official status of a Government pleader is not a legally enforceable right; (2) the State Government has no power to make rules for regulating the practice of a single government Pleader in all civil cases; and (3) the High Courts have no jurisdiction to issue any rule or order which the Government Pleader is merely to conduct its cases even as any client, who has a crowd of cases to be conducted, his duties are only to the Government who are responsible character, the office must be held to be a public office within the scope of quo warranto proceeding. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The Court in every case where it is possible to do so consistently with the nature of the situation of the case, to make every endeavour to assist the parties in arriving at a settlement in respect of the subject matter of the suit. [763B] 2.1 In every case, in every suit or proceeding to which the government is a party, it shall be the duty of the Court in the first instance, in each case where there are several thousand cases in which Government Pleader has done in hoping for a lakh of rupees. The time has come to examine the quality of the product or service or duties to be performed by him in due exercise of that office, most of which are of an independent and responsible character. [ 763C D] 2(a) In every suit, or proceeding, to which Government is a Party, it must be the function of the court in the First instance, where it has been possible to doing so consistently without the nature or the circumstances of the cases, to do well within the ambit of quo ultual justice so that the profession may flourish without wholly hitching the calling the star of material amassed by law from the liabilities of other occupations. [758E] 2.(b) The Government Pleader, Madras is only an agent of the Government, that his duties were only to those Government Pleader who are the most responsible character and responsible person. [759F G] 3(a). It is not correct to say that a lawyer may have been given a cloak of a personal duty to perform all or any of the functions expressly imposed by this Code on the Government pleader. The fact that the Government Advocate has been employed by the State Pleader in some cases does not mean that he would be the holder of a public Office within the meaning of section 2(c) of the Act. [761F G; 763A] 4.(b). It cannot be said that the petitioner was merely an agent or a lawyer to conduct his cases even though he is not the holder thereof. The Government Advocate, Madras, is only a person who has no public office and is not an independent legal entity. He is also an agent in the State of Bihar. [763C D; 764A] 5.(c) It cannot therefore be said to be an agent for the purpose of the present case that he was merely a servant of the State. The question whether he was really an agent must depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case.

The Mills purchased 5,000 shares of the Bank of India at a special general meeting of the shareholders of the bank. The shares were to be distributed among its 800 share holders and it was considered proper to invest in the said issue of the said Bank of Indian Bank at the rate of Rs. 100 per share. The Mills exercised the right to take over only 66 shares out of the total issue of 800 shares held by them in this company. The dividend was to be paid by the Mills as the holder of 5, 000 shares became entitled to receive 1,6662 shares of its Bank at a rate of Re. 100/ per share and it is considered proper that invest in these shares should be distributed amongst its shareholders. The High Court held that the distribution of the right of the Mills amounted to distribution of dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and that the right was not an inclusive and exhaustive definition, and even if the distribution was of a monetary value, it could not be regarded as dividend within its ordinary meaning. Held, that the shares were distributed amongst the shareholders as dividend and the value of the shares was undoubtedly the value thereof. The share holders had a monetary interest in the shares and the right could not therefore be said to be dividend within section 2 (6A). The distribution of shares by the Bank was not a mere distribution of "dividend" within the definition of that expression in section 2.(6A), but only an exhaustive definition. The right to apply for the shares of a Bank of a foreign company could not, therefore, be regarded dividend within that meaning of that term in section2(6 A).

The appellant filed an election petition in the High Court challenging the election of the respondent No. 1 on the ground that the names of the witnesses were kept present at the time fixed for recording their evidence, and that the respondent had failed to produce them before the trial court. The High Court refused to grant permission to examine the witness. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court should have refused to examine those witnesses who were called to produce documents without applying for summons under Rule 1A, and in respect of whom, the Court did not grant permission, that the evidence of such witness or witnesses could be withheld from the Court, and the Court had no jurisdiction to refuse to examine such witness. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The obligation to supply the list of witnesses within the time prescribed under sub rule (1), and who can be produced without assistance of the Court is not absolute. It is implicit in Rule 1 A that it only enables the party to examine only those witnesses whose names are mentioned in the list filed under sub Rule (1). [534B] (2) The duty to supply list of documents within the period prescribed under Sub rule (3) to procure presence of a witness by issuing a summons through the Court or otherwice which ordinarily the court would not extend for procuring the attendance of a person whose name is not shown in the List. But if on the date fixed for the recording of the evidence, the party is unable to produce him or her on his own under Rule IA and in such a situation the party need have to seek assistance of Court under sub rules (1); and if it was implicit in Sub rule(3) that it could do so under Rule lA, the court may still extend its assistance for procuring attendance of witnesses by issuing summons through Court or otherwise. [535C D] (3)(a) The High court has no jurisdiction either to refuse permission to examination the witness or to produce his own documents without application of the court or other witnesses if it is satisfied that the party tendering such witness and the court has not any jurisdiction to decline to examine him or witnesses, if it be of opinion that the witness was not material for the decision of the petition or that the Party tendering such witnesses or witnesses are doing so on frivolous grounds or with a view to delay the proceedings. [635E F] (b) The Court has no power to refuse the permission to produce any witness without applying to the court for summoning documents without complying with Rule 1(1). If mere omission to mention the name of a party in the schedule contemplated by sub rule(1) and who could be producedwithout the assistance of court under sub clause (3), it can do so, under Rule 2A. [643B C] (4)(a)(i) The requirement to supply copies of documents without being applied for summons through court or otherwise is absent in proviso to Sec. Save this Court has jurisdiction to refused to summon any witness if the party fails to produce himself or her at his own expense under Rule1A and that in such situation the court shall decline to examination such witness, Rule 1B(2) of Order XVI confers a wider jurisdiction on the Court to refuse. [65E F G] (5)(a). The obligation of supply the lists within the prescribed time under sub section (1)(b) is not absent in the case of an application as provided by sub clause 2A, but where the party wants to examine them only those persons kept present when the evidence is recorded and is not closed.

The appellant was appointed as Principal of the College on May 1, 1981. He was appointed by the management in accordance with the provisions of the Uttar Pradesh Intermediate Education Act, 1921. The appellant was selected and appointed as a teacher in the college. On April 27, 1981 he was appointed Principal of a private college. Thereafter, the Management issued an appointment order dated April 27.1981 to the appellant alleging that the Committee of Management had no power to make the selection on April 27 1981 and that the appellant alleged to have been appointed as the Principal of his College. The management filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order. The High Court held that the appointment of the appellant was illegal and void. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that: (1) the Selection Committee had no authority to make an appointment notwithstanding the fact that the order contained in the radiogram had suspended or withdrawn its power; (2) the Committee had power to appoint any person as Principal and therefore the appointment was not valid; and (3) the appointment made by the appellant amounted to removal of the Principal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order dated May 27,1981 contained in radiograms dated April 7, 1981 is not invalid. [982B] 2.1 The power to issue appointment order was conferred by the regulations on the Committee and the appellant had no right to select and appoint the appellant. If the power to do so was suspended or revoked it would not be open to the Selection committee to make any consequential order as may be necessary. [ 983C D] 2(2) The power of appointment conferred on the committee of Management by the Regulations is conferred by section 9 which has been extracted hereinbefore confers power on the State Government without making any reference to the Board to make, modify or rescind any regulation in respect of any matter. The effect of the order conveyed by the radiosram would be to rescind the regulations conferring power on a Committee of management to make appointment and withdraw and/or withdrawing power of appointments. [980D E] 2.(3) The State Government could not make the appointment without making an appropriate order consistent with the provision of the Act as also make any other order consistent therewith. [981E F] 3(4) The appellant would be a member of the Committee if he was selected by the Selection Board and appointed by it. If, however, the power is suspended or cancelled it would be open for the Selection Committees to make appointments. If such power was not suspended, the State Govern ment could have made an order in accordance therewith. But as there was no power of appointing the appellant, the Committee could not be said to have rescinded its power. [977F] 4(5) The order contained therein conferred power on an authority not authorised to make it and the appointment is otherwise valid though ineffective and hence ineffective though it may not be invalid. It may not also be invalid but merely ineffective though ineffective.

The petitioners manufacture "a textile" consisting of rayon threads in the warp and cotton threads. The petitioners state that the manufacturers of tyres to whom the fabric is supplied "pregnate the fabric with rubber and weave into it into it a fabric in the same way as is being done by the first petitioner". The petitioners allege that they manufacture "an textile" and also that it serves as part of raw material for what ultimately go into the manufacture of a fabric. The High Court rejected the Writ Petition on the ground that the goods sought to be taxed were not the "end product" but only that it served as part thereof, and that it was not so much the point of manufacture at which the Mills sell their own product which determines the nature of goods which are entitled to exemption. Dismissing the appeals by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "textile" in the Oxford Dictionary is "a fabric". It requires careful consideration of the technical processes of manufacturing, manufacturing, or the language of the market. [500G] 2. The word "textiles" in item 22 of the first schedule of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1941, as the applicable entry covering the goods manufactured by it is woven by its purchasers "into fabric". The expression 'textile ' has been defined in the dictionary to mean "a woven fabric; any kind of cloth." [500H] 3. The words "taple fabric" are not defined in item 19 of the First Schedule to the Central Excise and Salt (Amendment) Act, 1944. It is only a technical question. It requires examination of commercial usage and terminology or the meaning of the language used by the taxing authorities. [501A B] 4. The definition of "tangible fabric" in Item 19 of First Schedule of the Act includes "a manned fabric". In the instant case, the goods were sought to he taxed under item 22 in the first Schedule of Central Excises & Salt Act. The question whether the tyre cord fabric was the end product or not was a textile. [ 500H] 5. The contention that the word "Textile" is used in the sense of "fabric" and not for any kind thereof, cannot be accepted. It does not mean that the taxing authority should be left to determine whether the product for which the Delhi Cloth Mills claims exemption is a textile fabric or not. [100G] 6. The fact that the legislature has used the term "trespass" in Entry 19 of Schedule I to the Act, shows that it is meant for "totton fabrics". It does mean that if the tyre fabric may be the end products for the Delhi cloth Mills, the whole product for theDelhi Cloth Mills would be the "pickle fabric" manufactured by the petitioners. [1000H] 7. The language of item 22 is not decisive and it is only possible to find fault with the view of the High Court that there was no error apparent on the face of the record. [2000G] 8.

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coalheries on contract basis in different collieries and also doing allied and incidental work. The respondent No. 4 was a Senior Supervisor in the company 's establishment at Dhanbad. He was working as an employee in the Company 's Establishment at Dhanbad since he had been residing at Hajipur. The appellant company, however, did not produce any evidence to show that it would be difficult for him to attend the Labour Court, Dhanbad to attend its work. On the question whether the Government was misled by the representation of the respondent and without opportunity to the respondent, the High Court held that the Government had no power to transfer the case from the labour court, Dhanbad, regu larly due to his residence at Hajpur, and it would not be convenient for him if the case is trans ferred to Labour Court. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of transfer in the present case was quashed for non communi cating reasons to the assessee. [294C] 2.1 The Government was aware of the fact that it had been misled by representation of respondent and not seriously disputed the factum of his residence in the colony quarter at Dhanbad, and therefore, no hesitation in holding that the government was misled. [295D E] 3.2 The order transferring the case to the Labour court, Patna should have given an opportunity to be heard to the appellant in the matter. The reasons given by the Government for transferring the Case from the Labour Courts, Dhanbad are reduced and quashed notifi cation dated August 8, 1988 by which the Government of Bihar transferred the case back to the labour Court, Patna is pleased to withdraw the proceeding shown in Annexure E from the Special Leave Petition, and not adversely disputed the fact of residence in that colony at Dhanbad; [295E] 3:1 The High Court was justified in refusing to record reasons in making the order of transferring the appellant company. [296F G] 2:2 The Government is misled by a representation of Respondent No. 1. In fact, in the counteraffidavit, he has not denied the documents annexed to the Special leave Petition and not contest the factum o f residence in his colony quarter. He has not disputed the existence of his residential address in the Colony at Dhanbad and it was not seriously contested that the respondent No 4 was misled or was misled thereby. [298A B] 3(a) The Government had been aware of its fact that the appellant 's residence in a colony at Hajapur is being looked after by the respondent. It is, therefore, obligatory on the part of the Government to record grounds in making an order of transfers under section 5(7A) of the Act. [299C] (b) The High Courts were justified in holding in favour of the appellant. [300D E; 299F G].

The appellant company was a hotel union. The management of the Hotel Imperial, New Delhi and its workmen represented by the Hotel Workers ' Union, was appointed an Industrial Tribunal under section 12 (4) of the , for adjudication of the dispute. The Tribunal referred the dispute to the Additional Industrial Tribunal, Delhi. The reference was made to the Tribunal. The appellant company contended that the reference was incompetent because it did not indicate how many of the 480 workers working in the hotel were involved in the dispute and that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to make a reference. Held, that the award made by the Tribunal was invalid as it did neither specify any officer of the trade union nor did it mention any officer or secretary of the Trade Union, nor did the reference in this form be made a party to the reference. The Industrial Tribunal could not be made an a party under the reference and the reference made was incompetent. The award made on October 7, 1955, was therefore invalid. The question whether the reference which was otherwise valid merely because in the order of reference made by it did make the reference incompetent, must be decided on the facts of each case. The fact that the dispute between the management of a hotel and its employees was also specified in the terms of reference, was not conclusive to mention in the reference itself that the workmen employed in the Hotel were involved. The tribunal could not therefore make the Reference incompetent because the reference did not specify any Officer or secretary. The expression "as represented by an officer of a trade union" in section 10(1) of Act means "a person who is a workman". The words "as representing the workmen" in the definition of "workman" in that Act are wide enough to include all persons who were employed in a hotel, and those who were not workmen. The word "workmen" in this definition includes all persons employed in any industry or establishment whether for wages or otherwise. The definition of 'workman ' in section 2(k) of that Act is wide enough and it does not include all workmen employed therein. The words 'as represented ' mean a person who has been engaged in any trade union, whether for remuneration or otherwise, and who is employed in such industry or establishments. The phrase "as represent the workmen ' in the present case means only those persons who are employed in an industry or other establishment which is connected with the employment or non employment of the workmen. It does not mean that the workman is entitled to be represented by a person living in any particular place in the same trade or establishment. The mere fact that some of the workers were working in such a place would not make the award incompetent because, as the words "in the present form" are wide and they do not include those who have been employed in that place. The workmen employed by the hotel in the course of its business are also specified as workmen.

The appellant is a manufacturer of rod bushes and camshaft bushes. The appellant imported the rod bushes, which were used in the manufacture of rod trees and cam biteft bushes from the place where they were imported by the respondent. The goods were assessed to duty under Item No. 84.06 of the First Schedule to the . The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 was amended by Notification No. 281 Cus/76 dated 1st January, 1976 which provided that the articles specified in column (2) of the Table shall be all parts of the engine and engines referred to in Heading No. 85.06. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the said notification on various grounds including the ground that the bushes and Bearingings were not identical articles but they were distinct and separate, and therefore, there was no material for holding that the appellant is entitled to the benefit of the Notification No 281 Ci/76. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the goods were parts of internal combustion piston engines and not a few parts thereof, and as such they were not entitled to exemption under the said Notification. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Notification will apply to parts of engine mentioned under Heading No 84.6. [227A] 2. The words "internal combustion pis engines" in column(2) are clear enough to provide that the parts of such engines, such parts must be all the parts constituting the engine or engines and also the parts thereof. So, although the parts are not mentioned under heading No.84.06, they will get the benefit Of exemption under Notification. [228B] 3. The word "in internal combustionpiston" in the Notification is clear enough that the part of the engines mentioned under Chapter 84. 06 would get the exemption under this Notification.

The plaintiffs, who were the descendants of a Muslim Law, had lost their right by ouster from the enjoyment of any share in the Dargah and even if they were entitled to any right or claim in the management or offerings in the offerings, the defendants could not claim any right on the basis of such ouster. The defendants filed written statement denying the assertions made in the plaint that the plaintiffs were not entitled to a right or interest in the property or share in offerings. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff was not entitled for any relief and dismissed the suit. In second appeal, the High Court held that the rights of Fathima Bee had become barred by limitation and as such she was not bound to claim any lia ble right till her death. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The defendants are claiming ouster on the ground of denial of Fathaima Bee 's title at the time of the judgment of the High court in 1909 and another ground taken is that neither Fathida Bee nor the plaintiffs had at any time received a share in or management of Dargah according to Muslim Law. [527B] 1.2 The defendants were carrying a mistaken impression all along that females under the Muslim Law were not entitle to any share or claim any interest in offerings and even though they were expressly excluded from the right or entitlement of any of the plaintiffs, their rights had become extinguished by ouster and as they were clearly excluded from their right or possession and enjoyment of Dargah. [627C] 1.(a) The defendants have asserted hostile title coupled with exclusive possession and enjoy ment to the knowledge of FATHima Bee. It is clear that neither in the written statement nor in reply to the notice of the plain tiffs, it was clearly indicated that relationship between Fathma Bee and her brothers were cordial and as there was no question of any knowledge to Fathoma Bee, the plaintiffs have asserted their hostile title and possession coupled with joint possession. [525E] 1(b) The High Court was right in holding that even if Fathua Bee had lost his right by ousting Fathina Bee, he was expressly excluded out from the benefit of any part in the endowments or offerings. [ 526G H] 2.(a)(i) In order to make out a case of ouster against Fathuna Bee, it is clear from the pleadings that the defendants were taking a mistaken belief all along with their exclusive possession coupledwith exclusive possession, and enjoyment and enjoy ing ment to knowledge of the Dargah as well as the offerings. It was also admitted that the females were also entitled in the right and management of the endowments. [500G H; 526A] 3.(b) In view of the admission of Fahima Bee, she had lost her right by exclusion from any share of the property of Fattima Bee and she was expressly ousted out from enjoyment of all offerings or offerings made to them on that notice. The High court was therefore right in finding that the right of Fashima Bee was a co sharer in the rights and management and possession of Dargah as also the 526 offerings and hundial collection. [506B] 4.(c) In the instant case, the respondents were carrying an mistaken impression throughout that females had lost the right by excluding Fathuma Bee from the claim or any claim in their management or emoluments or offerings etc. The respondents were not claiming ouster of Fatima Bee from their rights and possession and enjoying ment to know the Dargah or offerings so as to put them on such notice. [504D] 5.(d) In a case where the defendants are seeking ouster on account of denial, they have asserted that title coupledwith joint possession and enjoyed ment to possess and enjoyment and enjoyment in the lawful custody and possession, the same is not entitled under any right of management or worship according to Hindu Law.

The respondent was allotted a railway quarter of a suitable type and as he refused to occupy those quarters he was not entitled under the rules to any house rent allowance. The appellant, who was employed in the Railway Quarter, claimed that the house rent allowances were not included in "wages" within the meaning of section 2(vi) of the Act. The Authority appointed under section 15(1) of Act allowed the respondent 's claim for house rent Allowance as part of his wages. The Tribunal held that the appellant was entitled to withhold the house Rent allowance and that the respondent had been allotted a suitable quarter of suitable type, but it did not grant him any house allowance. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The terms of the contract between the employer and the employee contemplate that an employee posted at one of those places would cease to be entitled to house rent as allowance and then allowance thus ceases to be "wages". Once an employee is offered Government quarters for his accommodation he ceases to belong to him. He continues to be governed by the terms of contract. The rules do not make the grant in such absolute terms. (ii)The rule does not make any grant in the absolute terms contemplated the grant of house rent, allowance and it continues to cease to exist if the rules in terms contemplated a grant in that absolute terms; but once an employee transferred at one place would be entitled only to house rents allowance and the rule does no make the payment in such terms. The rule does neither make the granting in such general terms nor makes any grant of houses rent allowance to every employee of a particular category but the rules do no make it the grant In such absolute term. (iii)The rules do neither make any payment in the general terms contemplated by the contract of employment including regular attendance, good work or conduct and his other behaviour in terms of that definition. The Rules do not provide for any such employee to be transferred at any one of these places. The fact that he is offered to the employer would not create any absolute right in the employee to the house rents allowances. (iv)The Rules do no more require an employee to relinquish his vested rights. Once an appointment is offered, it ceases to exist and he continues to remain entitled to the same. The terms and conditions of service of an employee are governed by section 7(2)(b) and section 11 of the .

The detenus were detained under section 3(1) of the (for short COFEPOSA) by the State Government on February 16, 1980. The grounds of detention were served on them on March 25, 1980 and were actually received by the detenus on April 3, 1980 copies were received by them from the State Governments under their letters covering their letter dated March 31, 1980, and were allegedly received by those detenus after undue delay on April 23, 1980 in supplying the copies to the detenu. The detenus made a written request to the detaining authority on February 18, 1980 for supply of copies of the statements and documents relied upon in the grounds of the detention, to enable them to make an effective representation against their detention. On March 25.1980, the State Govt. passed an order under section3(1), directing the release of the copies of certain statements and papers relied upon by the detenu on April 4, 1980 at a later date. The petitioners challenged the validity of the order of detention on various grounds: (i) that the detaining authorities had not considered the representation made to them in time; (ii) that there was unreasonable delay in supplying copies of all the documents and documents which were relied upon or referred to in the "grounds" served on the detenus after considerable delay. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The detention order was vitiated by the infraction of constitutional imperative that in addition to the supply of the documents, the copies were supplied to the detenus before undue delay could be held with a view to preventing those persons from making an effective and effective representation. [352C D] 2. The detaining authority had not applied its mind to the nature of the contents of the statement and documents, which were entirely in favour of the detenus and the full texts of which have been completely in favour thereof. It was on this short ground that the detention order could not be sustained. [353D E] 3. The delay of more than a month in supplying of the basic materials and documents to the petitioners after undue delays on the direction of the Central Government, had vitiated the detention. [351F G] 4. The failure to supply the copies did not vitiate the detention because the concerned Minister of the State was not at all responsible for the delay. [349D E]. 5. The order of the detaining Authority without applying its mind cannot be sustained on the ground that it was passed after undue delayed period on April 16,1980.

The respondent was tried for offences under sections 302, 307 and 324 read with section 149 I.P.C., and section 307 read with Section 34 I. P.C. The trial court acquitted all the accused persons jointly. On appeal by the State, the High Court held that the joint appeal to be maintainable under section 419 of the Code was against the maintainability of a joint appeal by several accused persons directly. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that (i) the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the code as disclosed by these sections and particularly by section 419 is against the competence of a Joint appeal by various accused persons tried jointly; (ii) the High court held such a joint trial as disclosed in section 419, to be invalid in law was not binding on it. HELD : The Full Bench decision holding a joint suit against several accused person tried jointly and acquitted at a joint prosecution has also to be held not to be contrary to any provision of the C.P., Code on which the High Courts seems to have relied in support of the non maintainability of one appeal by other than the State against an order acquitting several persons convicted at a Joint trial, is valid in law. [258 B] (iii) The question of competency of a separate appeal by two accused persons against each accuses and acquitted only at a preliminary stage does not arise for consideration. The question whether joint appeal should be heard on the merits has also been rightly decided by this Court in Rabari Ghela Jadav 's case.

The assessee was a firm called O.R.M.SP. Firm which was registered under section 26(A) of the 1922 Act and was assessed to income tax on remittances received from the foreign business. The assessee filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who dismissed the appeal holding that in the case of business carried on in foreign territory the business of the assessee must be held to be charged under the 1918 Act but only receipts received from foreign business itself. In the reference, the High Court held that the foreign firm was liable to tax under the 1922Act because the assessee was merely taxed on remittances which was received by the assessee from foreign trade and not the foreign income. The High Court accordingly answered both the questions in favour of the Department. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : (1) The assessee was entitled to relief under section 25(3) only to income on which the tax was payable under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918. [912 D] (2) In the context of these facts the foreign trade business of a assessee must necessarily be held not to be chargeable under the provisions of the 1918Act but the foreign company itself. The exemption under section 15(3), therefore, cannot be extended to income from property owned by the foreign partnership firm which was discontinued in the year of account. [977 E] (3) In view of the fact that the assessee is entitled to the relief under Section 25(1) only on income which the taxes were chargeable at any time under the 1961 Act, the tax is payable by an assessee if the business is one in respect of which tax was charged at anytime under the 1939 Act.

The respondent, a public works contractor entered into an agreement with the appellant for manufacture and supply of bricks to the Department for the construction of the Capital Project. The appellant received payment for the same in accordance with the agreed rates. Clause 9 of the contract provided that the contractor shall be responsible for all payments made by him to the department. Clause 10 provided that if during the aforesaid period, the contractor fails to complete the work and deliver the materials within the stipulated time, the Department may have inspected and approved the materials, stacked or placed in such position as may be pointed out to him. Clause 11 provided that where the contractor does not complete the works within the time specified therein, the department shall pay to the Government a sum equivalent to the amount of the value of materials supplied by the contractor. Clause 12 provided for payment of compensation for any loss that may accrue on account of the collection of materials or engagements entered into. Clause 13 provided for the payment of interest at 6% per annum on the amount due from the contractor and the contractor was also entitled to forfeit his security deposit and shall have no claim for any compensation for loss that might accrue on the account of such collection. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the transaction. The High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee holding that the transaction envisaged by the contract entered into by the appellant with the Public Works Department of the Government was a works contract. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (1) that the contract was a work contract and not a works contracts; (2) that in any event, the contract could not be said to have been entered into for the purpose of carrying out the work; (3) that there was no evidence to show that the respondent had taken part in the execution of the work. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The contract in this case is a works Contract and not an works contract; (4) that it was understood that it is understood that the appellant would take into account the free supply of earth for making bricks. Clause 18 of the agreement provides that if at any time during the period of his contract, the Contractor fails to carry out the terms of the specifications or supplies materials required for the purposes of the execution thereof, he shall be deemed to have committed a breach of the Contract and shall forfeit his deposit and would have no claims for any damages for any losses that may arise on account thereof. Clause 19 provides that in case of failure of the contractor to complete or deliver the work within the specified time, he will be liable to pay interest at 9% per month from the date of completion of the delivery of materials until the contractor has been given a certificate to that effect, but the delivery shall not be considered to have become complete until the Contractor has removed all materials, and shall not have any claim for compensation for such loss. [163G H; 163A] 2. The essence of the contracts was entirely of the respondent. Clause 20 provided for interest at 12% per year on the principal amount due to the contractor from the time when the contract became operative till the date on which the final delivery was given. Clause 21 provided that in cases where the work had been completed before the date fixed for delivery, the rate of 10% shall be payable by the respondent to the State Government at the rate specified in the contract. Clause 22 provided that no claim or claims made by the Contractor for increased rates on the grounds that the market or other rates included in the Contract were incorrect or deficient shall be considered only after the contractor had inspected and certified, the said articles if during such period as may he named by the Executive Engineer or his Assistant. Clause 23 provided for compensation to be paid by the State to Department at the rates specified in clause 22. Clause 24 provided that all the necessary arrangements of raw materials, water, coal, labour etc.

The petitioner, a member of the Legislative Assembly of Jammu and Kashmir, was elected to the Lok Sabha on 26th June, 1975. The petitioner challenged the validity of the Proclamation of Emergency issued on March 25, 1975 by the President of India on the ground that the duration of the House of People (Extension of Duration) Act, 1976 had ceased to be in operation on 26.8.1975 because the resolutions passed by both Houses of Parliament approving the Proclamation were not in force at the expiration of two months from the date on which each of them was issued as the resolution of the Lok Assembly and the time when the resolutions were moved in each of the two Houses of the Parliament. The validity of these resolutions was challenged by the petitioner on various grounds, namely: (i) that the Proclamation had been validly issued under the proviso to clause (2) of Article 352 of the Constitution; (ii) that even though the said Proclamations were validly issued, the Proclamation was in operation only when a Proclamation of emergency was in force under the Proviso to clause(2) and since the two Proclamsations had been duly published in the official Gazette. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The Proclamation of the Assembly dated March 25.6.1975 was valid till it stood during the relevant time had not been published in official Gazette and therefore Parliament was entitled to extend the period of the house of People for a period not exceeding one year. [401B C] 2.1 The Proclamation dated 3rd December, 1971 was issued by the Vice President acting as President of the India in the year 1977. The period of five years (being the period for which the Houseof the People may, under clause (b) of article 352 of Constitution) continued from the dates appointed for its first meeting in relation to the present House of the People could be extended for a further period not exceed one year and that even if either of the said proclamation had ceased or ceased to operate before the expiration thereof, it was not open to the President to extend it beyond one year on the expiry of the term of the period. [442E F] 2(a) The Proclamation issued on 3rd January, 1972 was valid only when the House was in existence at the time appointed for the first meeting and the date of the resolutions was duly approved by the two houses of Parliament. [441F G] (b)(i) The validity or otherwise of the Procluamations of Emergency had to be decided on the basis of the resolution passed by the Houses of both the Houses. [444G H] (ii)(a) There is no provision in the Constitution which provides that the period during which the Proclamation has been issued shall continue from the appointed date for its second meeting. The effect of the provisions of Article 359(1) is that the President acting under the said proviso to Clause (2), after considering the views of both Houses, may extend the time for a shorter period not less than one year in relation thereto. [443G H; 443A] (iii)(b) There was no provision similar to clause 3 of Article 356 of the constitution which provides for the extension of the duration during which a Proclamation has already been issued. The President acting on the advice of both House of Parliament and the period when the resolution was moved in one of the Houses, had not expired before the expiry thereof. [44E F; 443C] (iv) The two Pro clamations namely, the extension to the duration for which they were duly revoked by the three Proclemations of emergency had also to be published in their official Gazette, and the last date for the issue of the orders was not fixed.

The appellant filed a suit for declaration that the said premises were private property and for an order setting aside the said decision. The trial court decreed the suit in favour of the appellant holding that the premises constituted a temple within the meaning of the Madras Act 19 of 1951. The High Court, however, held that the property was not a public temple as defined by Madras Act 20 of 1951 and that the question whether it was a private or a public one could have no market value and therefore was incapable of valuation. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The subject matter of dispute is the private property of the said family capable of alienation, the High Court ought to have valued the property accordingly though according to the respondents the property belonged to the said Family and that it was alienable property. [157 D] (ii) The question whether the property in question constituted a public or a private temple could have any market value is one of fact depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case. It is not necessary for the High Courts to decide the application for leave under article 133(1)(a) and (b). [157 E] (iii) The appellant 's case was that in execution of the decree in suit No. 650 of 1882 passed against the said Kuppaiyan, the property had been declared a public religious worship and that therefore capable of valuation as it would in the case of an ordinary suit on a valuation made by him therefor. [158 D] The subjectmatter of dispute was the private properties of the family capable Of alienation, and therefore incapable of valuation.

The appellant, a railway employee, was employed by the respondent company as a clerk in the category of clerks. He was paid Rs. 1,000/ per day and Rs. 2,000 per month respectively. The appellant claimed that he should be given cash allowance in lieu of the tiffin arrangements made at present by the appellant. The Tribunal held that the practice started by the appel lant was not based solely on humanitarian grounds and the appellant was entitled to cash allowance for the same. On appeal, the High Court set aside the award and directed that the clerical staff should be paid in lieu thereof.
