In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Tribunal had erred in law in making an award in respect of the cash allowance; (ii) the award was contrary to the provisions of the Factories Act, 1948, and (iii) the workmen were entitled to a cash allowance. HELD: The Tribunal has overlooked the fact that the re employment of retired persons was mainly inspired by humanitarian considerations. It is in the light of these facts that the question posed by the respondents 's demand must be considered. [572 G] The history of the relations between the parties coupled with the prevailing practice in comparable concerns in the region strongly supports the view taken by the Tribunal that in the appellant 's concern it was an implied condition of service which cannot be ignored. [573 C D] (iii)(a) The question posed is whether the appellant is introducing a wage structure in respect o f the reemployed personnel which is definitely inferior to the wage structure devised for the employees of the respondent, and so, the question referred to the Tribunal was not pressed before it. [574 B] (b) The fact that some employees who had retired might have found it difficult to maintain themselves and their families, the appellant cannot be blamed for denying them the benefit of cash allowance on the ground that only 4 cases of re employment which could be ignored were brought to its notice.

The respondent was a subscriber to the State Railway Provident Fund. He elected to be governed by the Provident Fund Sterling Accounts Rules whereunder payment of the provident fund credited in his account in sterling was remitted to the Westminster Bank, Birmingham. The Union of India then applied for removal of attachment on the ground that the money represented provident fund and was immune from attachment under the law and that the attachment was "illegal and without jurisdiction". The Union Government applied to the High Court for a revision of the order passed by the executing court. The High Court confirmed the order. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Courts were in error in holding that the amount in the hands of the Reserve Bank of India was exempt from attachment and the money must be deemed to have been paid out to the subscriber of the Provident fund. [30E] (ii) The respondent was not a trustee for the subscriber, nor had sanctioned payment to the Reserve bank. He was a trustee of the Railway Administration for Browne. The Bank had no authority to receive payment on his behalf. The respondent had merely an interest to maintain the application for removal and not till then. [31F] (iii)The High Court was in error In holding that by sending the two cheques to the Bank draft and later to the Southminster bank, B.irmingam, the respondent was the agent of Browne, the ReserveBank of India had no power to receive the money on his own behalf. [32G] (iv)The respondent 's contention that the moneys were not liable to be attached under the Act and that he was entitled to recover the amount from the Bank by way of a demand draft or credit in sterling is without substance. The fact that the respondent had no interest to receive it on his account does not make him an agent of the Bank as the agent.

The appellant, a pump manufacturing enterprise, issued a notice terminating the services of its workmen under a standing order like cl.17(a) in the present case, issuing a notice ending the employment, stating that information regarding tenders was being passed on by the workman 's pay as authorized by the relevant Standing Orders. The Labour Court held that the action taken by the management amounted to retrenchment simpliciter and dismissed the appellant 's appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the termination of services of the workmen under standing order namely cl. 17(a), in the circumstances, amounted to a dismissal simpliciter; (ii) the action regarded as punitive was not a colourable exercise of power by the employer and therefore the Industrial Tribunal had jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination; and (iii) the form of the notice terminating services of an employee under standing orders like cl.(17(b), in that background, the appellant had no locus standi to meet the charge. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of termination simpliciter was not one of dismissal as it was a colourable exercising of power vested in the management or as a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice. [403 C] 2.1 The order terminating services was not an order simpliciter and the order did not amount to one of discharge simpliciter, if in reality it came to the conclusion that the termination was a camouflage. It was not based on any evidence, nor was the result of a misreading of the material evidence, or was the results of a misadventure or unfair trade practice. The form of notice terminating service was therefore, loath to interfere with a finding of fact recorded by the trial Court on this point. [406 D] 2(a). In the instant case, the action was held to be bonafide and the overall unsuitability led to a loss of confidence in the employee. It is needless to say that the employer must disclose to the court the grounds of his impugned action so that the same may be judicially tested. [409 E] (b) The power of the Tribunal to intervene, set aside or set aside an order of dismissal simpliciter, is loath to interfered with a view of good faith of the employer. If the exercise of such power is challenged on the ground of being colourable exercise or as an attempt of victimisation, unfair labour practices it would have the jurisdiction to interfere and set down the order so that it may be legally tested. But if the exercise is challenged, on the grounds which led to the order, look at the substance and set them fight, then the Tribunal can go behind the form Of the order. [504 F G] (c) The Tribunal was satisfied that the order of discharge was not genuine or mala fide or an act of victimisation. It would have been free if it had sufficient material and if so advised, to proceed against the workman for misconducts or on othergrounds valid in law. If such a finding is based on no evidence, the employer should disclose to him the grounds thereof. [404 C] (d) The order does not amount merely to one dismissal as by way of punishment but also to dismissal simpliciter. It does not create any stigma. It only provides that the employee shall be deemed to have been dismissed from service. If it is shown that the authority had lost confidence in him, it would be open to the employer to proceed with the enquiry against the employee for misconduct or on anothergrounds. [405 D] (e) The appellant ' has not filed a counter affidavit and the counsel for the Union and the Counsel for the respondent agreed that the impugned action was treated as punitive.

The petitioners, who were the victims of a serious breach of duty cast upon them to see over the safe functioning of the camp, filed writ petitions in this Court challenging the validity of the notifications issued by the State Government under section 3(1) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the State would not approach the matter not with the spirit of a litigant in any adversy action but would look upon the proceedings as a participatory exploration for relief to the victims. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (1) the State should have taken up the issue and its recommendations in regard to the norms for conduct of the 'eye Camp ' intended to extend facilities of expert Ophthal surgical services to the residents of the town; (2) the report of the sub committee of the Indian Medical Council may be consid ered by the Union Government for incorporation in their Revised Guidelines dated 9.2.1988; and (3) the guidelines for conduct and management of eye camps have been issued earlier and updated. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court HELD: 1.1 The State would approach the court not with its spirit and limited scope of proceedings no appeal could be made to the doctrine of State action. [255E] 2.2 The State will approach the issue not withthe spirit of the concept of State actions. It is unfortunate that some points made in the Report and Recommendation of the Sub Committee of the U.P. Government for incorporated in their revised Guidelines dated September 9, 2002 have been updated and revised. These matters would have to be gone into in the criminal and other proceedings that may be pending or in the contemplation of the Government. [256F] 2.(a) The State shall approach the Court not with these aspects. It will look upon all the proceedings that might be pending and in the pendency of the writ peti tion, the factual foundations laid before the Court and the limited scope for the proceedings no appeals could be make to the Doctrine of State Action. [257A] (b) The victims should be afforded some monitary relief by the Government, and on humanitarian consideration, the victims should also be afforded an monetiitary relief.

The Assam Rashtrabhas Prachar Samiti (Taking over management and Control) Ordinance, 1984 was promulgated by the Legislative Assembly of Assam. The Act provided for temporary transfer of management and control of the affairs and properties and properties of the Samiti to a Board. Section 3 of the Act empowered the State Government to make rules for regulating the administration and control and management of the Rashtrabi Prahahas Samchar Samiti. Sub clause (ii) of this sub clause provided that the Ordinance shall extend to all areas over which the Asom Rashtra bhas Prahachar Samiti had its jurisdiction immediately before the commence ment of the Ordinance by a Notification No. Act XXIII of 1984. The respondent No. 1, who was the Chairman of the Board, filed an application under Section 3(1) of the Assam Rahabhas Samachar Samiti (taking over management of Sthals and Control), Ordinance, 1985 for temporary injunction restraining the State from taking any steps to restore the Society back to its elected authorities and office bearers. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the Act was not intended to be a temporary measure and that it was only an enabling provision which could have been made by the Legislature in view of the provisions of Article 230 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the State it was contended that: (1) the Act did not provide for temporary transfers of management or control of any Rashtrabarbhas and therefore the Samiti was being run by its members having elected by a notification dated 1st October, 1984; (2) the provisions contained in Section 3 were intended to have retrospective effect from 1st November, 1984 when the Ordinance came into force; (3) the State had no desire to restore it back to the Society but had been taking over the management of Rashtraha Prachar Samachar Samitis and Control Ordinance,1984 and therefore there was no mala fide action of the then Chief Minister of Assam in taking over management. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "asom Rabhabhas" is used in the context of what was contemplated in that Act and not in the light of the provi sions of Article 19(1)(c) of th e Constitution. [171B C] 2. The word "asam Rabhabi Prachar" has been used in a sense which implies that the persons forming the Association have also the right to continue to be associated with only those whom they voluntarily admit in the Association. It is therefore clear that even on the basis of the Proouncement of the constitution Bench, the Government has no desire tain to restore its Society back and properties to the Samiti from the Board or the State Govern ment. [172G H] 3. The words "asmuch as Rabha Bi Prachar Samitis" in section 3 of Act No. XXIII of1984 are used in different senses. It would be clear that though the Act talks of a temporary measures coming to an end, the elected byabasthapika and Byabastha Pika Sabha which were functioning in 1984 has come to an ad hoc measure and byabakaparpika Sabha duly elected by its Members and all the functions, properties and affairs of the Society are taken over by this Board and it is further directed that the authorities appointed by the Board shall restore back all assets and properties belonging to the Committee. [173H; 173A] 4.

The appellant, a Hindu widow, made a gift of the four houses at Asansol in favour of her daughter and son in law. The gift was later confirmed on the occasion of the marriage itself, which was performed on May 10, 1940, some two years after the marriage. The deed of gift was actually executed and registered on March 10, 1941, some one year after the death of Kamala Devi, under the evil advice of her father and son, in law, the gift was subsequently confirmed on March 11, 1940. The appellant contended that the gift being of a reasonable portion of the estate of Ram Kishori Lal Sao and in pursuance of an ante nuptial agreement made by Sumitra Devi at the time of the final settlement of the marriages, the gifts were also given to her as her share on partition; thirdly, it was suggested that Sumitra Devi got an absolute right in the properties given to herself as her daughter, Kamala Devi. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court affirmed the decree. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) that the appellant had no right of alienation from the point of view whether Sumitra Devi was competent to make a gift under section 14 of the Hindu Law; (ii) that in view of the said provisions the plaintiffs respondents were not entitled to the reliefs which they claimed. The mere fact that the gifts made by her and the acceptance of such a gift by Nand Lal, father in law of Kamala Kumari, were not valid in Hindu law, did not make any gift at the stage of the execution and registration of the deed of gifted; (iii) that under section 15 of the Indian , the gift made to the daughter was not competent to be acted upon. The fact that Sumitra had been given a life time to her daughter as marriage was not sufficient to make it a gift, did no affect the validity of the gift in view Of section 14(1)(a). (iv)that the gift by way of a gift made at the instance of the appellant was not valid and valid in law; and (v) that there was no consideration, nor any discussion of the texts bearing on the question, and the learned Judges did not consider the alienation from point of the view that the marriage of the daughter had been a religious duty and the promise to make gift to the appellant as her son was a religious obligation flowing from the ante n uptial agreement.

The appellant, a candidate for election to the Punjab Legislative Assembly, was declared elected. The respondent filed an election petition in the High Court challenging the election of the first respondent on the ground that he had got circulated pamphlets and posters among the voters of the constituency which he had mentioned that Ruplal had withdrawn his candidature and any vote given to him (Tej Singh) would be deemed to be a vote for Ruplals. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the allegations of corrupt practices indulged in by the appellant were proved beyond reasonable doubt, and therefore, the election was set aside. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the allegation of corrupt practice as alleged by the first Respondent (Teji) was established beyond reasonable doubts and that the charges of corrupt conduct had been proved beyond doubt. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The allegations of the corrupt practices were established beyond doubt and that would have doubt materially altered the result of the election would have also materially altered its result. [419B] 2.2 In view of the very narrow margin of votes (123) between Tej Singh and Avtar Singh, a strong presumption and possibility that the votes polled in favour of Tej Singh would be considered as a vote given by Rupllal but at the instance of Tej singh, a grave presumption and probability that the voters who would have voted for Ru plal would now cast their votes in favour. [420B] 3.1 In view thereof, the irresistible inference and inescapable conclusion that can be arrived at that is that Tej Singh had actually paid for the posters which were printed at his instance and Rup Lal was not collected with the printing of the posters by Tej Singh. The inference and inevitable inference would have been materially altered. [406B] 4.2 The High court has rightly held that the appellant has proved beyond a reasonable doubt that Tej singh had indulged in corrupt practices particularly when the printing by the posters were circulated by him along with the return of expenses incurred during his election campaign which was verified by him to be true and correct.

The appellant was a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal. He was then the Chief Minister of the State. In his application for contempt, he alleged that one Shri Devinder Sharma was a forest Minister in Council of the Council headed by him and that he was not a fit person to be appointed as a Forest Officer. The High Court dismissed the application on the ground that no punishment was imposed on the respondent by the High Court in exercise of its jurisdiction under the Act. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have power or authority to punish for contempt. When the High court does not impose any punishment on the alleged contemnor, the High Cou rt cannot be said to be exercising its jurisdiction or power as conferred by Article 215 of the Constitution. [893B] 2.2 In a contempt proceeding there is only two parties, namely, the Court and the contemnor. It may be one of the reasons which weighed with the Legislature not in conferring any right of appeal on the petitioner for contempt; the High Courts cannot exercise its jurisdiction by punishing for contempt.[894C D] 3.1 Section 19(1) of the Act only when the High Curt erroneously acquits a contemnor guilty of criminal contempt, the court can exercise its jurisdic tion or power to punish. When no punishment is imposed by the Court, the contemnor, who has been punished for contempt is made in the exercise of jurisdiction to punish, for contempt and not that any contempt has been committed by the alleged contemner and acquits him. [994C E] 2.(a) The High Court cannot exercise jurisdiction under Article 215 or power of contempt. It does not even mean that when a court is conferred with the power or jurisdiction to act in a particular manner, the exercise thereof will involve the power of the High Commis sioner and power as given by Article 216 conferring jurisdiction or powers on the High courts to punish contempt. [794D E] (b) The jurisdiction of the Court to punish is discretionary and not appellate. It is for the first time under that provision that the High Power Court can exercise it. In such a case there would be no right of appeals under section 19(I) of t he Act, a person interested in maintaining the dignity of the court will not be without any remedy. [820E F] (c) The power to punishing for Contempt is discretionary.

The appellant, a tenant of the respondent, was let out to the respondent for a period of ten years. The rent note provided that the lessee would pay the rent at the rate of Rs. 100 per month and that he would not be entitled to any compensation for the period of the lease. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant on the ground that the rent note was invalid before the lease could be terminated, that the lease was therefore determined under section 111(g) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, and not under section III (g) as amended by 1929, and that the tenancy was therefore determinable under section 112(g). The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the provision in the rent notes was not applicable to the case of the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the amendment made in 1929 to section 111 (g), as amended, did not affect the rights of the tenant and that no notice as required by section 111 had been given. HELD : The High Court was fully justified in finding that in the present case the provision as to notice in writing to the lessee of his intention to determine the lease by the lessor bad been given and that could be done by filing a suit for ejectment based on forfeiture of a lease is not based upon any principle of justice, equity or good conscience. The principles of equity are not based on any principle or good faith but merely a procedural rule introduced in the statute with retrospective effect from 1929. [1023 H; 1024 A B] In the present ease the High court was fully right in holding that the provisions as to notices in writing were applicable to leases made prior to 1st April, 1930 and which still govern leases made before 1st May, 1930. The rule embodied a principle of equity is not founded on any principles of justice or good worth, but merely an express intention that he is going to avail of the forfeiture and that can be done in the case.

The appellant was a workman in the respondent No. 2, who was dismissed from service by an order dated 9th February 1970 on the ground that he had failed to give his explanation and that the enquiry held against him was vitiated because no second opportunity was given to him to show cause against the proposed punishment before the issuance of his dismissal order. The Arbitrator gave his award on 9th Feb., 1970 whereby he came to the conclusion that the Enquiry which was otherwise fair and proper was vitiated by not affording him such opportunity. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order on the grounds, inter alia, (1) that the procedure adopted by the Arbitrator was not fair and reasonable; (2) that no second enquiry was held to be invalid because no third opportunity was afforded to the delinquent before inflicting the punishment; and (3) that in the alternative, the High court had confirmed the finding of guilt on the basis of the evidence adduced before it. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The first part of the Standing Order No. 17 provides for giving an opportunity to a workman to offer his explanation. It contemplates giving of a second opportunity to the workman to showcause against the penalty proposed to be inflicted on him. The second part deals only with the punishment of dismissal and not with the second part dealing only with punishment inflicted upon a delinquent holding of a departmental inquiry into the charges in respect of each one of them. [417C D] 2. The High Court has confirmed the view of the Arbitrator that the opportunity spoken by para 3 does not refer to the opportunity to meet the charges but refers to the further opportunity being given to the charged to show causes against the punitive punishment before awarding punishment upon him. [518G H] 3. The language used in the Standing order No.17 is "all orders passed by the Manager or Acting Manager who shall do so after giving the delinquent an opportunity" to offer explanation". It is true that the Arbitrator has undoubtedly taken the view that the second opportunity spoken of by para.3 does not relate to the additional opportunity provided for the first time to show the cause against his proposed punishment and that in any event, the second stage deals only only with those punishments which are mentioned in the last part of paragraph 3. [618D E] 4. The expression "any order" used in para. 3 of the S.O. does not mean a whole or part of an order passed by a Manager or acting Manager who has to do so before giving the employee an opportunity of showing cause against such proposed punishment. It is only when the second or third stage deals with two different stages that the first stage is reached and the second, namely, the first and the third stage is concluded. [719G H; 720A] 5. The word "any" in para 3 of S.S.O., means "all". It does not include a whole of an administrative order passed before giving it to a delinquent employee. The words "any such order" are used in a very wide sense and they are capable of precise interpretation only if the first or second stage is followed by the second and third stages. [819C D; 820A B] 6. The question whether para 3 is mandatory or directory depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. It may be possible to say that the words "all" in a particular context are not intended to cover all cases where the charge against the delinquent employee is proved but they are only illustrative and not exhaustive. [820E F] 7. The object of the rule is to ensure that the disciplinary proceedings are conducted fairly and expeditiously and not arbitrarily or capriciously. It does so as to avoid any possible arbitrary exercise of power by the authorities concerned. [825F G] 8.

The Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969 was amended by Act 35 of 1969. Section 7D of the Kerala Land Reform (Amendment ) Act, 1970 provided that a person shall be deemed to be in continuous occupation notwithstanding any order of court for delivery of possession to another person who had no right over the land or who was not competent to lease the land. The appellant landlord filed an application under section 7D before the Revenue Divisional Officer claiming that he was entitled to continue in possession of the land and that the respondent was a tenant on the date of the amendment. The Revenue Divisional officer rejected the claim holding that the appellant landlord had no interest in the land, and that he had not surrendered his leasehold right to the landlord. The respondent filed an appeal before the Appellate Authority which allowed the appeal holding that he could not be deemed tenants under section 6D of Kerala Land Ceiling Act, 1960. The High Court held that the tenant was entitled for possession of land on the 11th day of April, 1957 and that as the lease was granted by a person who was in occupation of such land on 11th of April 1957, on the basis of an oral permission or an unregistered deed purporting to be a lease deed purporting ted to be the lease deed, he could be deemed tenant if he or his predecessor in interest was continuously in occupation thereof for not less than ten years preceding the 11 th day of May, 1955 or which was unsurveyed on that date. The landlord appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 7 D of the Act is a provision which provides that a tenant shall be entitled to retain possession of any land held by him as a tenant if the court has delivered a judgment or passed an order before the date on which the order of the court declaring the payment as modavaram or modavasam or modumavaram, or modvashtavaram etc. Certain persons who had paid amounts for occupation of land shall be presumed to be tenants notwithstanding anything contained in any law, custom or usage or in any contract, custom, or in some judgment, decree or order of any court, any person who on the11th day April, 1956 was in possession thereof on the 12th day Of April,1957, and was cultivating the nilam after the 11nd day of March, 1957. [112 D E] 1.2 The appellant landlords had no title to the land as they were not tenants within the meaning of section 6A of the Madras Land Reforms Act, 1950. They were in occupation for a period of ten years immediately preceding the 12 th April, 1967 and were cultivating the Nilam at nilam before the commencement of the Tamil Nadu Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1968. The tenant was in continuous possession of such property on the 13th day, April, 1969. [113 D E; 113 A] 1:3 In view of the fact that the lease granted by the appellant landlords was in respect of the Nila tial land and the respondent had not actually surrendered his tenancy right to landlord, but had not really surrendered possession of it before the expiry of the term fixed under the varam Reforms (Second Amendment) Act 1969, the question whether he was a deemed tenant or not would depend upon the facts of each case. [114 E F] 1 :4 The respondent was in actual possession of a part of the property on 11 th April 1957 and was paying rent to the appellant. He had no other right over it.

The appellant was found in possession of the goods on 21 4 1967. The goods were also seized from the custody of the appellant together with the Godrej lock and the keys produced by him together with his Godrejard and the iron lock. The appellant 's case that he had been falsely implicated in this case was that he was dealing with them knowing that the goods were smuggled goods and that the portion in which the boxes were kept was in his exclusive possession with all that was contained in it. The trial court acquitted him but convicted him under section 135(a) and (b) of the Act. On appeal, the High Court held that the appellant had not produced evidence to show that he knew that the articles were smuggled or imported in contravention of the law. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The prosecution was not required to prove that the gold was actually brought into India. It is true that the burden of proving that they were smuggled was on the person from whose possession the goods had been seized. But it was not necessary for the prosecution to establish that the article was smuggled or that it was in contravention with any law. [542G H] 2. The burden of proof that the accused knew that he must have been smuggled or brought into the country without payment of customs duty at a time when payment of such duty had become obligatory, and the onus of proving this fact was on him. [543A B] 3. In the instant case, there was no evidence to enable the prosecution, to come to the conclusion that the appellants knew that they might have placed the boxes or there were some reasons why he should allow them to use the portion reserved by him for himself. The very appearance of the articles and the manner in which they were found, for proving the place from where they were seized, was sufficient to enable it to come into the conclusion whether the goods must have actually been known to the appellant to be smuggled or not. [544G H; 543A] 4. In a case where the goods are not seized under the Act, as provided by section 111 of the , the burden is on the prosecution that the person concerned knew that it had been imported or brought in contravention thereof. The mere possession by the accused of such goods could not enable the Court to come tain that he might have had a chance of getting the benefit of doubt. [535B C] 5. In any case, the appellant was dealing in them knowing them to be smuggling goods without knowing that they are illegally imported or imported into India without payment thereof. It was immaterial that the possession by him of such articles could not be proved. The fact that the persons concerned knew about their origin and recent import did not admit the possession of those goods at all. [541G H, 543A B].

The appellants, who were the President of a registered Association, filed a suit for accounts of the Association. The suits were decreed by the trial court and the appeal was dismissed on the preliminary objection that the suits were not maintainable in view of section 4 Of the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellants had a right to bring a suit against one member of an illegal partnership in respect of the transactions and transactions. They had no remedy against each other to file a suit on the ground of illegality in the contract of partnership on which they sues was compelled to rely so as to make out their right to what he asks. [782 B] (ii) The suit for account must fail. The appellants were not entitled to any relief on the allegations made as the courts could adjudicate in respect thereof only if proceedings are instituted by one member against another in respect Of the partnership transactions and dealings. [779 C D] (iii) The contention that under the , an unregistered firm is not illegal cannot be accepted. It is true that under section 69(3)(a) of the Rewa States Companies Act 1935, a firm must be registered as a company under the Rewa state Companies Act. But, in the present case, the suits for accounts must fail because they were filed by one person who was not entitled. [777 E] (iv) The distinction between an unregistered partnership and an illegal one is that it has no direct compulsion that a firm should be registered if proceedings were instituted by another member of the association. In the present cases, the suit for the accounts must have been filed by two members of the associations who formed the Association in question and it was not a legal Association.

The respondents were charged with offences under section 9(1) read with section 9 (1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution alleged that on 8.6.1986 at 2.0 P.M., they along with two others named in the complaint, shot dead an elephant in compartment No. 1 and another named in it. The trial court acquitted all the respondents but convicted them under section 120B I.P.C. and sentenced them to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year each. On appeal by the State of Bihar, the High Court set aside the order of acquittal and directed issue of process against the accused. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court was persuaded to the view that this was a case to which section 210(1)(a) would not be attracted having regard to the position that cognizance of an offence can only be taken on the complaint of the officer mentioned in that section. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court will be justified in quashing the proceedings in exercise of its powers under section 482 of the Code. [463C] 2.1 In regard to an offence under section 429 IPC, on the facts of this case, it is not possible to explore the possibilities of this contention as indeed there has been no prior conviction and sentence for an offence Under any other law. The test is that taking the allegations and the complaint as they are, without adding or subtracting anything, if no offence is made out then the High Cou rt will be unjustified in quashing proceedings in exercising its powers thereunder. [464D] 2:1. In regard tain to an act alleged to constitute a contempt of court, it would be clear from the language of section 210 (1)(b) that cognizance can only take on the allegation set out in the charge sheet do not constitute any offence and that resort to criminal proceedings would, in the circumstances, amount to an abuse of the process of the Court or not. [465E F] 2(a). The test for determining whether a particular act constitutes an offence is whether it amounts to an attempt to commit a breach of trust. If the allegations are so patently absurd and inherently improbable that no offence can be said to have been committed in respect of a court subordinate to it, then the Court will not be justified to quash the proceedings. [467F G] 2.(b) The test would be whether the ingredients of an act under section 4(1), read with 5(2) of Prevention of Food Adulteration Act are satisfied or not and if no such offence is committed in the facts and circumstances of this particular case, then it would amount to abuse of process of court or not.[465E G] 3.2 The test that is applied by the High Courts is whether the allegations made in the present case relate to the specific act of killing an elephants, al1d that such an offence at all events falls within the overlapping areas between sec 42 and section 210 IPC on the one hand and 9(l) read along with 50(l). [465F G H] 3.(c) The High Courts have not committed any error in quashing a proceeding in exercise o f its powers Under Section 482 of Cr. P.C., even if no case is made Out then the high Court will, therefore, be justified In regardto an act or omission alleged to constitutes such offence. [446G H] 4.3 The High Cou nal has not committed a manifest error in passing the impugned order. [461B C] 5.1.

The petitioner was convicted by the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Meerut for offences under sections 363 and 366 I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years. The petitioner filed an appeal before the High Court which dismissed his appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that: (i) the poor accused has to fall back on touts and professional sureties; (ii) the rich as well as the poor are priced out of their liberty in the justice market, is the grievance of the Petitioner; (iii) the good is priced down from touts, and professional surety cannot be conditioned to attend at the appointed place; (iv) the court should always bear in mind that monetary bail is not a necessary element of the criminal process and even if the amount of bail fixed by the Magistrate is not high, for a large majority of those who are brought before the courts in criminal cases are so poor that they would not abscond, he can safely release the accused on his own bond without sureties; and (v) the petitioner has obtained an order for bail in his favour. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The court should normally bear in view of the liberal interpretation of bail covering personal freedom and indigent sections of society in general and in particular, socialist republic with social justice. [785B] 2. In a case the poor person accused is fleeced of his moneys by touts or professional sureties and sometimes has even to incur debts to make payment to them for securing release; in one case the rich accused is bailed out on bail, i.e., surety. [886C D] 3. The best guarantee of the court is the reach of the law not the money tag. It cannot be that an accused should ordinarily be released on his personal bond without bail or on his behalf bond. [783F G] 4. In order to read as 'bail ', it must be understood that monetary Bail is not the only deterrent and there are other factors which are sufficient deterrents against flight. The Court in its socialist Republic with social Justice has a power in the court to reject a surety because he or his estate is situate in a different district or State ? There is already a direction for grant of bail by this Court in favour of the appellant and so, the merits of that matter do not have to be examined now. [784H; 785A B] 5. The discretion to release an accused on bail or his own bonds without monetary sureties or financial security and release on his bond is a very wide power which must be exercised with care and caution. It is not necessary for the court in this case to consider whether in itssocialist republic, with socialism, individual freedom and economic justice, individual liberty and indigent considerations like family ties, roots in the community and roots in society, roots of stable organizations should prevail even if they are so weak that they will not abscond. [789C D; 786A B C] 6. The courts have to bear in regard to socialist countries with socialistic republic, social justice, and individual freedom. It must be remembered that the criminal law is a socialist democratic republic.

The assessee, a company carrying on business in the name of Eldee, was incorporated in the Indian Woollen Textile Mills Ltd. (Trading) Ltd., which was an industrial undertaking conducted in the names of its two partners with a share of /2/two annas each and one annas each. The Income tax Officer, Special Circle Amritsar, assessed the assessee 's income to include the amount advanced to 'Castle Manufacturers ' by the two undertakings, but the Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim. On appeal, the Tribunal modified the assessment and directed in clusion of the amount so advanced to the 'CTHle Manufacturers. The High Court also refused to state the case on the ground that no question of law arose. In appeal to this Court it was contended by the assessee that (i) the finding of the Tribunal was one of fact as it was based upon some evidence to support the finding; and (ii) the Appellate Tribunal had erred in arriving at its finding. HELD: The High court has the power merely to advise the Tribunal on questions of law arising out of the order of the tribunal. It is not open to the Court to reject the Tribunal 's finding of fact, if there is some evidence on which it can be regarded as a finding not giving rise to a question liable to be referred to the court. [440 F] The High Courts have the power to call upon the Tribunal to state a case and refer to it if it, if the Appellate Authority has refused to specify the case in its view. If the Tribunal has arrived at a different conclusion, it cannot be regarded a finding of not giving raise a question as having been raised by the Tribunal.

The respondent was a party in the writ petition filed by him against the order of the High Court directing that the Minister concerned might give personal hearing to the parties and thereafter pass necessary orders in the matter. The Minister concerned heard the parties, but did not file his affidavit. On February 18, 1975, the Minister made an order fixing the seniority of the engineers ned. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High court challenging the validity of the said order on the ground that the allegations made in the amended petition do not disclose any personal animus against the Minister and as such the High Commis sion was vitiated. The High Court dismissed the writ peti tion. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the respondent that (i) the Minister should file his personal affidavit; (ii) the Secretary of the Department had acted in a manner which amounted to violation of the principles of natural justice and (iii) the High Courts were wrong in directing that he be impleaded as a party. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order made by the High Cate General for the State of Punjab was not vitiated because it did not disclose anything personal animus on the part of the Minister. [97B] 2. The direction for impleading of the minister as a respondent is given by the Court with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegations in the petition. It is essentially for the Minister to decide in the light of the allegation made in his petition as to whether he should or should not file an affidavit. [98C] 3. The directions for impleading the Minister as a Respondent are not necessary or proper party, this Court should not interfere in the order made.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. The rent was due as arrears of rent on the basis of a lease in favour of the respondent. The respondent filed an application under section 259 of the Act for realisation of a sum of Rs. 64950 from the appellant, which was due to him as arrears. The trial court dismissed the application. On appeal by special leave the High Court held that the amount was due on the ground that the rent in favour Of the respondent was not claimable by the Board under section 260 of the Punjab Municipal Act (III of 1911) and therefore the suit was not maintainable. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the proceedings before the Magistrate were not one under the Code of Criminal Procedure and, therefore, no reference could be made by the Sessions Judge to the High court under section 438. HELD: The words "rent on land and buildings" in section 259 must also be construed as "any tax", and the word "any other money" must be construed accordingly. [259 B] In the present case the rent was not claimed or recoverable under any express provision of the statute. The High Court had no power to recover rent from the respondent on an application made by it even under the Act or the Rules. [260 C D] The words 'rent on lands and buildings ' in section 260 refer only to rent in the section refers only to rents payable by a Board etc. and not to any other money claimable under the provisions of the , and, consequently, action for recovery could be taken under section 258 of the Code.

The appellant was appointed as a Section Salesman in the respondent company. He was appointed on 12th July, 1973 and was confirmed in service by the Managing Director of the Company. The appellant challenged his termination before the Labour Court which held that the termination was illegal. The Labour Court held that it was not a "workman" and that the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act were not aplicable and the reference was incompetent. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Labour court has given findings in favour of the appel lant on the question whether the termination itself was illegal or not. [474B] 2.2 The finding of the Tribu nal on the nature of the work is a finding on a question of fact and it is also borne out by the document produced before the labour Court. It is seen from the documents produced before this Court that the appellant was employed to do canvassing and promoting the sale of the product of the company in any particular area or collecting the sale proceeds and depositing the same with the company. The supervising work of the other local salesmen was part of his work considered by the Tribunal as only incidental to his main work of canvassing and promotion in the area of his operation. [473B C] 2.(a) The appellant was engaged for canvassing and selling the product. He had been working as a section Salesman with his head quarters at Bikaner. He worked as a salesman with the head office of the local salesman. He also worked as an employee in the shop of the respondent Company. He did not work as a regular salesman or a local sales man nor the local Salesmen were employed in the place of his business. The supervision and conduct of the appellant is a fact finding on the character of the works. [476D] (b) The supervising and conducting of the various local sales men was part and parcel of his main function of canvassing, promotion and marketing of the products of thecompany. He has to reach and a study of the market condition. He is also required to send reports about the publicity and advertisement and advertisement of placing posters, holders, cinema slides and suggest to canvassed the sale in this area. [477E] (c) The supervision of the sales of the industry was part only incidental and not ancillary to his principal work of procuring orders for the company and promoting sale of products of its operation.

The Company was a Government lessee under section 181 of the M.P. Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, Samvat 2007 (Act No. 66 of 1950) for the purpose of carrying on its business in the Gwalior Dairy Limited. The Company had been granted a lease of the said land to the State Government for a period of 99 years. The company was also granted a licence for running a dairy farm. The lessee applied for renewal of the licence and the Collector, Gwalior, rejected the application. The respondent filed an appeal before the Additional Collector, who dismissed the same on the ground that the Company had not become an ordinary tenant earlier in Madhya Bharat under section 182(2)(i) of the Act No. 67 of 1950. The appellant 's writ petition was dismissed by the High Court holding that the company was not a Government lessees within the meaning of section 181 read with section 2(h) and was, therefore, not liable to be proceeded against in terms of section 182. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Company that the lease granted by the State was not covered by section 181 as it had not became an ordinary tenancy earlier in M. P. State under section 183(2) (i) and, therefore the Company was not liable for eviction. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that in terms sub section 2 of section 180 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue & Tenancy Act Samvat 1977 (Act 67 of 1960), which was the law in force in Madhya Pradesh under which the Company could not be evicted by summary proceeding provided for under that section, the Company has been at all material times a Government lease in respect of the land in dispute at any time prior to the coming into force of the Land Revenue Act. [179G H] 2. The Additional Collector was well justified in having recourse to the proceeding prescribed under section182 of the Code. In view of the fact that subsequent to the withdrawal of the appeal from this Court, fresh terms were agreed upon between the Government and the Company subsequent to its withdrawal from the appeal by the Company, fresh term was agreed upon. [180A] 3. The finding of the High court on the question whether or not the Company is deemed to be holding over under the old lease granted in favour of the State, is contrary to law. [181B] 4. The order of the Additional Commissioner dated 1.10.1977 in Misc. Petition No. 84 of 1978 was, however, set aside by the trial court and the High Curt held that the appellant Company had become an 'pakka ' tenant ' under section 185 of the code. In this view of things, the Additional District Collector was also well justified.

The Orissa Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1965 was passed by the State Legislature in exercise of its powers under article 246(1)(c) of the Constitution. The Act provided for the acquisition of certain lands in an estate and where any land comprised therein is held by a person under his personal cultivation, it shall not be lawful for the State to acquire any portion of such land as was within the ceiling limit applicable to him under any law for the time being in force. The petitioners who were owners of the lands filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the Act on the ground that the provisions of Ch. IV of the Orissa Land Reform (Amendment), 1964, which provided for compensation not based on the market value of the land but at fifteen times the fair and equitable rent was in consistent with article 3 1 A(2) of Schedule I to the Constitution and since the subsequent legislation seeks to restrict the ceiling limits and to vest the surplus land in the Government under section 45 of the Travancore Act 14 of 1124 (M.E.) into force, the notification issued by the Government of the United State was ineffective. The High Court held that the Act did not apply to the petitioners as they were not holders of any rights or interest in the lands and that the notifications were invalid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the provisions contained in Ch. III of the Land Reforms Act 14 Of 1965, which made the notification applicable to the landholders under the principal Act, were inconsistent with article 31(2A) of that Schedule and since they were holders of a personal cultivation of the holder, compensation would not be less than the market price thereof; (ii) the notifications issued by them were invalid as they contravened articles 14 and 19 of the constitution and (iii) the notification was void because it was inconsistent with the provisions Of article 31A. HELD: The notification issued in exercise Of the power under section 1(3) of Act 14of 1965 is not a law in force, but until the power is exercised by the appropriate Government to issue an appropriate notification, the provisions thereof are not applicable to landholders under any laws for the period time being In force. [924 C] The notification dated July 1, 1949 was issued by a notification and was repealed by Act 15 of 1965. It was not extended by a Notification under section I(3). The notification was therefore valid.

The widow of her husband, who was a Hindu widow, acquired the limited interest of a Hindu wife by adverse possession against her prior to the date of surrender and these rights would, in law, endure during the entire period of the widow 's natural life. The widow had no right to challenge it as she could not be surrendered to the reversioner. The question for decision was whether the widow could make a surrender of her estate by a Hindu husband to her husband or his spiritual benefit courts could properly refuse to annex rights to defeat rights to property during the whole period of her natural life, and if the title of such person has been completed, it could not prejudice the rights of persons acquired by grant from the widow. Held, that in case of alienation by a widow of Her husband 's estate, there is no principle of law under which the acts of the reversioner could bind him. The reversionary right of recovering possession of the property during her lifetime on grounds of equity, justice and good conscience in proper cases, is not an alienation but an absolute act on the part of the wife. In the present case, the widow herself was in capable of disputing the title to the estate at all and, therefore, could not, by any question of fraud or collusion that might arise, be in a position to recover possession of her property during his lifetime. The mere fact that the reversioner had no legal or moral obligation to surrender her estate does not detract from her own grant and disputing the alienation which she has made herself.

The appellant, a Director of the respondent Company, was appointed as a Receiver in respect of the Cotton Mills. He made an order under section 149 of the Land Revenue Act read with section 5 of the U.P. Government Electrical Undertakings (Dues Recovery) Act, 1958 appointing a Receiver for the Cotton Mill Company for a period of six months with various powers specified therein and in particular to seize the shares pledged by it. The appellant was appointed a Receiver on behalf of the State Government of Uttar Pradesh. He filed an application under section 169 of the Act before the Collector of Kanpur for appointment of a receiver of the shares of the Polytex Company held by him as a secured creditor. The Collector rejected the application and directed that the sale of the said shares be made in accordance with the order of the High Court. The respondent 's appeal to this Court was dismissed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The attachment of the share in the Poly Mills held by the Cotton Company had lost its right to the shares mortgaged in favour of the Government of U. P. under section 170 of the , and therefore, the sale was not a valid sale. [875F] (2) The order passed by the Collector being an order in the nature of a charging order under the English Law is not the same as an attachment of property or appointment of any Receiver under the Land revenue Act. [ 876A B] (3) The charge against the appellant was that he had lost his right to vote at the meeting of the company since the Cotton Corporation had ceased to enjoy the privileges of a member of the polytex Company in respect thereof. He had lost the right to participate in the meetings of the Company and could exercise its rights under section 171 of the . [876C] (4) The High Court was not justified in holding that the attachment of shares in the poly Mills held on behalf the Cotton mills amounted to a charge under the Indian Income tax Act. The order of Collector being a charging one, it was not open to the appellant to contend that the order passed under section 18AA(1)(a) of the Indian Incometax Act was an order made by the collector of Kanpur in respect Of the shares which had been pledged in favour thereof. [884D] (5) The fact that 3,50,000 shares have been pledged by the Government does not make any difference Sections 172 to 178 A of the deal with the contract of pledge. [874E F] (6) The statement of facts of the above decision itself shows that it has no bearing on the case before this Court.

The petitioners filed a suit in representative capacity under Order 1 Rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure for declaration that they were owners in posses sion of the suit land along with some others, that the Gram Panchayat, Mehal Kalan, Tehsil Barnala, District Sangrur in the State of Punjab had no sort of right in the suit property and that the suit was not maintainable before the civil court. The trial court dismissed the petition holding that the plaintiffs were owners of the land in question and that they had no right or title in it. The petitioners filed an appeal against the order of the Civil Judge, Barnala which was allowed by the Additional District Judge, Sangratur on the ground that the issue involved in the case was merely one of title to the suit lands and that since the question involved in that suit was merely a one of right or interest in it, the civil courts had jurisdiction to try the suit. The High Court held that since there was no specific plea raised by the petitioners in the plaint that the land belonged to them as shamlat deh, it had jurisdiction under section 13 read with section 13 of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961 to try it and accordingly dismissed the revision petition. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court was right in holding that since by virtue of section 13(2) of the Act the civil Courts had jurisdiction over the matter, the jurisdiction of civil courts to try such suits had been taken away by virtue Of section 13 and 13B of the Haryana Village Common Land (Regulation ) Act, 1960. [836C D] 1.2 The High Courts were right in dismissing the revision application. [820E F] 2.1 In the instant case, the plaintiffs who claimed to be the owners along with others of the property in question had not been impleaded as a defendant. They had also questioned the correctness of entries in revenue records which showed that the Panchayat was entitled to the land. The plaintiffs cannot by drawing their plaint cleverly by drawing his plaint clelly by drawing its plaint cleftly by draw his plaint, cleverfully by drawing the plaint clebyly by drawn his plaint. [825E F G] 2(a) In the present case, since the Panchayat had expressly claimed that the property belonged to it as shamat deh, the Civil Court had jurisdiction in the matter. The plaintiff has not claimed that he was entitled or deemed to have been vested in a Panchayat under the Act, nor is there any question of law involved in this case.

The respondent Board issued a notice to the appellant company under Section 49(1) of the Andhra Pradesh Electricity Supply Undertakings (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1976 for recovery of electricity dues from the appellant. The appellant filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the validity of the said notice on various grounds including that the demand of interest was illegal and arbitrary. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the levy of interest on the amount due to the Board under Section 48(1)(a) & (g) of Act is not justified as it does not contain any norm of guideline with regard to framing terms and conditions for supply of electricity and in particular, the demand for payment of interest is illegal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was entitled to continue the benefit of the provisions of Section 49 (1)(b) &(g) as it did not contain a norm of guidelines with regard thereto. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The levy of Interest on the amounts due to Board is illegal and unconstitutional. [278C] 1.2 The levy under section 48(i)(a), (b) and (g), as imposing an unreasonable restraint on the appellant from charging interest at the rate of 3 per cent was made in January 1987. [279D] 1.(a) In the instant case, the Board is clearly in the position of a trustee in respect of this money since the money is deposited by the consumer in trust with the Board to secure the payment of consumption charges. The obligation to pay interest to the consumer under section 49(i) (b), (c) and the conditions on which it is being supplied are statutory, the provisions under the Act to determine the conditions upon which supply is to be made. [280E] 1(b) In a case where the Board has been directed to allow interest at a rate of 12% per annum on the security deposit, the appellant cannot be said to be unreasonable and the consumer would not be entitled to continuation of the energy under section 4(2)(g). [278F G] 2.1 It is well settled that the power conferred by Section 49 is discretionary and has to be exercised in a reasonable manner. The discretion must be exercised judicially, reasonably and in accordance with law. [276G H] 1:2 In the present case, there was no order of this Court directing payment of any amount liable to be paid by the appellant to the Electricity Board as the liability of the Board for violation of any conditions of supply in the context of wide scale theft deposit being condition precedent for the supply of energy. [277F G]. 2.2 In a writ application filed under Article 226 of the Constitution, this court has been conferred with statutory power under Section 50(1). The challenge to the validity or otherwise of the notice issued by the Board on the ground that the Board had no authority to levy interest is not tenable because in the nature of contract it is liable to pay the interest.

The petitioners are members of the Telecommunication Research Centre under the Telecommunications Department. They were recruited through the Union Public Service Commission for recruitment to the various cadres in the TeleCommunications and Telegraph Department which is directly under the control of the P&T Board of the Ministry of Communications, Government of India. The petitioners belong to the Indian Telecommen tion Service Group A and Group B Field Officers who are working in the Telecom Research Centre as Assistant Directors and S.T.Os Grade I respectively with effect from 1.1.1973. They are also members of a Joint Cadre of the Central Secretariat Service Group B and Group C officers who are directly under that Department. The direct recruits to which the petitioners belong were not given Special Pay. The respondents in these petitions, who are presently working as Assistant Director and S, Grade I in the Indian Telecom Research Institute, have been denied the Special Pay on account of the irregular implementation of the rules of promotion contained in the Recruitment Rules. The Union Public Services Commission, by its letter dated 13.9.1984, recommended for granting Special Pay to the petitioners who belong to this category. The said recommendation was rejected by the Government on the ground that the petitioners were not eligible and were not able to discharge their duties. The writ petitions filed in the High Court challenging the validity of the aforesaid order were dismissed by a Single Judge of the High court. In these appeals, it was contended for the petitioners that the denial of Special Pay is sought to be justified by the Union Government in the counter affidavit filed by Shri C.L. It was submitted that the discrimination between direct recruits and the transferred officers regarding the payment of Special pay which is granted to the trans ferred officers who were directly under this Department, is attempted to be justify by the State Government in their Counter Affidavit filed by the Association on the petitioners (direct recruits) who are specifically recruited to the Tele Communication Research Centre in the Union of India discharge same functions and discharging the same functions as the petitioners. It is contended that the Special pay to the extent of Rs. 150 per month in addition to their pay scales in the grades of Deputy Director, Assistant Director, and S Grade I was being given Special pay of Rs 150 per day in addition thereto in the grade of Deputy Directors, Assistant Directors, and Assistant Director respectively with effects from 1st January 1973. The claim of the petitioners is that the Government had virtually admitted that all relevant things as such quali cations, functions, duties and responsibilities are the same as the scale of pay which was granted to officers working in Telecommunication Organisation and discharging these duties. It has been contended that there is no justification to deny the Specialpay at the same rates to the direct recruits working in a Telecomm tion Research Centre because the transfer of Group B officers from the Indian Air Force Service to the different cadres in Telecommi cation Centre is being made under the Semen Control and Telegraph Depart ment of the Union India. It had been contended on behalf of the respondents that the classification between direct recruit and the Transferred Field Officers was based on the basis of the policy of the Government and it was not open to the Court to interfere with the same. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The Special Pay has been rightly denied to the respondents by the High Courts. [1010F] 2.

The appellant was employed as a driver in the respondent company. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had failed to comply with the provisions of section 42(4) of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946. The Labour Court held that it was not necessary for an employee first to approach the employer or to follow the procedure laid down in section 42 (4) including the proviso before he could apply to the Labour Court for relief under section 8(1). On appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The scheme of the Act is that disputes should be settled as far as possible and primarily through conciliation and agreement. It does not stand to reason that an employee should be able to side all step side by all this step by a direct reference to the labour court. [707 D] (ii) A Labour Court is to have power to decide all the disputes covered by paragraph A of sub section (1) of section 78 and in particular, attempt must first be made by the employer intending to effect any change in respect of any order passed by the appropriate authority under standing orders applicable under this Act. [807 D E] (iii) The Scheme of the is that dispute should be resolved as far possible and exclusively through conciliation or agreement. If an employee wants a change in regard of any particular order passed under standing order which would affect his employment, he must give notice of such intention to effect such change in the respect of matters covered by section 42. [779 D E F] (iv) The object of the scheme is to provide for expeditious disposal of disputes between the employers and employees. It is not necessary that an employer should be allowed to take advantage of his own wrong or mistake.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground that they were occupying the property under a registered lease for a period of 20 years which expired on 31.7.1971 and the respondents had been occupying the premises under a valid lease for 20 years. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that in absence of a month 's notice under section 12(1) from the tenant, the application of the appellants was not maintainable before the Munsif. The High Court allowed the revision petition filed by the respondents and granted one month ' time to the respondents to vacate the premises. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the respondents would have to make another application under section 13(3) of the Act before the civil court; (ii) the appellants would have no right to continue in possession after 31.07.1971 as tenants from month to month and (iii) the suit was not barred by limitation. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The proceedings are governed by section 12 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease & Rent Control) Act, 1947. [975F] 2. The question whether a landlord after the expiry of the period of a fixed term lease is entitled to move the court under section 11 or making an application under Section 12 is wholly inapplicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case. [977B C] 3. The proceeding has to be treated as a suit and the judgment of the Munsif as a decree therein. If it is assumed that an application filed before the High Court under section12 of the was not competent, the civil courts would have the effect of a final order under section 47 which would be appealable as a judgment and decree therein.[977D] 4. The purpose for filing an applica tion under section 10 or making any application under s 12 is to enable the landlord to choose what he considers appropriate in the circumstances of his case. If the tenant fails to vacate, on the expiry o f a fixed period of time as it deems proper in the circum stances, the proceeding has become barred by time.[977E] 5. The fact that an order under s.12 is not one under section 9 or making application under S 12 is not conclusive. [980F G] 6. In the instant case, the respondents did not seek an extension of the term of tenancy. They were also directed to restore peaceful possession of the premises in question to the appellants within one month from today failing which the appellants shall be entitled to execute the decree in accordance with law.

The appellant Society filed a suit against the respondent 's election of its Secretary, who was elected as the Secretary of the Society. The trial court decreed the suit and accepted the case of Hari Narain Swami. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the application under section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not maintainable because the appellant had no locus standi to withdraw the suit, and that the trial court had committed serious errors in deciding the question as to who was the duly elected Secretary of a Society. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: The High Court has rightly held that the only remedy of the appel lant is to file a fresh suit. [237A] In the instant case, the appellant 's application under Section 15 1 was not competent to withdraw it and the trial Court had wrongly exercised its inherent power. The High court was therefore wrong in dismissing the appellant's application as not maintainable. [238B C] The High Courts were, therefore, not right in holding that the appellant invoking the inherent jurisdiction of the court was not entitled to withdraw a suit under its inherent powers. [236F G] In this case, it is the position that the respondent had actually consented to it and had made to the re sideration of the suit under the inherent power, if it is ultimately satisfied that Hari Narain Swamy was not the Secretary. The appellant 'S case was factually correct that Hari Narayan Swami was not its elected secretary and was, therefore not authorised to withdraw.

The appellant was a company carrying on business in the name and style of "Indian Fellow (Emergency Provisions) Act, 1940. The Ordinance was promulgated by the Indian Legislature with effect from April 1, 1946, whereby it was declared to have ended on April 1 , 1946. By the said order the period of emergency referred to in section 3 of the India and Burma (Eachmergency) Order, 1946 was declared a date on April I, 1946. The appellant contended that the Ordinance had been promulgated by him after April 1 1946, and that the Act could not be deemed to have concluded on April 27, 1946 when the emergency was declared under section 72 of the 9th Sch. of the Government of India Act, 1935, having been repealed by the Ordinance in question which had been passed by the India (Termination of Emergency) Order 1946, in spite of the words " for the space of not more than six months from its promulgation" the Ordinance was declared invalid on April l, 1946 and that it was void as being violative of article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the Ordinances were promulgated after April 27 , 1940, and the Ordinance having continued in operation even after the declaration of emergency had come to an end on April 2, 1946 the said notes continued to be ineffective as legal tender in India, though the position in Jammu and Kashmir in regard to which it was made on April 11, 1946 had been restored with effectfrom April 1. 1946, while determining the duration of the Ordinance, but the Ordinance could not therefore be deemed invalid on that date. The fact that the Government had issued a notification under section 3(3) of the Act did not affect the validity of the ordinance in question and the Government was competent to make it retrospectively from April 27. 1946.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge, Ambala. The High Court confirmed their conviction but reduced the sentence of death to imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the High Court was in error in confirming the death sentences passed under section 368(3) Cr. P.C.; and (ii) the Sessions judge had committed an error in awarding the extreme penalty of death. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The appeal must be dismissed. It is not possible to define or limit the connotation of the expression 'special reasons ' occurring in section 354(3), Cr.P., 1973, nor it can be legally permissible for this Court while dealing with an appeal confined to sentence under Art 136, to curtail the scope of death sentence under section 304 I. P C.C. [1070D] 2. The special reasons ' must relate to the crime as such but to the criminal 's in the country. If the general observations on sentencing imposed by this Court on an accused are constitutionally valid, it is neither feasible nor legally permissible to define and limit the scope or circumscribe the connotation so as to bring about a virtual abolition of the death sentence. [1170E F] 3. The question whether the death penalty should be awarded or not must depend upon the facts and circumstances obtaining in such case. If this means that even where the direct facts of an earlier case appear to be identical to those of the case before the Court, the Judge is not bound to draw the same inference as drawn in the earlier case One would find that in the decision in Rajendra Prasad 's case there are no rationes decidendi much less any ratio decidendi. [1270F G] 4. The Court has to choose between a sentence of imprisonment for death and a sentence for life, irrespective of the gravity of the clime as the surrounding circumstances i.e., the offence or the act which ought to be based on the facts, and the law applicable. If that is so, the Court would not ordinarily interfere with the sentence imposed by the High court under section 354 (3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [972F G H] 5. The death sentence passed under s. 368(a) of Cr. PC is a rule of universal application and the accused has right of appeal to the High Courts under 5. It would be manifest that it is not within the province of the Court while considering an appeal to lay down any legal principle applied to any legal problem disclosed by the facts or circumstances obtaining therein in such cases. [872F H] 6. The decision in the case of Rajendra Prasad vs State of Bihar, [1980] 2 S.C R. 869, relied on.

The appellant was a dealer in a cinema theatre. He was suspended on 30th September, 1953 by the Commissioner of Income tax, U.P., Lucknow, under section 3(1) (a) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, on the ground that he had entered into partnership with others, under the name of Gautam Cycle Mart, Meerut, in 1939, in contravention of the Government Servants ' Conduct Rules. The appellant was placed under suspension on 30st September, 1952, by the Assistant Director of Investigations, who was appointed by the Income tax Inspector, on 2nd April, 1956, reducing the appellant in rank from the post of an Income Tax Officer to that of an income tax Inspector. The order of suspension was confirmed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Commissioner. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant had been subjected to trial on allegations involving corruption and violation of service rules, and that the departmental proceedings were null and void. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the questions raised by the appellant depended upon findings of fact; (ii) the question whether the appellant was given a reasonable opportunity to meet a new case or not was essentially a question of fact, and (iii) the conduct of the trial court and vitiates the result. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether a departmental proceeding was null and invalid depends on findings of facts. It is only when an exclusion of evidence is of a kind which amounts to denial of natural justice or would have affected the final decision it could not be material. [583H; 583A] 2.1 In any case, it goes to the root of the jurisdiction and the conduct and the manner in which the charges were actually framed and fully enquired into by Officers whose integrity and sense of justice is not challenged. The questions raised are essentially a questions of fact which should be, initially raised in the departmental trial. [585B] 2(a) In the instant case, the question was whether the departmental proceeding were null or void. There was no allegation that the witnesses whose production was said to have been the subject matter of enquiry had formed about the work, efficiency and integrity of the applicant. The allegations made against him on each occasion were clearly established by the evidence on record. [584C D] 2.(b) In any event, it is only if an opportunity to produce nine witnesses in defence, that all the points sought to be raised on behalf Of the appellant capable of vitiating the departmental enquiry could have been considered and tried. The fact that some material facts were suppressed or misrepresented for the purpose of obtaining special leave would not vitiate the departmental inquiry. [58D] 3.(c) In a case where the authority has taken into consideration all the relevant circumstances, it may be possible to hold that the delinquent officer was given an opportunity of being heard and to be heard in support of such a technical objection to the nature of the charge which would cover the starting of the Gautam Cycle house at any time subsequent to 1939. [587E] 4.(d) The question as to whether the disciplinary proceedings were void or not depends on the findings of the departmental authorities. If the exclusion of all evidence is allowed, there can be no declaration that the disciplinary proceeding was void and invalid.

The appellants are the owners of manganese merchants who bought manganese from mines and thereafter sold the goods to their foreign buyers. The contracts between the appellants and the manganese merchants and the S.T.C. were interconnected with each other. The contract of the iron ore was the export and the exportation of the goods passed from the appellants to the M.M.T.,C. The appellants entered into a direct contract with their foreign buyer for the supply of manganese ores at the port of Andhra Pradesh. The terms and conditions of the contracts were that the manganese exporters would be entitled to import the goods on board the ship. The respondent, who was the exporter of manganese ore, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the contract between the appellant and the M/s.Mohmni International Ltd., which was dismissed by the Single Judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the contracts between them and the foreign buyers were inter connected with the contract entered into by the appellants with their Foreign buyer and therefore, the M,M. T.C., could not be said on the terms and condition of the Contracts in that case.
