Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The contracts entered into with the foreign buyer were inter co operative contracts between two parties. The export was an independent contract between them. The sale by the appellant to the foreign sellers was the first purchase in the State. The delivery of manganese was the second purchase in that State. In F.O.B. price the appellants were required to bring the goods F.o.B., price in contract between a merchant and the seller. The foreign buyer had no privity of contract with the appellant. The only question for consideration is whether the contracts entered by the respondent with the Foreign buyer were integrated activities in the course of export. [444A B] 1.2 The contracts were inter se between the parties and the appellants had to bring goods Fo.F.B, price in the contract. The fact that these contracts were integrated contracts was not a ground for holding that the contract was an integral one between the respondent and its foreign buyer. It is only when the export is complete that the goods pass through the ship that the export would be complete. [445C D] 1.(a) In the present case, the contract of sale entered into between the manganese sellers and the respondent was the master 's duty. The privity of contracts between Fo., the manganese buyers from the S/T. C. and the Foreign buyers were also different contracts. The question whether the contract in that behalf was integrated or interconnected is a mixed question of fact and law. [443E] 1(b) In view of the decision of this Court in Serajuddin 's case, it is clear that the High Courts have held that the appellants are not the last purchaser within the State of Andhra pradesh. The mere mention of Fo price in contracts between a Merchant and the buyer from the MM.M.,C., on board ship to be named by the buyer, is the first sale in the territory of India. [442E] 2(c) In Serajudduddin ' case this Court held that there was no privity contract between F o.B and the appellant with the respondent.

The appellant was employed with the respondent M/s Bharat Electronics Limited as Salesman at its Delhi 521 Sales Depot on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973. He was terminated by letter dated 12th October, 1974 with effect from 19th October 1974 with immediate effect from 1st October, 1975. The appellant challenged the termination order before the Labour Court which held that since he was not on probation and assuming maximum in favour of the respondent that he was a temporary employee, could not be said to be an retrenchment within the meaning of section 2(oo) and his case should be governed by sub section (1) and not by the provisions of section 25F. The Labour Court held that where termination was automatic, it would nonetheless be a retrenchment within Section 2(o) and in the absence of strict compliance with the requirements of section25F, termination was held to be invalid. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1)(a) The termination of service of the appellant was ab initio void and inoperative and a declaration follows that he continues to be in service with all consequential benefits. [529B] (b) The respondent had worked for 240 days in a period of 12 calendar months but has rendered service for a period exceeding 240 days during the period of twelve calendar months, it is not necessary that he should have been in the service of either the employer for one whole year. Therefore, both on principle and on precedent it must be held that section 25B(2) comprehends a situation where a workman is not in employment for a continuous period of 240 days but has served for a number of 240days during the periods of 12 months. [629C D] (c) The appellant was not in service for one year because he had worked continuously for a total period of one year and he had rendered service only for a short period of six calendar months. Therefore both on principles and on principle, it must also be held to have been validly terminated and a declared declaration follows the same. [729D] (d) The question whether the termination of the services of the workman was abruptly terminated is one of fact depending upon which calculation is to be made, in case of retrenchment date of retrenchment, there is neither termination nor cessation of work which is not due to any fault on the part of the employee. [829E] (e) The conditions are that commencing the date with reference to which calculation was to bemade, in cases where a person is not In continuous service within the definition of sub section 1(1), his case would be governed under sub section 2 (oo). Therefore, even on principle it must he held that Section 25B (2) covers a situation when a workman has been in employment.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953. He was served with a charge sheet setting out his mis demeanour, an enquiry was held in respect of the alleged misdemeanour and his employment was terminated because in the view of the Settlement Officer 's report with some warning that he should be dismissed from service without assigning any reason. The appellant submitted his explanation to the charge sheet stating that he had received Rs. 150/ as illegal gratification from one Ude Singh, but that he did not receive it as illegal bribe. The Deputy Commissioner agreed with the view taken by the Settlement officer and held that the appellant was a temporary servant and that no penalty was imposed upon him. On appeal to the High Court the appellant contended (i) that the order of dismissal from service was in contravention of article 311(2) of the Constitution as no reasonable opportunity to show cause against the order had been given; (ii) that it was not a case where the enquiry was made with the object of ascertaining whether disciplinary action should be taken against the appellant for his alleged misdemeanours and failure to obtain relief, because in his view, the order terminating his employment is one passed by the settlement officer without giving him an opportunity to make his defence; (iii) that there was no stigma affecting the future career of the public servant by the order dated March 17, 1965. Held, that the enquiry made by the Enquiry Officer was not in accordance with the rules governing the conduct of public servants for ascertaining whether the probation of the appellant should be confirmed or not and that the termination of employment was by way of punishment, because it put a stigma on his competence and thus affects his future career. The order terminating the services of the respondent was one passed under rule 8(1) (b) of Chapter XIV of the Punjab Civil Services Rules, 1934. The enquiry made against the respondent did not fall within the principle of Ram Narayan Das 's case.

The appellant, a Public Service Commission, was appointed by the State Government to fill up vacancies of Professors in the various departments. The State Government made rules known as the Jammu and Kashmir Public Service (Appointment by Promotion) Rules, 1969, for selection to posts of Professors. Under the said rules, the Commission was required to consult the Public Service Commissions on the suitability of candidates for such appointments, promotions or transfers. The Commission was consulted in regard to the principles to be followed in making appointments to civil services and posts and in making promotions and transfers from one service to another. The appellant challenged the selection made by the Commission before the High Court contending that the Public Services Commission had not been consulted either in regard thereto nor in respect of the principles laid down therein, and that the Selection Committee was not consulted in the manner required by section 133(2)(b) of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Commission had no consultation with the Commission under section 133 of the constitution and that it was not necessary for the Commission to consult a Public Services Commissions on suitability of the candidates for promotion as Professors, and the second requirement of clause (b) was also complied with. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High court erred in holding that there was no consultation between the Commission and the Commission. [875F] The Commission had been consulted in respect to the principle to be adopted in making the promotions to the posts of Professor. It is not provided by section 132(2) (b), that all the members of the Commission should have interviewed or all of the persons, so long as the Commission reserved to itself the right to approve or disapprove the Committee 's report and actually discharged that constitutional responsibility.

The petitioner was a member of the Bihar Legislative Assembly. He was elected as a member and was elected to the Bihar State Legislative Assembly from the said Assembly. The petitioner challenged the election on various grounds: (i) that he had been guilty of corrupt practice under section 123(3)(b) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951; (ii) that the House of Commons had not been duly constituted and was not entitled to be elected as members of the Legislative Assembly; (iii) that it had the privilege to prevent publication of its proceedings without the authority of the House to be expunged. Held:(i) The petitioner 's fundamental right under article 19(1)(a) is preserved despite the provisions of article 194(3) of that Act and, as in this case, the petitioner was not alleged to have been guilty, the Legislature has no power to take any action in respect of the said publication. (ii).The privilege conferred on a citizen under article 194 (3) is protected notwithstanding the fact that it infringes the fundamental right of a citizen. The privilege conferred by article 194 is preserved notwithstanding the provisions Of article 194. (4) is not made subject to article 19 of the Constitution and, therefore, if the House has never formally rescinded the orders from time to time it had made with regard to the publication of the proceedings without authority of that part of the proceeding directed by the Speaker to be deleted. The House of Lords in Council vs Harris, ; , referred to. (iii).The petitioner ' fundamental right is preserved inspite of the provisions contained in article 194 and the privileges of a House of Parliament are only those of the Houses of Parliament and the members and committees thereof must be such as may from time lo time be defined by the Legislature by law. The privileges, immunities and immunities of a house of such Legislature are only the rights, privileges and immunities which a House has not formally rescinded. The right to freedom conferred on the Legislature under article 195(3), is preserved even though it infringes article 19 (1) of its Constitution.

The Government of Orissa took over the management of a private college in the town of Behrampur, Ganjam District. The said college was administered as a Government College. The Government prescribed the requisite qualifica tions for appointment as Readers in different faculties in the private colleges. The State Government issued a formal agreement to that effect and a formal Agreement was executed between the managing committee of the College and the Governor of the State. The management had to meet with financial crisis in the past and obtained financial help in the shape of liberal endowment under a trust deed from the then zamindar of Khallikote, which was taken over by the Government on March 9, 1971. The teaching experience of the Readers in the college was also given as a qualification for appointment. The High Court held that the teachers were drawing salary more than Rs.600/ and therefore they were not entitled to be appointed as Reader. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants (1) that the High Court erred in directing the Government to take into account the experience as a Reader in the Government College; (2) that since the teaching experience was only a confirmed Lecturer, the salary drawn by the Readers on the date of taking over were in receipt of pay of Rs. 600/ and (3) that even amongst the Readers who were drawing a salary less than Rs..600/ were drawing more than what was being paid to them as Reader, they were drawing an salary higher than Rs .600/. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The teachers were drawn on the basis of pay drawn by them in the College on the dates of takingover. They were drawing less than what were being paid. [775F] 2. The salary drawn on a date of take over was not in receipt but was drawn by a Reader, but whether he is suitable for appointment to the post. Whether they will be suitable for employment as Reader or later for consideration of their suitability by the Public Service Commission for appointment, for consideration, of their ability by the public service commission for appointment and later for consider ing his suitability by it, are entirely different matters. [777A B] 3. The question whether the teaching Experience of Readers in a college is completely effaced to the extent that they will not be even eligible on the plea of absence of teaching experience in Government service, for considera tion of their eligibility by the Commission for selection as Reader and later on for consideration his suitability was also a matter entirely different. [779C] 4. The fact that the teaching knowledge is only a confirmation Lecturer and not a mere confirmation Lecturer makes no difference to the position that the Readers are selected for appointment in the same college. [780D E] 5. The principle of equal pay for equal work has been laid down by this Court in several decisions of this Court. In the instant case, the High Courts have taken the view that the salary was drawn on an earlier date and not on a later date. It is also clear from the record that the respondents were drawing higher salary than what they were getting.

The appellants applied for temporary permits under section 68 F(1) A of the U.P. Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. The State Transport Authority rejected their applications on the ground that they were not in accordance with law and therefore an application for temporary permit could not be granted. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the order of rejection of their applications. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the Corporation had no power to grant temporary permits, and that the State Transport Appellate Tribunal was wrong in rejecting the applications on that ground. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that (i) the scheme has been prepared and published under section 69C of Chapter IV A of Chapter V A of . The route in question is an inter regional route and therefore the Corporation alone could grant temporary permit; (ii) the State Government had power under sub section (1 C) to grant permanent permits only for the full strength but not for the entire number of vehicles operating on the route. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The scheme has already been published in respect of the route under section68C and further enables the Corporation to apply for temporary or permanent permits. [985F] 2. The Regional Transport Authority or the Regional Transport Officer as the case may be, in exercise of power conferred by sub section(1 C), can grant temporary or temporary permits only if the Corporation applied for all the permits. But if the corporation is willing to operate on the issue of a permit to any one else it will have to apply to the State transport Authority for temporary and permanent permits, once the Corporation made an application in respect thereof for temporary temporary permits not for full strength. [ 985F G] 3. The provisions contained in section 68F(1 A) are mandatory and do not require that the Regional or Transport Authority should grant temporary and temporary permits to any person in respect only of the area or route or part thereof specified in the scheme. If the Corporation is willing, to operate the maximum strength undoubtedly the State Govt. will have power under subsection (1C) to permit any one other than the Corporation. [977F] 4. The Corporation has power under section 67 F(I C) only to mean that even though there are 7 vacancies and the Corporation applies for temporary licences not for a full strength, yet if the State or Transport authority applied for some other suitable person willing to obtain temporary permits then the Corporation would be entitled to all the temporary permits. The mere fact that there are certain vacancies in respectof which the scheme is published will have no application by the Corporation and section 68 G(1A) would not be attracted. [980F H] 5. The words "if any one otherwise applies" occurring in section68 F(l C) of Chapter VI A of 'the Act indicate that the scheme should be made applicable only to temporary permits and not to temporary permit. If, however, the Corporation has applied for any one, then the State, Transport Authority will have the right to grant such temporary or Permanent permits. If there is no application for a temporary permit it would be equally attracted. But where the Corporation does not apply for all temporary permits the State of Transport Authority cannot grant temporary temporary orpermanent permits unless the Corporation makes an application under section 66 F( 1 C) for temporary, permanent or permanent permit. [981H; 985A B] 6. The word "if" in section 69 C of Chapter VII A of "the Act means that if the scheme contains a situation where a scheme has not been published and yet if it is open to the Corporation, then such scheme can be made by the State Road Transport Authority. [983F G H] 7. The expression "if no application is made under section 63 F(i C) would be squarely attracted.

The appellant, a son of the respondent, was born in his ancestral property. He died leaving behind him two sons and three daughters. The respondent 's father died leaving him surviving his widow and four daughters. After the death of her husband, the respondent filed a suit for partition of the properties which were inherited by her from his maternal grandfather. The appellant contended that the property inherited by respondent 10 was not ancestral property qua the appellant and so it allowed the appeal preferred by respondents 1 to 9 and dismissed the appellant 's suit. Held, that the decision in Narotam Chand 's case (2) did not rest upon any evidence relating to custom of the Punjab which had been concluded by the earlier Full Bench decision. The law on the doctrine of stare decisis is applicable only to cases where a daughter succeeds either in preference to or in default of male heirs, and does not alter the character of the property merely because she happens to be a female. The principle of stare overruling was applied in the case of Mohammed Husain Khan vs Mushammat Thakri (I.L.R. , followed. In the present case, the decision of the Full Bench was wholly unsustainable as a decision on the point of the relevant custom. The only effect of the said decision was to confer upon the son of his maternal grandmother the property from his paternal grandfather and it was governed by the custom of that community since 1895. The fact that the respondent ' son acquired an interest jointly with him does not affect the character or status of the ancestral property of the appellant.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Birbhum, for offences under section 449 and section 307 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the night of 14th November 1950 when Haji Ebrar Ali was sleeping on the Verandah of his hut, he inflicted an injury on his neck with a dagger. He sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for four years under section 302/34 and to rigorous Imprisonment for two years under Section 449 of the Code. On appeal by the State, the High Court acquitted all the appellants but convicted them under section 307/34 of the Penal Code and sentenced them to rigorous rigorous imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the charge under section 27 read with s 34 of Indian Penal code is not sustainable in law; (ii) the offence under section 448 of the I.P.C., if committed by any person in furtherance of the common intention of all, the legal position that results is that each person shall be held to have committed the entire criminal act; and (iii) the fact that one of the other who did not use the dagger must in law be considered to have done the entire act of holding Ebrarar Ali down and applying the dagger. HELD: The offence under s. 449 of I. P.C. is punishable with imprisonment for life or to suc h punishment as is hereinbefore mentioned. [982 B] (i)(a) It is not necessary that there should be a charge under s 307 read along with section 149 of the Criminal Procedure Code. But it is clear from the fact, that when it is decided that the act was so done by a number of persons in furtherance or common intention, the law has to be considered whether each person would be held liable to imprisonment for his life or not. [882 C] (b) The position is no way when different persons are acting jointly in furtherance and in furtherance thereof the common intent of all is that the legal status that results was that each individual must be held guilty of murder, unless he has done the whole act of using the dagger himself. So, he becomes punishable under section 149 I.I.P.,C. [977 D] (c) The fact that a charge Under s 307/149 read with Section 34 of I P. C. is not made punishable under s 302 or section 34 I. I.p.C.; and so, each person must be considered as having committed the whole criminal act. [980 E F] (d) In the present case, when it was found that the four appellants attacked Haji EBrar Ali with the dagger on the neck of Ebrrar Ali, one used the dagger in furtherance Of the common object of all and so the other three who did use the weapon on him were jointly acting in furtherance o f the common purpose of all. The position was not in any way when Matiullah was not acting alone but several others were acting jointly with the common motive of all; so, the position is that one person shall have committed an offence punishable with death. [981 E F]. (e) In order to commit theft it is necessary to show that the accused had committed the crime trespass in order to committing the house trespass. The fact of holding the accused guilty of the offence punishable under Section 307 readwith section 34, I.PC., if the intention was to commit the house enter into the house, it will be proper to say that he has committed the offence of house trespass and not the dagger, so as to attract the provisions of section 34. [983 E F H] (f) The distinction between a charge for house trespass is that when the act is done by one person in pursuance of the intention or knowledge referred to in the section and so where the act consists of a number o f persons in pursuance or knowledge, it can have no application.

The appellant, a Sarswat Brahmin of the Gurdaspur district, was a Sarwat Brahmins. He had two sons and one daughter, who were born in the family of his father. The respondent claimed that he was entitled to succeed to the self acquired property of her father and that the properties in suit were not ancestral. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the appellant was not a collateral of the father who was the last male holder excluded the collaterals from succession to the ancestral property of his mother. In appeal by certificate, Held, that the respondent had failed to discharge the initial onus that was thrown on her as a result of the production by the appellant of the Riwaj i am of 1913 and which stood contradicted by the instances collected and set out in Appendix 'C ' of the same Riwi am. The High Court was right in holding that the suit for a mere declaration was not maintainable in view of the provisions of the Indian Succession Act relating to succession certificates, (ii)that the appellant had failed in proving the custom of the district of Gurdaspur which was compiled by him as to what the custom should be, and (iii)that according to the custom prevailing in the Gurdasparpur district the collateral's properties were ancestral. Held, further, that even if the general custom in favour of the daughter excluded her collaterals in preference to collaterals even though they were within the fourth degree exclude the collateralS from succession, the appellant must succeed.

The respondent was a Managing Agent of certain companies registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The managing agents of the said companies were acting as Managing Agents of several companies registered in respect of each of those capacities. The respondent was assessed to duty on the basis that the properties in question were joint properties and that the instrument was chargeable with the aggregate amount of duty payable if separate instruments were executed in respect thereof. The appellant contended that under section 5 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, the instrument in question was a power of attorney liable for a single duty under article 48(d) (1) 850 of the Schedule to the Indian Stamps Act, 1908 and that as the instrument fell under two or more of them, it was chargeable to the aggregate duty payable on any one of them. Held, that the deed in question did not comprise distinct matters but comprised only one matter and that matter was the execution of a general power of Attorney by the donor in favour of the donee in respect Of each of these capacities. It is within the very nature of the general powerof attorney which all the distinct acts which the donor is capable of performing whether in his individual capacity or in his representative capacity as trustee, etc., are comprised within the instrument and are not distinct matters to be dealt with so as to attract the operation of section 5. The instrument in dispute did not fall under article 47(d)(1) but was merely a single delegation. The fact that the donor of the power of executes it in different capacities is not sufficient in his opinion to constitute the instrument comprising one distinct matter and thus requiring to be construed as distinct categories.

The assessee, a company, was carrying on business in the Mahalaxmi Mills Ltd., in the other two (C.A. No. 600/1962) and its business was carried on by it as a dealer in the said mill. The assessee claimed that the depreciation should be computed by deduction from the actual cost of depreciation allowance which would have been allowable under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, if the Indian income tax Act was in force in the past, but the Income tax Officer rejected the claim and held that this expression "or which would be allowed to him if the India Income tax Ordinance, 1949, was in operation in the previous year" did not permit the Income Tax Officer to make any deduction under this head. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner as also the Incometax Tribunal took a different view and held in favour of the assessee. In appeals by the Revenue, the High Court answered the question in negative but gave a certificate that it was a fit case for appeal to the Supreme Court under section 66(1) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1961, if it had been in force and a claim had been made or could be made for such allowance, was rejected by the Income ' tax Officer. In the appeals to this Court, HELD: (i) The words "or Which would have allowed the depreciation that would have read as "all depreciation actually allowed under any laws or rules of a Part B State relating to income tax and super tax on profits of business" in paragraph 2 of Removal Difficulties Order, 1949 were apt and sufficient to express and give effect to this intention. [231 E] (ii) The word "or" used in the Ordinance was not intended to convey that it should be so construed as to include depreciation actually allowable under any law relating to tax on income of business. It is well settled that the words "any law relating t o tax on profession" are not sufficient to give effect thereto. [232 E] Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City vs M/s. R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala, ; , referred to. (iii) The expression "any Law relating to profits of a business" is also a law relating lo income tax or super tax and so, depreciation actually permitted under any rules of the Part B States relating to Income tax and Super tax on business would be taken into account in computing the written down value under section 10(5)(b) of that Ordinance.

The appellant, a contractor, entered into an agreement with the respondent for supply of certain essential items. The contract was to be completed within six months from the date of execution of the agreement. The respondent submitted its tender form on or before 31st December, 1989. The appellant accepted the same and sent it to the respondent on or about 1st January, 1990. The work was completed by the respondent in June, 1990 and the appellant was informed that the contract would be completed only after the completion of the work. The Respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the award of the contract. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the pre requisites for supply were only the three conditions set out in para I of the N.I.T. and other details called for vide para 5(c) of the said N. I.T., and that the details called "the three conditions mentioned in para 1" were intended to verify the fulfilment of the three prequalifying requirements as stated in para 2. The learned single Judge dismissed the petition holding, inter alia, that the appellant had fulfilled all the prequalification requirements and as such the respondent was much better qualified for the contract and that he was also entitled to be considered for the work which he had done. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts should not have entertained the tender form to the appellant even before the final award of contract. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts were right in holding that para I and para I are intended to be verified with the fulfilment o f the three essential requirements as mentioned in Para I and that all the documents referred to in para V could be supplied at any time before the Final award of Contract. It was for the respondent to satisfy the preliminary Tendering requirements and that only three pre qualifying conditions were prescribed in the NIA.T, and other relevant details called 'the three pre requisites ' for supply '. The requirement in para. I is also a part of the specific requirements in para l. [236B C] 1.2 The High courts should not ordinarily interfere with their decision unless there are some special circumstances which would justify interference by the Court. In this case, the respondent had no experience in this line of work and that even if he did not comply with the requirements of paras I and V, he was much more better qualified to tender for the contracts. [237C D] 1.(a) The High court should not interfere with its decision unless it is shown that the decision of the single Judge was perverse or based on no evidence or that there was some material which could justify interference. [238F G] (b) In the instant case, as the respondent did not strictly comply with paras I & V of the F.I., the High court rightly held that para 1 is intended to apply only to NIA and not to para I. The other conditions set forth in para II are also relevant for the purpose of determining whether there was any difference between the requirements in paras I, V or VI of theN.IT. [239F G; 239A] (c) In para I, the appellant has no doubt stated that the respondent is much better than the other tenderers who had already supplied all the relevant documents referred in para IV. The only condition set out therein is that before the tender forms are supplied to any intending contractor. It may be said that the rule was likely to be relaxed. [240F G H] (d) In this particular case, whatever may be the interpretation that a court may place on the NAC or in the K.P.C. would not have been found to be in order. The fact that the contractor had fulfilled the pre requisite qualifying requirements as set out by para I is no doubt sufficient to warrant the issue of a tender form.

The appellant was a Custodian of Evacuee Property, New Delhi. He was appointed as the Custodian of evacuee property under section 5 A of the East Punjab Act XIV of 1947. The Custodian General issued an order of confirmation of the Additional Custodian and Deputy Custodian of the Evacuee Property on the 20th March, 1952. The appellant filed a revision petition before the Custodian General against the order of the Custodian and the Additional Chief Custodian. The Additional Custodian held that the order was not subject to appeal or revision but it was made final and conclusive. On appeal by special leave the Custodian held: (i) that the original order passed by the Custodian, Additional Custodian or an Authorised Deputy Custodian under section 27 of the Central Act XXXI of 1950 were not subject matter of appeal or revisions and it was specifically declared to be final and binding; (ii) that in view of the provisions of section 5A of the Act the appellant could not challenge the confirmation order passed on the original orders of confirmation. Held, that the revisional order of confirming the order passed in 1952 would clearly be subject to the revisional power of the Deputy Custodian and an Authorised Assistant Custodian under s. 27 of Central Act LXVII of 1950 and that clause (c) thereof must be construed as referring to matters ejusdem generis with clauses (a) and (b). The order of confirmed was perfectly bona fide, and could not be challenged in a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution. The order passed under appeal was one passed by virtue of the wide powers of revision vested in the CustodianGeneral under section27 of the , and that the orders of confirmations were not relevant matters for consideration by the custodian General himself in his order under appeal.

The appellant company was a seasonal industry. The workmen claimed bonus for the relevant four years, which was founded on custom or custom prevailing in the establishments before 1965 were recognised as customary and traditional in the establishment of the respondent company. The claim for bonus based on custom was founded upon custom or practice prevalent in the Establishments before 1965. The Tribunal made short shrift of the jural stream. The appellant company claimed bonus based only on custom, which did not detract from the claim of customary bonus. The Industrial Tribunal held that the claim for payment of bonus based upon custom was justified and directed the respondent to pay the same. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the award made by the Tribunal was invalid as it did not provide for those categories of bonus and confines itself to profit based on customs or conditions of service; that the Tribunal had made short spilled over the banks of jural stream, and therefore, the claim was justified. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Industrial Court was right in holding that the appellant company had not established any case of customary or traditional bonus. [603 C] (2) The question about the policy of the Parliament to allow an invasion from flank in that manner is not a matter of implied agreement between the employers and employees, creating a term of employment for payment for those who are either excluded or exempted from the Act, it would have made an express saving provision to that effect as it had done for employees in Coal Mines. [503 D] (3) The claim of bonus on customary and contractual basis is not barred by the general principles of res judicata. It is true that if the Bonus Act is a complete Code and is exhaustive of the subject matter of bonus, there may be a bar, but it is quite conceivable that the codification may be of everything relating to profit bonus in which case other types of bonus are different from unconnected or exempted. [403 E] (4) The scheme of the Bonus Bill is not an exhaustive one and does not provide any prohibition for those classes of bonus. It does not bar claims based on profits bonus based solely on custom. The question of payment of Bonus based on conditions of services of workmen to employees employed in Coal mines, therefore, cannot be decided by this Court. [525 G] (5) The Tribunal was called upon to decide one cause of action based on profit bonus based purely on custom and practice prevailing in establishments before the 1965 is not such a matter as has to be adjudicated and it also does not fall under the provisions of Bonus Act.

The Punjab Superior Judicial Service Rules, 1972 were amended by the Haryana First Amendment Rules, 1973 providing that seniority of members of the service, whether direct recruits or promotees appointed to the Superior Judicial Services of Punjab and Haryana shall be determined by the length of continuous service in a post irrespective of the date of confirmation. The High Court issued a notification fixing the inter se seniority of all officers appointed to that Service by promotion and by direct recruitment. In pursuance of the said notification, the State Government amended the Rules from time to time providing for the fixation of seniority of the members of service in accordance with the Haryana Superior Judicial service Rules, 1963. The petitioners who were promotees to the Higher Judicial Services filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the aforesaid rules and the notifications issued thereunder on the ground that they had been discriminated against by the State. The main contention was that the rule of rotation at the time of confirmation was discriminatory inasmuch as it conferred the power of control over district courts and subordinate courts vested in the High Courts by Article 235 and the power conferred upon the Governor under article 235 was thus expressly, by the terms of that Article alone; therefore, it was not open to the High court to give an arbitrary date of confirmation to the promotees. The writ petition was dismissed by a Single Judge of the High Curt holding that the rules of rotation were discriminatory and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, it is contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the rule prescribing seniority of officers in the judicial service of the State was governed by a rule of quota only and not by the rule or rotation; (ii) the power to frame rules regulating the recruitment and conditions of service of persons appointed, promoted or promoted to the higher Judicial Service was governed under a rule which the State legislature may pass for regulating the Recruitment and conditions in service of judicial officers of the state; and (iii) the High courts were not justified in applying the rule as it confers the power on the Governor to frame Rules regarding seniority of judicial Officers in the Superior judicial service. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The power of the Governor, in the exercise of power conferred by Article 234, has the power vested in him by article 235 and is not in the Governor. [1038F] 2.1 The power to make rules regulating recruitment and condition of service is expressly by the words "in a post" in that Article itself made subject to the law which the state legislature may passing for regulating recruitment or conditions of services of persons employed, promoted, appointed or promoted. In so far as the rule is concerned, under the amended Rule 12, the quota prescribed by rule 8 is not the criterion of seniority but the method of determining the interse seniority of direct recruits and promotees. [1138F G] 2(a) The power conferred on the High Power Court by article 236 is a part of the control of the Supreme Court vested in it by Article 233. It may be recalled that in Haryana, continuous officiation on a post in the service irrespective of whether the date or dates of confirmation so that after every two promotees are confirmed one direct recruit has to be confirmed and until that is done, promotees cannot be confirmed even if vacancies are available within their quota in which they can be confirmed. [1238F H] 2.(b) The High Courts were not right in applying rule 8 of the Superior Civil Service Rules of Punjab & Haryana. [1339C] 3(a).

The respondents Nos. 4 & 5, who were working as Junior Assistants in the State of Andhra Pradesh, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order dated October 6, 1989 passed by the Government of Andhra pradesh, appointing them to the post of Junior Assistants and Senior Assistants respectively. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the creation of a division and maintaining separate seniority of Junior Assistant and Senior Assistant was illegal and contrary to the orders issued in G.O.Ms. No. 10 dated October 20, 1975. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The creation of an integrated division and maintenance of separate seniority is not a matter for the purpose of administrative convenience nor is it a matter of policy. [569E] 2.1 It is the President alone who has been given power under proviso to paragraph 3(1) before the expiry of twelve months prescribed in sub para (1) of paragraph 3 of the Order, by an order to organise classes or classes of posts in the civil services of the State into different local cadres for different parts of the state. [570E] 1.2 The power given to the State Government under paragraph 3 (1), by an Order to organise class or classes or categories of posts is only to organise a separate cadre in respect of any category of posts, and not for the purposes of administrative necessity or for any part of the States in the manner provided therein. [568F] 2(a) The power conferred on the State Govern ment under paragraph (3) of the said order by an express provision is only for organise a single cadre in relation to any class or categories in respect o f which a local cadre has been organised, in respect Of such category exist in each department. [567B C] 2.(b) The State Government may organise different classes or groups of posts within a zone under para 3(i) before its expiry of the twelve months from October 20 1975. No person can be appointed to any post in any department for any period when more than one cadre exists in respect thereof. [571D E] 2 (c) The creation or maintenance of a separate seniority list is not an act of administrative expediency but only a device to organise the local cadres in relation thereto. It is only in the purpose for administrative convenience that the State may organise a particular class or category of post in a zone. [572F G] 3.(d) The Government has been empowered under paragraph 2(1), to organise different categories of civil services, and classes of civil posts under the State in respect whereof a local cadres have been organised. It cannot be said that the power given by an authority under paragraph 4(1)(a) is only administrative or executive. [573D E; 573A] 3. The creation and maintenance, separate seniority lists are not relevant for the object of recruitment, seniority etc., as the case may be. [574E F] 4.(e) The Central Government has power under paragraph 5(1).

The plaintiff, a mortgagee in possession of the mortgaged property, purchased certain properties from one M. P. Singh who was the auction purchaser in execution of that mortgage decree and sold them to the defendants. The defendants filed a suit for recovery of khas possession of these properties on the ground that they were subrogated to the position of the Bank, that the decree which had been passed in the mortgage suit was binding the defendants, that he was the mortgagee 's security insufficient; and that the plaintiff was not entitled to recover khas possession from the defendants as the sale was by a mortgage decree. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court held that the mortgagor could grant leases which were not wasteful in their effect the mortgagee had no power to grant a permanent lease of the property so as to bind the mortgagee. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The plaintiff was entitled to khas possession and he was entitled only to recover possession from defendants. [110 F] (ii) The High Court was clearly in error in holding that the mortgagee did not exercise his right of redemption by making a lease for a term. It is only relevant consideration whether the mortgagor in possession had power to lease the mortgaged properties in the usual course of management by making the mortgage and so long as nothing took place to impair the value, or impede the operation of the mortgage the mortgagor would be well within his powers in making a temporary lease for the term. [111 F] The fact that the mortgagors dealt with the property in the normal course must be deemed operative against the mortgagee does not alter the value of the mortgagee and so far as it takes place to impaired the value or impede its operation or impede, the operationof the mortgage. [119 G H] (iii)The plaintiff was a mortgagor in the ordinary course of administration by the mortgagor. The mortgagor could thus in the prescribed course of business create a lease of his property by making an arrangement for the sale of the properties in usual course. It was not necessary that the lessee should have been permitted to do so. [121 A] (iv)The mortgagee ' had no authority to deal with the mortgaged land in the well known course of the management and the interest which was thus created by the mortgagee in his ordinary course must rightly deemed operative from the mortgagor 's right of sale. The only relevant considerations are whether the lessee in possession has power to let out the property by a lease granted by him can be lawfully deemed operativeagainst the mortgagee.[121 C] (v)The fact that a mortgagor is not restricted in management of the land by making any mortgage and that so longas nothing takes place,to impair the valuation or impede his operation or influence the value etc. does not make a lease in respect of the entire property by the lessee to the mortgagee even though he may have no power under the law to grant such a lease. [122 D] (vi)The question whether the mortgagee was entitled in possession to the permanent lease granted to him could be considered with reference to section 66 of the Transfer of Property Act and it was held that as the object of the burial ground was to grant leases for a period, the mortgagor did not choose to exercise his rights of redemption, that there was no answer to the plaintiff 's claim and the permanent leases granted by the defendant could not prevail against the plaintiff. [123 E] (vii)The High Court had rightly held that in view of section 66 the mortgagee could not be deemed to have leased the land in question to the respondents. The fact, however, that a mortgage was not restricted does not affect the value and impede the operations of the mortgagor by making it a lease within the meaning of section 65 A of the Act.

The petitioner sent a notice on Nov. 28, 1989 to the respondent for reference to arbitration. The respondent sent the bills on July 12, 1979 and paid the amount but not made. The petitioner filed an application under section 8 of the Arbitration Act before the High Court for referring the dispute to arbitration and for appointment of an arbitrator. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the period of limitation was not applicable to arbitrations as it applied to actions in the High Courts and the courts below had justifiably exercised their discretionary power, and jurisdiction under sections 5 and 12(2) (b). Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of the Limitation Act would apply to arbitrations and notwithstanding any term in the contract to the contrary. [363B] 2.1 In the instant case, the respondent sent a letter on Nov., 28,1989 to the petitioner and relieved the parties from the arbitration agreement for reference. The notice was received by the petitioner on Nov, 28, 1990. The period of Limitation is not applicable in the present case as the proceedings before the arbitration are like civil proceedings before an arbitrator within the meaning of section 14 of the . [363C D] 2(a) In the present cases, the High court has exercised its discretionary power and jurisdiction Under sections 5 & 12(1)(b) of the Act for appointment an arbitrator and when the petitioner had legally invoked clause 68 of the Contract providing that if an arbitration is not so commenced the claim concerned shall be barred. [364E] 2.(b) The Court has been given power in circumstances given to grant leave to a contracting party to have the arbitrator or umpire removed, in effect, from the jurisdiction of the court within the term of section14 of the 1963 Act. [365C D; 365A] 3.2 In the case of arbitrations, the claim is not to be put forward after the expiration of specified number of years from the date when the claim accrues. The Court should exercise its discretionary powers and jurisdiction in cases where the claim was not to he put forward within the time prescribed by clause 68. [366E] 3.(a) The court has been conferred power under sections5 and 12 (2)(b). The courts below have justifiably exercised its discretion, and jurisdictions under sections 4 and 12 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908. [367F G] 4.3 In the facts and circumstances of the case, it is an exceptional case and the Courts below have rightly exercised their discretion, jurisdiction and jurisdiction by applying the principles of analogy to arbitration proceedings, and like interpretation was given to section 14.

The appellants were the tenants of certain lands in Bihar. The decree holders sought to proceed against them under section 47, Civil Procedure Code. The executing court held that the objection was barred by res judicata and further on July 23, 1960 for default of the judgment debtors. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the objections were barred by the principles of res judicata as well as further on the principle of resjudicata and further that the same had no merits. HELD : (i) The objection raised by the judgment debtor was overruled by the executing court on two different grounds namely (1) that the execution was barred under section 4(d) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950; and (2) that it was 'so barred because the execution proceedings were barred on the principles Of res judicata. [110 D] (ii) The question whether the execution is barred under the provisions of the Act did not fall within the protection of the section 4 (d). It was not the object of the legislature which was merely to provide for the transference to the State of the estates as specified. [1110 C] (iii) The fact that a notification issued under section 3(1) of Bihar Land Reform Act, 1951 is only to provide that on and from the date of vesting all lands used for agriculture or horticultural purposes which were in khas possession of an intermediary on the date Of vesting shall subject to the provisions contained in sections 7A and B be deemed to be settled by the State with such intermediary and he shall be entitled to retain possession thereof and hold them as a raiyat under the State.

The respondents were recruited to the Indian Police Service in the year 1973 and they were promoted as Assistant Sub Inspector of Police. The respondents filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the second proviso to Rule 4 of the C.S.E. Rules, 1988 on the ground that they had been allocated to the I.P.S., and who have appeared in Civil Services Main Examination, 1988 or 1989 under the interim orders of the Tribunal and are within the permissible age limit and have succeeded, were to be given benefit of their success subject to the provisions of Rule 17 of the Central Civil Services (Main) Rules,1988. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the second Proviso to Rule 3 of the said Rules was not applicable in the case of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes candi dates who were otherwise eligible for appearing in the next CSE (Main). In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the proviso to rule 4 of C. S.E., Rules, 1989 is only a procedural provision which has been enacted with regard to the procedure to be followed for selection and promotion to higher posts in the Indian Administrative Service. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The second proviso is not applicable to the case where Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes cates are made available to the members of the IPS or Central Services Group 'A ' but who have been allocated under Rule 17 to a service group of officers. [58G H] 2.2 In the instant case, the respondents were appointed to the CSE in the years 1973 and 1989 respectively. They had not been allocated any of the services to which they had already been allocated on the basis of the previous CSE. The Tribunal has held that the respondents could not be given the benefit of the proviso only with regard t he main examination as now contended by the Additional Solicitor, according to whom those candidates were not eligi ble for being considered again in the CSC (Main), 1988 or1989 under the Interim orders of this Court. [59H; 60A] 2:3 The Tribunal had rightly held that there was no provision in the Rules for the purpose of determining the eligibility of Scheduled Tribes and Scheduled Castes cates to be eligible for promotion to the post of Sub Inspector. The proviso to sub rule 4 is only procedural provision and not substantive provisions. [60F G] 3:4 It is well settled that a candidate who has been allocated by the CSS/Central Services Group to a Service, Group 'B ' can have more attempts in the sub quent Civil Services Examination for competing for IAS, IFS, IPS, IPS etc. for competing under Rule 4. The second Proviso is only an procedural provision. [61G H; 62A] 3.5 In the present case, there was a clear cut cut off date of 1st April, 1987 and the respondents had been given the opportunity to appear in the preliminary examination as well as the subsequent examinations. They were not eligible for being promoted to the next Civil Service Examination. The question whether they should be considered at the next Criminal Services ( Main Examination) Examination was a matter which fell for consideration before this Court in the earlier case. [62F G H] 3(a) In the facts and circumstances of the case, it is not necessary to issue any direction as prayed for by the respondents. The directions issued by the Tribunal are only procedural provisions and cannot be said to have been violated.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the (COFEPOSA for short) by filing a writ petition before the High Court and that application has been dismissed. The High Court, however, rejected the same on the ground that since the detenu had no statutory right to be represented by a lawyer before the Advisory Board, he was not entitled to assistance of a friend at the hearing and that the order of detention is vitiated. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (1) whether the detaining authority or the Government should have the facility of appearing before the Board through a legal practitioner or a legal adviser; and (2) whether in the facts of the case, the detenu was entitled to the assistance of an advocate before the advisory board. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The order of the High court is set aside and the appellant is directed to be assisted by Sundararajan as a friend. [792C] 2.2 The Advisory Board has given its finding in rejecting the detenu 's request for assistance of his friend at that hearing and for reasons and in the manner indicated in the counter affidavit. It was not justified on the part of the detaining authorities or the government to allow such assistance to the detenu when it allowed the facility to be representing by an array of lawyers. [ 793D] 2:1 The Advisory board has given their finding in favour of the appellant and that is why he had sought assistance of Sundararajan, in order to ensure due observance of the policy of law that a detenu is not entitled only to the aid of a legal lawyer but that the said facility should be denied to him. [789E] 2(a) The Advisory Boards have given their findings in favour and that it was for the Advisory board to allow the appellant to be defended by an counsel before the Government or the Board. It is not for this Court to examine and assess what prejudice has been caused to the appellant on account of such denial. [788F] 2.(b) The order passed by the Advisory Boards to permit the appellant, when it permitted the assistance to him, was therefore a friend of the detenu before the appropriate Board. [893G H] 3(c) The detaining authority and the Government must have the facilities of appearing in the proceedings before the board through a Legal practitioner or an advocate but that they should be allowed the opportunity of appearing after the Advisory Committee. [878F G] 4.(d) The detention order is vitiated because it was not for the advisory Board to allow any assistance of the friend at this hearing and assess whatever prejudice has caused to him on account thereof. [877A B] 5(e) The High court had rightly rejected the contention that if the detaining Authority or the State Government takes the aid Of a legal practitioners or a Legal adviser, it must be deemed to be in the position of a legally binding practitioner. [880C D] 6.(f) The appellant was not afforded legal assistance by a counsel before an Advisory Board and the refusal of such assistance could not be justified. [879F] 793 (g) The detenu had a statutory right under section 11 of the Act to be heard by a legal professional or a lawyer. He had no legal authority to represent the case of the petitioner.

The appellants were the owners of certain goods. The respondents filed a suit for possession of the goods on September 30, 1946, and claimed that they had passed to hand over the goods to the mills as their representatives who were not present at the time when the goods were delivered. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the acquisition was valid and binding on the respondents and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants (i) that the order of requisition must be brought to the knowledge of the person whose interests are being affected by it, and (ii) that there should be a service of notice on the owner, and that the orders of requisition were not valid and enforceable. HELD: (i)(a) The question whether the Government of India will be estopped from challenging that order of requisitioning was not properly served and, therefore, there could be no doubt in view of section 18 of the Act that the title in these cases had not passed to the holders of the pucca delivery orders on September 29, 1946. [745 B C] (b) The Government of india will have also contained that the managing agents were being addressed and the names 837 of the mills whose managing agents was addressed and those who were present at that time were served on the managing agent of particular mills. [777 D E] (c) The word "in" in section 18 is not defined in the Act but it is used in a wide sense to include all persons who are interested in the property or who have been affected by the acquisition. In the present case, the Government had no authority to acquire any property and the properties were acquired under the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act. [77 D E F] (d) The expression "in any other case" in the section means that where the owner is interested in a property which has been acquired for the purpose of the acquisition, he may be given notice of his intention to acquire it and the property shall thereupon vest in the Government.

The assessee was a Private Limited Company. The assessment year 1963 64 was the relevant accounting year. In its books for the year ending March 31, 1956, there were no provision and no addition was made in respect of any amount set apart for contingent liability. The assessee claimed that it may become liable to pay additional tax under the said provision, but no such order was passed with respect to the assessment year 1964 65. The Income Tax Officer did not agree and the matter was ultimately taken to the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal. The High Court answered the same in favour of Revenue and against the assessee. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) amount set out for contingent obligation, (ii) Amount set apart towards contingent liability, (iii) Amount setting apart for other reserves and reserve funds were appropriations of profits, the assets by which they were repented to form part of the capital employed in the business. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The amount set as a provision is a charge against the profits to be taken into account against gross receipts in the P & L accounts. [111D] 2. The expression "in any other case" in section 23A means a reserve and not a reserve. It does not call it a reserve nor is set apart as a reserve, but it was set apart or appropriated as a reserves. [112E F] 3. The word "in the balance sheet" in the context of the provisions of the Companies Sur Profits Tax Act, 1964, means a provision and not reserve. [113G H] 4. The distinction between a provision made towards a liability which had attached on account of the issuance of a notice is settled by this Court in Metal Box Company of India Limited vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Andhra Pradesh etc., ; , followed.

The petitioners were appointed as temporary Assistant Engineers in the Indian Railway Service of Engineers (Class 1) every year, and were given weightage of half the length of service as temporaryAssistant Officers subject to a maximum of five years. The petitioners challenged the classification of their personnel into Class I, but the High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the classification was arbitrary and not permissible under the equality clause in the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the classification made by the Union Public Service Commission was neither discriminatory nor violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution, for the reason that it had nexus with the object sought to be achieved, which was mainly achieved, and (ii) the petitioners ' claim of equality in matters relating to employment on appointment in service was not justified. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The distinction between two services is well marked in Katyani Dayal 's case, and the important question of equality was once settled for all. When there has been complete absorption of the personnel of one service into one service, and when there has already been complete absorbed of the staff of one Service into the Indian Railways Service of Engineer Class I as stipulated in their appointment matters and held that both the services had started separately and never became one. [1022B C] 2. The principle of constructive res judicata is not applicable to cases where the claim of equal treatment has been made before the Court, but all the same approved of the measures of the Railway Board in lessening the Iona day of absorption into one Service of Temporary Assistant Officers subject only to a minimum of five year. [1122C] 3. The doctrine of constructive Res judicata is applicable to all cases where there has not been complete absorb ment of the employees into one services and the seniority of the absorbers is to be reckoned from their date of absorption as stipulated by their appointment matter and held as such. [1223D E] 4. The concept of equality by making one as an isolated one, and not providing for promotional avenues reasonably falls to the ground in view of the bar of re agitation erected by Direct Recruit 's Case (supra). It needs to be noted that while absorption had been made possible and its pace quickened with weightage, it is difficult to find fault with the scheme at this point of time to dig up old issues. [1323F] 5. The argument that the State is prohibited to create separate channels of service and create discrimination by making a one as one isolated one and not provide for promotional opportunities reasonably falls only to the grounds in view in view, of the embargo of re spitation erected by direct Recruit' case (supra) and the relevant question of equal opportunity was once again raised before this Court. [1423C] 6. The State is restrained from creating separate channels or service of service on appointment to any post in a representative capacity. It needs no emphasis that the posts are created by promotion, promotion etc., and the employees who have been recruited by selection cannot claim the same benefit as an independent one. The fact that the petitioners were given preference for promotional chances was not brought to the notice of this Court at all. [924D E; 925A] 7. The question of discrimination by giving weightage of full length of services subject to maximum of 5 years, because of its being questioned elsewhere, cannot be said to be barred by principles of res judicata as also in the rule of constructive constructive res bar. [826F G] 8. The contention that the temporary Assistant Officers were not so represented at all is misconceived and untenable.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1949 and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court acquitted him but on appeal by special leave it was contended that (i) the language of section 11 of the Saurashtra Ordinance which authorised the State Government to direct any class of cases or classes of offences to be tried by the Special Court constituted under the West Ben. Act, and (ii) the notification issued thereunder offended against the provisions of article 14 of the Consti tution and as such were void under article 13. Held, that section 11 was not ultra vires the State Legislature and was, therefore, void under articles 13 and 14 of its Constitution. The object of the Ordinance was to provide for the establishment of a Special Court and to direct investigation into offences or classes o f offences or sections of the Indian Penal Code and to appoint a Special Judge to try such cases by the special tribunal constituted under that Act. The notification issued by the State of Saurashtra in that behalf was, however, different from the notification dated April 1, 1950, issued under that part of section 5 (1) Of the West India Special Courts Ordinance, 1949, which authorised certain individual cases in which speci fied persons were involved to be charged with offences or class of offences. The State Government had power to direct a particular classes of cases to be try by the different special courts constituted under this Act and that delegation of such power could not be tested with reference to any definite legislative policy or standard.

The appellants were convicted under section 396 I.P.C. and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge. The High Court confirmed their conviction and sentence on appeal by special leave. In this Court it was contended for the appellants that (i) the evidence of P.W. 1, who had seen the occurrence as well as the deceased being injured in law, was not reliable; (ii) the prosecution has proved the case against the appellants satisfactorily beyond all reasonable doubt and that the conviction of the appellants for the offence under section 395 I. P.C., was not justified; (iii) the High Court erred in holding that the evidence was corroborated by the evidence on record and that it was not improbable that the appellants were seen by P.Ws. 1 to 7 and 8 at the time of the occurrence, and that their evidence could not be relied upon because they had intentionally made improvements in his version about the occurrence; (iv) the fact that P. W. 7 had been injured in the house and that he was also injured in a fire incident did not affect the prosecution case; (v) the conviction for the offences under section 397 I.PC. was not sustainable because the evidence given by P,W. 2 was corroborated from the evidence as well; (vi) the trial court had rightly rejected the evidence and convicted the appellants of the offence of murder. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The prosecution has established the case beyond all doubt and beyond all reasonably doubt. [901C] 2.1 In order to prove its case against an accused under section 302 I. PC., it is necessary that the prosecution must establish the circumstances which led to the death of the deceased or the manner in which the offence was committed, the circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is drawn and the circumstances of the case. The circumstances from where the conclusion is drawn should be such as to exclude every hypothesis but not to exclude any hypothesis except those that may be possible. [1001D] 2(a) In order that the court may convict an accused on a charge of murder, it has to satisfy itself that the circumstances have been fully established and all the facts and circumstances of each case have been properly established. The evidence of the prosecution witnesses should not be discarded merely because they are interested in the success of the defence. [1101E] 2.(b) In cases where the court is satisfied that the accused has committed an offence punishable under section 307 I.p.C, it may convict him on a finding that he had caused death or was guilty of murder and that his evidence should be accepted as true. But in such cases, the court must not accept the evidence unless it is corroborated by other evidence. [1201F] 3.(c) The High Courts have rightly rejected evidence of PWs 1 to 5 and 8 who were injured in fire incident. There was sufficient moon light at the place of occurrence and it is not improbable, that P, 7 could have seen some of the offenders and that her evidence could be relied on because he had intentionally omitted improvements in her version about his occurrence. [1191G] 4.(d) The reasons given by the learned Judges of the High court for rejecting the evidence are totally irrelevant and do not call for any interference. [1202E F] 5(a).

The appellant Corporation created a State Road Transport Corporation under the State Act, 1950. The employer of the respondent Corporation created an Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and the employees were probationers and the order of discharge in every case was on account of unsatisfactory service. The Labour Court held that termination of services of the employees while on probationers was not amounted to retrenchment and for non compliance with the provisions of section 25F of the (Disputes Act ') for short), the termination is bad, and directed reinstatement of the appellant Corporation with back wages. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the Corporation that in view of the decision in Hindustan Steel Ltd. vs Shambhu Nath Mukherjee, [1971] 1 SCR 591, the services of a probationer were terminated on the ground of unsuitability and for not compliance with section 25FFF. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: (1) The termination of service of a workman by an act of the employer even if such termination was involved a consequence of transfer or closure of the undertaking was to be treated as retrenchment for the purposes of notice, compensation etc. [793G] (2) In Hindustan Steel Limited vs Shambhu Dayal Mukherjee, ; , it was held that retrenchment as defined in section 2(oo) of the Act includes every termination of the service of any workman by the employer of a service of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract of employment between the employer and the workman concerned contains a stipulation in that behalf. [893A] (3) The expression 'retrenchment ' must include every termination which is embodied in the definition, discharge or termination of employment of a person by an Act of the employee concerned containing a stipulation In that behalf, it means the discharge of surplus labour or staff by the employers for any reason whatsoever. [789B C] (4) The word 'ret retrenchment ' in section 25 F has no wider meaning than the ordinary accepted connotation of the word; it means discharge of Surplus labour or Staff by the employee for any reasons whatsoever.

The assessee South Eastern Railway disposes of unclaimed and unconnected goods for money consideration. The assessee South East Eastern Railway, disposes of the unclaimed and unrelated goods for cash consideration. In assessment proceedings for the four quarters ending March 1959, the Commercial Tax Officer examined the case and found that the sale effected by the assessee was a regular feature of the assessee 's activities, and therefore the assessee fell within the scope of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes held that the sales effected by it were not "dealer" within the meaning of section 2(c) read with C.P.C. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the Revenue, it was contended that the assessee could be treated as a dealer under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941 and therefore liable to assessment under that Act. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The activity of so disposing of the goods remained un claimed for a period the Railway was entitled to dispose them of. There can be no doubt that the activity of such disposal of the unidentified and unserviceable material lying with it. It is an activity which may be regarded as necessarily incidental or ancillary to its business as carrier of the Goods by the Railway. It seems to South Eastern railway, that South Eastern Railways was a "dealer". [782B C] 2. The expression "business" in section 2 (c) of the Bengal Sales Tax Act, 1940 is not defined in the Act but it is an inclusive definition which includes business carried on by the railway. In the case of the appellant South Eastern railways, what were sold unclaimed and unserviceables material lying in the premises of the Railway were unclaimed goods. The High Court held that a transfer of property was involved in the auction held by the appellant and that therefore a sale of goods took place. [785C D] 3. The word "business ' is not necessarily incidental to its main activity of the carriage of goods by the Railways. It means something which may incidentally be regarded an integral or ancillary one to its trade as carrier. It does not mean anything incidental or auxiliary to its principal activity of carriage of the property by the railways. [779E] 4. The definition of "business " in section 3(c), read with section 2, (d) and (g) of that Act includes business which may actually be regarded by the person who is actually carrying on the business of buying or selling goods. It also means any activity which is necessarily incidental and ancillary to the main activity carried on as carrier or otherwise. [780E] 5. The words "business of so disposed" in the definition of the term "business", in section 4(c)(i) are wide enough to include business which can be regarded to be an integral part of the trade. It may also mean that a business which is actually carried on with the object of buying and selling goods, but it does not necessarily include business carried out by the owner or the person carrying on such business. [781F] 6.

The appellant, a company incorporated in India, was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling securities. The appellant had been carrying on its business as a dealer in securities under the name and style of M/s Bbagwati Trading Company. In the course of its business it had purchased certain shares from the respondent Bank of India at Bombay and paid them to the Union Agencies, who were also the agents of the appellant. The respondent Bank was to be made over to the appellant by the appellant on receipt of the advice of the Exchange for confirmation of the contract of purchase or sale of securities and after consulting the Reserve Bank of the United States Agencies with the Banks at Bombay, and to pay money out of the Insurance Company 's account with the Chartered Bank, Bombay. The prosecution case was that the amount was received in cash and not through transfers which transactions had to be adjusted by the Union Agency when funds were needed and also providing funds in the Insurance company 's accounts with the Bank of Baroda at Bombay. It was contended on behalf of the respondent that the money was received from the Insurance Companies, and that the moneys were credited in the account of the Bank at Bombay Office in the name of M /s Bagwati Trading Co., and that as the business had been entrusted to the Bank Agencies, it was not good and that there was no evidence of any loss or damage caused by the said transactions. Held, that the appellant was liable to be convicted under section 409 I.P.C. for having committed an offence under section 408 I. P.C., and the respondent bank was liable under section 405 I.p.C.; but the prosecution case had not been established beyond reasonable doubt. The Bank of Bombay was a private limited company, and it was carrying out its business in the course Of its business. It had no concern with the banking business of the company and its branches. The money was paid to the Reserve Agencies by the Bank and the Bank was not liable under s. 409 I P. C., because the moneys received were credited to the account at Bombay office in the names of M and Bbagni Trading Company, and the receipt of cash or the other transactions, his role had ceased according to the prosecution, after consulting with the Reserve Agency, and as such the funds of the insurance company was not bad.

The appellants were holding permanent posts in the ministerial service of the Secretariat of the State of Saurashtra and Kutch. They were allotted to serve in connection with the affairs of the new State of Bombay. The appellants were serving in the Secretariat as officers in the Ministerial service of that Secretariat. On November 1, 1956, the appellants were allotted a permanent post in the secretariat cadre. In the year 1957, the services of the appellants came to be transferred to the Secretariat and they were posted in the same Secretariat. The State Government issued an order dated August 19, 1966 transferring the former Saurashtra and Saurashtra States Secretariats of the former Kutch and Kutch States to which the members of the ministerial department were allotted. On October 1, 1957, a large majority of the members were transferred to Secretariat of Bombay and later in the State. In December 1958, the respondents were allotted the permanent posts of the secretaries of the Government of Saurashtra, Kutch and Saurashtra. The respondents challenged the order by filing a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court contending that the transfer of the latter Saurashtra and Gujarat Secretariat personnel to the secretarial service of their Secretariat was not open to objection.
