The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the transferred of the erstwhile Saurashtra and Ahmedabad States Secretaries of former Kutch State and Kutch State was not a case of absorption within the meaning of section 115(7) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The proviso to sub section (7) was intended to provide for the conditions of service applicable immediately before the appointed day in connection With the affairs or affairs of another State and were allotted thereto. [518 D] (2) The words "regularised" in section 115 are not used in the sense of a word of regular appointment. It is only when the Government makes an order under article 309 that it can be challenged by the aggrieved party. [619 E F] (3) The High Courts have rightly held that when the State 'regularised service ' was obtained, their right to be absorbed in equivalent posts in each department must be regarded as provisional and to continue in service of those who were already entitled except with the previous approval of the Central Government.

The petitioners who were dealers in the goods manufactured by them, purchased cotton and sold it after the period provided for in section 5(2)(a) of the Central Act. The petitioners contended that since the tax was levied, whether on sale or purchase at the first stage, the stage was fixed and that the dealer could always claim exemption under section 5 (2)(b) or a refund under section 12 of the Act. Held: (i) that the normal rule is that the tax can be collected only at one stage and that stage must be in respect of declared goods and such goods are sold in the course of inter State trade or commerce, or in the Course of export out of the territory of India. The distinction between the first purchase in the case of imported goods and last sale in the State and similar goods imported in the country and similar Goods imported in that State is prohibited by that clause. (ii) that where a person has purchased cotton at one time after the close of the year, to a registered dealer, a declaration in the prescribed form and duly filled and signed by him to whom the goods are transferred, is furnished by the dealer claiming deduction. The tax is also levied at more than one stage. (iii) that there was no liability for payment of tax unless this stage was so stated in the Act or the rules thereunder. (iv) that a person who is not liable to pay tax must nevertheless pay it in the first instance, and then claim exemption from payment of sales tax and the tax is further levied at one Stage and that is also the tax levied at different stages.

The respondent, who was the decree holder in a mortgage suit, filed a suit against the present appellant for recovery of a mortgage debt. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court held that the amount payable by him under the decree was to be settled at Rs. 3,215 and put in a petition under section 47 and Order 21, rule 2, Civil Procedure Code. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the decree being passed against them, the decretal debt might be scaled down in favour of the agriculturist; (ii) the amount paid by him as a result of the scaling down under the Agriculturists Relief Act may indirectly get the benefit of the decree which has been scaled up in favour Of the agriculturist and hence entitled to have his debts scaled over in accordance with the provisions of the Act. HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the mortgage debt and the security had been split up and, therefore, the benefit under the compromise decree could not be given to the agriculturist. [299 B] (iii) The decree passed against the appellant was scaled off by the High court in favour o f defendants 2 to 7 only and the amended decree directs that on payment of the amount directed to be paid by them as a consequence of the compromise, the decree holders were bound under the terms of the mortgage decree. [300 C] (iv) The subsequent agreement between the parties arrived at in course of execution proceedings by which the decreeholders agreed to release the interest of defendant No. 2 and that by opera tion of the principle ofigenceisibility of the mortgaged property including their interest would be sold for the entirety of the loan including their interests would be put into a petition Under section 47, Civil procedure Code. [298 E] (v) The compromise decree does not contain any clear directions but merely directs that the said defendants do pay into court the sum of Rs. 1,05,000 and odd and it is on payment to the mortgagee.

The appellants, who were the tenants of the first respondent, filed a suit against the respondents for possession of certain premises on the ground that they had been in occupation and occupation of the premises as subtenants thereof. The City Civil Court held that it had jurisdiction to entertain the suit but dismissed the suit on the view that there was no lawful subletting by the first plaintiff of the said premises to the second and third plaintiffs, and that the appellants were not entitled to possession, use and occupation, and occupation as sub tenants thereof. On appeal the High Court reversed the decision of the City Civil court and held that the suit filed by the appellants in the City civil Court could be entertained by that Court having regard to the provisions of section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 (Bombay Act No. VII of 1947), the City Court had jurisdiction in the area in which the premises were situate or if there was any such Civil Judge, the court of the Civil Judge (Senior Division) having ordinary jurisdiction, could entertain the same suit. Held, that the City Curt had jurisdiction under section 28 to try a suit relating to possession of the property and the right of the landlord to evict any of the appellants was not one relating to the premises in question. The provisions of Part 11 of the Act were intended to enable the court to deal with such claims or questions arising out of the provisions Of Part 11, and no other. The jurisdiction to try such a suit was exclusively vested in the courts specified in section 28 and no more.

The appellant was a private company incorporated under the name of Oriental Metal Pressing Works Ltd., hereafter called the Company. On July 7, 1955, Dadoba executed an agreement with one M/s. New India Metal Pressings Ltd., hereinafter called the company, for the sale of its business to the company. The company agreed to sell the said business to M/S. New Indian Metal Presses Works Ltd. on May 26,1955. On June 7, 1956, Dadindra executed an oral agreement with M/M. New Delhi Metal Pressers (India) Ltd., which was registered under the names of two directors of the company and M/O. New New India Metals Pressing Company. The appellant was appointed as managing director of the said company by the will of Dadoba on May 27, 1955. On August 7,1955, Dado executed an unregistered agreement with the company for sale of the business to its subsidiary M/o. New Baxers (I) Ltd. and M /O. Baxer (II) Ltd.; but the appellant was not appointed as the managing director. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant on the ground that the appointment of the appellant Govind as the Managing Director of the Company by the said will of the Dadoba, amounted to assignment of his office in his place and so such an appointment would also be void under the section. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the word "assignment" in the main part of section 86B of the old Act did not include the appointment by a director of another person as the director of M/or Baxing Company, and so the appointment was also void under section 312 of the new Act. The High Court took the view that the words "assignation" in section 312 were intended to make it clear that an appointment by the company of one of its directors was not an assignment but only a transfer of office of the director within section 312 and so, such an order could be made void under sections 3 and 4 of the Act. Held, that the proviso to section 86A did not apply to the present case because the word 'assignment ' in the proviso meant a transfer by the directors of one or more of their respective offices but it was intended to cover only such transfers as were done by one of them. The words "his office" in this proviso must be construed as including an appointment of his successor by another director, and not merely a transfer simpliciter of office.

The respondent landlord let out a shop to the appellant firm under clause 13(3)(iv) and (vii) of the Central Provinces and Berar Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. The appellant filed an eviction petition against the respondents on the ground that they were sub tenants. The Trial Court held that the appellants had unlawfully and without the consent of the respondent sublet the said shop let out to the said M/s Adeshwar Glass Mart without joining any of the partners of the said firm as respondents or serving them as partners and hence, the eviction petition was not maintainable at all. The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal holding that the appellant had unlawfully sublet the premises to the firm and that firm was carried on business in the name and style of M/S Adeshwar glass Mart without joined any of its partners. In an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Code of Civil Procedure is not applicable to proceedings under the said Rent Act and either the Rent Act or the Rent Control Order, 1949 are applicable to the proceedings under that Rent Act. [420B] 2.2 The provisions of the Rent Acts are not applicable in the proceedings before this Court. The question whether a firm can sue and be sued in its own name without joining its partners as repondents is one which would have been fatal to the eviction Petition. In the instant case, no such objection has been raised at all till the stage of Special Leave and it was surely not open to the appellants to raise such an objection at a very late stage and thereby delay matters for a number of years. [419C D] 2.(a) The question as to whether a partnership firm can be sued or not without joining itself as rerespondents, is one that would have to be decided by the Trial Court on its own merits. In this case, the partners were before the Court though in a wrong name. There could be no doubt that the partners are before the court although in a correct name. [406B] (b) The High Court was right in holding that there was no evidence in the case to come to the conclusion that the respondents had sublet the shop to M/ s Adeshwar glasses Mart without join any of their partners as res pect edents. [409C D].

The Andhra Pradesh Urban agglomeration (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 was enacted to provide for the imposition of ceiling on land situate within such area. Section 2(n)(A)(ii) of the Central Act provided that in an urban agglomerations referred to in section 2(p)(A), the Central Government shall not impose any ceiling on lands situate within the urban agglomeration, but may impose a ceiling on the total extent of land held by a person in excess of the ceiling area. The Andhra Pradesh Act was enacted with a view to provide that the ceiling areas in the State of Andhra Pradesh including land situate in urban agglomomerations shall be deemed to be an urban Aggomeration and the Andhra Pradesh Legislature would have legislative competence to provide such ceiling on holdings of land situated within such areas. Section 3(f) provided for imposition of Ceiling on land situated outside the urban Aggomerations. The Act was challenged by the landholders before the High Court in Writ Petition No. 1872/77 etc. In the said writ petition, the landholders contended that the Andhra State Act was ultra vires and void as being outside the legislative competence of the Andhra Legislature and that the Act was intra vires and invalid as being beyond the legislative power of the State Legislature to provide ceiling on holding of land situate outside the rural agglomeration. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that (i) the Andhra Act was an expensive concept and any area with an existing or future population of more than one lakh could be notified as an urban precomeration under section 2 (n)(a)(ii), the State Act would apply in relation to land situate beyond the urban immovable agglomerated areas; (ii) the Central Acts were not ultra vires the Andhra legislature inasmuch as being within the legislative competency of the A.P.

The respondent workmen, who were directed to be taken back in employment without any condition, were dismissed from service. The Company filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of dismissal on the ground that the workmen had failed to produce satisfactory evidence of their absence and that the reasons given by them for not giving the compensation were not justified. The High Court held that the Industrial Tribunal had in each case acted illegally or amounted to victimisation and that there was no reason why they should be taken into back employment without leave, and that it was for the Company to decide whether the charges had been proved and the Industrial tribunal should not have interfered with the decision of the company. The appellant contended that the Labour Appellate Tribunal had no jurisdiction to give compensation for the period anterior to October 2, 1953, because the workmen were near Burnpur and might have joined another, but failed to prove satisfactory evidence in which case they could not be taken up back as of right and without any conditions. Held, that the Company having held a regular and proper enquiry in which Samar Sen was said to be suffering from fever and blood pressure, the question of giving compensation for this period did not arise. The Industrial Tribunal was wrong in refusing to give the compensation for these periods. The company had been acquitted in a criminal proceeding on the footing that the work of the Company would be paralysed if the Company was forced to give leave to all of them for a "more or less indefinite period". The Industrial Court was wrong, and the High court was right in interfering with what was really a finding of fact.

The appellant University of Rajas than invited applications for the post of Professor in Botany. The Selection Committee constituted under section 5 of the Urea Kant Act, 1974 put a reserve list of candidates selected by it in order of merit and recommended the name of the appel lant Dr. Ureakant who was already selected and kept in the reserve list. The appellant University submitted that once a selected person joins the post, the reserved list was to remain valid upto six months from the date of approval of the Syndicate as per the resolution of the syndi cate. The selection committee constituted under Section 5 of Act, 1975 put a reserved list of selected candidates by it and recommended that the reserve List be valid for one year instead of six months. The respondent University filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order on the ground that once the selected person joined the post he was not selected for the concerned post and objection was also raised that once he joins the same, the reservelist was to remained valid upto 6 months from th e date of the approval of Syndicate as well as the resolution passed in its resolution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that once an selected person join the post the reserved List would be invalid for one month instead of 6 months. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant University that once once a candidate joins the said post, he is not entitled to be appointed and his selection is set aside. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The very purpose of preparing a reserve List would become extinct if the view taken by the High court is accepted that once one person selected by the selection committee has joined that post then selection made by the Selection Committee which is constituted for selection of teacher in Botsany and his name was recommended in the reservedlist will be considered as having been selected for that post and shall be entitled for appointment if any 424 vacancy is caused during the validity period of the reserve pate. [403B C] 1.2 The selection Committee constituted for the selection of a teacher or officers for which the selection Committee was constituted, has to prepare a reserve select list in the same order and to the extent of 50% of the vacancies for the posts of teachers or officers of the post as per resolution of Syndicate dated 10th July, 1978 and sub section (4) clearly provided that no teacher in any university in Rajasthan shall be appointed except on the recommenda tions of the Selection committee constituted. [416C D] 1.(3) The selection is not vitiated if the views taken by it are accepted that after a person selected for appointment on a vacant post caused during a period of one year, as no person selected has joined the same post can at all be expected to join for such a long period of time. [420D] 2.1 In the instant case, the Selection Com mittee had joined the said posts and several appointments had been made in the last decade from the reserve panel.

The appellants were owners of certain lands in the development plan originally published on January 9, 1964. The appellants challenged the validity of the acquisition proceedings contending that they had been wrongly acquired by the local authority and that the land was earmarked for recreation centre and green belt by the first respondent in the Development Plan finally adopted. The High Court held that the appellants were entitled to compensation under section 16(1) (a) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the local authorities had no power to revise the development plans and to publish them in the prescribed manner for inviting suggestions from public within a period of ten years from the date on which the final development plan comes into force; (ii) the reservation of land for the purpose of preparing a development plan was not something left to the pleasure or discretion of the local body concerned; (iii) the preparation of the final Development Plan was an act done in accordance with law and the rules framed thereunder were not ultra vires. HELD: The appellants were not entitled to any compensation under the Act as they had not been given a reasonable opportunity of being heard before the acquisition was made. [284 B] The provisions of sections 4 to 16(both inclusive) of 'the Act were borne in mind and the Rules framed thereunder complied with, as appears to have been done in these cases. [285 C D] (iv) The preparation of a development Plan by which the local Authority had to guide itself was nothing left to be entrusted with the work of appeal or revision. If the provisions of the statute were borne In mind and rules framed under section 13 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 were borne on the record and the draft of a section of the development Plan was prepared, the question was a simple one as to whether the commencement certificate could be given without doing any violation to the development planning.

The appellants, who were the owners of certain lands in the State of Gujarat, challenged the validity of the award on the ground that it was beyond the competence of the Executive wing of Government and no constitutional amendment was necessary. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the dispute was to be decided by arbitration, and that the award did not show a continuous boundary acceptable to the parties now or in the past, nor did it operate as giving rise to an obligation to cede Indian territory. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The award does not purport to, nor does it operateas giving rise thereto any obligation to supply, a claim to the Government of India to exercise fundamental rights in respect of which Parliament has power to make laws. [289 D] (2) The question whether the territory is now part of India or not was essentially one of fact and it cannot be said that there will be a cession of Indian territory and that there would be a migration of what is now Part of the territory of India from and to the award, does not operate as making rise to any obligation, acceptance of the Award. [288 E] (3) The decision to implement the Award by exchange of letters, treating the Award as an operative treaty after the boundary has been marked in this area is within the competence or authority of the executive wing of the Government and any constitutional amendment is necessary. [287 A B] (4) The High court was right in holding that there could be no cession of territory over which the Maharao of Kutch had sovereign rights and deprivation of the rights of citizens under article 19(1)(d) & (e) can only be achieved if the cession of what was now part, for part of the year.

The mortgagor, a proprietor of a five annas share in Mauza Bansjora, Simitanr and certain interest in Mauza Khora, was sold on January 16, 1937 by the auction purchaser who purchased the mortgaged property. The mortgagee 's rights in Bahaldih were sold on February 16, 1940, and after th sale was confirmed possession of Mauza Bans jora, the mortgagor 's right, title and interest in that property was sold to the mortgagees. The plaintiff filed a suit for enforcement of the two mortgages by sale of the mortgaged properties. The trial Judge rejected the defence raised by the defendants and held that the suit in respect of the first mortgage was within limitation because the mortgage was partly simple and partly usufructuary and partly simple, and even though the plaintiff could not rely upon part payment of principal or interest, after the date of dispossession, she could maintain the suit relying on the dispossession of the mortgagee on April 7, 1937, by the sale of his right, interest and upon the cause of action furnished by the mortgagees in respect thereof. The High Court also held that there was no bar to extend the period of limitation for the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (i) the mortgage dated August 27, 1922, was not barred by the law of limitation because, as the mortgage money was partly usufructuary, and partly perpetual and partly ordinary, the plaintiff had lost all his interest in Mauzas Bansjorora and Simitanar and therefore the suit to enforce the mortgage on August 27 , 1922, could not operate to extend time for the same. HELD: (ii) The High court rightly held that Mauza Bansjiora was not given in mortgage to extend period of Limitation for the Suit. [602 B] (iii) The plaintiff 's claim to enforce a mortgage on the mortgagor "was barred by limitation because it was barred by law of time. It was not open to the mortgagee to sue where the mortgagee is deprived of his interest, part payment will not extend the periods of limitation.

The appellants, who were in supervisory grades, were charged at the rate of Rs. 2 per month for transport of employees from Chinchvad to TELCO factory at Pimpri and back. The appellants contended that they were liable to pay the tax as also the penalty. The High Court dismissed their appeals holding that the challenge to the tax sought to be realised by the Revenue was not tenable and the appellants were liable only to pay tax as well as the penalty, but also the penalties. In these appeals by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the levy of a tax on passengers carried in certain classes of public service vehicles fell within the ambit of the charging section 3 which is the charging Section 3 which was the charging sections of the Act and therefore, the tax could be levied only if the passengers were carried by a stage carriage. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The word 'public service vehicle ' has not been defined either by the Act or by the Rules but that does not create any difficulty because having regard to the Preamble of the act it is clearly clear that vehicles which could not be termed as public service vehicle in any sense of the term. [362 A B] 2.1 The word "public service" has not even been defined by the Bombay Motor Vehicles (Taxation on Passengers) Act, 1958, hereinafter called the Act. It cannot by any process of reasoning or stretch of imagination be deemed to include employees of a private company who are given facilities not as members of the public but as holding a special status, namely, the employees of that company. [363 A B C] 2(a) The word `public service ' has been defined in section 2(7) of the Bombay Act and it is clear from the preamble of the enactment that vehicles used as a contract carriage within the meaning of the definition would be exigible to passenger tax. [364 D] (b) The words "public services vehicle" have not been mentioned either by or the Act nor by the rules, but that did not create difficulty because being a nominal charge is realised from the employees and they would provide free transport as in the case of supervisory staff. It could not by any method of reasoning stretch or stretch any process or reason of reasoning be deemed not to include employee of a public service Vehicle. [365 C] (c) The expression `public services vehicles ' has also not been described either by Act or Rules but it does not mean that the transport vehicle provided to the employees by the appellants could be a public Service vehicle in view of the Preamble. [366 D E] 2.(a) Rule 2(i) and section 2 (7) are the charging provisions of section 3, which is as defined in Section 2(8) of that Act. The words `public goods vehicle ' have not also been defined anywhere by the legislature or by Rules but have been defined under the Act to mean a motor vehicle carrying passengers for hire or reward at separate fares paid by or for individual passengers either for the whole journey or for stages of the journey.

The appellants, who were the residents of a temple in the vicinity of the place where the proposed cinema house was to be constructed, applied for a licence under Rule 101 and 102 read with rule 103 of the Madhya Pradesh Cinemas (Regulation) Rules, 1972. The application was rejected by the licensing authority on 6th March 1978. On appeal the State Government set aside the order of rejection and directed that the appellants should have been heard and decided the decision arrived at by the State government. In an appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that (i) no objection certificate specifying therein whether the application is in respect of a permanent cinema having a permanent Cinema licence having been opened in the locality there was no need for a cinema house with a temporary 'temporary ' licence and (ii) no objections were invited from the local residents who had objected to the grant of a "no objection" certificate. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the detailed provisions for the grant Of a "No objection" Certificate are without prejudice to the right of the licensing Authority to refuse a licence. [795G] 2. The appellants were not entitled to challenge the grant on short ground that on the facts and circumstances of the case, the order granting no objection was violative of principles of natural justice. [896A B] 3. The State Government did not give any opportunity to the successful objectors and decided their appeal at their back and thus the decision was rendered in violation of the principles of Natural Justice. [997B C] 4. The order granting a " no objection" is violative of the principle of natural Justice. It is not a fit case for interference of the High Court. [980C D] 5. The appeal must fail.

The appellant, a lessee of the mining lease granted to him by the respondent, executed an agreement dated September 2, 1957. The respondent agreed to assign the mining leases in respect of 184 acres of land in Kudrekan Kaval, Hosadurga Taluk, and claimed specific performance of the contract. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court reversed the decree. In appeal by special leave it was contended that the agreement was concluded on September 2 , 1957 and that the respondent had agreed to transfer the mining rights in favour of the appellant. HELD : (i) The plaint in O.S. No. 46 of 1957 was not an acceptance of the offer but was communicated to the appellant before November 6, 1957 by his letter dated September 1, 1957, and that in breach of the original contract the respondent was at liberty to revoke the offer. [584 B] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the assignment of the lease could not be lawfully made without the sanction of the State Government and the approval of the Central Government and that as the governments concerned could not get a possessory right before execution of a conveyance of the mine lease, the plaint was not a acceptance of offer. The appellant relied on Bloxam 's Case (4) to contend that the communication of an acceptance was not necessary. [585 C] (iii) The respondent had made an offer to assign a mining lease in respect Of 184 acres. The offer was communicated by letter dated November 2,1957 to the respondent before November6, 1957 and the acceptance was communicated on September 1 , 1957. There was no concluded contract unless there was an acceptance or communication of the application for shares. [58 D] (iv) The correspondence between the parties showed that the appellant had agreed not to purchase the mining right but only to remove iron ore from the leased area. In the peculiar facts of Bloxin 's case a contract to take shares was concluded by an oral application for share and the offer was conveyed to assign to the applicant. [583 E] (v) The letter dated October 31, 1957 was a communication of acceptance by serving a copy of the plaint along with the writ of summons alongwith the writof summons alongwith a writ of Summons. It was not intended to be an acceptance. It is not usual to accept a business offer by a plaint; nor is it usual to communicate an acceptance by a serving copy of a written statement through the medium of the Court.

The appellants were prosecuted under section 3 of the Bihar Sugar Factories Control Act, 1937 for having committed an offence punishable with three years ' imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1,000/ . The trial court acquitted them but convicted them on appeal by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) sugarcane did not come within the ambit of the Act and hence the power conferred on the Government under section 2 and 3 of that Act was incompetent; (ii) the regulation of the price at which sugarcane may be bought or sold, and in addition to the Sugar Control Order 1955, the Central Government had also powers to control the production, supply and distribution of essential commodities and trade therein; (iii) the power to fix the price of sugarcane under section 4(1)(f) was not validly issued under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act. HELD: The Bihar Sugar Factory Control Act is a complete code in itself and it does not confer any power on the Central Govt. to make rules for regulating or prohibiting production, sale and distribution thereof and trade in essential commodities. [616 C] (iv) The regulation of price of cane under section 5(1) of the , was subject to the control of the Central Govern ment by notification dated 27th August 1955 issued by the Central government on 27th September 1955. It was well within the competence of Parliament to enact the Act, and hence it was well beyond the competence Of Parliament to legislate in respect of sugarcane and direct payment thereof as also the controlling of price atwhich sugarcane may or be bought and sold. [716 D E] (v) The power conferred by section 3 is a part of agriculture. It is not necessary that there should be an agreement between the parties to the effect that the price should be paid in cash or in kind. The word 'agricultural produce ' has been defined in section 2(f) of that act and it means any article which is used for agricultural purposes, whether or not for growing thereon of food crops. [816 D] (vi) The expression 'agricultural production ' in section 3(2)(c) includes the production of sugarcane as also processing of sugar. It does not include the production or manufacture of sugar and it is only when there is an agreement in writing to the contrary that the same must be held to have been altered in view of article 372 of the Constitution which empowers the Parliament to make laws in respect thereof.

The Government of Karnataka decided to adopt a policy to encourage rapid industrialisation and that the earlier orders had given room for many types of misuse but such concessions were not permissible under the said order. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court claiming that the benefit granted by the earlier order dated 30th June, 1969 was being misused and undue advantage was being taken of the same. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable in the present case because it was found by the Government of Mysore that the concessions granted under the order dated 12th January, 1977 were being misused or undue advantage had been taken of which was being used and undue benefit was being given to them by the former order as the said grant of concessions constituted a promissory estoppel against the Government on the basis of which they had acted by starting new industries requiring investment of considerable funds and the Government was not entitled to go back or promise as permitted by Section 8A. The State Government, however, issued another order dated 20th January 1977 directing that the incentives would be given to new industrial units requiring investment in the State on raw materials purchased by it for the first five years from the date of industry goes into production as set out in the Order. In pursuance thereof, the Government issued another Order dated 12.1.1977 which recited that the incentive would be granted to new industries require investment of substantial funds and that promise was not admissible under the Order and that assurance was not given to the new industrial unit requiring investment. The said order also stated that the concession granted by it earlier had been utilised and undue benefits were being taken away from the Government. In the writ petition filed before the Karnataka High Court, the appellants contended that the State Government had no authority to provide for the grant of refunds as the grant was given to entrepreneurs by starting fresh industrial units in the Mysore State. The learned Single Judge dismissed the Writ Petitions holding that there was nothing on record to show that any such misuse was being made or undue benefit taken of it. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The doctrine of promissory estoppel is not applicable because it is a rule of law and is not an absolute rule of evidence. It is well settled that the principle of estoppel is a part of the rule of equity. [950G] 2.2 The doctrine is not intended to be extended to cases where there is no statutory provision under which such concessions could be granted. In order to test the validity of the order, it is clear that in effect, the benefit was given by the previous order and not merely certain words used out of context. [980B] 2.(a) The doctrine has been applied only for the purpose of determining whether a particular provision of law is applicable or not. It does not apply to cases of promissory estoppels.

The appellants were charged with the offences under Sections 147, 148 and 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C. for causing the death of Madda Lakshamandas. The Trial Court acquitted A 1 and A 2 but convicted them under Sections 148 and 323 I. P.C., and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. On appeal by the State, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellants under Section 302 readwith 149 IP. C. and dismissed their appeals. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The non applicability of Section 149 Cr. Pc. is, therefore, no bar in convicting the appellants Under Sections 148 & 302 read along with Section 34 I.PC. [849C] 2.1 In order to attract Section 149 IPC, it is necessary that there must be a common object of the unlawful assembly which is to commit an offence. The prosecution has to establish that the accused persons formed an unlawful assembly within the meaning of Section 141 I. PC. If the evidence discloses commission of an offence in furtherance of the common intention of the accused, all the accused are liable to be punished as sharers in the commission of offences. [949C D] 2(a) The non application of section 149 I P. C., is therefore, not bar in conviction under Section 7 read with section 34 I PC. [1049D] 2.(b) The offence committed by the appellants was one under Section 148 and on applying to the aid of Section 34 IPC, they were convicted under Sections 302 read and Section 34, I.I.P.,C. and sentenced to imprisonment of life. [1150E F] 3(a). In order that the appellants may be released on bail, it must be shown that there was a previous enmity between the parties. The evidence of P.W. 1, the wife of the deceased, PW 2, the daughter of the decease sion of the appellant and the deceased caused his instantaneous death. [1250E] 4(b) In order whether the appellants can be convie ded under Section 149 or Section 34 Cr.Pc., it is not necessary that the common object should be to commit the offence. It is in evidence that all the appellants formed an assembly within a defined meaning of section 141 I PC, and committed the offence punishable under Sections 143 and 302 I.Ps. [980F] 5(a)(i) The High Court clearly fell into error in confirming the conviction of the Appellants under Section 147 read with 149 I PC and keeping them on bail. [981G] 6(b). In view of the manner of attack as disclosed by the eye witnesses and the number of injuries, it cannot be said that there is no bar to convicting the accused under Sections 149 and 34 I P C. The appellants being only three in three numbers could not have formed an unidentified persons. [983F] 7(c) The prosecution had failed to establish any common object for which they were charged. [984D] 8(d) The evidence on record discloses commission Of an offence under Section 307 read with 34 IP C.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax on the total value of the property as on the date of transfer. The assessee claimed that the transfer was effected with the object of avoidance or reduction of the liability of the assessee to tax on capital gains on the basis of section 52 sub section (2) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The Income tax officer assessed the sum of Rs. 48,500/ as consideration for the transfer and it was enough to attract the applicability of sub section(2) to tax. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of assessment. In appeal by the assessee, the Tribunal held that the assessee had not proved the actual consideration received by him and that the transaction was a capital asset within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of Act. On reference, the High Court held that sub section 52(2), which required the assessee 's consent to transfer of the capital asset in question, did not require the assessee as a condition precedent that there should be no application in respect of the transfer. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that sub s.(2) applied only where the consideration for transfer is shown at a lesser figure than that actually received by the assesse and the assessee has actually received more than what is declared by him, and that therefore sub section 2 did not apply. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that sub sec.(2), as it stood before its amendment by Act of 1976, provided for a condition that it would apply only where there was an intention to transfer the capital assets or any other type of income. [601C D] 2.1 In the instant case, the assessee did not produce any evidence to show that the consideration was received by it and it must be confined to cases where the actual receipt received by a assessee is not disclosed and the consideration declared in respect thereof is more than that originally received. The mere fact that the amount was shown at the lesser figure as that actually was received would not result in an amount being taxed which has neither accrued to the assessee nor been received by them and it would be difficult, if not all, to determine and prove the exact quantum of suppressed consideration, sub section 3(2). [602D E] 2.(a) The High court was right. (b) The fact that there is no understatement of the consideration, subsection (2), does not mean that the fair market value of a capital assets transferred by the assesses as on date of thetransfer exceeds the full value of consideration declared by the assessees. [643E] 2(a) In the present case, sub sec. (2)(b) provides for the statutory measure for determining the consideration actually received and the transfer is correctly declared. The fact, however, that the total consideration received was not disclosed or in other words, shown at any lesser figure, than that which actually received was more than once does not make the assessee liable to tax under the Gift Tax Act. [641F G] 3(b) In order to determine what is actual consideration the real value of transfer exceeds the entire consideration declared, sub s.

The appellant was charged with an offence under section 7(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, and sold it to the Food Inspector. The Food Inspector stated that he had written on the cash memo when he sold these Til seeds to the appellant. He denied the presence of Tambe on the ground that he did not write on the Cash memo but only on the packets. The trial court acquitted the appellant holding that the evidence of the Food inspector was more probable because it was supported by what the Inspector described ashandling. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) It is true that black Til seeds are not used as food. But if they were sold in a shop, it would be difficult for the prosecution to prove that what he had stored was not really meant food. [330 B] (2) The evidence of P.W. 2 who said that Tambe was probably not present at the time when the seeds were sold by the appellant to the Public Analyst cannot be implicitly relied upon in this case. It is more likely for reasons already given by us, that Tame 's testimony tends to demolish more than corroborate to the version of the food Inspector. [331 C D] (3) The prosecution has not been able to prove what the appellant had stored or sold. He could have been kept for the purpose of being sold only 11 days after all, if it was shown that he was more likely. [328 B] In Bhagwan Das vs Delhi Administration, ; , referred to.

The plaintiff, a Government servant of Madhya Pradesh was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13th January, 1966. He preferred an appeal to the Divisional Commissioner and that appeal was dismissed on 31st August, 1966 on the plea of limitation. The plaintiff 's suit was one for declaration that the order of dismissal was bad and he continued to be in service. The trial Court decreed the suit holding that the dismissal was not valid because the order had merged in the order passed in appeal therefrom and in the final order of the lower authority in the appellate order dismissing the appeal, it was held that the plaintiff 'S suit was within time. In the second appeal before this Court, the question for consideration was whether the order in the proceedings under Article 226 of the Constitution was an order prior to the Constitution and the revisional order passed by another officer in the department and an order rejecting an application for revision by the head of the department could hardly be equated with any propriety with decrees made in a civil suit under the Code of Civil Procedure by the Court of first instance and the appellate decision which was rendered on the ground of limitation and jurisdiction had not greater efficacy by the subsequent order of dismissing the appel lant 's appeal. Dismissing the appeal to this Court. ^ HELD: 1. The cause of action shall be taken to arise not from the date when cause of a suit has arisen but where such order is either reversed or modified it is the order which is the operative order and if the High Court has no jurisdiction to issue a writ to the appellate authority it cannot issue a Writ to the original authority. [54B C] 2. The principle of merger applicable to decrees of courts would not apply to orders of departmental tribunals, and if, the High Courts have no jurisdiction, Article 58 may not be invocable in view of the special limitation. In every such case only when the appeal or representation provided by law is disposed of, cause of actions there is no getting behind these words in spite of apparent inequity of applying the same. [55D E] 3. The civil Court 's jurisdiction has been taken away by the Act and, therefore, the order dismissing a suit on the doctrine of merger would not be open to attack under article 226 of thi sution. [56F G] 4. In view of this legal position, the Civil Court 'S jurisdiction has not been taken off by the State Government and it is not the appellate judgment which was pronounced in appeal from the order confirming the dismissal of the suit or revision. [57G H] 5. The High Court was right in its view that the cause of the action shall not arise from the dates when the original order merged in a decree made in civil suit by an officer in an authority subordinate to it. [58F G; 59A] 6. In this case, the claim has been dismissed on the basis of the apparent inequities of applying it. The Civil Court had no jurisdiction. [59D E F] 7. The question whether the original decree had merged into the order or not is not at all referred to or examined. It is the appellate view which was taken by the High Cou rt that the original judgment merged in its order of transfer and became opera tive in law and was capable of enforcement. [60F G H] 8. The suit was filed within a period of six months from the passing of the final ord er.

The appellant, who was the decree holder of a decree for Rs. 1,000/was directed to pay interest at 6% per annum on the amount awarded by the trial court and also to pay costs of Rs. 500/ . The appellant contended that the word "decision" in article 133(1) should mean the whole of the appellate decree and not the grounds stated in support of the decision or the grounds given for it. Held, that the words "decision", in article 134(1), are wide enough to cover all cases where the appellate court makes a variation in the decision of the trial Court. The word " Decision" in the context of section 110 literally means the whole and not merely the decision on which the variation is made. It does not mean that the judgment or decree of the High Court varies the decision according to its own view. The words "decree of affirmance" in section 110 clearly indicate that the appellate order makes a modification in respect of the order as to costs, though it may be of very minor importance and may be a similar approach to the part of the decree. The appellant was entitled to go to the Privy Council for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court under article 133 (1) of the Constitution. The expression "decision ' in article 136(1)(a) means the decision which is directly in the discretion of the court under section 35 of the Code of Civil Procedure as an order of affirmances. The phrase "decision of the suit by the appellate Court" in that clause means the judgment of the first appellate court and not by reference to the whole or any part of it. The High Court was therefore right in holding that the expression " decision" did not mean the entire of the appeal as a whole; but only makes a difference in regard to the order which is entirely in the power of costs, and that if the appellate judgment makes any variation in respect the decision would be affected either by the extent of the variation or by the fact that the variation was made in favour of one party or the other.

The High Court had exclusive jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 to entertain a revision petition filed by the respondent against an order of the District Judge exercising revisional powers under section 25, Provincial Small Cause Courts Act disposing of a revision application filed on and after that date. The High Court in exercise of its revisional power under section 116 of the Civil Procedure Code, dismissed the revision petitions filed by respondent. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant (petitioner) that the High Court exercising revisional jurisdiction under Section 115, Code of Criminal Procedure, could not have arisen of invoking the revisional powers conferred upon the District Court under section 100, Code, of Civil Laws (Amendment) Act, 1976, and that the revisional power enjoyed by the High Courts from time to time was barred. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The revisional jurisdiction of the High court under section115, Code is not amenable to the revisional jurisdiction conferred upon a District Court by a District Judge or Additional District Judge under section25, Provincial Civil Laws Act, in respect of cases arising out of original suits or other proceedings of any valuation decided by a district Court. [975B] 2. The provisions of section 115, C.P.C., are not applicable to the High courts exercising revisional power of the State under section 23, Code. [973D E] 3. A revision petition under section 114, Code cannot be entertained against a revisional order made by the District court under Section 25, Code unless it is satisfied that there was sufficient cause for doing so. The jurisdiction conferred on the High Curt under section 24 of the Provincial Small Causes Courts Act, is not subject to revisional jurisdiction. [976D E; 975A] 4. A revisional order passed by a subordinate Court under Section 100, Civil Procedure code, is amenable to revisional power vested in the High Criminal Courts under section 151, Code Of Civil Procedure. The revision petitions must be dismissed. [977B C] 5. In view of the fact that a revision proceeding pending immediately before 1st August, 1978 would vest in the District Magistrate, the case would be amenable to his revisional jurisdiction, the matter would be governed by section 115 C. P.C. and no question could have arisen under the revisional order under section 26, Code or any question could arise of invoking revisional power conferred upon him by section 25. [980D E].

The respondents, who were owners of certain lands belonging to the appellant Trust, filed a writ petition in the High Court for quashing the notification issued by the State Government under section 52(1) of the Act on February 8, 1984. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the alleged need of the respondents was just bona fide and their real object was just to get the land released from acquisition on one ground or the other. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the cause of action culminating in the acquisition of the land under section 51(1), Or, as the case may be, arose within the territorial jurisdiction of the Rajasthan High Court at Jaipur Bench and that the writ application filed by the respondents under article 226 of the Constitution was not maintainable. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The cause of actions arising out of acquisition of land under Section 52(l) or (2) of Act arose within a State of Rajasthan i.e., within the local jurisdiction of Jaipur Bench. [605B] 2. The entire cause of the action culminating into the acquisition was wholly or in part, arisen within the State of Jaipur and that it was necessary for the respondents to plead the service of notice on them by the Special Officer , Town Planning Department , Jaipur under section 53(1). [606C D] 3. The writ application under article 227 of the constitution is maintainable only if there is a manifest abuse of the process of the Court. It is not necessary for this Court at the Jaipur Bench to plead and service of the notice on the respondents by the special Officer , town Planning Department, Jaipur under Section 53(l). or (3) of Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959, as it was not necessary that the land should be acquired by the Government under Section 51(2) or the notification under section 54(1); and the ad interim exparte prohibitory order made by the High court at Jaipur bench in the writ peti tion is set aside and proceedings before the Calcutta Bench are restored. [706D E] 4. The respondents were not justified in invoking the jurisdiction of this Court under article 136 of the Consti tution of India, 1950. [807F G] 5. The State Government issued the impugned notification dated February 8 1984 under section52(1 ) or the Act and the notified land vested in the State government free from all encumbrances. The said notification was duly served on the Respondents by the Collector , Town planning Department, Jodhpur. It was not required to plead or serve any notice on him by the 'State Government at Jaipur. [783A B] 6.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the respondent tenant from the premises in suit. The respondent tenant resisted the claim contending that the building was constructed by a co operative society and the landlord had purchased it from the society and, therefore, the new Rent Act had no application to the building during the period of ten years from the date on which its construction is completed. The Additional District Judge dismissed the suit holding that the appellant would be entitled to the benefit of s.39 of the new Act. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the construction in question was constructed not ten years old on the date of the suit and, consequently, the old Rent Act having no application, the additional District Judge had rightly held that the buildings were not ten year old on 1st October, 1971. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: The Additional district Judge has found that the premises which was not ten, years old at the date when the revision came to be decided by the High Court and, thus, there was no question of giving the benefit under s.40 of the Act to the appellant. [337B] In the instant case, the building had become ten years on 1 st October, 1970 and not on the dates of assessment which will be deemed to have been completed on the day of assessment. The additional District judge has found in favour of the appellant and against his liability for eviction on ground that the said building was not five years old. [437C] In view of the matter, the Additional District judge had found that there was a change in the cause of action. He did not give the benefit to the respondent because the appellant could not get any protection of the old Act. The High Court, however, accepted the finding of the Additional district judge that the suit would be deemed as completed on 1th October, 1972 and not from the day on which it was actually occupied.

The appellant company entered into three contracts for the construction of a building contractors. The respondents entered into two contracts with the appellant company, and the latter entered into four contracts with them. The first of them was an agreement to refer to arbitration. The second contract was in respect of the construction work of aerodrome, hangarettes, buildings, stores and other works at Ranchi. The third contract was for the execution of a work contract. The appellant company made two contracts on November 5, 1942, and December 21, 1942. In the first of these contracts the respondents entered upon three contracts with M/s. D. P. Roy & Co., and the second of them were also an agreement for arbitration. On February 25, 1948, the Executive Engineer wrote to the appellant that certain formal corrections should be made in the agreement and signed by both the parties. The Executive Engineer informed the appellant on February 25 that the draft agreement had been slightly modified in consultation with the Government Pleader and he wrote to him that some formal corrections were made in his agreement and signing by both of them. On March 26, 1948 the Executive engineer wrote to M/S. D P Roy & Company that certain corrections should not be made as quickly as possible. The Superintending Engineer wrote a letter to the Executive Engineers that certain modifications should be effected in the draft contract and that the necessary corrections should also be made. The respondent filed a suit for specific performance of the contracts on the ground that the agreement was not one relating to execution of works as that had been completed and the dispute related only to payment of bills, and that it fell within item 12 K. Lall. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the award passed in favour of the appellant was a nullity and that no decree should be passed in terms thereof. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The agreement dated February 6, 1948 was not an instrument relating to the execution or execution of work as that having been completed, it would fall within item 2 and the Executive Officer was authorised to execute the arbitration agreement. [830 C] (ii) The High Court had rightly held that there was no valid reference to arbitration in view of section 175(3) of the Government of India Act 1935. [820 D E] (iii) The question whether the award which was sent by the arbitrator to the court is the original instrument or a copy thereof, depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. It is not necessary that the original document should be produced in Court and it must be produced before the court. [821 G H] (iv) The arbitration clause does not provide for the levy of any penalty on lost documents.

The appellant, a retired Executive Engineer in Public Works Department, was working as Executive Engineer, in Public Health Department in the State of Punjab. He was working under the respondent in Public works Department in Punjab. The First Information Report against him was lodged by the respondent on the basis of an information received from the Vigilance Department that he had committed certain irregularities in the construction of a road and had been found guilty of misconduct, negligence or misconduct by the appellant. The respondent filed a complaint before the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Patiala alleging that the said report was not correct and that the First Information Reports against him were false and that he was falsely implicated in the case. The Chief Judicial Magistrte, Patiala, dismissed the complaint on the ground that the allegations made against him had been proved by the prosecution as against him. The High Court quashed the First information Report and acquitted him of all the charges leveled against him under section 161 I.P.C. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the third proviso to clause (b) of Rule 2.2 is in the nature of a beneficent legislation and in case of doubt has to be interpreted in favour of the person for whose benefit the Rule had been framed; (2) the fourth proviso to sub rule (b), which provides that where the conditions stated therein are satisfied, the competent authority may either dismiss or withhold the pension of a Government servant on the expiry of four years from the date of cause of action or event mentioned therein. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The third proviso is in nature of an exception to the power of the government in the matter of withholding or withdrawing or withdrawing pension of any class of Government servants. It does not cover cases where the competent authorities have exercised their discretion arbitrarily or capriciously or arbitrarily or where the exercise of such discretion is arbitrary, unreasonable or capricious. [920D] 1.2 The third Proviso to clause(b) has been framed for a different purpose namely to provide an exception thereto to the powers of the Government in the matters of withholding pension of the retired government servant contained in clause (a) with regard to pension of such a government servant. This purpose can be achieved if the said proviso is interpreted to mean that even if a government employee is prosecuted and punished in judicial proceedings instituted in respect of cause or action which took more than four years before such institution, as has been held by the High Court can be treated to be a rule regulating the condition of service of such an employee. [1020E F] 1:2 The fourth proviso cannot be interpreted as laying down an absolute or general embargo on prosecution of a government Servant on the expiration of a period of four year from the time of cause, if any, that may have occurred more than three years before the institution of the departmental proceedings. It is not to place an embargo on the prosecution of the employee for whose benefits the Rule has been made. [1120F] 1 :3 The third provisos to clause 2.1 are in the very nature of things a beneficient legislation and, therefore, cannot be construed as layingdown an absolute prohibition on prosecution.

The respondent company was floated as a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act 1913, to acquire and carry on the business of manufacture and sale of "Amrutanjan". The authorised capital of the company was 7,000 ordinary shares and 3,000 preference shares of Rs. 7,500 ordinary shares. In September 1936 the authorised capital was 7000 ordinary share and 8,000 equity shares of the respondent company were allotted to the shareholders as dividends by the authorised Capital of the Company. On March 31, 1951 the respondent filed a petition under section 23 A of the Indian Income tax Act for an order under section 24A of the Income tax (Investigation Commission) Act, 1922, for an amount of Rs 1,10,000 shares representing the value of the shares held by the company up to the end of the sixth month after its accounts for that previous year were laid before the company in general meeting. The respondent contended that the provisions of section 23A were correctly applied for the three relevant years and on a view different from those which was taken by the High Court, the Income Tax Officer had no jurisdiction to pass the order under s.23 A. Held, that the Explanation to sub section (1) of section23 A was in reality a clause which defines what a company in which the public are substantially interested and to a subsidiary company of such companies as would render the company one in which it is substantially interested. The Explanation has raised a conclusive presumption in those cases where shares of a company carrying not less than twenty five per cent of the voting power have been allotted unconditionally or acquired unconditionally by the public, it must be presumed that the company is one in whom the public were substantially interested, having regard to the purpose for which the holding of fifty one per cent. of the votes power has been allotted partly or wholly acquired unconditionally or partially and acquired unconditionally. The word "Amritanjan" in section 23(A) means a person who holds or is entitled to a fixed rate of dividend, whether with or without a further right to participate in carrying profits not less that twenty five percent of the paid up capital of such company. The expression "Amratanjan" has been defined by the Explanation as meaning any company which carries on business in concert with another person and includes a company which is engaged in the business as well as in any other manner whatsoever, whether incorporated or not. The definition of "amrutanjan" is wide enough to include a company whose shares are held by it. It does not mean that a company has been formed by a single individual or a group of individuals acting in concert, the company would be regarded as one in Which the public is substantially concerned and to an subsidiary company which would render them the company equally interested.

The first appellant, who was the agent of a firm, sold the bales to one Dwarkadas Khetan & Company on behalf of another quota holder Beharilal Bajirathi. The goods were delivered to the same Dwarkadans and the sale proceeds were credited in the account of the purchaser. The first appellant sent them to Dharsi Moolji for delivery to the quota holder or his agent but they did not deliver them. On the same day, i.e., on 21st February, 1947, the first appellant despatched 13 bales on 28th February, 1948, and sent them again to Dharliji through a letter dated 17th February. The sale proceeds of the goods were credited into the account by the purchaser on behalf Of the first respondent. On 21st March, 1947 the first Appellant sent them with a cheque for Rs. 2,000 on the same date. The cheque was returned unpaid and the first Respondent paid the amount in advance to the first appel lant on 21 st February, 1949. The second appellant filed a complaint against the first and second respondents under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (Act No. 1 of 1881) for the recovery of the amount due from them. The trial court acquitted all the three accused but convicted the first two appellants under section 420 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced each of them to imprisonment for one year. On appeal by the second appellant, the High Court held that the transaction remained in the physical possession of the firstappellant at all material times and were not physically delivered to Messrs. Dwarkadasi Khetan & Co., but it was one which was not physically supplied to the second appel late appellant. The High Court further held that even if there was physical delivery to Dwarkada Khetan, the statement is inaccurate and misleading. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) that the entry in column 3 of the register showed that the first appellants had passed and so the goods had passed, and so they were handed over to DwarILLans Khetan & company on behalf o the first respondents. The fact that the goods remained in physical possession was not a ground for holding that there was any physical delivery of the bales by Dwarkadan Khetan or the agent. (ii)that the first information appellant had made a sale, and that he had been authorised to take delivery of those 13 bales.

The respondent was a public servant. He was prosecuted under section 5(1)(d) read with section 5 (2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 for having committed an offence punishable under section 161 I.P.C. and section 5 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted him but convicted him under section 165 I. P.C., and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for one year. On appeal by the State, the High Court set aside the acquittal order and convicted him thereunder. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the offence of criminal misconduct in the discharge of his duty was not a public service; (ii) the use of the word "obtains" in clause (d) of section 5, as it stood at the material time, was not necessary that the remuneration by any of the Government or remunerated by fee or commission for the performance of any public duty should be paid by the Government as a public officer; and (iii) the remuneration which was to be paid to him was by the government as a reward or commission. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The word "public servant" in clauses (a), (b) and (c) of s 5(2) read along with section 4(1) of Prevention of corruption Act, is wide enough to cover all kinds of public servants. It would be reasonable to put on clause (e) a construction which is consistent with the other clauses of the sub section. [723 A] 2. The abuse of position as a Public servant is clearly implied. The use of words "obtain" in cl.(d) is not decisive. The words "public servants" are wide enough and they must be construed according to their ordinary meaning. It may be used in the wider sense, but it would not be reasonable for the purpose of the opening part of section5(1). [724 C D] 3. The expression "obtaining" is a term which has been defined by section 2(g) of that Act. The definition of public servant means any person who is remunerated or by fees or commission, whether paid to the Government, or to any other person for rendering his position as public servant, and includes any person in receipt of remuneration from any other public servant without there being any question of his misconducting himself in the performance thereof. [824 D E] 4. The object of section 405 is to prevent corruption or abuse of official position by a public authority which is not an offence under section 6(1), and it is not necessary for the prosecution to prove that the public servant was guilty of any corrupt or illegal conduct. It is, therefore, clear that the use by the public officer in the exercise of his official duties would be the essential ingredient of the offence. [825 E F] 5. The section does not exclude the concept of abuse of the position as an public servant because the abuse of his position would be sufficient to sustain the construction or interpretation of section 6 (1) (d). It is also erroneous to hold that the essence of an offence is the use which is consistently with the provisions of the section. The misuse by a corrupt or unlawful means or by otherwise abusing his position, as apublic servant, is clearly implicit.

The petitioners, who were working as casual labourers in the Construction Department of the Signal Unit in the Signals Unit in Northern Railway, challenged the validity of their temporary status on the ground that they had put in continuous service for quite a long period and that their services should be treated as temporary servants. The petitioners contended that since prior to the issue of the Railway Board 's directions on January 1, 1984, casual labourers were not entitled to all privileges like House Rent Allowance, City Compensatory Allowance, Temporary Status, Casual Leave etc., they are now entitled to only those privileges as applicable to open line. Allowing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: (1) The petitioners should be entitled to the same pay as is 1) admissible to either category of employees. [144H] (2) The Railway Board and Northern Railway Headquarters were placed before this Court for consideration. The Administration was anxious to take appropriate steps to remove the difficulties faced by casual labour but there was a break in such continuity the previous service is also taken into account. [145A B] (3) The Administration will have to be blamed. It is not necessary to create temporary posts to accommodate casual labourers who acquire temporary status, will not, however, be brought on to the permanent establishment unless they are selected through regular Selection Boards for Class IV staff. [146C D] (4) The Railways Board and the Northern Railway Headquarter were placed in a similar manner as that of the petitioners. They had also been directed to be absorbed against a permanent vacancy in the open line, and therefore, that retiral advantage is not available to either categories of employees.[144E F] (5) The Government should take prompt steps to screen such casual labour who acquire Temporary status, would not, ordinarily, be bring on to permanent establishment until they are appointed through regular selection Boards for class IV staff, and that retiral benefits are not admissible to other categories of persons. [147F G] (6) The respondents cannot be denied the same benefit as is applicable to temporary railway servants who acquire permanent status. [149G] (7) The claim of pension is not admissible in either category or in the project or in open line acquired temporary status. It may, however be brought to the regular establishment unless it are selected by regular Selection Board for Class III staff. The Railway Administration cannot be avoided. The Railways Boards and Northern Railways Headquarters were put up before this court for consideration and decision. [150F] (8) The Central Government should consider the question of granting relief to casual labourers as per the existing rules, if they have been selected through a regular selection Board for class III staff, in accordance with the instructions issued by the Railway Administration. [151G H] (9) The Court directed that seniority of project casual labourers should be combined for the purpose of screening and forming panel on the basis of panel on merits depending upon the days of work put in. This Court directed a scheme for absorption in Yadav 's case which has been framed and is operative. [152H; 153A] (10) The Union of India, Ministry of Defence, Government of India and the Railway Boards are requested to consider the matter afresh and take appropriate action to remove difficulties faced in future.

The Forward Markets Commission was constituted under the Forward Markets Act, 1951. The Forward Markets (Amendment) Act, 1956, which came into force on January 24, 1956 provided that the Central Government may, either on a request in writing received by it in this behalf from the governing body of a recognised association or if in its opinion it is expedient so to do, make bye laws for all or any of the matters specified in section 11 or amend any bye laws under this section. The said Act was amended by the Forward Market Commission (Amendment). The said amendment provided that "the Forward Markets Commissioner shall not exercise any power conferred on him by or under the Act, or as may be prescribed by the rules made under the rules". The appellant who was a member of the Forward Marketing Commission filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the amended bye law. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Forward Contracts (Amendment), Act, 1957, did not confer any power on the Central Govt., to make a bye law with retrospective effect and that the powers of the Central Govern ment under section 12(1) of the Act were not competent to confer any such power on it under the amended Bye law. Held, that the power conferred by section 12 was merely co extensive with the power of the Commission to make bye law conferring on the Commission a power which it purported to do under the unamended bye law and that it was beyond the powers conferred by the Act. The power of making a bye laws is not competent either to confer upon the Central or the State Government any such powers. The impugned bye law, therefore, cannot be said to have been validly made by the Central Gov ernment.

The assessee, a shareholder of a company, was granted long term leases for the grant of long term mining and other leases. The Income tax Officer brought the entire amount to tax declared as dividend for each of the three years in question and grossed up the amounts under section 16(2) of the Indian Income tax Act 1922. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that part of the amount distributed which was attributable to salami received by it for the granting of longterm leases was not taxable as dividend but only a part of it being dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of that Act. The High Court also recorded answers on all the questions in the negative, and dismissed the reference. In second appeal, HELD : (1) The distribution to the assessee of the amounts attributable to Salami received for the grants of long Term leases after 31st March, 1948 was not in the hands of the assessee but only part of its accumulated profits. [33G H] (2) The Explanation to section 2 (6A), capital gains arising after 31 st March, 1949, was a receipt of income in the hand of the assesee and taxable as the income of the company from other sources. The Explanation did not apply to the case of the appellant. [34B C] (3) The High court had to decide on the facts of each case whether any amount of salami was capital gain, and whether any part of compensation received for compulsory acquisition of land was capital gains, and if dividend be distributed to the shareholders of the Company out of those capital gains to the shareholder of the respondent. [35C] (4) The expression "other sources" in section 2 of the Income tax Acts, 1922, means "other source". In the instant case, the assessee had not been able to show that the amount attributable to the salami which was received for granting long term lease after 31th March, 1947, was not part of accumulated profits and if dividends were distributed to shareholders of a Company out Of those capital gain it could be said that the distribution to him of the capital gains was taxable. [36D E] (5) The word "other Source" in the Explanation to Section 2( 6A) is wide enough to include within its ambit all sources of income which form part of fixed assets of a fixed asset acquired compulsorily for public purposes. It is not necessary that the expression " other source" should be understood as including within its ordinary meaning any other source of income.

The respondent was prosecuted for offences under the Kerala Forest Act, 1963 and the Kerala General Sales Tax Act, 1957. The trial court acquitted him of all the charges. The High Court in appeal held that Sandalwood oil is not a forest produce within the meaning of section 2(f) (i) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that Sandals and wood oil are not 'forest produce ' as defined under section 2 (f) of Act. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The word 'forest ' has to be construed in its technical sense but in an exhaustive manner it cannot be restricted in such a way so as to defeat the principle object and purpose of the statute. [164B] 2.1 The term wood oil is a forest produced by the appellant. It must also be construed, in the context in which it is used and the purpose the Act seeks to serve the tribals in the forest area. In the instant case, Sandal wood is not wood oil within the definition of 'forest Produce ' as envisaged under section2 (f). The word wood oil has to bear its colour from its context and connotation. [165C] 2(a) The term "forest produce" defined in section 2 of the Kerala Act means any produce which is a Forest produce or not, whether found in orbrought from a forest or not. It is used in the sense in which they are understood in trade, business or transaction known to the trade. [166D] (b) The word "forest" has to mean wood oil as defined in Section 2(k) of Kerala Act. Therefore, the word wood is also included in its ambit cut pieces in the background and purpose for the Act sought to serve. [167E F] 3.2 The expression 'forest' is not static vehicle or ideas of concepts and concepts as they are bound to do in any country like ours with the establishment of a democratic structure based on agalitarian values, the meaning and content of the word forest produce. It should also be interpreted in its popular sense but it cannot, in an absolute sense, be restricted to a exhaustive manner so as not to defeat or frustrate the principle and object which legislature seeks to subserve.
