[168E F; 168A] 3(a). The expression "forest ' is used by the legislature in the Act to include forest produce which includes wood oil. It cannot be confined in such manner so that it can be restricted, but to enable the wordwood oil to meet its ordinary popular sense and meaning in an inclusive definition has to he understood in commercial parlance. [169F] (c) The expression is not necessarily wide enough to defeat a principle or object which Parliament seeks to achieve. It may be used in a wider sense so as that it cannot possibly be restricted. But the word ' forest produce ' must be construed strictly in the light in which its meaning is being understood in the commercial parlance and in the ordinary sense in Which it is being used and its meaning will have to be discovered having regard to the intention and object of the legislature which seeks to serves the tribals. [170F] 4(a)(i) The words 'forests ' are not static vehicles or ideas as they may be understood in common parlance.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 and sentenced to transportation for life. The High Court acquitted the accused on appeal by special leave. Held, that there was no evidence against the appellants sufficient to warrant a conviction and the High Court should set aside the judgment of acquittal. The fact that the doctor was young and that his statement was not in accord with the opinion expressed in books on Medical Jurisprudence by authors like Modi and Lyon showed that he had been most young and had been asked to mention it, did not make any weight and value to the statement of Gyaniram. The evidence in the present case was sufficient to sustain a conviction on a charge of murder. The other piece of evidence which the prosecution relied upon was insufficient for sustaining a conviction of murder, but the High court should not set aside that finding unless there are " substantial and compelling reasons" justifying interference with the findings of the trial Court. The judgment of the High ' Court does not disclose any such reasons justifying interference in the findings. The appeal must accordingly be allowed. Held further, that the evidence in this case was insufficient to sustain the conviction of the appellants. The prosecution had relied upon the dying declarations made by Shivlal and he must have been asked whether he was young or that his statements were false. The statement of the deceased alleged to have been made in the circumstances of this case is not sufficient to support the conviction. The trial court was therefore, right in holding that the High Curt should set it aside.

The appellant company was an all India complex having establishments in different parts of the country. In Bihar, it had two factories at Jamshedpur and the factory at Jamshedpur were situated at Jamshedpur. The workmen represented by the Indian Oxygen Workers ' Union which represented the workmen of the appellant company were also allowed special leave to attend the union meetings without loss of pay. The Industrial Tribunal held that the dispute raised by the union was in respect of employees of the respondent company and that as the said reference was made in October 1963, i.e., after the said amendment, purported to have been amended, it did not affect the position that the disputes raised by it were in respect thereof. The appellant 's appeal to this Court was dismissed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Tribunal had rightly held that an obligation to grant special leave under section 10(2) of the , is a condition precedent for the exercise of its jurisdiction under section 11(3). [501 B] (2) The Industrial Court has rightly held in favour of the workmen. The Tribunal 's conclusion, therefore, cannot operate only in respect the workmen concerned and not the workmen directly connected with the dispute referred to it. [502 C D] (3) The award is operative in respect only of the employees of a company where they may be stationed. If the overtime rate allowed by the Tribunal is in respect or of the workers employed in that factory, the company would be liable to pay at double the ordinary rate of wages as provided by the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act, the Company would be entitled to special leave demanded by the Union.

The assessee was a partnership firm carrying on business in timber at Abdullapur, and the business of the firm was taken over by two partners of the assessee. The firm was dissolved on March 31, 1939, and on that account the assessee was entitled to relief under section 25(4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1918, as amended by the Indian Finance (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939. The assessee contended that the firm alone was entitled only to relief in respect of income from business after April 1, 1939 and not in the alternative under section 26(3), or in the alternate under section 24(4). Held, that the assessee could not be said to have commenced business immediately after March 31 , 1939, when the Indian Incometax (Amendment Act 7 Of 1939 came into force. The partnership was dissolved by a deed of partnership dated April 1 , 1939. It was not necessary for the assessee to prove that the partnership was in fact carried on by him at the commencement of the Income tax (Amendment). Act 7of 1939, as it stood before its amendment by the Finance Act 7th of 1939, to bring into force the provisions of the Act. The mere fact that the partners were members of a joint family did not make them separate from the 1st April, 1939. In the absence of other evidence, it could not, therefore, be said that the business was carried on at the date of dissolution from April 1. 1939. Held further, that in the absence Of other evidence the firm of Hakam Malani Tang Malani Mal did not carry on the timber business allotted to it at the time of dissolution. The fact that a partnership deed was executed by the partners in favour of one of the partners, and that the partner had become separate from his 1st of April 1939, would indicate that the said firm was carrying on the business immediately before the dissolution of the partnership firm.

The appellant was granted a stage carriage permit under section 48 of the , for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by the Regional Transport Authority, Shimkot. The appellant produced the relevant documents and the certificate of registration for making necessary entry in the permit. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal holding that there was no period of limitation under rule 151 of the old Rules which was applicable to his case. In the appeals before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the issue of a permit was made beyond the prescribed period of time from the date of grant of the permit and, therefore, the appeal lay under section 64 of the Act to the State Transport Authority. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The appeal must be dismissed. [190 B] The appeals before the State Government and further in second appeal by the Mysore Revenue Appellate Tribunal are, therefore not competent under section64 of the . [191 C] The appellant was entitled to the permit on the ground that there were no period for limitation under Rule 151 of Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1963. [192 D E] The appeal before the High Court and further appeal to the Mysore Appellate Tribunal were, therefore. not competent Under section 64. [191 F] The provisions of the new rules are only a ministerial act necessarily following the grant of permit and other matters with which we are concerned here. There is no dispute that section 64 has to be read with rule 178 of the Rules which prescribes the procedure for appeal to various authorities Appeal.

The appellant was a sitting member of Parliament. He challenged the election on the ticket of the Republican Party, to which the appellant belonged. The respondent filed an appeal against the election petition and contended that the appellant had committed corrupt practice in relation to the personal character and conduct of the appellant and threatened his workers. The High Court dismissed the election Petition holding that the meeting was held at Hapur on 7 February 1967 and there was no attack on the office of the Federation. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The evidence of the respondent is not sufficient to prove that respondent Vir Shastri committed any corrupt practice. [895 C] (2) The appellant failed to prove the contents therein. The oral evidence of P.W. 18 was in support of the rival contentions. The evidence on behalf of the respondents was not sufficient. The appellant 's case about the Nagola incident at Chhajjupur is unacceptable because there was an assault on Elahi, a worker of the petitioner and his election agent. [ 895 D E] (3) The oral testimony of the witnesses on behalf Of the respondent was in respect of the allegation that the respondent had attacked the office and the supporters of the Congress Party. The alleged incident at the meeting which was held on 7 2 1967 did not mention the name of the candidate as having been assaulted or chased or chased by the workers of the party. [869 D] (4) The High court rightly came to the conclusion that no meeting was conducted at Hapur and the oral evidence on record was in favour of the election petitioner.

The respondent, a Hindu Undivided Family, filed an application under Order XXI Rule 95 of the Code of Civil Procedure for delivery of possession of the property purchased by him. The trial court dismissed the application holding that in view of the provision of Explanation I to section 47 of the Civil Procedure Code, the application was within the period of limitation as prescribed by Article 136 of the . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that since the sale was confirmed, the decree holder auction purchaser filed an applica tion for setting aside the sale and that the application for delivery was barred by limitation. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The application for settingaside the sale on the ground of fraud was within time as prescribed in Article 136. [361D] 2. The High Court was right in holding that Article 134 will apply to an application for set aside a sale. It is true that the sale becomes absolute only under the circumstances mentioned in Rule 92, and not Article 134 of the Limitation Act. But after a sale becomes complete on the dissal of the application of the judgment debtor for setting it aside the auction sale, another application for the setting aside of the sale is made within one year from the date of decree irrespective of the date on which the decree has been passed. [362E] 3. The expression "the date of sale" in Explanation II to section47 of the C.P.C. means the date when a property is sold in execution of a decree. It does not mean that the auction purchaser will be deemed to be a party in the suit in which the judgmentdebtor has been passing, as provided in clause (a) of Explanation II of Section 47 of Civil P.C., and by virtue of clause (b) all questions relating to delivery of posses sion have been expressly repealed by section 47 read with Article 134. [367F G] 4. The word "the" occurring in Explanation I means the word "sale" as defined in clause(a) or "sale". It is not correct that the expression "sale", in Explanation 2 to Section 47, an application is made for setting up a decree for delivery at a sale in execution. [368F G]. 5. The words "the day of sale", in the Explanation are wide enough to include within its scope all questions pertaining to delivery and all questions regarding delivery of possess ment. Such an application can also be made within a period of 12 years from the passing of the decree irrespective as the date or order disallowing the application to set aside the sales on the grounds mentioned therein. [364F G; 367A] 6. The language used in Explanation 1 to Section47 is plain and unambiguous. It cannot be said that the word 'sale ' has been used in a restricted sense. The use of the expression 'sale" in the explanation is not decisive. [366B C] 7. In the instant case, the sale became absolute on the dismissal of the second application for making it absolute on August 21, 1979, and the decreeholder respondent having filed the application within one month from July 21, 1980, it was within that period of time as provided by Article 134(b) of the Act. [365C] 8. The question whether the application under order XXI Rule 94 of the CPC for setting off the sale could be made after the disposal of such an application, even though the application is not one as contemplated by Rules 89, 90 or 91 of Order XXI of the code will be governed by Article 137 of the , does not arise in view Of the provisions of Explanation 1. [363D] 9.

The appellant, a candidate for election to the Kerala Legislative Assembly from Mattancherry Constituency No. P 14 and P 15, was declared elected by the Kerala State Legislative Assembly. The first respondent filed an Election Petition in the High Court challenging the election of the appellant to the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly on the ground that the said poster was published in a public place and that it was intended to create an impression that the incident had taken place a previous day but that it did not create an apprehension and did create an assurance. The High Court dismissed the Election Petition holding that exhibit P 1 was printed and pub lished only a day prior to the election, and that the publication was meant to create impression that it would create an indication and did not believe either to be false or does not believe to be true in relation to the personal character or conduct of any candidate. The appellant 's appeal against the judgment of the High court was dismissed by this Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The publication in question on the said days is intended to creating an impression and did creating an assurance that the event of murders had taken places a previous date before the election. It is not necessary to prove that the words complained of were reasonably calculated to prejudice the prospectus of that candidate 's election. [701C D] 1.2 The publication by a candidate or his agent or by any other person with the consent of a candidate, being a statement reasonably calculated as to prejudice his prospectus of the defamed candidate ' s election is not defamatory or that it is not possible to prove the words spoken by him in a defama tory sense, in an election action. [801C] 1.(a) The publication was intended only to create some impression and does not create any impression that what the appellant himself had stated in his examina tion as alleged in exhibit P1. He has also in his examination in chief stated contrary to what he had stated earlier.

The respondent No. 5 submitted a plan to the Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay for the construction of a five star hotel. The Municipal Corporation rejected the plan on the sole ground that it was proposed to earmark the said land under reference as a recreational ground with suitable internal network of roads during the revision of the development plan which was in the offing. The respondent No, 5 filed an application before the Municipal Commissioner for sanction of the plan submitted by the respondent No., 5 for the constructions of a ten star hotel on the said plot. The Corporation rejected its plan on two grounds: (1) that it had been proposed to be earmark, and no proposal to exclude it therefrom; (2) that the draft revised development plan was not in accordance with the direction of the respondent NO. 2; and (3) that there was a proposal for revision of a draft revised Development Plan. The High Court rejected the application on the ground that the proposed revision could be taken into account as one of the relevant factors. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the Municipal corporation that the impugned order granting sanction of development plan had been published and the plan was submitted by respondent No . 5 for construction of the five star hotels. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order granting exemption should be quashed. [924D] 2. The appellant is only interested in seeing that sufficient area is kept reserved for a park or recreation ground for the benefit of the members of the public. They are not, in our opinion, concerned with the question as to the legality or otherwise of the exemption granted by the Government to the respondent no. 5. [ 925F] 3. The impugned order of the High Court sanctioning the development plans of the appellant No. 1 is, therefore, set aside and the appeal is allowed.

The appellants, who were the employees of the two concerns, were dismissed from service by the Industrial Court. The employer filed a complaint before the Labour Court under section 28 read with Items l(a), (b) and (c) of Schedule II of the Maharashtra Recognition of Trade Unions and Prevention of Unfair Labour Practices Act, 1971 alleging that the employers had committed an unfair labour practice by imposing a lock out and continuing a lockout as provided in Item 6 of Schedule I of the Act. The Industrial Court framed an issue whether the employer had committed unfair labour practices. The appellants contended before the Industrial Tribunal that the employer was guilty of unfair labour Practice and that the workmen were not recdent to work, and that there was no closure of the industrial undertaking. The Labour Court held that the appellants were guilty of misconduct and that they were entitled to reinstatement with full back wages. On appeal by special leave, the Industrial court framed an additional issue as to whether the employers were guilty or not. The Tribunal answered the said issue in favour of the appellant union. In the appeals before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the industrial undertakings of the employers having been closed down, there was a closure of their business itself and that no new workman will be recruited in full and that as resumption of work is gradually expanding and that till all the old workmen are re inducted into service, no new employer would be recruited. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The industrial undertakings which have been closed by the employer cannot be said to be unfair labour Practices within the meaning of section 2(L) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. [67F] 2. The closure is not necessarily temporary or permanent and that lockout is necessarily temporary and permanent. It is only when the true test is that when it is claimed that the undertaking was carried out in letter and spirit and not closed down that the new employer has closed down the industrial establishment, it is not necessary to approach the matter from this angle that the closure would be adjudged a device or pretence to determine the intention and bonafides of the employer at the time of closure but is not decisive of the matter. [68F] 3. The question whether the appellant had resorted to closure of an industrial undertaking and it was not a case of lock out has to be determined with accuracy whether the closing down of the industry was a result of impose lockout or has closed the industrial unit. [69G H] 4. The fact that the business activity was not closed up is the refusal of the management to continue employ any number of persons employed by him even though the business activities were not closed off but was a case where in case of closure there is only closure of its business itself permanent and permanent lockout, it would be difficult to find out what was the intention of the employee at the date of closure. [70F] 5. The real test is whether the closure has been a device for determining the intention or bonafides. If the employer has imposed a lock-out or had closed down its industrial undertaking, then the question of lockout would not arise. [71G H; 72A] 6. The workers employed by the appellant even though they were rec closing down the industry are the refusal to continue employment even though it is bona fide and for reasons beyond the control of the owner at the relevant time of the closure but was not decisive. [72B C] 7. The mere fact that a lockouts have been permitted or closed down does not necessarily mean that the workers employed in such a situation must be deemed to be guilty of an unfair trade practice. In such a case, the employer is not guilty of any unfair labour conduct. [73F G] 8. The burden of proving that the employees had committed a breach of an illegal lockout has to rests on the employer.

The assessee company was a dealer in shares, securities and properties. The objects set out in the memorandum of association and particularly in sub cl. (1) of that clause were to deal in investments and properties and to make profits. The Income Tax Officer held that the assessee company could not be treated as a dealer for the purpose of section 66(2) of the Act, but on appeal by the assessee the Appellate Tribunal held that in the case of the assessee it was a "business" and that since the objects contained in the Memorandum of Association and the previous assertion made by the appellant company that it was an investor, it could be taxed as business profits. On further appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the assessee Company can be treated a dealer or an investor is a mixed question of fact and law. It is not necessary for the Income Tax officer to decide whether the particular facts are relevant or not. If it is found on an examination of the transactions themselves that the essential characteristics of the business of the company were of an investor it cannot be said that the profits and losses arising from the sale of shares, properties and securities acquired by the company can be taxed in its profits. [527 C D] (ii) The fact that the appellant was a 'dealer ' in investments or properties and not merely an investor ' is a question of law. If the facts are found on examination of these transactions themselves the essential features of the trading business of an assessee were of a mixed character and law, it would be necessary to make a fresh statement of the cases on the following questions of fact: (i ) Whether on the evidence and in reaching its decision on the point the assessee was a company or an investment; (ii ) Whether the profits or losses arising therefrom from the transfer of shares etc. of an industrial concern were a mixed questions of law and fact. [627 D E] (iii) The High Court has not decided on the question whether the relevant legal principles have been mis applied by the Tribunal in reaching the decision on that point; nor has it decided on any other question of facts. It was not necessary to decide on the questions framed at present.

The appellant was recruited to the Madras Provincial Judicial Service as Munsif in 1935. He was promoted to the office of Subordinate Judge, and on June 19, 1950, he was posted as Subordinate Judge of Masulipatnam, Krishna District. The appellant was appointed to the service as Subordinate judge of Masalipatnam. On April 28, 1954, he made an elaborate enquiry into the conduct of Government servants on a monthly salary of Rs. 150 and above. He submitted his report to the Government for action, and after making an elaborate inquiry in which several witnesses including the appellant were examined, he sent a report to enquire into the charges, and that the proceedings in the High Court of Madras after October 1, 1953, ended in the order of suspension dated January 28,1954, resulting in the orders of suspension. The Government issued a notice to the appellant on August 12, 1954 to show cause why he should not be dismissed or removed from service. On September 29, 1954 the appellant filed an application under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order dated January 27, 1954 passed by the High court of Madras, and for a writ of certiorari quashing the said order. The High Court held that the enquiry was vitiated as it was in contravention of article 311 of the constitution and dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of the High Commis sioner dated January 29,1954 was merely one of suspension pending final orders by the Government, and such an order could not be said to conclude the question against the appellant. [419 C] (ii)The order passed by it on January 28 1954, is merely one that authority appointed him was the Governor of the Province, and, in fact, the order passed on January 27 was only one of dismissal pending final disposal of the matter finally. The order passed in the matter must be held to have been made without jurisdiction. [420 D] (iii)The Government had issued a show cause notice to all the members of the State Judicial Service, and it was for that authority to pass the ultimate order in the case. But under r. 4(1)(a), the Government could not make any order on the basis of the report submitted by the enquiry officer. The report was then sent to the Governor for action and, therefore, the proceedings were bad.

The assessee, a registered holder of 2674 shares of Gannon Dunkerley & Company, was assessed to income tax under section 23(4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The assessee claimed that he had made and published a will disposing of his extensive estate in the United Kingdom and in British India, but that the liability to pay the tax on the dividend so deemed to have been received by him or her legal representatives after the death of the deceased was made after the date of the order of the Income tax Officer. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that section 24B did not authorise the levy of tax on receipts by the legal representative when the order was passed, and that the assessee had no right to claim any income from the estate of the person in the hands of his legal representatives. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the provisions of section 24A were not intended to be applicable to the case of the assessee. The High Court, on a reference, answered the question against the Revenue. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the expression "assessee" in section 2(2) of Indian Income Tax Act, 1961, meant a person who had died before his death and therefore the income received by the deceased could not be deemed to be taxable as income of the legal representatives; (ii) the word "assessee", in section 24 B, was not intended merely to cover cases where the income was notional but also to include cases where it was not actually received by a legal representative of the estate before its death. HELD: The expression "person" in s. 2(1)(a) means a person whose income tax is payable under the Act and includes any other person who has died before the date on which such income is assessable to income of that person. [597 G] (iii) The word "person", in s, 24B, means a legal representatives of a deceased person who dies before his or her death. It cannot be said that they were income which may be deemed by fiction to have supplied the machinery for taxation of income received after the expiry of the account year in which such notional income must be deemed. [658 C] (iv) The expression 'assessee" is not defined in section 3(2). The word 'person ' has been used in a wide sense and it means a body corporate, a firm or an association of persons. It may include a firm, a company, a partnership firm or a firm. [559 D] (v) The legal personality of a person for the purpose of assessment is to be regarded as extended to the end of the year in Which such notional Income must be regarded to have received by his legal representative. But if the Legislature has failed to set up the procedure to assess such income, the Courts cannot supply it. [596 E] (vi) The words "any tax which would have been payable by him under this Act if he had not died" in the course of which such person died would have become assessable to tax as income. But the Legislature having made no provision generally for assessment of income receivable by a Legal representative of a estate of a dead person should not be permitted to escape tax to the detriment of public revenue. [593 F] (vii) The legislature has not provided that the income which might be deemed as income received or of the loss sustained by a person or of his death, have been collected by such legal representative, but for the death or of any loss sustained in the previous year, it could be taxed as income and tax had therefore to be in accordance with the provisions.

The appellant was a Ruler of the State of Baster. He was then a Ruler and absolute owner of the villages specified in Schedules A and B of his petition under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution. The appellant claimed that he was still a Sovereign Ruler and was entitled to recover rent or revenue from persons holding land in such village. Held, that the appellant was an ex Ruler and not as a Ruler. The fact that the Ruler had no right to recover rents or revenue did not make him a Ruler for the purposes of the Act. The effect of Merger Agreement was clearly one by which a factually a Ruler ceased his status as a sovereign owner of those villages. The nature of Merged Agreements was clearly different from the scope and ambit of the word 'proprietor ' in the definition of the term 'proprietor in the Act, and therefore a Ruler could not conceivably be a maufidar. The question whether the appellant had given any evidence to establish that the villages in question were not assessed to land revenue did depend upon the nature of the Merger Agreements and the fact that it was entered into by him in the wajib ul arz with respect to some of his maufi villages. Held further, that there was no material on the record to show that the appellants had given evidence to prove that the village in question had not been assessed to lands revenue but only a grantee from the State or Ruler and therefore the appellant must be regarded as an ex ruler. The mere fact that some of the maufaidars were not entered in the sajib Ul arz did not by itself make him an "proprietor" within the meaning of article 366(22) of the constitution.

The respondent was transferred from Shillong to Pauri (U.P.) by the Senior Administrative Officer, office of the Director General, Botanical Survey of India, Eastern Circle, Shillong. The said order was challenged in a writ petition before the High Court which quashed the order of transfer on the ground that it was sitting in appeal over the order passed by the respondent. The Division Bench quashed the said order of the Single Member who passed the impugned order of his transfer. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the guidelines contained in Government of India O.M. dated 3.4.1986 have not been followed and that the respondent is liable to transfer anywhere in India. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the order transferring the respondent 's transfer. [475B] 2. The Administrative Tribunal has exceeded its jurisdication of the Central Administrative Tribunal is akin to the jurisdiction of the High Courts under Article 226 of the Constitution of India in service matters. It does not enable any spouse to claim such posting as a matter for the appropriate authority to decide. Unless the order is vitiated by malafides or is made in violation of any statutory provisions, the Court cannot interfere with it. [ 432E] 3. The administrative instructions/guidelines contained in the administrative instructions andguideline are not followed, much less can it be characted as malafide for that reason. [ 433F G] 4. The respondent has been transferred from Meghalaya to Pouri (U .P.) on the basis of certain guidelines issued by the Government. He is liable for transfer anywhere at one station if it is possible without any detriment to administrative needs and the claim of other employees. [ 435G H] 5. The order of transferring the appellant was passed in violation o f the statutory provisions. The Tribunal has clearly exceeded its powers in interfering in the order dated 31.3.1991.

The appellants were tried for the murder of Jawahar. The prosecution case was that the deceased Jawahar had caused injuries to him by aruval (bill hook) and a stick (spear stick). The trial court acquitted all the accused persons but reversed their findings in respect of A1 to A7, A2, A3 and A4. The High Court maintained the acquittal of A4 to A6 on the ground that the commission of offence by A1 was proved beyond doubt. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The intention of the appellants was to cause grievous hurt and as such the offence committed by them comes within the parameters of Section 325, I.P.C. [312B] 2. The participation of the accused in the occurrence which resulted in the death of Jawahar has been proved beyond doubts. Even according to Jawahar 's statement (Exhibit P 6) all the first accused had remarked that the attack on him was in retaliation for the injuries caused by the deceased. There is no evidence to show that the appellants were responsible for causing such injury as would be sufficient in the ordinary course of nature, to cause death. [412C] 3. The offence committed is punishable under Section 304 Part I read with section 34, IP.c. and instead convict under Section 325 read with Section 34, i.e., Part I, I,I.P., C.P.; and conviction under Section 302 read with Sec tion 34, IPC read with Sections 34,I,I and 34, is set aside.

The appellant Bank was constituted a special Indian law by the Banking Companies Act, 1949. The Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970 came into force on 1st April, 1971. Section 4(e) of the Act provides that the provisions of the , shall apply to a corporation formed or created by any special law enacted by an Indian Legislature. Section 3(27)(a) defines `special law ' as meaning a law made by Parliament and not by the law itself. The appellant Bank, therefore, was constituted under the Banking companies (Acquisition & Transfer of Undertaking) Act 1970. The banking Companies Act is a special law made in pursuance of the provisions contained in section 4(1e). Section 4 (e) provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, no court shall have jurisdiction to entertain or try any suit or proceeding relating to any matter which is within the competence of the Reserve Bank. The respondent Bank was formed by or under a special Law enacted by the Indian Parliament and was not a corporation within the meaning of section 4 (a) of that Act. The question for consideration in this appeal is whether the Banking Company Act, 1950, is a 'special law enacted in the United Kingdom 'and before the words `an Act of Parliament ' refer to the action taken under the law and not the by the Law itself. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 Section 4 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1969, which is a general law, does not apply to corporations formed or constituted by any other Indian Legislature, but by the provisions thereof. The expression `any special law ' refers to a law enacted under the Indian , and it cannot be held that it was created under a Special Law in respect of matters covered by the Act. [968D] 1.2 The words `any general law ' refer only to a statute made by the Parliament and does not include any law made under the ordinary law. It is well settled that the word `any other special law" in section 3( 27) of a special Act refers to an enactment of Parliament, but it cannot mean that the legislature has not intended that the corporation in question should be formed by a third party in pursuance or by the laws itself. [ 969D] 2.1 The words 'any special Indian Law ' refer and 'under a special statute applicable to India. It will be highly unreasonable and illogical to think that as a corporation had been formed by and under a general Law, whether it is created in pursuance thereof, it will not come within the purview of section4(e). [969D E] 2.(a) The words "any special India law" refer only when there is a conflict between the words 'in pursuance of any law ' and 'in accordance with the provisions relating to such law. [977F G] (b) The word `an Indian Law" in Section 4 has been used in the sense of a general statute, but not by its own language. It has been defined in section 2(e), which means a law passed by Parliament or by any Legislature of a State.

The petitioners who were manufacturers of sugar in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar, challenged the validity of the impugned notification on the ground that it was violative of article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The contention was that fixing of price arbitrarily, and did not take into account the cost of production of a large number of units in the country and didnot provide for a fair and equitable distribution of sugar within the country. Held, that the impugned notifications were invalid as it contravened article 19 (1)(f) of Schedule VII to the Constitution and the petitioners were entitled to the protection of article 31(2). The impugned notification was therefore void and inoperative. The impugned Act was not violative of articles 14 and 19(6) of Part III of the constitution. The State of Bihar vs Kameshwar Singh, ; , followed. The object of the Act is to secure essential commodities for the consumer, i.e., the general public, at fair prices; but it does not follow from this that this object can only be achieved if retail prices are fixed for factories in other States which are said to be mainly deficit, and that there is no reasonable safeguard against the abuse of power and no provision for a check by way of appeal or otherwise. The Act was therefore invalid as the impugned Notification did not authorise the Central Government to fix the price at a loss, (ii) it fixes the prices arbitrarily, (iii) there was discrimination in effect, and (iv) there is discrimination in fact between factories in Bihar and North West Bihar. Held further, that there was no discrimination between factories within the State of Uttar Pradesh, and the impugned Act could not be said to have been passed by the Central Legislature under article 19 of the Consti tution of India. The provisions of the , which are intended to secure the essential commodities in the interests of general public must therefore be held to be violative of the fundamental rights guaranteed by article 19.

The appellant company was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The Company had its registered office at Calcutta and it had its head office at Kolkata. It had its principal office at the relevant time. On April 26, 1951, the Government of West Bengal issued an order in exercise of powers conferred by section 7A of the , that the working class of employees should be paid a minimum of Rs. 100 per month for each year and that the said amount should be deducted from the wages payable to them. The company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order on the ground that it was not passed under section 19(6) of the Act, and therefore the present reference was bad in law and without jurisdiction. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the award dated June 21, 1951 was not terminated in accordance with the provisions of section 19 (6) Of the Act and therefore it was bad. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The award dated April 26 was binding between the parties and therefore, the reference was valid. [148 C] (ii) The Tribunal wrongly relied upon Exhibit 3, corrected on the basis of information given by the State Statistical Bureau West Bengal, for ascertaining the working classes cost of living index. It came to the conclusion that full neutralisation of the working conditions of living Index in the year 1957 had not been produced. [149 D] (iii) The fact that the Tribunal wrongly applied the said award was irrelevant and did not affect the validity or otherwise of the award.

The appellant, a religious institution dedicated to the propagation and promotion of the tenets of the Veera Saiva Mutt, was the Matadhipati of Sri Gavi Mutt. The said management continued as before and the fact that an Executive Officer had been appointed under the relevant provisions of the earlier Act, was not actually enforced before the 26th January 1950, it could not be challenged on the ground that some of its provisions contravened the fundamental rights guaranteed to the citizens of this country under article 19(1)(f). The appellant contended that since the scheme was framed under the provisions of 1939 as early as 1939, the Act had been enacted and the Executive Officer continued as in 1952. Held, that the scheme having been framed under section 63 of the old Act, it must now be deemed to have been settled or modified under the earlier statute. The scheme was not merely enforced before 26th February 1950 but was also executed by legal proceedings and partly because the appellant had continuously challenged the implementation of the scheme by legal proceeding and partly Because he has otherwise obstructed the said implementation. The provisions of section 103(d) of the new Act were clearly justified by the fact, that they contravened the Matadavat Rules in respect of the properties which were actually taken over by the Executive officer. The appellant was not entitled to seek protection of article 19 (1)(g). The scheme had been framed and a challenge made by the appellant to its validity in the light of these provisions was rejected by the learned Judge with the observation that where the fundamental right is clearly infringed, it is the duty of the Court to interfere in favour of the citizen unless there are reasons for policy which make it inexpedient to do so.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in a school under the Orissa Aided Educational Institutions (Appointment of Teachers Validation) Act, 1989. He joined the school on July 12, 1982 and worked for repeated spells of 89 days and thereafter he joined the School with repeated spells. The appellant continued to serve the school with repeated spell of 89 day appointments but no action was taken by the said authorities. The managing committee of the school in its resolution dated July 6,1987 informed the educational authorities of the State Government that the appellant was still continuing to serve as Hindi teacher in the school and that he would continue to serve him with repeated periods of 89 months and 89 days. The management of the School filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court claiming regularisation as Hindi Teachers with effect from July 12 1982. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioner was entitled to be regularised in terms of the provisions of Section 3 of the Validation Act, on the ground that his initial appointment for 89 days or till a candidate selected by the State Selection Board was made available. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The validation Act does not arise from the date of regular appointment i.e. July 12.1982 and has been enacted by the legislature with the obvious object of granting relief to those members of teaching community who are being exploited for years together by keeping 995 them in short spells appointments like day 89 days break in between the spells, and one day break which deprives a teacher of his salary for the period of summer vacation as long as they hold the office under this order. [901A B] 2. The impugned Act does no more than provide for regularisation of service in a post created by an enactment. It is well settled that the validation Act has been passed with the avowed object of giving relief to certain members of the teaching community which are being misused for years along with one day breaks and other service benefits, is wholly arbitrary and suffers from the vice of discrimination. [1001C] 3. The State Government has stated that the appellants were still continuing in service as Hindi teachers in the schools under the orders of the managing committee. The appellants have not been able to show any approval by the educational authority for the periods subsequent to 1986. The appointment by the managing Committee is still utilising his services though there is no approval by educational authorities for the Period subsequent to1986. [1101D] 4. The question of issuing any direction to regularise their service in the a post does not arises because of the validation act which was followed by the Government for a long period has led to the breach of Article 14 of the constitution. [1202E F] 5. The scheme or any other appropriate measure to regularise the services of the appellants is wholly unfair and suffersfrom the viceof discrimination. The school in question had been functioning with the approval of the authorities for almost 4 years with short breaks.

The respondent was a Chairman of a Panchayat Samiti. He was elected to the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zila Parishads, for performing all official duties. The appellant challenged the election of the respondent on various grounds including that he was disqualified from being a candidate for being a member of a panchayat Samiti and that his ground that he had been disqualified from appearing in the election was based on Rules 3 to 7 of the Punjab Panchayats Samitis and Nagar Parishads, Non official Members (Payment of Allowances) Rules, 1965. The High Court held that the allowances paid under rules 3 to7 were not admissible as they were not made by a person who was defeated by respondent No. 1. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the payment of travelling allowance and daily allowance under r. 3 to the Chairman, Panchayat Samiti at Rs. 3 per day for journeys performed outside the district was illegal and void as the same had been made without any authority or jurisdiction. HELD : (i) The High court was correct in arriving at the conclusion that the allowance paid under rr. 3 and 7 were not allowable as they did not convert the office of Chairman of Panchayat Samiti into an office of profit. [401 C] (ii) The payment of daily allowance to a Chairman, Vice Chairman or Member of a Zila Parishad is in addition to the payment to the consolidated monthly allowance under rr 3 to 8. [441 D] (iii) The appellant has failed to establish that the payments were made by him for journeys outside the District.

The appellant was the tenant of a shop in Dholki Mohalla, Sadar Bazar, Meerut Cantt. The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction against the appellant on the ground that the tin shed marked by letters ABHG had been constructed by him with the consent of the erstwhile landlords predecessor in interest of the respondents and that the roof wall did not constitute material alteration in the accommodation. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the partition wall did no constitute material alterations as the same were temporary in nature which could be removed without causing any damage to the accommodation, and dismissed the suit. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in interfering with the findings of fact recorded by the First Appellate Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court committed error in interfering in second appeal. [771A] 2. The question whether tin shed and the partition wail was permanent or temporary is a relevant consideration in determining the question of material alteration. The essential element which needs consideration is as to whether the constructions are sub stantial in nature, they alter the accommodation or not. The construction carried out by the respondent had the effect of altering the front and structure of the accommodation and it was enclosed by Bamboo structure, and a tin shed which did not make any material alterations in the premises. [775B] 3. The appellant has failed to prove that the wall was constructed on the open land adjacent to the accommoda tion. The constructions were made with the permission of the District Magistrate but if the tenant, without the permission or permitted to make construction in the building did not create any change either in the form or structure of a building, it took care to use the word materially altered the same as the one which makes material alterations. [764C D] 4. The structural features of the disputed constructions which make material alterations are not permanent or permanent. The nature of construction, whether they are permanent or Temporary, is a question of fact and depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. In determining the questions of 'material alteration ', the Court must address itself to the nature, character and character as materially altered the accommodation; but if so, whether those constructions are temporary or permanent in nature does not provide a ground for eviction without obtaining permission of t he District Magistrate. [784D E] 5. The material alterations made in the structure or the structure of tenanted building should provide a sufficient ground for ejectment without causing damage to it. In deciding this question, the court has to consider whether the construction had been made with consent of land lord and if so whether those structures are permanent in character which could not be removed at any time without causing damages to the premises; but every construction made by a tenant in the shape of kitchen and bathroom did not effect any change in the front structure or structure. The mere fact that a construc tion is permanent does not create a ground of eviction. [794E F] 6. The word 'material alterations ' means something which brings about substantial change in front and structures of the building.

The respondent company filed a suit against the appellant for setting aside an ex parte decree for Rs. 28,479/ passed in favour of the respondent firm on 22 4 1975. The trial court decreed the suit on 29 7 1975 and dismissed it on 21 7 1975. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that (i) the summons in the suit was duly served on the company and it came to know about the decree on 29 8 1975 about the passing of the ex parte order; (ii) the company remained in dark and as stated above, learnt for the first time on 29 9 1975 asking the company to appear at Indore on 25 3 1975 asking it to appear on 25 4 1975 itself; (iii) the notice was not duly served upon the company; (iv) the suit had been filed within one year of the passing the exparte decree and the ex p parte decree was passed in the absence of the company. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The words "Principal Officer" in clause (a) of Rule 2 would include managing agents and it can, under this rule, be on a juristic person. [1032D] 1.2 In Rule 17 of Order 5 it has been provided that managing agents shall affix a copy of the summons on the outer door or some other conspicuous part of the house in which the defendant ordinarily resides or carries on business personally or works for gain, 1032 and shall then return the original to the Court from which it was issued with a report endorsed thereon or annexed thereto stating that he has so affixed the copies thereof. [1133E] 1.(a) The meaning of clause (b) has got to be understood in the background of the provisions of the Code in Order 5 which is meant for issue of service and summons on natural persons. In Rule 2 is not an exhaustive provision providing for all modes of service on the Company in the sense as to what is meant by service of summons on a natural person. The meaning has gotto be understood according to the provisions contained in Order 6 which is intended for issue or service of summon on natural person, unless the contrary is shown, will be presumed to be service on company itself. [1233E F] 1(b) In Rule 3 it has got been provided: "Where the defendant or his agent or such other person refuses to sign the acknowledgement or where the serving officer, after using all due and reasonable diligence cannot find the defendant, and there is no agent empowered to accept service of the summon on his behalf, nor any other person on whom service can be made, the serving Officer shall affix the copy of summons upon the outer gate or some conspicuous part thereof as required by Order 5. [1334F G] 1 (c) In order to avoid any doubt about the applicability of the said provision it is necessary for the court to examine the facts and circumstances of each case. The language used in Rule 2 makes it clear that the meaning of the words " Principal Officer" has got a meaning which is given to them by the Code. [1434G] 1:2 In order that the summons may be served on a person who is not a person entitled to be served upon him, or where he refuses to accept the service of such summons on his authorized agent or where there is none empowered to receive service of notice on his authorised agent or other person as aforesaid refuses to affix a Copy of the same on the inner door or any other conspicuous portion of the House in which such defendant ordinarily reside or carrieson business, it has to be presumed that service of a summons on such authorized person or such person as is mentioned in the first part of clause(b), is not necessary.

The respondents were tried under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for having committed an offence punishable under section 146(1) (b) of the Criminal Procedure Code. The Magistrate passed a preliminary order on 17th July, 1978 declaring the appellant to be in possession of the land in dispute. The High Court, however, dismissed the petition and remitted the case to the Magistrate for passing a final order on the 29th July. 1978 declaring him to be the in possession. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the final order of the Magistrate was vitiated in absence of a finding that breach existed at the time when the order was passed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The final order in the preliminary order cannot be said to have been made without there being clear evidence to show that the dispute has ceased to exist so as to bring the case within the ambit of sub section (5) of section 145. [941 C] 2. In a case where a Magistrate finds that there is a breach of peace, it is not necessary that the breach of the peace should continue at every stage of the proceedings unless there is clear evidence showing that the disputed dispute has been ceased to exists so as not to bring it within the purview of sub s.(5) and pass a final orders under sub section(4). [942 D] 3. The order of Magistrate was based on a finding of existence of breach of law which existed at that time. It could be said that no dispute existed, as contemplated under section145, Cr. P.C., requiring such a finding in the final orders. [953 E F] 4. In the instant case, there is nothing to show in the instant cases that any prejudice was caused to any of the parties who had the full opportunity to produce their evidence before the Court so it was not necessary for the Magistrate to repeat what he had said in the Final order. The fact that a finding has been recorded by the Magistrate in the provisional order does not necessarily mean that the question of the dispute having ended so as would bring the matter within the scope of sub sec.(5). [954 E F; 95A] 5. In view of the conflicting stands taken by the two parties, it cannot be held that a breach existed even in the earlier final order passed by the magistrate so it is unnecessary to attract the extraordinary jurisdiction of the High Court under section 482 Cr. The finding of the magistrate in the impugned order was implicit in the order passed in the main order and not in the circumstances as mentioned above.

The appellant, a resident of Madras, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1941 42 and 1943 43. The Income Tax Officer held that the intermediaries firms were benamidars for the appellant and that the profits had accrued to it both in British India as well as in the legal sense and that liability to tax had arisen. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Tribunal held that a question of benami was one of pure fact or mixed question of law and fact and that there was no evidence in support of it or that on the evidence it was perverse. The High Court, however, held that as the appellant sold its goods to the ultimate purchasers and received the prices, there could be no question but that the profit had accrued only to it and that therefore a finding thereon was open to review under section 66(1). Held, that the decision of the Tribunal in Com Missione was not correct. The fact that the appellant had sold its products to the actual purchasers and receive the price did not make any difference as regards the character of the payments made to the appellant. The question whether the profits were remitted to British India or not was a mixed question between facts and law, and it could be decided on the basis of evidence. In the present case, the fact that there had been no evidence to show that the assessee sold its product to the purchasers did not amount to sale within the meaning of section 2(c) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, was a question which could be referred to the court under section 67(1) and the decision in Com missione Mission of Income tax vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai and Co. (2) was not open to challenge as it had not been treated as profits by the appellant nor was it supported by evidence.

The assessee, a firm carrying on the business of manufacturing and sale of blankets and other woollen cloth, was appointed as an employee of the General Manager. The remuneration paid to him was to draw a fixed salary of Rs. 75,465. He was also paid a sum of Rs,75,465 as commission paid to the General manager. The assessee claimed deduction of Rs 75,467 as commission on account of business considerations but the Income Tax Officer rejected this claim and held that the commission paid by him was not wholly or exclusively for the purpose of carrying on business. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the view of the Income tax Officer and held in favour of the assessee. The High Court, however, held that it was not possible to accept the view taken by the Incometax Officer that the post of General Manager carried the equal responsibility of that of the Director who was given the charge of the conduct of business after the death of Shri Vaish. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Courts were wrong in taking this circumstance into consideration. [753 B] (ii) The principle of commercial expediency for determining whether an expenditure was wholly and exclusively laid out for the purposes of the business has to be decided on the facts and in the light of each particular case. In the present case, both the Appellate Tribunal and the High Court have not accepted this view. [764 C] (iii) The fact that the company had taken over the mill at a time when it was old and dilapidated and it never made profit and Shri Vaish was able to secure an order from the account of which the mill made some profit, cannot be said to be decisive in determining whether any expenditure was laid out or wholly exclusively for carrying on its business. [774 D] (iv) The question as to whether an amount claimed as expenditure was lay out or expended wholly and primarily for the object of the company and a host of other related circumstances.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of Bata Shoo Company (Private) Limited, since October 1943. He was an employee of the Union and was represented by a representative of his union. The appellant filed his application to the Patna High Court under article 226 and article 227 of the Constitution for a direction on the Tribunal not to record the compromise in so far as it related to the appellant 's case and praying that the agreement should be accepted and that he should not be accepted. The Tribunal rejected his prayer for a writ, but granted him a certificate of fitness. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) that the Tribunal committed an error in refusing the appellant to enter into any agreement in his case and on proper adjudication of the matter. (ii)that section 36 of the Industrial Disputes Act did not contemplate that the machinery provided therein should be set in motion to settle only disputes which involve the rights of workmen as a class and that a dispute touching the individual rights of a workman was not intended to be the subject of adjudication under the Industrial Dispute Act, unless it was taken up by a Union of the workmen or by some other workman employed. (iii)that the Tribunal erred in rejecting the appellant's application for a separate representation on the question of representation as well as regarding the award that had been made. The fact that when an individual workman becomes a party to a dispute under the Act, he is not independently of the union which has espoused his cause cannot be said to be an error of law in refusing him relief on the ground that it was not entered in what was considered to be his best interests of the workman himself. (iv)that a dispute between an individual workmen and an employer cannot be an industrial dispute as defined in section 2(k) of the Act unless it is taken up at any stage by a union of workmen or otherwise by a majority of workmen.

The appellants instituted a suit for ejectment and recovery of rent against the respondents on the allegation that they constituted a joint Hindu family and the surviving plaintiffs could continue the appeal in view of r. 3 Of O.XLI, r. XXII, r., XXII, and not of rs. 3 of O.XXII, r, XXII, R. 33. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal by the surviving appellants the High Court reversed the decree holding that the surviving respondents were competent to continue the Appeal even after the death of Kedar Nath and the other appellants constituted a Joint Hindu family. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants (i) that the original decree proceeded on a common ground to all the plaintiffs or defendants jointly, and therefore, the provisions of 0. XLI, rs., XXII and not o. XLII, rr. 3 and 4 were not applicable to an appeal to which the provisions Of OXLI r. 33 were not intended to apply; (ii) that in view Of the provisions ofs. 41, r . 4 when an appeal has been filed by all the appellants as an appeal against the whole decree in pursuance of the provisionsof 0. XLIII, r,. XXII, rr., 3 and 5 the appeal could not have been taken to be an appeal from a common party under the Code or under the Letters Patent of the High court; (iii) that since the surviving defendants were competent in law to continue their appeal even though the appeal was filed by some of the plaintiffs jointly, they could not continue the appeals even though they had a common right and interest in getting a decree against them. HELD: (i)(a) The provisions of OXLLI r., 3 Of 0. XXI, r.( XXII), r. 4 of O XLI, rr, 3 and 6 are not applicable. [558 B] (b) In the present case the surviving appellant had a joint right to appeal against his entire decree in view, and such decree could have been on a ground common to all of them. The provisions Of 0, XLI, R., r. 34 of O I, r; XXII, are not intended by 0. XXXII, R, 33. [559 C] (c) In order that the appeal against a part of the decree should be heard together it is necessary for the Court to exercise its discretion in favour of such a party. The appellant landlord sought to break through these defences by urging that the lease had expired by efflux of time, limited thereby under section 111(g) of the TP Act, as amended by the Amending Act of 1929. The Rent Control Law (Amendment) Act, 1929 was enacted with a view to protect tenants against eviction on certain grounds. Section 111(a) and (g) were introduced in the TP Acts by the amending Act of 1928. The appellant landlord seeks to break into these defencess by urging: (i) that the tenancy caused by sub letting contrary to the terms of the deed of demise could be availed of by the landlord even in the absence of a notice as contemplated by section 111 (g), and no notice terminating the tenancy under section 106 is needed; (ii) that there was no requirement in law of a written notice to quit and no such notice terminating tenancy under Section 106 was required, and (iii) that since the lease has expired by lapse of limited time under section 112(g), the forfeiture of the tenancy created by sub let contrary to terms of lease is not based on the principles of justice, equity and good conscience. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the appellant landlord 's termination of the lease was not due to any statutory provision or rule which required the tenant to give notice in writing of his intention to determine the lease. [920C] 2.1 Section 111 (a) of TP Act is a procedural and technical rule introduced in 1929, but on the application of the principles embodied in section 111, the breach by the lessee with the right, if he so chooses, to determine such lease was of a technical nature or could be said to be consistent with the English rule regarding forfeiture. [1020D] 2(a). The statutory law as it now stands, as it stood, is a substantive and procedural rule introduced by the section 111. It is a fitting finale to this part of justice equity and sound conscience. [1121C D] (b) The essential principles of equity and justice are not the technical rules of equity or good conscience but are merely procedural andtechnical rules introduced in 1930, and therefore, in consonance with the principles contained in section 112 (g). [922D E] 2.(a) The statutory rule regarding the forfeiture on forfeiture is not founded upon any principle of justice.

The respondents were the employees of the Assam State Electricity Board. They were dismissed from service by an order dated July 26, 1967 on the ground that they had been dismissed without giving any reasonable opportunity to show cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to them. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order and the High court allowed the writ petition holding that the order was invalid as it was passed without affording an opportunity of hearing to the respondents. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The amended Article 311(2) of the Constitution is not intended by the amendment to bring about a substantial change in the legal position which was intended by that amendment. [487 E] (2) The Governor has been satisfied under sub clause (c) of article 311 that in the interest of the security of the State it is not expedient to give the government servant an opportunity to showing cause against action proposed, but only on the basis of the evidence adduced during such inquiry, to impose on him a reasonable opportunity of showing cause. [488 E] The amended article 311(1) has been reproduced in the judgment of my learned brother. It is not necessary to give an opportunity for showing cause to the government servants. The satisfaction under the unamended provision, therefore, that the Governor had to arrive at his satisfaction that in public interest it was not expedient or expedient to hold such inquiry is not imperative to give him an opportunity. [489 E] In the instant case, the Governor has given a reasonable and fair opportunity of show cause to all the respondents before passing the order impugned. The Governor 's satisfaction under article 311 (2), therefore, cannot be said to have been vitiated by any error of law or fact. [490 G H; 490 A B] (3) The High Court was in error in holding that it was necessary for the Governor to arrive on his satisfaction whether in the interests of the public it was expedient to grant an opportunity and that the satisfaction under that provision was required to be recorded by that authority in writing.

The petitioners and respondents 5 to 8, who were the Shia Wakfs in question, filed a suit for specific performance of their religious ceremonies and functions on the plots and structures in question. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the said plots and structure had been registered as Shia wakfs for purposes of performing their religious rites and functions thereon under sec. 5(1) of the Act and published in the U.P. Gazette dated 26th February, 1944. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Notification dated 26 th February, 1943 issued under section 5(2) of U. P. Muslim Wakfs Act, 1936 on the ground that the notification dated 26.2.1944 was not published in accordance with law and that the same had been published in exercise of its power under section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that since the petitioners were not parties to the suit, they could not be regarded as between the same parties who were before this Court and that their individual capacity and functions over the other plots and constructions thereon. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the Notification issued under Section 5(l) of Act by the Sunni Board is of no avail to the Sunnis for the purpose of defeating the customary rights of the Shias to perform their religious functions and functions in violation of the lawful exercise of their legal rights; (ii) the mosque on Plot No. 9 was registered as a Shia Wakf for purposes Of performing their ceremonies and function thereon under section 6(1), and (iii) the notification issued by the Shiya community of Mohalla Doshipura is not valid because it was published in pursuance of the powers conferred upon the Shiisas to discharge their religious duties and functions; (iv) the Shiaya Community of Mohalla, Doshipsura had established their customary rights to perform its religious ceremonies, practices and functions as Shias and they were also immobilised in the writ petitions. Dismissing the Writ Petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Notification dated 25th February 1944 issued under s.5(1)(a) of Uttar Pradesh Muslim Wakfs (Amendment) Act, 1954 is not a valid piece of legislation. [1112E] 2.2 The notification dated 27th February 1943 issued by Shia Board on 1st December, 1956 under Rule 54 1136 (vii) was the Notification under s 5(I) of that Act and publication in the Gazette dated 25 th February 1944 refers to the mosque in question and structures thereon. [1213E] 3.1 In view of the fact that the Notification No. 26/1944 issued by a Shiya Board on January 1, 1954 under Rule 936 (viii) was not produced in the earlier litigation either before the Allahabad High Court or before this court, it cannot be regarded to have been decided by this Court in Civil Appeal No. 5 (1) Of 1976.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer disallowed the claim for set off on the footing that when in the assessment year 1957 58 the loss was claimed it was excluded in the computation of the profits of the assessee 's claim for setting off and set off before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and he dismissed the appeal by holding that there was no genuine loss; it was essentially notional in nature and that the claim was essentially a notional loss. The Appellate Assistant Commis sioner allowed the claim of set off but held that there had been genuine loss, and set aside the order of the Income tax officer. In further appeal to this Court, on behalf of the Revenue, it was contended that the assessee had filed its return showing the loss and the loss suffered by it was merely notional in character and that no claim for carry forward and setoff could be allowed. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The claim of setting off was admissible in the case of set Off. [1164B] 2.1 In order to attract section 74(1)(b) of the Act, it is necessary to show that the loss has been actually determined under the Act or as the case may be, the assessee sustains a loss falling under the head 'capital gains '. The wordings of section 80 are not exhaustive and they are only illustrative and not exhaustive. [1064D] 2.(a) In order that section 74 (1)(c) should be read in its entirety, it must be held that the benefit conferred under section 24(3) was intended to be given effect to under the 1961 Act. The expression "capital gains" is a wide and comprehensive expression which has been used in the Income Tax Acts. [1264D E] 2(b) In the instant case, the loss sustained by the assessee was not merely notional but had been determined as required under section 23 of the 1922 Act. [1365E F] 3.(c) The benefit conferred by section 24 (3) is intended to cover short term capital assets and it would be carried forward to the following assessment year and so on. 1961 or any subsequent assessment year which is car ried forward in accordance with the provisions of sub section (2A). [1266E F G] 4.(a)(i) The assessee has not filed its returns showing the losses and the income tax Officer neither computed the loss nor passed an adverse order, the Incometax Officer was not entitled to take advantage of his own failure and reject the assessee's claim. [1466F G] 5(ii) In so far as it relates to capital assets other than short term assets is concerned it must also be held in view of the provisions contained in section 74A that the right conferred under Section 24(2A) was not available to the assessee. [1566D E; 1567B] 6.(iii) The claim for carrying forward and setting off under sub section(1) of Section 73 or sub section 1 of Section 74 or sub s.(3) of section 73 or subsection (1) is not entirely set off except against any profits and gains falling under that head. [1666D] 7.(iv) In view of this provision, the benefit of Section 24 (2B) was available to an assessee who sustain a loss which has not been determined in pursuance of a return filed under section 139. The benefit of section 24 is intended only to cover the short term asset and not to be set off against capital gains.

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Air) and Production, Air India, Ministry of Defence, Government of India, and was posted at the relevant time, i.e., on November 12, 1967. The respondent was appointed as a Scientific Officer in the Department of Defence Research & Development Organisation (DRDO), on October 13, 1966. He joined service on October 11, 1966 and was promoted to the post of Scientist 'E ' on October 14, 1966, in the defence Science Service, and thereafter he was posted to the Directorate General of Technical Education and Production. The Respondent was recruited to the Defence Engineering Service by the Defence Research and Development Organisation, Ministry Of Defence, and subsequently he was transferred to the Department on November 13, 1967, and joined service as a Junior Scientific Officer. He challenged the order of his transfer before the Central Administrative Tribunal, Hyderabad Bench, holding that he had a right to prescribe different conditions of service for the members belonging to the different units, namely, DAQAS and DQAS, and that the respondent was not liable to be retired at the age of 58 years. The Tribunal held that the repondent was not entitled to continue in service upto the superannuation of 60 years, and directed reinstatement of the respondent with all consequential benefits. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant Union of India that (i) the respondent had a fundamental right to be governed by the Service Rules; (ii) the Government had no power to vary the conditions of his service from time to time, and (iii) the order passed by the Tribunal was neither proper nor valid. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The denial of the benefit of enhanced superannuation age to the members of the other unit amounts to discrimination, violative of Article 16 of the Constitution. [23F] 2.2 The denial is not expressly provided for in the Service rules. It is later in the year 1979 that the Defence Training Service was reconstituted into three different units and their services were inter changeable between the three units. The service conditions of the employees belonging to two units, therefore, belonged to one single service. [24F] 3.3 The denial was not expressly made for some other legal reasons, it became necessary to discontinue his services before that date. The denial in the facts and circum stances of the case is neither proper or valid. There is no substance in the present appeal. [25G H; 26A B] 4.4 The denial to the respondent in service was not specifically provided for by the Rules. The Government had power to alter the conditions, of service from a date to time. The order passed was neither legal nor proper. It was not open to the appellant to contend that the Government has power to modify the conditions. [26F] 5.1 In the instant case, the denial of benefit of enhancement superannuation age was made by the Government in exercise of its powers under Rule 12(2) of the Rules and the same was approved by the President. The said decision was extended to all Scientific and Technical personnel of the DRDO i. e., DAQA and DZAS. [27F] 4.(a) The denial made by this benefit is not justified and there is no basis in the appeal. There are no substance or reason for denying the benefit to the appellants.

The appellant was elected to the Sangli City Municipality. The election of councillors to the Kolhapur City Municipality was held under the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, 1965 (hereinafter referred to as the Act). The appellant filed an application before the High Court for quashing the order of the Judge and praying that he be declared elected to a local body. The High Court dismissed the petition on merits but the High court dismissed it on the ground that there was no fair trial of the two witnesses called as court witnesses. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The appellant was guilty of corrupt practice and made an order disqualifying him under the Act from taking part in municipal elections for the next five years. [975B] (2) The High court was not right in refusing to quash the order on the grounds that there were two publications in the Maharashtra Gazette, one of June 15, 1967 that the first publication having taken place on the 8th June the time limit of ten days fixed under section 21 sub section (1), of the Act began to run from that date and the petition which was filed on the 24th June was beyond time. [977C] (3) The trial Judge accepted the evidence with regard to distribution of the pamphlet by the appellant but he found the appellant guilty of a corrupt practice, and made the order disqualified him under section21 sub section(1) of the Bombay Municipalities Act. [980D E] (4) The allegation about the distribution of pamphlet was not sufficient for the Judge to come to his conclusion as to the period of five years ' disqualification.
