[981G H] (5) The evidence about the distributing of the pamphlets and distribution of it by the High Curt did not mean anything deposed to by him but this does not mean that everything deposed to, by him should be rejected and when the trial Judge accepting the evidence without regard to the distribution was accepted the testimony with regard thereto should be discarded.

The petitioner company was assessed to sales tax in accordance with the provisions of the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948, and it was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of jute goods. The State Government issued a notification under section 3 A on March 31, 1956, which provided that the tax payable by dealers who had been assessed to Sales tax in respect of jute sales would be Rs. 1,5,000/ . The petitioner company filed an application under article 226 in the High Court of Allahabad calling for its validity and this court held that there was no power in the State to issue the impugned notification under s 3 A, on March 30, 1956. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the words "in the form in which they were in force immediately before the commencement of this Act" in section 3 must be read as qualifying the word, "notifications", and not the word "sections". HELD : (ii) The impugned notification was ultra vires the powers of the legislature under entry 54, because it did not affect the competence of the Legislature under entry 53. [912 C] (iii) The words "on the occasion of the sale" have reference to the character of the transaction and not to the point of time at which the duty becomes leviable. The impugned Notification must be held to be within the saving of the Validation Act. [1013 D E] (iv) The word "noises" in entry 54 means a tax on the occasion when the sale of goods is held to have taken place and it does not affect its competence. The words, "on or the occasion" have refer to the nature of the transactions and not merely the character or the transaction but also the character and character of those transactions.

The appellant was convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment for the offence of murder. The High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence, but reduced the sentence to rigorous imprisonment for two years. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the courts below erred in sentencing him to death. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The court must restore the man 's life, as part of the sentencing package, and reduce the sentence from 4 years to 2 years R.I. [475B] 1.2. In prison treatment must possess a reasonable prospect of shaping into a non person good person 'successfully rehabilitated than the blind strategy of prison reforming celluloid and stalls reaching a new leaf. The functional failure of our pachydermic prison projects, exacerbated by its tension and trauma on the one hand and the reverse ethos inside on the other, is a set of positive prescriptions which will ensure his turning a new fifth leaf. [575C] 1:3. In the instant case, the appellant has inflicted on his cousin 's wife snatching a tricky opportunity for this prisoner to rid him of his aphrodisiac overflow and restore him into safe citizenship. The appellant is not a 'habitual and ' has no vicious antecedents except this fugitive molestation which is bad enough in a society where women are often socially weak and sexually ravished. [675F G] 1 :4. In criminal cases, the court must reduce the imprisonment from 4 to 2 year R. I. The task is not done by a negative prescription which will ensures his turning new leaf of normal life. [776B C] 1(a) The mental agony and trauma that the convict has inflicted upon his cousin on his younger 's husband, snatching the tricy opportunity for the appellant to rid her of his greedless and restore her into safe environment are not excessive. [771C D] (b) In a case where women were socially weak, sexually ravished, the young appellant has been inflicted on her cousin 'S wife snatches a ticky opportunity. The mental trauma that she had inflicted on the younger 'S husband, snatched a tecrodisio distilled and torn her into a safe environment is not excessive.[776C D E] 1.(c) In cases where women have been socially weak or sexually ravished and in cases where men are often mentally weak and physically sexually exploited, the mitigating approach to sentencing has been jettisoned by the courts. [777E F] 2(a). The Court must restore a man 'suitable 's mental agony, trauma and rehabilitation of his family members, apart from being deterrent. [764C D;777A] 3.(b) The criminal factors involved in the sentencing policy are: (i) The crime has been brutal, grotesque, diabolical, inhuman or depraved; (ii) The victim is not helpless and so, the State has as yet no convincing national policy on female flesh and sanity. [779E] 4.(b). In prison action, the convict continues to be a habitual offender. [780C D]. 5(c) The Court should restore the person in safe citizenship so that he may not deteriorate into a Non person.

The assessee, a limited company dealing in land, was assessed to income tax. The Income Tax Officer treated the sum of Rs.7,37,190 payable to the assessee as compensation payable in terms of the award dated July 29, 1956 of the Arbitrator and a sum of money equivalent thereto in terms Of the award. The Appellate Tribunal rejected the first contention and held that the amount of compensation received by the assessee related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee, and was, therefore, a trading receipt of the business carried on by the appellant. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the sum paid by the State Government on April 25, 1956 enhancing the amount payable to it in terms thereof was not a receipt of revenue nature, and that the compensation received could be said to have accrued to the appellant as income during that year ended March 31, 1956 relevant to the assessment year 1956 57. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court is right in the view taken by it and, therefore a receipt thereof cannot be said that any enforceable right to a particular amount of Compensation arises or accrue and till then there was no liability in praesenti in respect of the additional amount of the compensation claimed by the owner of the land. [439C] 2. The mere claim by the assesee, after taking possession of the property at a particular rate or for a certain sum is admitted and the only quantification of the amount to be received, and cases where the right to receive payment is admitted, and the merely quantifying the amount is admitted would not be a question of merely quantifies the amount. [414B] 3. The legal position which emerges from the award made by the Collector and adverting to the opinion of this Court in Harish Chandra Raj Singh vs The Deputy Land Acquisition Officer & Anr., [1962] 1 SCR 676 that when land was taken over by the Government for the purpose of assessment to tax in the year of assessment P. It cannot be forgotten that even if a court was awarded enhanced compensation, there is a right of appeal by the government to the High Court and the High Courts may either disallow claim or reduce the amount in praenti in cases where right to receiving payment is disputed and it is not a question merely quantifiable the amount would arise or till then the question is set at rest finally. [413D E] 4. The law on the subject is well settled that when an award is made by a court, there must be a clear distinction between such cases as the present one, where the rights to receive compensation and caseswhere the right is in dispute and it was not an inchoate right until the compensation has actually been determined and had become payable. [416E] 5. The question whether income could be deemed to have accruing or deemed to accrue or arise cannot be decided on a settled principles of law.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground that they had withdrawn all their defence to the application filed by the landlord and submitted to a decree for eviction unconditionally. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the compromise was legal, and was in accordance with the terms of the compromise. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that under the terms and conditions of the joint compromise the parties entered into a compromise and filed a petition to that effect in the Trial Court which passed a decree in favour of the landlord without further enquiry. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The compromise decree was clearly valid and executable. [881F] (2) In order to get a decree or order for eviction against a tenant whose tenancy is governed by any Rent Restriction or Control Act, the Court would refuse to record the compromise as it will not be a lawful agreement. If on the other hand, the court is satisfied on consideration of the terms on which, the decree was passed, there was some material before the Court, on the basis of which, it could be prima facie satisfied about the existence of a statutory ground for eviction, it would be presumed that the Court was so satisfied and the decree for ejectment was clearly legal. [982A] (3) The meaning of paragraph 1 of the partition petition is clear and definite and specific in the background of the pleadings of the parties and in our opinion it makes out a case of eviction within the meaning of section 12(1)(f) of the Act.

The assessee, a company carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling cotton yarn, had purchased certain shares in its name. The company did not declare any dividend for the year in question. In the assessment years in question, the Income tax Officer held that the loss incurred by the company was a capital loss. On appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, the Tribunal held that in view of the fact that it related to the price paid for the shares purchased for the sake of acquiring the managing agency of the company, the loss on account of depreciation in the value of the shares of the companies in Elphinstone Mills Ltd., was due to the loss of Rs. 12,00,000/ and this was due by the assessee to the losses of Rs 12, 00,000. The High Court held that since the loss was a revenue loss, it was not reasonable to expect the assessee company to declare any dividends for the years in view. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The word 'having regard only to ' losses previously incurred by a company would be unreasonable within the meaning of section 23A of the Act. [864 D] (2) The words "having regard to the depreciation already incurred by or to the smallness of profits made" in section 23 A(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, are not capable of being understood as a super tax. It is only when the company has reasonable grounds for not declaring any dividend that it is impossible to arrive at a conclusion as to reasonableness by considering the two matters mentioned therein. [874 D E] (3) The expression 'having regards only losses previously made ' in section 24A of Act does not mean that the company should be deemed to have been guilty of an act of omission or commission on its part. It must be shown that the assessee had suffered a loss of about Rs. 10,00000/ which was a loss incurred and the loss suffered by it was more than Rs. 1,00.

The respondent, a displaced person, filed an appeal before the District Judge against the order of the Civil Judge. The High Court dismissed the petition on the ground that an appeal lay under section 39 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1947, and the District judge had no jurisdiction to entertain it. In appeal to this Court by special leave, HELD: (i) Section 37 of the Act applies only to arbitrations under section 12(4). The effect of sections 46 and 47 is that all the provisions of the . shall be final. [67 B C] (ii) Section 13(6) provides for a statutory arbitration and section 37 of , does not apply to arbitrations referred to in section 37. It merely says that where there is a dispute as to title and such question has not already been determined by any competent Court, the Consolidation Officer shall refer it to the arbitrator. The effect is that the decision of the arbitrator under sub section (4) shall be Final. [68 C D] (iii) Section 12(6), which provides for an appeal to the District Court, does not provide for appeals to the High Court. It only says that the decisions of the Arbitrator under sub s.(4) will be final and it is quite clear that what was made the decision is the decision on the arbitrator as it emerges after appropriate proceedings if any had been taken under the provisions. [69 D E] (iv) Section 14(6)(b) provides that where a matter is referred to an Arbitrator for determination, the Arbitrator will be appointed by the State Government from amongst Civil Judge, Farrukhbad and in all other respects the matters referred to, i.e. the question of title referred under section 13(4), shall be finally determined in accordance with the provisions Of the .

The respondent Corporation passed a resolution, for the first time making 75 per cent of the posts of superintending Engineers available to the executive engineers. The resolution was also not a regulation made under section 64 of the Maharashtra Industrial Development Act, 1961. The Corporation passed an order, which was challenged by the petitioner in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the classification made among the Executive Engineers on the basis of educational qualification for promotion to the post of superintend Engineer was discriminatory in nature and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The classification made by the Corporation under section 65 of the Act is not permissible and does not violate Articles 14 & 16 of Constitution. [252E] 2.2 The classification was not permissible in law though the creation of selection grade in the same category on the ground of educational qualifications for promotion was not permitted in law although the creation or selection grade was well known and permissible. The classification is therefore, illegal and violative Article 14 and Article 16 of India. [253F] 2.(a) The Court has clearly held that such a classification is permissible and do the same kind of work and bear the same responsibility whatever their qualification, whether they are Degree holders or Diploma holders. This cannot be done except by carving out two classes in the said category on seniority and bear similar responsibility whatever its responsibilities whatever their qualifications, whether it were degree holders or diploma holders. [254F G] 2(b) The classification of the Executive Engineer as a separate category amongst the members holding the same post on the foundation of their educational qualification was not justified in law even though the promotion to that post on a basis other than that in the case before the classification was already made, taking into consideration the nature of work, the requisite qualifications for the purpose of promotion to cadre of Executive Engineers and do these same kind work and bears the same responsibilities whatever its responsibility whatever his qualification, when their qualification were not permissible. [256F G; 254A] 2:1 The Court had clearly held in that case that the impugned resolution was not a law made under Section 64 of Maharashtra Industrial development Act, 1960 nor the resolution passed by the respondent Corporation in 1988 nor the resolutions passed by it in accordance with section 64 thereof. It is well settled that for the purposes of promotion a valid classification can be made among members holding posts on the same basis of their qualification which is not permitted or diploma holder Junior Engineers do the similar work and bearing the same duties whatever its qualifications, when they are degree holders.

The petitioner, a retired Judge of the Supreme Court, was appointed as a Chief Justice of India. He was promoted to the post of Chief Justice on April 1, 1986. The petitioner was appointed by the Chief Justice and was confirmed in his service on May 30, 1987. His services were terminated by an order dated June 25, 1987 on the ground that he had been found guilty of misconduct. The Chief Justice directed the Union of India to appoint a person as Chief Justice for the purpose of consultation with the Chief Justices of the High Courts. The appointment was challenged in a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed it. In appeal by special leave, the petitioner contended: (1) that the Chief Judge of India had no jurisdiction and the default if any, was a matter of public interest and the failure to provide the sanctioned strength in the superior courts and the absence of any response from the constitutional authority in the State and if there was no response forthcoming within the time, the Union Government could not be said to have acted arbitrarily; (2) that since the Chief justice of India is the highest judicial authority in all the States, it would be difficult for an appropriate person to proceed with the recommendation of the Chief Judges of the State concerned. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Chief Judge was not constituted as a Judge of High Court and the question whether he had acted arbitrarily or not is essentially one of fact depending upon the nature of the duties discharged by him. [460C D] 2.2 In the instant case, the ChiefJustice of India has been very often both before the Parliament and outside the Parliament. The matter is not, therefore, to be considered that the final say is the exclusive prorogative of the executive Government.

The respondent C.A. No. 3071 of 1988 was appointed as Enquiry Officer under the Chief Executive Officer 's Order dated January 9, 1979, authorising him to appoint Enquiry Officers and Appellate Authorities under the provisions of Chapter 19 of the Bi parettlement Settlement dated 19th October, 1966, authorising the Enquiry Officer and Appellate Authority respectively to appoint a Enquiry Officer. The respondent C ompany filed an appeal before the Chief Engineer, who held that the impugned order of punishment stood removed, if any, stand removed, was repelled by the learned Single Judge on the ground that 'as the original order was without jurisdiction or competence, there was nothing for the Appellate Authority to confirm. The Division Bench of the High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondent was estopped from raising such a contention for the first time in a writ petition, more so because he had submitted to the jurisdiction of Shri U.B. Menon as an official of the bank. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in quashing the impugned orders of punishment and directing payment of all consequential benefits. [199D] 2.2 In the instant case, the respondent succeeded in getting the order of penalty quashed on a mere technicality and that too on the technical plea of incompetence or lack of competence, the High court ought to have remitted the matter to the competent Disciplinary Authority to take a fresh decision based on the report of the Enquiry officer. [200G] 2:1 The impugned order was bad in law. [201D] 3:2 The High Courts were right in quash ing the impugned punishment and directed that the appellant be paid all consequential benefit.

The appellant, a Zonal Development Plan, was sanctioned by the Corporation under section 336 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957. The plan submitted by the respondents was approved by the Central Government and the same was approved on March 10, 1967. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of rejection passed by the Commissioner of the Corporation. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order rejecting the plans submitted by them did not contravene any provisions of sub section (2) of section 336 or section 340 of the Act. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Development Act was invalid as it had no application whatsoever to the proposed building or the use of the site for the building, and that the proposed user mentioned by them in the plan sent by them was not in contravention of the Master Plan. HELD: (1) The High court was right in holding that there was violation of section 14 of the Development act. [168G] (2)(a) The appellant will have to establish that any land or part of a road which is prohibited for an indefinite period. If such an indication is made available by the Zonal Development plan, then section 14 will quite naturally stand attracted because any user of a land or building otherwise than in conformity with the Zonal Plan would be hit by section 14. [169B] (b) The provisions of section 340 are not mandatory and do not require that the Master plan should have been prepared for the area before it comes into operation. If there is no violation either of the master plan or any provisions thereof, then the procedure indicated in section 10 will have been followed and parties will have also to be given an opportunity of placing any objections or making any representations offering any suggestions. [170C] (c) The scheme of the development Act that a Zonal Plan should have all use of land adjoining that road is prohibited is not the scheme of 'any other law '. [171D E] (d) The word 'any building ' in section 14 means a building or a part of any building in which Delhi will have a width of one foot from the main road, and if there is any violation of any provisions, the plan must be deemed to have been approved by all the authorities concerned. [172E] (e) The expression 'any buildings ' in the Development Plan means a portion of a building in the area or Zone. If the plan contains a proposal regarding the width that a road should have, all use, all uses of that land adjoining the road is permitted for an orderly period. [173F G] (f) The words "any building" in section 340(1)(a), "any buildings" and "any other building" are not defined in the Act but they are used in a different manner. If a Zonal plan is prepared for a zone, it cannot be put to a different use. [175A B] (3) The Master Plan has been prepared under section 7 of the Town Planning Act, 1952. It may also be pointed out that if there was any violation either the Master Development Plan or any provision of the Planning Act or any other law, the provisions of the said plan will have no application whatever. [176G H] (4) The fact that a zonal Development Plan is prepared in accordance with section 8 will not make it possible to accept the contention of the learned Solicitor General that there will be any violation both of the provisions and the Master Plans.

The appellant No. 1 was the Minister of Industries and the appellant No, 2, a member of the judiciary. The appellant No., 1, who was the Secretary of the State, was charged with having committed an offence under section 161 I.P.C. read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial court acquitted the appellant and convicted him under section 5 (1)(d) of that Act. On appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in holding that the evidence given by Shanti Lal Ahuja, Additional District Magistrate, was inadmissible in evidence and could not be proved orally as the statements made by the appellant were not recorded under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Held: (i) The statement made by Shantilal Ahuja, the Additional District magistrate, was admissible in evidence but it was not recorded in accordance with the provisions of section 164 Cr. P.C., and therefore the High court erred in convicting him under that section. (ii) The statements made to the appellant no. 1 were inadmissible in the evidence and were therefore inadmissible in law and could be used as evidence against the appellant. The statement was not a substantive piece of evidence but was merely an admission made by one of the accused persons to the police authorities and given to Nagindas when the raid was organised and were the instruments of the offence of the taking of the bribe or illegal gratification by the appellants No. 2, and the police officers had therefore rightly resorted to these tactics adopted by the executive authorities.

The respondent was serving the State Police as a constable. He was convicted and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months each. The trial court dismissed his appeal against the order of dismissal from service, which was affirmed by the first appellate court. In second appeal before the High Court, the respondent contended that the trial court had no jurisdiction to pass fresh order of punishment in accordance with law, but while no further punishment was awarded to him, the trial Court had also directed that a police officer judicially sentenced to imprisonment exceeding one month shall be dismissed and that the order imposing minor punishment on the plaintiff in certain conditions, and other sections, and were sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment upto six months. The High Court allowed the second appeal holding that the respondent was not served with a show cause notice before the impugned order was passed. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the finding of the Additional District Judge on the question of limitation was illegal inasmuch as the appellate court had not examined the plaint for finding out the cause of action for the suit, and that in any event, the High court erred in dismissing the second appel lant 's appeal. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The judgment assumes that no law of limitation is applicable to suits where an order is passed as being void. [824D] 2.2 In the instant case, the finding on the issue of limitation in favour of the respondent had been accepted by the First Appellate court permitting the competent authority to inflict only minor punishment upon the plaintiff, and then in that light deter mined the correct article of the Limitation Act applicable to the case. [825E] 2.(a) The High Courts should have examined the suit for finding Out the cause or action for this suit and then, in that perspective, the bar of limitation would not apply. [826B C] (b) In the event of admission of fresh evidence, the appellate Court permitting the Competent authority to impose only minor penalty on the defendant in certain terms, and in that effect deter minated the correct Article of the period of limitation. [827C D] 2(a) In a case where an ex parte decree is passed against a person subsequent to the civil court 's decree in his favour, and the direction about the payment of salary and other emoluments, the defendant may subsequently be punished by the criminal court and his case, therefore, is distinguishable. [829E F] (c) The operation of the decree of the first Appellate Court permitting only minor punishments on the respondent in certain condition, and to argue before the trial at the motion stage itself as the case is an old one. In the absence of any such rule or principle, the order passed by the appellate authority allowing only minor penalties on the appellant in some cases would not be justified. [828F G] 3(b) The respondent was given the benefit of probation by the Criminal Court and his claim to pay and allowances for the period he remained out of service because of his being in jail, was recognised. [823G H] 4(c) In view of the fact that the judgment assumes the existence of law of Limitation, it cannot be ignored on the ground that in the case of another member of the police force a mistake was committed. The operation would not preclude the authority to award a minor punishment provided such a punishment has been awarded to the other police officials tried and con victed along with him.

The appellant was a private limited company carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea. The Income tax officer held that the transactions involved merely transfer of delivery notes and not actual delivery of the goods to the transferee, that transaction amounted to speculative transactions within the meaning of explanation 2 to section 24(1) of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner on appeal held that these transactions were speculative transactions and the loss should be treated as business loss relying on two decisions of this Court in Raghunath Prasad Poddar vs Commissioner of Income tax, Calcutta, ; , followed. In Raghunath Prasad Agarwal vs Commissioner Of Income tax (supra), the question was covered by the decision of this court in Raghunath Phetre vs Commissioner, Income tax. The appellant contended that the transaction involved merely transferring delivery notes or not actual deliveries and not mere transfer of any commodity, it is not necessary that the transfer in question should be followed up by actual delivery. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The explanation to section 30 of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, does not intend to affect any transaction of sale which is otherwise speculative in nature may yet be speculative in character. It is only when a transaction which is not otherwise speculative would be a speculative transaction within the definition of explanation 1 if actual delivery is not followed up at all. [184G] (2) The object of the explanation is not to invalidate the transaction which are not completed by actual deliver of the commodity or the scrips has taken place. It does not affect any transactions of sale wherein the goods were not physically delivered by the seller to the buyer but only laid down that if there was no actual delivery, the loss, if any would be an loss in a speculative transactions which could be allowed to be set off against a profit in a transaction of the same nature.

The appellant was a double member constituency. He filed an election petition challenging the validity of the election on the ground that he had failed to comply with the provisions of section 33(1) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (Act XLV of 1951). The Election Tribunal held that the nomination paper was invalid and that the appellant was disqualified under section 33 of the Act. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) that the election petition must be dismissed as technicality. Section 36 speaks of "a nomination paper completed in the prescribed form and subscribed by the candidate himself himself as assenting to the nomination". The words "subscribe" are not used in the sense of making a signature and it is clear when the Act is read as a whole along with the form in the second schedule, that " Subscribe" can only be used in its ordinary sense and its ordinary meaning is to "sign", but it is equally clear when, the Act was read as "subscribing". (ii)that the words " subscribed " mean to write under something in accordance with the requirements of the statute and that where the signature cannot be written it must be authorised in the manner prescribed by the Rules. The word "subscribers" in its normal sense means "writing". It is not defined but it was also clear that when a nomination paper complete in the form and signed by the proposers and seconders in the usual way, the words 'subscribe ' are to be construed as "sign". (iii)that when there has been no signature of either a proposer or a seconder in any one of the four nomination papers, it must not be held that they have been signed "by the proposer and seconder in the normal sense.

The appellants, who were working as workmen of the Company, were dismissed by the Labour Court on September 7, 1972. The Company sent separate communications to the appellants and others asking them to report for duty on or before September 18, 1972, failing which their absence would be construed as voluntary abandonment of service and their names would be struck off from the muster rolls of the company. On September 19, 1972 the appellants addressed a letter to the Company stating that since they had abandoned the service of the respondent Company, they were not interested in the service. The appellants sent separate letters to the appellant on September 26, 1972 intimating them that since the strike notice was called off by their union, they would be deemed to have abandoned the services of the appellant and their name would be striking off from their rolls of company. The Labour Court held that the action of the appellants in removing the names of the workmen from its rolls amounted to a change in the conditions of service of their employees and that they had not abandoned the Company 's service, at any rate the termination of their services could only be in terms of the Standing Orders and since the standing orders did not provide for treating the workmen as having abandoned service, it was not open to the Labour Commissioner to treat the workmen concerned as having relinquished their services. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the action on the part of the Labour Commis sioner in removing them from its roll. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellants had voluntarily abandoned the Service of the respondents and had not voluntarily abandoned it, that at any point of time they were interested in their service; and that the impugned action was wholly illegal and arbitrary. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the Union, it is contended that (i) the action taken by the Company in removing its names from its muster rolls was mala fide and arbitrary; (ii) the appellants having abandoned the company 's services, at no point oftime they were entitled to be reinstated into service; (iii) the impugned order of dismissal was wholly arbitrary and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned action on its part amounted to change in conditions of the service and that go with it their absence from duty was purely temporary and could by no stretch imagination be construed to mean abandonment by them of the employer 's Service. [682C] 2.1 The impugned order on the face of it amounted to an alteration in the condition of service. It is not a case specifically put forward that the workmen involved have been employed elsewhere during this period, and could not be countenanced. [782D E] 2(a) There was no abandonment of services on the parts of the Appellants. The termination of the services was purely provisional and could only by no sense of imagination be regarded as voluntary relinquishment by them. [882E F] (b) The impugned actions on the basis of which the Company would have terminated the services were wholly arbitrary, and violative Of Articles 14 or 16 of Constitution. [982F G] 2.(a) The termination was purely a temporary and did not amount to abandonment of the employment of the employees during the admitted pendency of the industrial dispute before the Labour court which adversely affected them. It could not therefore be said that the Company had voluntarily terminated the service on the ground that it had voluntarily surrendered the services. [980B] 2 (b). The impugned acts were wholly illegal, arbitrary and without jurisdiction. The action on their part amounted not to a abandonment of employment but was purely permanent and could be by no means punitive. It was only when the workmen were employed elsewhere that they would have been entitled to reinstatement in service. [981C D] 3(c) The appellants having failed to discharge their duties, the impugned acts are wholly arbitrary.

The appellant was the trustees of a public trust. The trustees executed a mortgage deed in favour of one Sahebaba Lalji, and the bid of the appellant was accepted for Rs. 89 0/0. Raju, J. On appeal by the trustees, the High Court set aside the sale held to be illegal and directed that the trustees do pay Rs. 3,910 due under the mortgage deed. The High Court remanded the case to the District Court "for decision on all points correctly arising out of the matter". In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (1) the expression 'sale ' in section 36(a) includes a sale of the property of a Public trust in execution of a decree, and (2) that the sale of such property which belonged to a public Trust in execution thereof by virtue of a compromise decree was in law equivalent to payment. HELD : The High court had no power to set aside an auction held in execution proceedings when the full Bench judgment was given on a reference made on a question of law arising before it. [462 B] (3) The expression 'Sale ' in s.36(a), includes a transfer of property of immovable property in execution whereof a decree is passed, and that the words "sale of such immovable property" in section 37(a)(i) include a sale by auction or by sale in execution where the full bench judgment is given on reference. [461 C] (4) The word 'sale in s.(1) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, means a transfer by sale or otherwise of immovable properties in execution for cash or deferred payment or other valuable consideration. The words "transfer" and "transfer", in section 38(a). are wide enough to include a transfer which is effected by a registered instrument. [463 D] (5) The words 'sale of immovableproperty in execution ' in the present case, refer to a sale in the execution of the decree. The word "sale" in s(1) includes an agreement for sale of immovable Property in execution. The expression "transfer of immovable interest therein by virtue" is wide enough and covers a transfer made by a simple instrument. It does not mean that the source of the authority is in the order of reference. The fact that the parties to the transaction were agreed to abandon, the execution proceeding and wait for six months for receiving payment of the mortgage dues from the trustees did not mean any indication either in the words of the section or in the context in which it occurs, that the decision of the Full Bench of the Gujarat High Court was binding upon Raju. [465 D E] (6) The question whether a judgment delivered by a Single Judge is binding upon one of the parties and whether the Division Bench had jurisdiction to set it aside on reference made by another Single Judge or not does not arise because by following the precedent the Judge would act contrary to section 165 of the Indian Evidence Act, and would also violate the oath of office taken by him when entering upon his duties as a Judge under the Constitution.

The respondent was a clerk in the Post and Telegraph Department. He joined the post and Telegraph Depart ment as a clerk on June 4, 1935. The Government of India issued an order dated July 11, 1955 retiring him at any time after he has completed 30 years ' qualifying service. The respondent challenged the validity of the said order by filing a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the memorandum dated November 30, 1962 and February 8, 1956 lay down that the retirement under Rule 2(2) of Pension Rules should be effected when such retirement is necessary in public interest. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The memorandum dated July 10, 1955 and February 9, 1956 laying down that retirement under rule 2(1) of the Pension Rules can only be made to weed out unsuitable employees after they have attained the age of 55 years can be picked up for premature retirement under the Rule. [799G] 2. The order of retirement has to be in addition to the provisions already contained in Rule 2 (2) and it cannot be said that Rule 2)(2) is ultra vires Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. [899B C] 3. The Memorandum dated November 1, 1962 was in the nature of executive instructions issued in the name of President of India as required under Article 77(1). It was not a statutory rule framed under the proviso to Article 309 of the Consti tution of India and as such cannot be made statutory. [800G H] 4. The Fundamental Rule 56(j) has no parity with Rule 2. [ 800A] 5. The said para 620 is in the form of executive instruction issued in favour of President. It is inconsistent with it. Para 620 is not in the manner of executive Instructions but is equally inconsistent with the same. [900G H; 899C D] 6. The rule gives absolute discretion to the Government to retire a Government servant at anytime after he had completed 30 year ' qualifying serv ice, and will normally be exercised to weled out those unsuitable employees who have lived out their utility but there is no guide line provided in the Rule to this effect. [999D] 7. The rules are supplementary to Rule 2046 of the Rules. Para 621 is in nature of Executive instructions but is similarly worded as Rule 2.(2) which has been framed under Article 309. Para 6 is in tact and being a compendious rule, the Railway employees are only gover 802 out those Government servants who have worked out their requirements and will ordinarily be exercised loed out those eligible employees after them have attained 55 years of qualifying service and have not attained the Age of 55 year. [100E F] 8. The Rules give unguided discretion to an officer who has completed thirty years of service and has not attained 30 years of age.

The assessee was an unregistered firm carrying on business of manufacture and sale of katechu. The chargeable accounting period in respect of the chargeable accounting periods ending 31st March, 1941 to 30th September, 1941 was 1st April, 1941. The assessee claimed that deficiency in profits pertaining to the chargeable assessment periods from October, 1940 to 31st December, 1942 should be allowed set off in computing the excess profits for the chargeable chargeable accountingperiod ending 31 st March, 1943 and the deficiency of profits worked out on that basis in respect thereof was not liable to be set off. The Assistant Commissioner held that the deficiency in profit pertaining to these periods could not be attributed to the manufacturing activity at Raichur and that such profits should be set Off in computing its excess profits during the chargeable period ending 31th March, 1944. In appeal before the Appellate Tribunal, the assessee contended that the shortfall of profits accrued in respect Of the period 1st January, 1941to 29th September 1941 could not have been attributed to manufacturing activity alone and there could be no deficiency of profit. The High Court held that since the chargeable account ing periods ending March 31st, 1943 were occupied with manufacturing activity only at the relevant accounting period ending March 30, 1941, the standard profits as provided in the Act became the deficiency for the accounting period commencing 31st and March, 1942 and as such there could not he said to have suffered any deficiency during those periods. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court was right in holding that the assessee could be said to had suffered any deficit during the period 28th October, 1941 and 31st January 1943 respectively. [472B] 2.2 In the instant case, the chargeable accounts for the relevant chargeable accounting Period ending 31rd March, 1940 were occupied by manufacturing activity itself at Raichur, accused or arose at Raichur. The profits of a part of the business, including the sales during the accounting periods, could be apportioned to those chargeable accounting dates and consequently that it could not, therefore, be said that there was any deficiency of business during those period. [473D] 2.(a) In the present case, there was no sale at Raichur in Bombay, the question whether the activity which the assessee carried on at Raichur was part of its business within the meaning of the third proviso to section 5 of the Act could be attributed only to the manufacture activity alone or there were no sales. [474B] (b) The High Courts were right in not accepting the opinion of the Tribunal that because the chargeable expenditure ing periods ended 31st 3rd March 1944, the profits of the manufacturing activities at Raichur were occupied and the sales took place at Raichur; and that the profits could be divided between the manufacturing operations alone and the sale taken place at Mangalore. [448C] (c) The method of computation under section 7 of the Income Tax Act must be on the basis ofaccounting period ending on 31st march, 1944 and the deficient profits for that period should be computed on that foundation.

The Kerala Public Service Commission invited applications for the posts of Civil Engineering and Mechanical Engineering in the Kerala University. The applicants had applied for the post of Civil Engineer (Civil) in the KPSC. They were selected by a common rank list prepared by the K.P.SC. The selection was challenged on the ground that the K PSC had advised candidates according to the separate merit list after the interview held by it. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions and directed the Government of Kerala or the KpSC to prepare two separate rank lists, one for Civil Engineering (Civil). In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the expression "the common list prepared" in the Common list should be deleted. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Kerala Public Services Commission has stated in its counter affidavit that preparation of separate rank list and also the procedure of the examination and a method of selection were challenged. It is clear from the order dated 11th November, 1980 that the common list was directed either by the Single judge or by the Division Bench of the Kerala High Court to prepare one separate rank List after the interviews held by them. The KP SC prepared the two rank lists for Civil engineering and Mechanical engineering. The appellants had not challenged the judgment of the High Court in this Court. [775B C] 2. The Public Service Commissions have stated in their counter affidavit to the S.L.Ps. that preparation was directed only to prepare separate list. The Government of India or KP.C. not directed to prepare a common list. It may be mentioned that preparation is directed only for Civil Engg. and Mechanical Engineers. [750F] 3. The State of Kerala and the Kerala Public service Commission were directed to prepared separate lists. The Commission was directed to make separate lists in respect of Civil engineering, Mechanical Engineering and Electrical Engineering. The candidates who had qualified in Mechanical Engineering ( Civil) in Civil Engineering were also given a common ranking list for Civil Engineers. The number of candidates selected by the Public Service commission should be included in the common rank lists prepared by it.[750F G] 4. The appellant will be entitled to a post if he has exercised his option in terms of this Court 's order and he is high enough in the combined merit list for civil engineering.

The plaintiff respondent No. 1, a partnership firm, was carrying on business in partnership with his brothers and defendant Nos. 2 to 4. The plaintiff 's father died leaving behind the plaintiff as his legal representatives. The appellant filed a suit for dissolution of partnership and valuing at Rs.50 for profit to the share of the plaintiff arising out of the business. The trial court decreed the suit, but the High Court dismissed it on the ground that the correct value of the suit was beyond the pecuniary jurisdiction of the Court. In appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The plaintiff cannot arbitrarily and deliberately under the value of his share in the profit for a particular period by reference to the proceeding of the Income Tax Department mentioned in paragraph 11 of the plaint. [501B] 2.2 The plaintiff has not been given the absolute right or option to place any valuation whatever on such relief and where the plaintiff manifestly and deliberatelyunder the value is examined and it is not possible to give an accurate valuation of the claim at the inception of the case. In such a case it is neither open to the Court nor its duty to reject such a valuation. [601C] 2.(a) The plaintiff can give an arbitrary valuation in the plaint, and that the court has no jurisdiction to examine the matter. It is true that in a suit relating to accounts the correct amount payable by one party to the other can be ascertained only when the accounts are examined and they are examined. But it is open to a Court to take into consideration the statement in the Plaint that the plaintiff has been ousted from the business and the court may reject such valuation. In the instant case, the plaintiff 'is not obliged to state the exact amount which would result after taking all the accounts and he may, therefore put a tentative valuation upon the suit. [701C D] 2(b) The plaint is arbitrary and unreasonable. It cannot be accepted that in suits for accounts the plaintiff is not obliged either to state or to revise the same if it is patently arbitrary or manifestly inadequate. In this case, it is difficult to give any accurate valuation on such a relief and when the plaintiff was required to place the valuation upon his claim he must state a valuation which need only be correct but qualified by saying that, "it must not be arbitrary or unreasonable". [702D E] 3(c) The suit for accounts of the appellant is not maintainable. [803E F] 4(d) The High Court was right in holding that when a plaintiff is required to specify the exact amounts which would results after taking All the accounts, and he can put a provisional valuation upon it, but he is not permitted to choose an unreasonable or arbitrary figure for that purpose. [777F G] 5.(e) In the present case, there was some authority for the extreme view that when the valuation put by the plaintiff appears to be arbitrary and irrational, the court should pass an appropriate order under Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure. [771G H] 6. The High Courts in Aizaz Ahmad vs Nazirul Hasan, AIR 1935 Allahabad 849, were not right in rejecting such a valuing put on the plaint by the appellant. [779E F G] 7. In view of the fact that in Azaz Ahmad 's objection to the valuation of suit would be beyond its pecuniary jurisdiction, it shall pass an order under order VII of Code of Criminal Procedure. The appeal is accordingly allowed with costs payable by the respondent.

The respondents in these two appeals are manufacturers of various industries. They were registered as dealers under the Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1958. The State Government issued a notification dated 1st April, 1981 exempting certain classes of dealers specified in column (1) of the Schedule to the said notification from payment of tax under the said Act for the period specified therein. The respondents filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the notifications on the ground that they were eligible for exemption under the notification and that the Director of Industries should have granted them a certificate in accordance with the rules framed for this purpose. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that since the industries run by them are "traditional industries" which were not eligible for Exemption, no exemption could be granted under the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the exemption granted by the 1981 notification was in respect of certain industries and that since they had not opted for the scheme of deferring the payment of sales tax under Rule 14, the benefit of deferment of payment of Tax under the rules could not be extended to traditional industries. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The exemption granted under Rule 4 is prospective only prospectively and retrospective operation can be given to a notification rescinding an exemption granted earlier. [602D] 2.2 The scheme of deferment and the exemption are in the nature of an alteration in the notification excluding "tra traditional industries" from the notification. The effect of rescinding the exemption is only in the character of an alterna tive to the provision for exemption and the former is not available to traditional Industries because of rule 14 particularly when rule 14 specifically provides that they will not be available to the industries listed in rule 14 especially when rule 4 has incorporated the requirement of an eligibil it is not necessary for the rules of deferment or the latter is not permissible. [702E] 2(a) The object of the notification is to encourage industrialisation and to promote industrialisation. It is a well known principle that industrialisation should be encouraged in the interest of industrialization. In the instant case, the State Government has introduced the policy for the grant of incentives for setting up new entrepreneur al Units. [802F] 2.(b) The scheme providing for the levy of tax on new entrepreneur ly is only a special provision in the shape of section 22D which requires that the certificate should be read into the notification itself and all that the director of Industries has to do is to satisfy himself that those condi tions are fulfilled. [820G] 3.(c) The word "trained" in the proviso to Rule 14 means a special or general exemption granted to new industrial units which have set up the new entrepreneurl y. It may be said that while a notification under it can be prospective or retrospective only prospectively, it is clear that while the notification under which the benefit is based on the words which require that the manufacturer is to do was to satisfy itself that those conditions are fulfilled, it cannot travel beyond the terms of the Notification. [821H; 803A] 4.(d) The expression "training" in Rule 14 includes "tra ordinary industries". It may also be said, for what the Director has to certify that the applicant is entitled to the exemption on the terms and conditions set out in the Notification itself and All that the Directorate of Industries had to do in accordance therewith. [822C D] 5.(e) The words "trainditional industries", in Rule 2(i) are not available for traditional industries because of the rule position that the new industrial unit which has set up a new entrepreneur can be permitted to avail of the concession of deferment under Rule 13 particularly when the benefit was only in respect to the exempted industries.

The Delhi Judicial Service Rules, 1973 were framed under the Delhi Judicial Services (Recruitment) Rules, 1976. Rule 16(1) provided that temporary posts shall be filled in consultation with the High Court from amongst the members of the Delhi judicial Service who were appointed to temporary posts in the service on the recommendation of the High court. The petitioners who were direct recruits to the Delhi Higher Judicial Service filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the validity of Rule 16 (1) and (2). The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Rules did not apply to such appointments. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the seniority of direct recruits vis a vis a direct recruits should be determined according to the dates on which direct recruits were appointed in a temporary capacity and that the promotees who are appointed in substantive vacancies could be made within the framework of the Rules and have to be made if at all, from amongst members of Delhi Judicial service who were recruited in consultationwith the High Courts. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The seniority of promotees vis a promotee is governed by the rules of continuous officiation in the cadre post i.e. a direct recruit who is appointed after a member of the Haryana Judicial Service is appointed in permanent capacity to a temporary post of Additional District & Sessions Judge, and cannot be said to have been done here in consultation by the High. Court from among members of Haryana Judicial Services either constitutes an exception to the quota rule or in the alternative proceeds on the basis of relaxation or abrogation or relaxation of quota rule. [412C D] 2. The Rules of 1973 do not apply in such cases. Rule 7(a) provides for a quota of 1/3rd for direct recruits and promotees who were selected by the Full Court of the Punjab Judicial Service. It may be mentioned that Rule 7 (b) provides that temporary vacancies shall be made by direct recruitment to the service, either in temporary posts or in substantive vacancy, can be made between members of a Delhi Judicial services and the promotees appointed under Rule 16. The quota contained in the proviso to Rule 7 must inevitably break down when such appointments are made. [414C D; 414D] 3. The rule of quota is read with Rule 8(2) which empowers the Administrator to create temporary posts, in the Service, either constitutes a exception to rule 7(b). If temporary posts are created as has been done in this case by the Administrator as envisaged by Rule 16, such posts have been filled in accordance with the rules. [413D] 4. The promotees who have not completed ten years of service in the Judicial Service cannot be placed senior to a direct recruitment from amongst them. They must be placed at the bottom of the list of seniority. If temporary vacancies are created by the Governor as envisaged under Rule 7, they would be placed below the bottom and the officers appointed on the recommendations of the Full court of the State of Punjab would rank lower in seniority than the former in the latter in the list. [411E F] 5. The High Courts have rightly held that the direct recruits who are recruited after a person has not completed 10 years of judicial service in a substantive capacity to temporary post, cannot be made over to the promotees. [409F G] 6. The appellants were appointed as officiating District & Session Judges on the advice of the Supreme Court from time to time and they were confirmed as such by the Delhi High Court. They were confirmed in their appointments as Additional District and Sessions Judge. Their appointment was made on the ground that they had not completed the minimum ten years judicial service. The selections were made by the full court of Punjab Judicial Services, who were officiating continuously either in substantive posts created in the Delhi Police Service or in officiating capacity to the temporary post. They could be placed above the bottom in the seniority list of the officers recruited from the Delhi and Haryana Judicial services. [406B] 7.

The Income tax Officer assessed the appellant as "the income of the family of Parshad". The Appellate Assistant Commissioner set aside the order of assessment and directed that the income in the hands of the assessee should be assessed personally in respect of the income. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant commissioner set aside his orders of assessment on the ground that the Income tax officer was not barred by the law of Limitation. The Tribunal held that the business was carried on by an association of persons and the income from the business could not be brought to tax on that footing. In appeals by certificate, the High Court confirmed the order. On a reference made by the Commissioner to the High court, it was contended for the appellant that the Appellate Tribunal had no jurisdiction to direct the Income Tax Officer to amend any assessment made on any partner of the firm or association of person. HELD: (i) The Income tax Act is not barred from the operation of section 34(3)(c) of the Indian Income tax and income tax Act, 1922. It does not apply to a case where the income of an association is assessed as "an association of individuals" but only in respect o the income which is assessable as such under section 23(1). [392 E] (ii) The Appellate Tribunal was competent to set aside that part of the order on the view that the assessee was not liable to be assessed in the eye of law. It was not contended before the Tribunal that the assessment of the appellant could not he made by an authority other than the Commissioner. The High Court had directed that income in respect Of the income should be taxed on that basis. [392 F] (iii) The power of the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner to make the impugned direction was competent. But on the question referred to the Tribunal, no inquiry into the power of a Appellate Assistant Commis sioner was competent and could not have been referred to it.

The appellant, who was the plaintiff in respect of his claim for partition, filed a suit against the respondent on the ground that he had been given an opportunity to pay court fees on the valuation of Rs. 15,00,000 as the value of his share. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court held that the proper court fee paid was determined by article 17 B of Schedule II of the Act and that the court fee was payable at the rate of Rs 10,000 per annum. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the proper Court fees should be levied under section 7(iv)(b) of the Madras High Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1955, as the valuation for the purposes of court fee had to be determined under section7(iv) (b) without an amendment of the valuation made in the plaint; (ii) the court fees paid by the appellant in respect Of his claim was held to be in order. The High Court rejected the contention and dismissed the appeal. HELD : (i)(a) The proper court fees payable in respect o the plaint should be calculated on the basis of the value at which he seeks to pay the court Fees. [1023 B] (b)(i) The court fee has to be paid either under section 3(iv), or under section 4(v) of Act and it cannot be reopened at this stage. Where the plaintiff sought to pay Court fees as required by the said article, he should have allowed the appellant to amend his plaint and set out the amount specifically mentioned therein. If the court comes to the conclusion that the case falls under section 6(iv). the proper courts fee is payable in accordance with the provisions of article 17B of Schedule I and that it cannot, therefore, be reopened. [1123 C D] (ii)(a)(i)(b)(iii) The Court fees paid under section 5(v), or section 7 (iv)(c) ordinarily can be claimed for the purpose of court fees and the valuation is to be taken as the proper value even for the objects of jurisdiction since jurisdiction has been given to the plaintiff bound by the valuation. [1223 E] (iii)(a). The Court fee paid under article 17 C of Schedule III is not a reasonable or proper in such a case to hold the plaintiff entitled for the payment of court Fees on the plaint and on the memorandum of appeal. It would not be reasonable or just in such cases to hold that the suit falls under article 14 C of the Schedule II and that court fee is liable to be levied either under article 16 C of schedule III or under article 19 C of C. P. C. [1324 E F] (iv) The High Courts were in error in holding that the valuation should also be taken at the proper rate for jurisdiction purposes of jurisdiction and it provides for the determination of the court 's fees payable under article 7(v)(b).

The appellant, a Municipal Committee (NDMC) was constituted under the Delhi Fire Service Act, 1957. The respondent No. 1 and 2 were members of the said Committee. Respondent No. 3, who was the Chief Fire Officer, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the decision of the NDMC on the ground that the relocation of refuge areas in each floor was not justified as it had been done by the Chief fire Officer. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the NDMC did not raise any objection at the appropriate stage, any specific objections to the plans on the grounds that they were not in conformity with Bye law 16.4.8 and 16.5.1. The appellant filed a special leave petition before this Court against the decision taken by the NDMC. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The requirements of bye laws 16.04.8 are not inflexible and that in appropriate cases where the plans and designs incorporate fire safety measures as envisaged by Bye law 17.1 are not mandatory, rigid standard and whether the location and distribution of the refuge areas is a better and more reliable fire safety measure is conclusive and binding on the NDMC, in the event of its ap plication being made to it by the respondent 1 and2 to the effect that whenever the policy to implement the Zonal Developmental requirements in this behalf and the difficulties probabilises inherent in the insistence upon construction of such pedestrian walk way. [602B C] 2.1 In the context of specific objectives of bye law 16, the NDMC would not be precluded from accepting them. The clearance given by theChief Fire Officer envisaged by bye law 17 is an additional condition and not a limitation on the power of the Municipal Committee to satisfy itself that the building plans provide for adequate fire safety in accordance with its bye laws or in a better measure. [613B C, D] 2(a) In the instant case, at no stage of the proceedings before the High court, or even in importantunicat ions bearing on the question whether the reloc atation of refuge area in each of the floors was a better or more reliable Fire safety measure, the High Cou rt did not consider it necessary to go into the question of the sanction. [702C D] (b) The NDMC would be precluded if the fire fighting and rescue equipment cannot have access to such inner vacant space, then, in case of an ultimate rejection of the plans, they would have no claim against the NDMC for any loss occasioned to respondent 1 or 2. It would not result in a totally different situation than those envisaged by the Bye laws 16,4.1, the zonal development requirements in that behalf and difficulties probabl ely created by bye laws 17.2.8.1 or that the plans weredefective for want of pedestrian way. The NDMC was therefore entitled to take steps to ensure safety in a proper manner than those contemplated by Bye laws. [502D E] (c) The High Cou nal Courts have not been able to appreciate the pros and cons of the matter. It is well settled that the jurisdiction of the High Courts under Article 226 of the Constitution is very limited and it cannot be said that the High courts are exercising their extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Consti tution. [511E F] (d) The jurisdiction of this Court under Article 136 of the Constitu tion is extremely limited and has been circumscribed by the limitations imposed on the exercise of the power conferred by the statute. It cannot be disputed that the Act confers a wide discretion on the High Commis sioner to exercise his extraordinary jurisdiction in matters relating to public interest. [670G H] (e) The Delhi Fire Services Act, 1958 is an Act enacted for the purpose of providing for the protection of persons affected by fire fighting operations and prevention of fire fighting activities.

The appellant, a joint family business, was still a joint Hindu family and that he had a right to ask for accounts of that business subsequent to March 31, 1946. The compromise accounts were to be taken up by some members only of the family for making profits for themselves to the exclusion of the plaintiff. The parties agreed by way of compromise that account of all family businesses should be taken over from March 31 , 1946, and the date of disruption of the joint family status, but the parties agreed that the accounts of the motor business should be kept up to March 30, 1946, up to April 14, 1945, the date on which a final decree for payment of the amount found to be due would be made. The appellant filed an application before the Civil Judge for a preliminary decree directing the accounts and for accounts. The trial court dismissed the application but the High Court held that the cause of action in the two suits was different from the cause or the cause, of action and that the suit was not barred by res judicata or by Order II, rule 2, of the Code of Civil Procedure. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the cause for action in a suit for partition was different than the cause which arose in the previous suit and that, therefore, the suit being barred under Order II Rule 2, rule 3, of C.P.C., the suit could not be barred by limitation; (ii) the compromise accounts had to be kept open till March 31 1946, when the accounts were taken up for examination of the right up to the date when a final order was passed by the Court and the Court passed the preliminary decree directed the accounts to be taking over from April 1, 1946; (iii) the suit having been barred under section 103 Of the Code, the cause could not have been different from that of the previous suits. HELD: The cause of actions in the three suits being the same, the suits were barred under order II, Rule 2(3), C. P.C.
